facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Account planning fails when it becomes an inventory. Focus on a short operating plan that helps you decide where attention goes this week.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritization requires saying no. AI can assemble customer, pipeline, renewal, whitespace, partner, and investment signals. You decide which account deserves action and why.
discussionQuestions: Which accounts get your attention by habit rather than evidence? Where is the account plan missing a decision? What signal would change your priority list?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prioritize account action for this week'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from account list discussion to one AE selecting a top account and naming the next action. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the account priority list', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Prioritization improves when account signals change where you spend attention, not when the list grows. Separate supported priorities from assumptions before choosing the next account action. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account deserves attention that it is not getting? Which account gets attention mostly by habit? What evidence would change your top three?
How does another AE distinguish evidence-led priority from an account that gets attention by habit?
listenFor: Planning as annual documentation, prioritization by revenue alone, unclear next actions, missing role coverage, and customer priorities not connected to pipeline.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-account priority table: dated signal, customer priority, role gap, next action and AE judgment. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore an account priority view, with or without AI, and consider whether it suggests a worthwhile next action. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share one priority you checked and whether it clarified the next action. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: Two accounts both appear urgent: one has a recent relationship signal, while the recorded ranking favors the other. Compare the dated evidence and identify the next account action without changing the plan automatically.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Account prioritization connects recorded signals with relationship context to decide where AE attention is useful next. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review how the example's dated priority signal relates to the existing account plan.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Habitual attention is not evidence of account priority. Look for a next account action linked to a recorded signal and relationship context.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: habitual attention is not evidence of account priority. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Schedule account or opportunity checks
activities.description: Run a recurring MSX and interaction-grounded check In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: For [account/opportunity scope], run a one-time, read-only check for material changes, stale engagement, missing next steps and new risks. Show dated sources, gaps and one proposed seller action per issue. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline. Don’t schedule, send messages or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run opportunity review with actual source coverage, signals and proposed seller actions. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides what the scheduled check should be looking for. A check scoped too broadly reports everything and stops being read, and only the person reading it knows which signals would change what they do.
activities.requiredContext: A small named account/opportunity scope; approved source-access confirmation or permitted extracts; previous verified result if one exists; and a human reviewer. Recurrence, if separately chosen, needs explicit approval of scope, reachable sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Read that first result against opportunities you already know. Every flagged item should name a source signal you can check; discard anything it got wrong.
5. Make one correction you own off the back of that read, so the check has earned its place.
6. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
7. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recurring checks should reduce review burden, not create another inbox.

activities.description: Locate the largest current-quarter pipeline gaps in the enabled certified report, distinguishing volume, progression and timing signals.
activities.prompt: In [Report Name], for [portfolio scope] this quarter, identify where pipeline is furthest behind plan. activities.name: Review applied pipeline fixes and resolve judgment items
activities.description: Check supported Auto-Fixes against the real deal, then resolve the hygiene items that still require seller judgment.
activities.expectedOutput: A reviewed hygiene queue distinguishing verified applied fixes, accepted or reverted changes where supported, seller-resolved items, and unresolved corrections routed to their owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE owns record accuracy whether or not they authorized the change. A fix can satisfy the rule and still misdescribe the deal, and the only person who can tell is the one who had the conversation. Reverting is the seller exercising ownership, not overriding the system.
activities.requiredContext: Your authorized MSX opportunities; access to Pipeline Hygiene and supported Auto-Fixes; the enabled rule configuration; verified deal timelines and evidence for any correction.
activitySteps: 1. Open MSX, then Pipeline Hygiene > Auto-Fixes if available to your role. Confirm which supported rules are enabled; do not assume a default configuration.
2. Separate changes already applied from items awaiting your judgment.
3. Compare each applied change with verified deal dates, customer evidence and forecast context.
4. Use the supported accept or revert controls where available. If a correction cannot be made there, use your authorized record-correction process.
5. Resolve surfaced items yourself, confirming the exact correction before changing the record.
6. Discuss a rule-correct change inspected in this activity that did not describe the deal; if none occurred, use the facilitator's illustrative example. Do not expose sensitive account detail.
activities.whyThisMatters: Rule compliance is not deal accuracy. Reviewing applied changes protects the forecast while reserving seller judgment for context the rule cannot see.

activities.name: Keep pipeline hygiene current between reviews
activities.description: Stand up a recurring sweep of your owned pipeline so hygiene problems surface on a schedule instead of the night before a review. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: Check [pipeline/portfolio scope] read-only for past close dates, no activity in 30 days, weak next steps, or unchanged stages with moved close dates. Draft the question/correction for each, ranked by current-period revenue at risk. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline and flag gaps. Don’t change records, schedule checks or send follow-ups.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run baseline or change hygiene list ranked by revenue at risk, with a drafted resolution for each flagged opportunity. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE confirms each flagged item is genuinely stale before updating, and makes every record change themselves rather than delegating the write.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your owned pipeline; your current period close dates; your team's definition of a healthy next step. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Confirm your team's definition of a healthy next step so the check flags the right things.
5. Review the first list and confirm each flagged opportunity is genuinely stale rather than deliberately paused.
6. Make every record change yourself; do not let the check write to MSX.
7. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
8. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: A source-checked change list can make hygiene review more focused without letting an unattended check alter the deal record.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on restoring trust in the pipeline signal before it becomes a forecast argument.
keyTalkingPoints: Bad data creates bad inspection. Stage, close date, next step, customer engagement, and partner attach should reflect reality. AI can flag issues; you verify and decide the correction.
For a chosen MSXI practice, check the relevant report/visual, portfolio filters, period and plan measures; progression needs history, not just a snapshot.
discussionQuestions: Where does your pipeline data most often mislead you? Which field do you trust least? Which opportunity would you hesitate to defend in a review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Ask what the certified business data says'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the individual records the check surfaced to the aggregate gap they add up to, then decide which correction would change the forecast conversation. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Tell the applied fixes apart from the ones waiting on you', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pipeline trust comes from checking material signals and routing corrections to the record owner. An AI explanation is a hypothesis, not a verified stage or forecast change. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Which opportunity would you not want inspected right now? What field, date, or next step might be telling the wrong story? What correction would change the forecast conversation?
What recurring inspection check has a peer used to catch a misleading date or next step before the review?
listenFor: Manual reconciliation, stale dates, close-date optimism, missing customer engagement, and records corrected only right before reviews.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a pipeline inspection row with the metric, baseline, uncertainty and record-owner question. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did inspection reveal about the pipeline or forecast story, and which correction or caveat changes the decision?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could run one pipeline signal-quality check and correct or flag one material issue. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share the type of issue verified, corrected or routed and whether it reduced a misleading pipeline signal. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An opportunity's close date is current, but its next step is generic and its last recorded engagement is old. Check the available source before deciding whether to flag a record correction.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Pipeline quality depends on whether opportunity fields reflect the deal, not just whether the record is complete. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged pipeline gap example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check portfolio filters, period, plan baseline and stage/timing measures in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. For discovery or definitions, start from the goal or metric; a known report name is optional. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A rule-correct field can still misrepresent the deal, and a snapshot does not establish slow progression without movement measures. For the optional pushed-metrics activity, the guide's read-only Insights widget is not evidence of subscriptions, sending preferences or delivery; keep setup on hold unless those features are separately confirmed.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a rule-correct field can still misrepresent the deal. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

WF-X-PIPE-01.keyTakeaway: Separate a signal from a verified deal state; record source, scope, and as-of timing before changing the forecast or route.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a rule-correct field can still misrepresent the deal. Manager support can reinforce source checking without turning the exercise into a seller data-quality score.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help the facilitator distinguish a record-quality question from a seller inspection; leave corrections with the opportunity owner. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check portfolio filters, period, plan baseline and stage/timing measures; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test. Where available and relevant, the IAP executive-summary starter can locate the role view; drill from the pipeline question into supporting metrics/opportunities, not a blanket readiness assessment.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations without scoring individuals. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check the report/view, relevant visual, scope, period and source basis before one focused question: Which gap is measured, which needs progression history, and which needs seller evidence? Narrow a broad query using the visual's terminology; keep consequential judgment with its accountable human owner and do not turn the practice into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to reinforce source checking without turning the exercise into a seller data-quality score? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan
activities.description: Review digital signals and conversation context to prioritize lead follow-up; return source-backed fit, consent status, and the next contact action.
activities.prompt: Using approved lead or attendee context for [solution area], draft a prioritized lead follow-up plan, not a general account or deal review. Favor current, relevant signals; flag context that may be stale, outside the intended scope or uncertain. For each lead, concisely show source, account, likely interest, solution relevance, suggested message, known or proposed owner, and next action. If scope or evidence is unclear, ask for clarification or a supporting document or link. A signal alone is not confirmed customer interest. State consent/contact-history status only where supported; otherwise mark it unknown and identify the check needed before outreach. Do not send outreach.
activities.expectedOutput: Prioritized lead follow-up plan with digital signal source, conversation/contact context, fit, consent status, owner, and next action; unverified signals are flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP validates the digital signal and prior-conversation context, checks consent and contact history, and decides whether to engage; a signal alone is not customer intent.
activities.requiredContext: Approved lead or attendee context, the selected solution area and relevant account or interaction context; recorded consent/contact history where available.
activities.whyThisMatters: A sourced fit assessment and verified contact status make outreach selective rather than treating every digital signal as demand.

activities.name: Identify missed solution-area opportunities
activities.description: Use sales signals to identify solution-area opportunities the SSP may be missing.
activities.prompt: For [solution area] across [active account list or territory scope], identify opportunity signals I may be missing. Show the source signal, likely customer need, possible relevant FY27 Conversation or solution context, clearly labeled as a hypothesis unless customer-confirmed, uncertainty, and the next discovery action. Separate facts from recommendations. State the coverage and gaps in the available evidence. Prioritize hypotheses where supported relevance and timing allow comparison; explain ties or an unsupported ranking, and say when no hypothesis is supported. Activity alone does not establish demand, qualification or consent. Align Stage 1 follow-up with the AE/account team; do not create or advance records or contact anyone.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked opportunity hypotheses with next discovery actions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides whether a signal represents a real opportunity or activity that resembles one. An opportunity created from a weak signal fills pipeline with something somebody has to explain later.
activities.requiredContext: SSP scope; solution area; available MSX and approved customer signals.
activities.whyThisMatters: Unnamed solution opportunities never get an owner.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Draft the first contact for the top-priority lead
activities.description: Turn the top-ranked lead into a specific, short first message that connects the signal to a reason for the customer to respond.
activities.prompt: Here is the top lead from my follow-up plan: [the top lead's source signal, account, role and recorded prior interaction]. Draft a first contact message under 100 words that references the specific signal, states one evidence-supported reason this is relevant to their business now, or frames relevance as a respectful question when it is unknown, and asks for one small next step. Give me two versions: one for a business decision maker and one for a technical decision maker. Do not claim knowledge of their environment we do not have, and do not assert a product feature I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: Two short first-contact drafts, one business and one technical, tied to the originating signal.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms consent and outreach appropriateness, verifies every factual statement about the customer, and owns the wording before sending.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized lead plan; the source signal; the contact's role; prior interaction history; consent and outreach appropriateness.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the lead's source signal, account, role and contact context.
2. Draft the messages and check consent, facts and tone.
3. Discuss which version gives the recipient a useful reason to respond.
activities.whyThisMatters: A prioritized list that never becomes a message is just a better-sorted backlog.

activities.name: Close the loop on what the follow-up produced
activities.description: Review what happened after follow-up and decide which signals are worth testing again.
activities.prompt: Here are the leads I followed up this week and what happened with each: [the leads, source signals, actions and documented responses or confirmed silence]. Tell me which signal sources produced a response and which did not, what the responses have in common, and which two signal types I should prioritize next week. Be direct about small sample size; do not overstate a pattern from a handful of leads. If the sample cannot support a change, say what further evidence is needed rather than forcing a new priority.
activities.expectedOutput: A short evidence-limited read on source signals and a proposed priority change only where supported, otherwise the next check needed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP judges whether the pattern is real or coincidence given the sample size, and owns the decision to change prioritization.
activities.requiredContext: The leads worked this week; the originating signal for each; the action taken; the response or lack of one.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the leads, source signals and documented outcomes.
2. Compare the responses, silences and size of the sample.
3. Discuss whether the evidence supports a priority change or only another check.
activities.whyThisMatters: Lead follow-up improves only if you find out which signals were worth following.

activities.name: Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer
activities.description: Track the outreach you have sent so the follow-ups that matter are surfaced and drafted rather than remembered.
activities.prompt: Review the outreach in [sent-message/account scope] over the last 30 days and identify every message where I asked for something - a meeting, an introduction, a decision, or information - and did not receive a substantive reply. For each one, tell me how long it has been waiting, how important it looks based on the opportunity involved, and draft a short follow-up in my own voice that adds a new reason to respond rather than simply repeating the ask. Do not send anything. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of unanswered asks with elapsed time and a drafted follow-up for each that adds new value rather than repeating.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP reviews and edits every draft before sending, and removes any follow-up where the silence is itself the answer.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your sent messages; your current lead and opportunity list; your team's follow-up cadence norms.
activitySteps: 1. Choose permitted sent-message evidence and run the prompt.
2. Check one unanswered ask and edit its follow-up to add value.
3. Discuss whether another message is useful or the silence should be respected.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most lost specialist opportunities are not rejected - they are dropped. The follow-up that would have converted was never sent because it was never surfaced.

agents.name: Scout
agents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
agents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Lead and account signals are noisy. Focus on turning them into a focused follow-up plan.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritize relevant lead follow-up rather than a general account or deal review.
Distinguish source signals, inferred interest and confirmed customer intent; keep uncertain or out-of-scope context explicit.
Keep suggested messages and owners provisional, and check contact history and consent before any outreach.
discussionQuestions: Which lead or signal deserves attention first? What evidence makes it real? Who owns the next action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from noisy signals to one prioritized follow-up plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Lead prioritization matters when credible demand leads to appropriate, consent-aware follow-up. Activity or a high AI ranking alone does not establish customer intent. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Which signal supports relevance to the selected solution area, and what is only inferred?
What may be stale or outside the intended scope?
Who is the known or proposed follow-up owner, and what should be checked before any outreach?
listenFor: Undifferentiated lead lists, vague ownership, weak message fit, and missing consent/context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-lead ranking: source signal, customer relevance, missing context/permission, known or proposed follow-up owner and next question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which signal warrants a customer action rather than just a new record, and what evidence would disprove the opportunity?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore whether a priority lead warrants first contact and adapt a possible follow-up. Contact is not a huddle assignment; any outreach still needs appropriate permission and human judgment. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized lead signal and whether the reviewed follow-up clarified interest or avoided a poor contact; no sent message is required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An attendee engaged with a solution-area event, but there is little evidence of a current need. Compare the source signal and known interaction context, distinguish interest from inference, and choose a useful follow-up question without assuming consent or accepted ownership.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Lead follow-up tests a digital or conversation signal against qualification evidence before pursuit effort is prioritized. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example's lead or attendee context and selected solution area. Note what supports relevance, whether timing changes the interpretation, and which questions remain.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A contact or interest signal is not confirmed customer intent. Look for a prioritized follow-up question and a known owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a contact or interest signal is not confirmed customer intent. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Align on a useful follow-up question, not a requirement to create pipeline; keep contact history and customer intent in view.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Build the executive technical deck
activities.description: Create a bounded executive-ready presentation package.
activities.prompt: Using only [the approved CXO briefing and supporting emails, transcripts, roadmap and source materials], create a new draft executive technical PowerPoint deck for the customer identified in that briefing. Align the story arc to stated outcomes and the Azure/AI roadmap; include proof, architecture implications, risks, open technical decisions and review flags. Carry through the briefing's options/tradeoffs, named decision and sourced Microsoft support mechanisms; do not introduce a new recommendation or imply review/approval. Preserve consequential source references. Do not edit a shared source deck or share the new draft.
activities.expectedOutput: New draft executive technical PowerPoint deck preserving the approved briefing's options, tradeoffs, named decision and sourced support mechanisms, with proof/review gaps visible; not shared or approved.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS is accountable for every roadmap statement made. Roadmap language is heard as commitment however carefully it is caveated, and a slipped date attributed to you is remembered.
activities.requiredContext: Approved emails, transcripts, roadmap, and source materials; the approved CxO briefing with its options, tradeoffs and named decision.
activities.whyThisMatters: An executive deck should preserve the briefing's real options and sourced support, not turn roadmap language into a new commitment.

activities.name: Translate architecture into business value
activities.description: Create a concise business-value summary from approved architecture content.
activities.prompt: For [Customer/Account], turn the supplied approved reference architecture and customer-priority evidence into a one-page business value summary. Map technical choices to customer-stated priorities and expected outcomes, citing the evidence behind each connection. If a priority or outcome is not customer-confirmed, label the mapping as a hypothesis and give the question needed to validate it. Keep Azure consumption implications sourced or explicitly provisional. Include risks and assumptions requiring review; quantify only when the source supports it.
activities.expectedOutput: One-page technical-to-value summary distinguishing sourced customer priorities from hypothesis mappings, with provisional implications and validation questions clearly marked.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS owns the numbers once they are said out loud. A value translation persuades precisely because it simplifies, and the simplification is where a defensible figure becomes an indefensible one.
activities.requiredContext: Customer/account name; approved reference architecture; customer-stated priorities/outcomes and their sources where available; supporting evidence. Missing customer confirmation remains a hypothesis to test.
activities.whyThisMatters: Architecture matters more when the customer can see the business consequence.

activities.name: Pressure-test the options and tradeoffs with an executive
activities.description: Practice putting the real decision, its options and its tradeoffs to an executive.
activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the executive who has to make the decision identified in [paste/describe fictional or de-identified options and tradeoffs]. I will present the options and their tradeoffs rather than a recommendation. Push back where an option sounds like a pitch, where a tradeoff has been softened, or where what this executive is personally backing has not been named. Pause for my response before coaching me on whether the decision was put clearly and the tradeoffs stated honestly. Do not invent customer facts or commitments. Keep responses fictional; this is rehearsal, not a customer interaction.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed decision conversation, the objections raised, and coaching on where an option was pitched rather than offered.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which tradeoffs are material enough to put in front of this executive. Review the downsides the rehearsal raises and add the material ones it missed, since not everything it raises bears on the decision being made.
activities.requiredContext: The approved narrative; the decision being asked for; the options and their tradeoffs; who the executive is and what they are accountable for.
activities.whyThisMatters: An executive decision put badly sounds like a pitch. Rehearsing it is how you hear the difference before they do.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on assembling an executive technical customer narrative.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is an executive-ready technical narrative with sourced claims, proof points, decision questions, and a technical ask. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: When did an executive last stop you to ask what something meant?
Which part of your technical story do you find hardest to say without jargon?
What is this executive personally putting at risk by backing your recommendation?
What decision do you actually need from the executive, and have you ever asked for it directly?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Translate architecture into business value'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the technical story to the one decision you want the executive to make, and the proof they need to make it. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Executive technical narratives translate options into customer consequences and an explicit decision. Preserve the difficult trade-off instead of hiding it behind technical detail. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Read your opening line aloud. Would a CFO know what you meant?
Which claim in your narrative rests on a proof point you do not have?
What are you asking the executive to decide, stated in one sentence?
How would another ATS translate your strongest technical claim without losing its caveat?
listenFor: Architecture described rather than translated, value asserted without evidence, narratives that end without an ask, and jargon that survived because nobody in the room questioned it. Also note a narrative aimed at the technical stakeholder while claiming to target the executive.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one executive technical narrative: business decision, technical option, sourced proof, caveat and one-sentence ask. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which technical trade-off became clearer in customer terms, and what proof does the executive still need?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could adapt a technical narrative for an executive audience, clarifying the decision, options and trade-offs without needing to present it. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized trade-off made clearer and whether a reviewer better understood the executive decision. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A technical recommendation lists capabilities but does not explain the executive decision or risk. Rework one paragraph around the decision and flag an unsupported proof point.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A technical executive briefing translates evidence and tradeoffs into a recommendation and a customer decision ask. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the proof point and executive decision in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Technical detail is not an understandable executive recommendation. Look for a recommendation, its evidence and a clear executive ask.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: technical detail is not an understandable executive recommendation. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when technical detail is not an understandable executive recommendation. Manager support can help involve the executive-conversation owner without prescribing the technical answer.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which decision the briefing should support; encourage understandable tradeoffs without treating the huddle as technical sign-off.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that technical detail is not an understandable executive recommendation; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help involve the executive-conversation owner without prescribing the technical answer? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

activities.name: Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief
activities.description: Synthesize approved customer and technical context into a brief that names the customer decision, constraints, evidence gaps, and criteria.
activities.prompt: Use [customer and technical sources plus confirmed attendee list] to draft a discovery brief: business outcome, owner, architecture, constraints, open questions and five questions that advance the decision. Identify who must authorize funding/staffing and who is attending; flag unknowns. Separate customer-agreed decision criteria from proposed criteria, citing evidence and who must confirm each. Don’t turn hypotheses into agreement.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical discovery brief with questions, evidence gaps, the business outcome and its owner, decision-maker coverage, and explicit decision criteria. Each criterion identifies customer-agreed versus proposed status, supporting source where available, and the person who must confirm it or an unresolved ownership gap.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides which questions are appropriate to ask this customer. A technically sound discovery question can be premature or presumptuous given where the relationship is, and discovery is where that costs most. The SE also decides how directly to ask who can approve, since the question is fair to ask and can still land badly depending on who is in the room.
activities.requiredContext: Selected approved customer/technical sources; confirmed meeting attendee list; sourced decision-authority or decision-maker measures where available; any recorded customer-agreed criteria and their evidence.
activities.whyThisMatters: Discovery becomes useful when it produces decision criteria the customer and team can inspect.

activities.name: Rehearse the technical discovery conversation
activities.description: Practice questions, listening, objections and the intended next decision.
activities.prompt: Role-play the customer or stakeholder for the upcoming technical discovery conversation. Use [paste/describe an approved fictional or de-identified discovery brief] only. activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns what is said in the room. Rehearsal makes phrasing fluent, and fluency makes an unverified claim sound exactly as certain as a verified one.
activities.requiredContext: Approved discovery brief.
activities.whyThisMatters: Practicing discovery questions reduces the chance that the real meeting ends with ambiguity instead of criteria.

activities.name: Map evidence gaps against decision criteria
activities.description: Test each decision criterion in the discovery brief against the evidence you actually hold, so the gaps are visible before the customer finds them.
activities.prompt: Using [the discovery brief and permitted supporting evidence], map each proposed decision criterion to evidence, missing evidence, assumptions and required reviewer input. Cite material conclusions and distinguish customer-confirmed criteria from proposed ones. Identify the evidence or reviewer role that could close each consequential gap; use known contacts only where supplied and mark ownership unconfirmed otherwise. Do not invent criteria, weights or customer agreement.
activities.expectedOutput: Evidence-gap map tied to customer decision criteria.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides which missing evidence actually blocks the decision. Discovery can always find another gap, and pursuing all of them delays the decision the criteria were built to enable.
activities.requiredContext: The discovery brief with its proposed decision criteria; the evidence you currently hold for each; the reviewers who could close a gap.
activities.whyThisMatters: The gap map shows what must be proven before architecture, demo, or PoC work proceeds.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Discovery should end with decision criteria, not a second discovery meeting. Today focuses on making the customer decision explicit early.
keyTalkingPoints: Start from the customer decision and work backward to criteria and evidence.
Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and open questions.
Capture what must be validated before architecture, demo, or PoC work begins.
discussionQuestions: Which decision is the customer actually trying to make?
Who has to say yes for this to happen, and were they in the room last time?
What evidence gap would make the next technical step unsafe?
What criteria need to be agreed rather than inferred?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from discovery discussion to building the actual decision-criteria brief. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Map evidence gaps against decision criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical discovery separates customer-agreed criteria from assumptions and identifies who can say yes. Write criteria before the conversation, then revise them as evidence changes. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which discovery question would most change the technical decision?
What evidence is missing or only assumed?
Which criteria must be agreed with the customer?
Which question has a peer used to turn assumed criteria into a customer-confirmed decision?
listenFor: Vague decisions, inferred criteria, missing evidence, and questions that sound impressive but do not advance the decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one discovery-criteria brief: customer decision, confirmed versus assumed criterion, evidence needed, discovery question and confirmation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore discovery criteria and the approval question using existing context; a new customer conversation is not required. Any real discovery should keep proposed criteria distinct from customer-confirmed criteria. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized criterion confirmed or corrected and whether it focused discovery or clarified approval ownership; it need not have been wrong. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A discovery conversation produced feature requests but no agreed technical decision criterion. Prepare one question that distinguishes customer evidence from the team's inference.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical discovery turns requests and constraints into criteria that the customer can confirm. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the discovery question and sourced customer constraint in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: The team's inference is not a customer-confirmed technical criterion. Look for a sharper criterion and a named authority for its confirmation.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: the team's inference is not a customer-confirmed technical criterion. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when the team's inference is not a customer-confirmed technical criterion. Manager support can support the next customer clarification rather than substitute an internal guess.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which uncertainty is worth exploring; keep the team's inference separate from a customer-confirmed technical criterion.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that the team's inference is not a customer-confirmed technical criterion; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the next customer clarification rather than substitute an internal guess? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Build the commercial decision brief
activities.description: Prepare commercial talking points, decision needs, and authority boundaries for a live customer or deal review.
activities.prompt: Prepare a read-only commercial decision brief in chat for [Account Name or TPID] or Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID] on [decision or proposed structure; one labeled Enrollment Number or Agreement Number only if contract-specific]. Use existing records and current applicable guidance; do not create, initiate, update or submit a pre-approval, DealBook or other commercial workflow. Cover contract terms, commercial positions, concessions, approval status, authority limits, renewal/consumption risks, customer discussions/questions and the next decision with recorded owner or owner role. Distinguish facts, approved positions, proposed but unapproved positions, risks and unknowns. Cite sources; flag missing, conflicting or stale evidence. Do not infer approval or customer commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: Commercial decision brief with authority boundaries, risks, questions, and next decision.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides what commercial position is stated in the room. Authority limits are theirs to hold, and a position offered in a live review is difficult to withdraw once the customer or the account team has heard it.
activities.requiredContext: Account name or TPID, or Opportunity ID for a particular deal; the commercial decision or proposed structure under review; available contract/proposal facts and known approval or authority references. One labeled Enrollment Number or Agreement Number only for a contract-specific question.
activities.whyThisMatters: A commercial review needs an explicit proposed position and authority boundary, not an implied approval hidden in a fluent brief.

activities.name: Identify commercial risk and escalation priorities
activities.description: Prioritize commercial risks from approved evidence, test assumptions, and identify escalation needs; return risk rationale, evidence gaps, and the next decision/handoff.
activities.prompt: In [Report Name], for [account/portfolio scope] during [review period], prioritize material commercial or renewal risk signals using available measures. Cite the relevant visual, filters, dates and comparison basis. Separate observed changes from risk interpretations; flag missing measures and the intervention, ownership or escalation questions the report cannot resolve.
activities.expectedOutput: Commercial-risk brief with dated report signals, provisional risk priorities, evidence gaps and escalation questions. A next decision owner is named only from supplied confirmed context; approvals, eligibility and commitments are not inferred. Unavailable report access or comparisons remain gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides which commercial risks warrant action and whether the evidence supports escalation; no approval, eligibility, or customer commitment is inferred.
activities.requiredContext: Report name; permitted account/portfolio scope and filters; review period and comparison baseline; available commercial or renewal measures; approved agreement context and any confirmed decision owners.
activitySteps: 1. Check the right report/view, permitted scope, period, relevant visual and measure definitions, including any comparison baseline.
2. In the available report Copilot Pane, ask the concise business question using the visual's titles and report terms.
3. Compare the answer with the report metrics. Inspect missing measures or unsupported conclusions, and refine the question if needed; optional book prompts can help.
activities.whyThisMatters: Commercial risk found early is a conversation. The same risk found at approval becomes delay.

activities.name: Set the trigger for each commercial risk
activities.description: Give each prioritized commercial risk an observable trigger, so it is acted on at a defined point rather than watched until it is late.
activities.prompt: For each risk in [the prioritized commercial risks], state the observable condition that means it has to be acted on now rather than watched, who acts when that condition is met, and what they do first. Keep internal steps separate from anything the customer is asked to do. Separate risks within my documented CE authority from those needing a more-authorized role; use supplied authority/owner evidence to identify who can decide and what they need from me. Where a risk has no observable trigger, say so rather than inventing a threshold. Distinguish documented triggers from evidence-supported conditions proposed for CE review; do not present a proposed operational trigger as policy. Preserve confirmed acting owners and mark missing owners unconfirmed rather than inventing a person or implying acceptance. Use the supplied material and flag gaps.
activities.expectedOutput: Each commercial risk with its acting trigger, the person who acts, their first step, and the risks that have no observable trigger named as such.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE owns the escalation route and confirms it before the plan is used. An escalation that arrives through the wrong channel is slower than none, because it must be re-routed after it has already alarmed someone. The CE also decides whether each trigger is one a person would actually act on, since a threshold set where nobody would move produces a register that looks governed and changes nothing.
activities.requiredContext: The validated commercial risk view; the approval owners; the escalation route your team actually uses.
activities.whyThisMatters: A risk everyone agrees is real still waits, because nobody said what would mean now.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Risk you find this week is a conversation. The same risk found by the customer is an escalation. Focus on finding it earlier.
keyTalkingPoints: A health score can tell you something is wrong. It rarely tells you what to do.
Every risk needs an owner and a date or it is an observation.
AI is good at surfacing signal. Prioritizing it is judgment.
For a chosen MSXI practice, inspect the risk visual, permitted scope, dates and defined measures; a report signal is not a policy interpretation, financial approval or confirmed escalation owner.
discussionQuestions: Which account is at risk in a way the reporting does not show?
What stops a known risk from getting an owner?
Which part of this carries policy or precedent risk?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Identify commercial risk and escalation priorities'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the one deal you just briefed to where commercial risk is concentrated across the book, then back to what you will act on first. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test assumptions behind the commercial risk view', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commercial risk prioritization needs current authoritative evidence and an accountable intervention owner. Ranking risks does not authorize pricing, exceptions or commitments. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Which commercial risk is most consequential this week, and what dated evidence supports it? Who can act and by when? How does a colleague distinguish a risk score from a cause that changes the intervention?
listenFor: Risk described without an owner or a date; health reported by score rather than cause; and interventions discussed but never started.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a commercial-risk row with dated fact, provisional consequence and governed decision-owner question. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could compare commercial risks and explore a proposed intervention for the most consequential one, without having to initiate an owner conversation. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized commercial risk verified or routed and whether it made the intervention clearer; keep agreement and pricing details private. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A commercial structure appears workable, but an unresolved policy question could block the next step. Inspect the approved source and identify the governed decision owner.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Commercial risk review connects a structure or timing signal to its consequence and authoritative decision route. CE clarifies commercial options and routes; only the designated authority can approve terms, exceptions or funding.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged commercial risk example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check portfolio filters, dated risk measures and authoritative agreement context in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A commercial trigger is not a policy interpretation or approval. Look for a consequence and intervention question tied to the authoritative source.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a commercial trigger is not a policy interpretation or approval. Confirm who can explain the commercial judgment and governed approval boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

WF-X-HEALTH-01.keyTakeaway: A health signal is actionable when its evidence, accountable owner, and next decision are clear.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a commercial trigger is not a policy interpretation or approval. Manager support can support access to the commercial decision owner without promising an exception.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which commercial risk question is useful to explore; keep interpretation and escalation within the applicable authority. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check portfolio filters, dated risk measures and authoritative agreement context; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations without scoring individuals. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check the report/view, relevant visual, scope, period and source basis before one focused question: Which risk is a report observation, and which intervention or approval question needs the commercial decision owner? Narrow a broad query using the visual's terminology; keep consequential judgment with its accountable human owner and do not turn the practice into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support access to the commercial decision owner without promising an exception? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Compare only transactable constructs
activities.description: Test options against customer intent and confirmed route mechanics.
activities.prompt: Using only [dated requirements, agreement facts, route mechanics, economics, policy/licensing/pricing evidence and partner capability], propose a comparison plan and pause for review. Then compare only demonstrably transactable constructs, showing sources, customer/Microsoft impact, assumptions, disqualifiers and conflicts. Keep unresolved routes unresolved. Draft decision questions for authoritative owners in chat; don’t approve a construct, invent policy, query systems or assume Deal Agent/Sales Home integration. Flag missing access without claiming a completed run.

activities.humanCheckpoint: CE recommends the construct after authoritative questions are resolved.
activities.requiredContext: Already-enabled Cowork authorized for these materials; output of SMEC-CE-DEAL-01 and dated customer requirement, agreement facts, economics, transaction route, current authoritative policy/licensing/pricing input and recorded partner capability. 3. Build a source-linked matrix of confirmed transactable constructs; keep unsupported or conflicting route facts unresolved.
4. Draft customer/Microsoft impacts, assumptions, disqualifiers and authoritative-owner questions. Verify citations and do not choose or approve a construct.
5. CE recommends the construct only after authoritative questions are resolved. Keep the packet in chat; no files, sending, scheduling, approvals, assignments, submissions or record updates.
