facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A transition or committed milestone is ready for another role to review. Focus on one evidence-backed decision within your organizational remit.
keyTalkingPoints: ATU: inspect the AE-led integrated account transition. STU: validate customer commitment and send to CSU. CSU: accept or return milestone through its own receiving owner.
Boundary: Each org discusses this in its own huddle; the receiving owner accepts separately. No joint ATU/STU/CSU huddle is assumed.
discussionQuestions: Can the receiving role act from this transfer?
What commitment or evidence is still missing?
Who must accept separately under the applicable organizational process?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Check the handoff packet against explicit acceptance criteria'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the selected evidence or rehearsal to one human-reviewed decision, its authority limit, accountable execution owner and next check. Keep individual-contributor and receiving-owner decisions with those owners. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Draft a precise acceptance request or return reason', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Handoff inspection distinguishes sent requests from accepted responsibility. Discuss gaps in your own org huddle and seek receiving-owner acceptance separately. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Could the receiver act from the handoff and its explicit criteria? Is acceptance actually recorded or only requested? How does a peer manager resolve a blocker within their own org without claiming the receiving org's decision?
listenFor: Assumed authority, unsupported evidence, or a cross-org huddle. Each org discusses this in its own huddle; the receiving owner accepts separately. No joint ATU/STU/CSU huddle is assumed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one acceptance checklist: handoff requirement, missing evidence, sender/receiver role, recorded/requested acceptance and bounded blocker. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What showed acceptance rather than assumption, and what remains for the receiver to confirm?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: A suitable Featured practice or manual discussion could support your exploration. If relevant, you could check a consequential handoff input and request separate receiving-owner confirmation or a precise gap; no joint cross-org huddle is assumed. Keep approvals, people decisions, record changes and messages human-owned. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open; do not infer status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized acceptance gap clarified and whether it reduced ambiguity; pending is valid. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A de-identified transition packet is ready to send, but the receiver may not be able to act. Inspect the evidence and keep receiving acceptance a separate decision.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A management handoff review asks whether the receiver can act, with acceptance separate from sending a packet. Manager authority depends on the organizational remit and formal delegation; the huddle must not rank, score or evaluate employees.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the de-identified handoff and known sending and receiving owners.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Sending a packet is not receiving-owner acceptance. Look for a receiving-owner decision with its evidence, conditions and next action.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: sending a packet is not receiving-owner acceptance. Confirm who can explain the management decision quality within organizational remit boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

WF-X-HANDOFF-01.keyTakeaway: A handoff is complete when the receiving owner accepts the work and knows the decision, evidence, boundaries, and next step.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when sending a packet is not receiving-owner acceptance. Manager support can help settle acceptance and ownership without reconstructing the entire history.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish local acceptance criteria from a universal process; do not presume a joint cross-organization huddle or receiving agreement.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that sending a packet is not receiving-owner acceptance; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help settle acceptance and ownership without reconstructing the entire history? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

Preserve known constraints and confirmed responsibilities; label suggested owners, timing or dependencies proposed. Flag missing evidence and ask only if a critical gap prevents a useful plan. activities.expectedOutput: Draft technical intervention plan with suggested next steps and measures, separating hypotheses from validated causes; owners and dependencies remain proposed until confirmed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A gap in planned usage does not tell us why it exists. Explore the customer and workload context, distinguish possible causes, and decide what to check next. Plan a technical intervention when its cause has been validated.
keyTalkingPoints: Separate observed usage or consumption signals from possible causes; be clear about the measure and period.
Use Cowork to investigate when the cause is unclear, or choose the planning alternative when validated causes are already available.
A report can show movement, but it does not establish a technical cause. Researcher can check public technical plausibility, not private customer facts.
For optional MSXI analysis, check the relevant visual, permitted scope, period and consumption/plan measures; missing comparisons are gaps, not technical causes.
discussionQuestions: Where do consumption or usage signals become technical work for you?
Which shortfall signal is most likely to hide a technical cause?
What evidence would you need before owning an intervention?
suggestedTransitions: Start with 'Investigate risks to planned usage' in Cowork when the situation or cause is still unclear. If validated causes are already supplied, choose 'Plan from validated consumption causes' instead; it is an alternative, not a required second live step. Extended choices are certified-report analysis (where available) and public-guidance evidence critique. Neither requires an MSXI run as a prerequisite.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Summarize what is known, which explanations remain provisional, and the next useful check. Choose a proposed technical action only when the cause and measure warrant it; keep commercial and customer-priority decisions with their accountable owners. Treat an unavailable report or missing comparison as a gap, not evidence that the underlying data is wrong.
facilitatorQuestions: What do we know about the situation, and which missing detail would change the next decision?
Which explanation is evidenced, and which is still a hypothesis?
What check would distinguish technical, adoption-related and other causes?
If using a report, are its scope, period and measures suitable for this question?
listenFor: Relevant supplied context reused; observed signals separated from cause hypotheses; an evidence check that could change the decision; honest access or measure gaps. Proposed owners and dates are not accepted commitments. Public technical guidance does not verify private customer evidence.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Keep the sanitized situation or clearly fictional manual hypothesis/options table when inputs or host access are missing. Only for a chosen MSXI report question, optionally use a starter/book prompt or narrow to the relevant visual; if the route or measures remain unavailable, use an approved excerpt or continue without a measured result. Fictional practice is not a tool result, customer finding, diagnosis or approval. No additional Team Member prework is required.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your interpretation, and which assumption or ownership question needs checking before action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a consumption-gap hypothesis against permitted evidence and confirmed metric definitions, and consider an intervention or owner question. Keep the cause provisional if evidence is incomplete. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized consumption hypothesis checked and whether it changed the diagnosis or intervention owner. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A workload is not reaching planned usage. A project note mentions an integration problem, while a customer note suggests rollout has been delayed. Neither establishes the cause. Compare the explanations and identify one useful evidence check before recommending a technical intervention.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A consumption gap can have technical, adoption or nontechnical causes; the measure alone does not choose the intervention. Start with Cowork to frame the situation and hypotheses, or choose the validated-causes planning alternative when that evidence already exists. Certified figures still require an authorized source; Cowork is not a replacement MSXI data retriever. CSA owns the technical judgment, not commercial approval or overall consumption-plan ownership.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Keep the existing Cowork investigation or validated-causes planning choice as alternatives, not a tool sequence. Arrange a sanitized situation or approved supplied figures. Only if optional MSXI analysis is chosen, check the report/visual, customer filters, period, plan/consumption measures and available report Copilot Pane; the home link alone establishes no access or successful retrieval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Usage variance is not proof of a technical cause; a Cowork hypothesis is not validated analysis. Researcher checks public technical plausibility, not private customer data. For optional report analysis, check the applicable report, scope, period, permissions and measures. Use the report's Copilot panel where available, not Take Action / MSXI Action Agent; do not assume a report run has succeeded.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree whether the example needs hypothesis framing or already has validated causes; choose one Featured alternative. Keep team-member attendance free of new artifact requirements. Agree who can help check technical assumptions or interpret the measures if questions arise.

WF-X-CONSUME-01.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when usage variance alone does not prove a technical cause. Manager support can help obtain the right diagnostic expertise rather than impose an unsupported cause.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish competing explanations before discussing a technical action; keep metric definitions and missing evidence visible. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check customer filters, period, consumption definitions and any plan/milestone comparison; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations without scoring individuals. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check the report/view, relevant visual, scope, period and source basis before one focused question: What changed in the measure, and what evidence would distinguish a technical cause from adoption or other causes? Narrow a broad query using the visual's terminology; keep consequential judgment with its accountable human owner and do not turn the practice into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help obtain the right diagnostic expertise rather than impose an unsupported cause? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

WF-TRANSITION.todayObjective: Reflect on the team’s progress over the past eight weeks, identify the AI habits to keep building, and agree how to continue learning through team huddles.
WF-TRANSITION.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
WF-TRANSITION.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Reserve the final five-minute Close & Survey block for participants to complete their own Impact Survey through the approved link. Priorities and the continuing structure should already be agreed in Recap & What's Next.
2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Look back on experience from the first eight weeks without assuming everyone completed every huddle. This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion: keep sharing, explore workflows that matter, and build on what works.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the shared Transition HTML, not the ordinary AI-in-Action practice format. Share recent experience and journey-wide reflection; the facilitator or manager briefly explains why practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue. Then agree the ongoing huddle rhythm and a Week 10 topic, and close with feedback. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
discussionQuestions: Since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well or did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?

Looking back across the journey: Moments that mattered—what changed in how you think about or use AI, and what are you doing differently? Habits worth continuing—which habits and peer learning should we keep building? Make it our own—what has worked about our huddles, what would we change, and what should ongoing huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep a team-owned rhythm, and which topic will we use for Week 10?
suggestedTransitions: Open with the purpose (2 minutes). Use Share Your Experience (15 minutes) for both the since-last-huddle check-in and the journey-wide reflection. The facilitator or manager then presents Sustain (3 minutes): practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Move to What’s Next (8 minutes) to agree the ongoing rhythm and a Week 10 topic using All Topics or Huddle in a Box as appropriate. Close & Feedback (2 minutes) welcomes questions and points to the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the habits worth continuing, the team's ongoing huddle rhythm, and the agreed Week 10 topic. Use Close & Feedback for questions and the Team Member Impact Survey invitation. Participants who already completed the survey do not need to repeat it; this is the beginning of Sustain, not the end of the motion.
facilitatorQuestions: Share Your Experience—since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well, and what did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?
Looking back across the journey:
Moments that mattered: What experience changed how you think about or use AI? What are you doing differently today that you were not doing at the beginning?
Habits worth continuing: Which AI habits are becoming part of everyday work? What have you learned from one another that you want to keep building?
Make it our own: What has worked about our huddles, and what would we change? What should our ongoing team huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep learning together, and which topic will we choose for Week 10?
Close & Feedback: What questions, comments, or ideas would you like to share before we close?
listenFor: Listen for concrete changes, honest uncertainty, habits worth continuing, peer learning, and support needs. Include people with mixed experience or access gaps without assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Seek a shared Week 10 topic, not a tool quota or a ranking of participants.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If app, topic-library, customization, or survey links are unavailable, continue the team discussion and agree a Week 10 topic without a live build or download. Raise the access gap through the approved support route. Do not invent personal impact evidence or generate survey answers.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What has changed in how we think about and use AI, which habits should continue, and where would more practice or support help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Agree how the team will keep learning through huddles and choose a Week 10 topic. Existing All Topics content or Huddle in a Box are options described in the supplied HTML, not required live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; each person supplies their own feedback.
bringBackEvidence: Keep bringing useful experiences, questions, and friction into the existing team rhythm. No new individual report, artifact, or survey-completion proof is required. Distinguish an observed benefit from an untested idea and keep human judgment explicit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Help the team move from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Reflect on the first eight weeks, identify useful habits and remaining support needs, agree how huddles will continue, and choose a topic for Week 10. This is a shared team review, not account planning or technical strategy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the shared Transition HTML and its five-part agenda. With the manager, agree who opens the session, facilitates reflection, presents the brief Sustain explanation, and guides the Week 10 planning. Locate the All Topics, Huddle in a Box, and Impact Survey links before the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Follow the shared 30-minute agenda: Overview 2; Share Your Experience 15; Sustain 3; What’s Next 8; Close & Feedback 2. Sustain is a short facilitator/manager explanation of why ongoing practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue—not another open discussion or AI-practice block. Do not require a success story, a new artifact, or live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to draw out experiences and friction, reinforce why huddles continue, and help the team choose its Week 10 topic and continuing rhythm. Keep the same shared Team Review content across audiences; do not substitute a role-specific planning exercise.

activities.name: Draft coaching questions from a de-identified business scenario
activities.description: Prepare evidence-focused coaching questions for a de-identified business decision without taking over the team member's judgment.
activities.prompt: Using only [the fictional or de-identified business plan, handoff or technical decision], write three coaching questions: one testing evidence, one exposing a material tradeoff and one letting the person choose their next action. Explain each decision criterion; propose a team-member-owned follow-up and work evidence to revisit. Do not rewrite the person's answer or assess employee ability, behavior or performance; use business evidence only, not employee profiles or history. Draft only and flag unavailable inputs.
activities.expectedOutput: Three judgment-focused coaching questions with decision criteria and a proposed owner-led follow-up evidence check.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The manager chooses questions appropriate to the situation; the team member owns the real decision and follow-up. No employee evaluation is generated.
activities.requiredContext: A fictional or de-identified business artifact, its intended customer outcome, known evidence gaps and a review point; no real employee/customer identifiers.
activitySteps: 1. Choose this activity or another Featured option; use an existing relevant business artifact rather than completing every activity in sequence.
2. Confirm your remit and permitted inputs, then run the prompt with the evidence listed here. If the tool/source is unavailable, use a permitted extract or manual review.
3. Check source dates, access gaps and the distinction between evidence, proposal and agreement.
4. Make the stated human decision or confirmation request, with owner-role acceptance and a review point; any real record update or communication follows the separate authorized process.
activities.whyThisMatters: Coaching improves judgment when it probes evidence and trade-offs rather than replacing the person's decision with an AI answer.

activities.name: Rehearse a judgment-focused coaching conversation
activities.description: Rehearse an evidence-focused coaching conversation using a fictional business scenario and clearly simulated reactions.
activities.prompt: Role-play a fictional colleague discussing [paste/describe the fictional or approved de-identified business scenario]. I will open with a coaching question. Pause for my response in each of three exchanges, then coach whether I tested evidence, explored a trade-off and left the next action with the colleague. Label all reactions simulated; do not invent actual customer agreement or make any employee evaluation. End with one revised question and the business evidence to verify in real work. Keep this to business evidence, not employee assessment. Draft only. Flag unavailable sources.
activities.expectedOutput: Three simulated coaching exchanges, feedback on the manager's questions, one revised question and a business-evidence verification point.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The manager judges the questions before any real conversation and verifies business facts separately; simulated reactions are not evidence about an employee.
activities.requiredContext: A fictional/de-identified business scenario, intended decision, coaching question and evidence boundaries; no real employee or customer data.
activitySteps: 1. Supply a fictional or de-identified business scenario with its evidence and boundaries; no real employee/customer data.
2. Rehearse three exchanges, responding yourself before the coaching.
3. Distinguish simulated reactions from verified facts and choose one question or explanation to improve.
4. The manager verifies any real-work evidence and owns the next conversation; nothing is sent or recorded by this rehearsal.
activities.whyThisMatters: Rehearsal exposes when a coaching question supplies the answer or takes ownership away from the colleague.

activities.description: Test one proposed next action against the plan evidence and applicable criteria, producing a coaching question rather than a seller score.
activities.prompt: For the de-identified plan and next action I supply, compare the evidence with the applicable decision criteria or role guidance I identify. Cite current guidance and source dates, keeping general guidance separate from the scenario. Name one unsupported assumption and the evidence that would settle it; if none is found, say so rather than inventing a defect. Write the coaching question that helps the person make that judgment, and a proposed follow-up check. Do not rank or assess employees. Keep this to business evidence, not employee assessment. Draft only. Flag unavailable sources.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidence-to-criterion check, one unsupported assumption and the evidence needed to settle it if found or a clear statement that none was found, a coaching question and proposed follow-up evidence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The manager verifies the criterion fits the local work and leaves the actual decision and evidence gathering with its owner.
activities.requiredContext: De-identified plan, proposed next action, dated evidence and applicable decision criteria or authoritative role guidance.
activitySteps: 1. Choose this activity or another Featured option; use an existing relevant business artifact rather than completing every activity in sequence.
2. Confirm your remit and permitted inputs, then run the prompt with the evidence listed here. If the tool/source is unavailable, use a permitted extract or manual review.
3. Check source dates, access gaps and the distinction between evidence, proposal and agreement.
4. Make the stated human decision or confirmation request, with owner-role acceptance and a review point; any real record update or communication follows the separate authorized process.
activities.whyThisMatters: A coaching question needs a defensible decision criterion, not an AI assessment of who made the plan.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A customer decision stalls when its next action rests on an unsupported assumption. Focus on a coaching question that exposes the evidence gap without taking ownership away from the accountable role.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Coach within your remit: account-plan ownership, technical decision criteria and customer-success responsibilities are not interchangeable.
2. Test the customer hypothesis and compare realistic options without turning the discussion into a performance score.
3. A useful question makes the remaining evidence check and its owner clearer; internal rehearsal is not customer agreement.
discussionQuestions: Which weak assumption blocks the next customer action?
What coaching question tests it without rating an employee?
What evidence should return after the decision?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft coaching questions from a de-identified business scenario'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the selected evidence or rehearsal to one human-reviewed decision, its authority limit, accountable execution owner and next check. Keep individual-contributor and receiving-owner decisions with those owners. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test whether plan evidence supports the proposed next action', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Coaching improves decisions through evidence and questions, not seller scores. People and performance decisions stay with the manager and outside AI evaluation. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Which observable business decision needs better reasoning rather than a seller score? What question lets the owner explain their judgment? How would another manager test the reasoning without asking AI to evaluate an employee?
listenFor: Assumed authority, unsupported evidence, or a cross-org huddle. Never rank, score, or evaluate individual employees; keep people and performance decisions with the manager.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one de-identified business-decision coaching card: observed evidence, reasoning question, owner-led action and follow-up test. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Rehearse with a peer; if alone, write both sides and mark the exchange untested, not a validated customer or coaching response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which question helped the team member examine a decision criterion without inferring performance or intent?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: A suitable Featured practice or manual discussion could support your exploration. If relevant, you could rehearse or use a coaching question from a de-identified business scenario and agree a team-member-owned next check; do not rate people. Keep approvals, people decisions, record changes and messages human-owned. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open; do not infer status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a de-identified question or criterion refined and whether it improved the decision discussion; exclude employee and performance details. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A de-identified decision depends on a weak assumption. Try a question that reveals the missing evidence without rating the employee or prescribing an unsupported answer.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Judgment-focused coaching tests the evidence behind a decision while leaving ownership with the accountable role. Manager authority depends on the organizational remit and formal delegation; the huddle must not rank, score or evaluate employees.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the de-identified decision and unresolved assumption in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Coaching a decision must not become scoring an employee. Look for an evidence-testing question that leaves ownership with the accountable role.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: coaching a decision must not become scoring an employee. Confirm who can explain the management decision quality within organizational remit boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Draft a one-decision technical intake
activities.description: Makes the first build-with conversation actionable while respecting technical judgment and actual intake governance.
activities.prompt: Create a scoped PTS/PSA intake for the recruit/use case identified in [approved requirements, architecture/gap excerpts and current intake rules]. State the single technical decision requested, user need, and scope exclusions; mark missing required inputs unavailable. Map the supplied evidence to intake fields with document/page/date references, separating verified requirements from recruit claims. Return a one-page intake with dependencies, risks, proposed reviewers, and separate questions for PTS cross-solution direction and PSA design judgment; leave capacity and prioritization unconfirmed. Ask the PDM-R owner to attest intake completeness and the PTS/PSA owners to review their respective questions. Stop before submitting, assigning resources, declaring technical readiness, or inventing intake rules. If required context is missing, return only a targeted gap list.
activities.expectedOutput: One-page intake with traceable requirements, scope exclusions, gaps, dependencies, and distinct PTS/PSA review questions, or a required-input gap list.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PDM-R checks intake completeness; PTS/PSA validate direction/design and applicable intake owners confirm routing/capacity. A complete draft cannot certify readiness or allocate resources.
activities.requiredContext: One recruit use case; approved requirements/architecture/gaps; current intake criteria owner/version; named PDM-R and proposed PTS/PSA reviewers. Cowork access/spending policy; supplied sources only.
activitySteps: 1. Define one technical decision and exclusions (1 min).
2. Draft against supplied intake fields (3 min).
3. Inspect missing evidence and reviewer questions (2 min).
4. PDM-R checks completeness and routes review proposal (2 min); stop before submission.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Makes the first build-with conversation actionable while respecting technical judgment and actual intake governance.

activities.name: Check one build-critical technical assumption
activities.description: Surfaces the dependency most likely to derail the build conversation before it becomes an assumed technical fact.
activities.prompt: Investigate [build-critical assumption] for the use case identified in [approved requirement and recruit architecture summary], and up to three supplied official technical sources. Bound the research. Restate the assumption and relevant environment/version; mark unavailable implementation details explicitly. Verify documented capabilities, prerequisites, and limitations with dated citations, distinguishing product documentation from evidence of the recruit's actual implementation. Return a five-row technical evidence brief with supported facts, unresolved applicability, contrary evidence, and one proposed validation question or test for each material gap. Ask the PDM-R owner to confirm context, the PTS reviewer to validate cross-solution implications, and the PSA reviewer to judge design applicability. Stop before certifying readiness, approving architecture, running tests, or promising build support; unavailable sources require an evidence request.
activities.expectedOutput: Maximum five-row cited technical evidence brief with applicability limits, unresolved inputs, and owner-reviewable validation questions/tests.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates cross-solution implications and PSA judges design applicability; PDM-R confirms recruit context. Documentation is not implementation proof, and no technical readiness certification is permitted.
activities.requiredContext: One technical assumption; approved requirements and architecture summary; environment/version; up to three official sources; PDM-R and PTS/PSA reviewers. No production access or secret material.
activitySteps: 1. Scope one assumption and environment (1 min).
2. Check official technical evidence (3 min).
3. Inspect applicability gaps and proposed tests (2 min).
4. PDM-R confirms context and assigns technical review (2 min); stop before execution.

Fallback: If Researcher is unavailable, inspect supplied approved extracts or approved official URLs manually. Preserve citations/dates and mark inaccessible claims unresolved; do not broaden the source boundary.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Ask: What exact technical decision would help this recruit move toward launch? Separate an intake that is complete enough to review from a solution that is technically ready to build.
keyTalkingPoints: Use supplied current intake and prioritization rules; do not invent regional SLAs or resource entitlements. PDM-R owns intake quality, PTS cross-solution direction, and PSA technical design judgment. Official documentation is evidence, not proof of recruit implementation. Proposed reviewers and milestones are not accepted assignments.
discussionQuestions: Which missing requirement would prevent meaningful technical review? Which dependency is cross-solution versus design-specific? What must the technical owner validate before a build plan can be trusted?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft a one-decision technical intake'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Choose the bottleneck: incomplete intake, uncertain technical evidence, or an unclear dependency. Run one Featured practice and inspect whether the draft asks for a decision rather than presuming approval. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Triage an existing prototype's cross-solution launch gap', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: PDM-R confirms what is complete enough to ask; PTS/PSA questions remain explicitly pending. Record the smallest next validation step and who must accept ownership before work is planned. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one recruit opportunity/use case, supplied intake rules, approved requirements and architecture excerpts, known gaps, and relevant official technical sources. Confirm tool access and Cowork spending policy. Exclude secrets and unnecessary customer data. Select one practice; no resource booking, technical approval, deployment, or system changes.
facilitatorQuestions: Is the requested decision small enough for an owner to answer? Can requirements be traced to evidence? Are proposed success checks owner-reviewed rather than invented acceptance thresholds? Who confirms capacity and prioritization?
listenFor: Explicit scope and exclusions, cited requirements, unknown inputs, appropriately separated PDM-R/PTS/PSA responsibilities, and unconfirmed resource requests. Challenge assumed access, technical readiness, or acceptance from a completed template.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If access or current intake rules are missing, prepare a one-question intake clarification with the known requirements and label rules unverified. Use supplied official excerpts for a manual evidence brief; do not fill technical gaps with a plausible architecture or assume resource availability. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did we remove from the request to make the next technical decision clearer?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could examine an intake gap or dependency and adapt a scoped PTS/PSA question. Review must not be treated as resource approval; no request or response is required. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized intake dependency clarified and whether it sharpened the PTS/PSA decision without resource approval. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on preventing late commercial involvement by making the CE trigger and requested decision explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Use when pricing, agreement route, concessions, funding dependency, renewal, procurement, partner transaction, or approval complexity requires CE judgment.

Fallback: Use a structured engagement brief and named CE acknowledgment if no intake workflow exists.
System of record: MSX for opportunity context; authoritative agreement/licensing and approval sources for commercial facts.

discussionQuestions: What commercial decision requires engagement now?

What would become unsafe if terms were shared before review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test whether CE engagement is required'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. facilitatorQuestions: What trigger makes CE engagement necessary on this deal? What is the exact commercial decision and working boundary? How does a peer establish CE acknowledgment without taking over seller execution?

activities.name: Design one bounded experiment you can finish this week
activities.description: Turn the real end-to-end bottleneck into a one-week test tied to an outcome, with explicit permissions, human review, leading evidence, and a capability or improvement worth learning about.
activities.prompt: Here is the business outcome and end-to-end workflow I want to improve: [paste the outcome and workflow map]. Here is the bottleneck: [bottleneck step and its observed consequence]. Design a one-week experiment. Specify the exact input, action, output, permissions, reviewer, stop condition, human accountability, downstream effect to watch, and leading evidence across time, quality, risk, customer value, or capability added. Keep it small enough to run in under an hour total. Suggest a best-fit tool only after the test is clear. If the scope is too large, narrow it rather than proposing a bigger plan.
activities.expectedOutput: A bounded experiment card with outcome, input, action, output, permissions, reviewer, stop condition, downstream effect, and leading evidence of efficiency, quality, risk reduction, customer value, or capability added.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide whether the experiment is genuinely small enough to finish, and you own the judgment about what output is safe to use in real work.
activities.requiredContext: The business outcome; end-to-end workflow map; selected bottleneck; accessible data and systems; required permissions or approvals; downstream users; and an available human reviewer.
activitySteps: 1. Take the step your group identified.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut the experiment down until it fits in an hour.
4. Name your reviewer and your stop condition out loud.
5. Put it in your calendar before you leave the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A fast task is not transformation if it moves the bottleneck downstream. A bounded test should improve the whole workflow or prove a capability the team could not reasonably use before.

activities.whyThisMatters: Designing a test is not enough; the team needs to learn from the evidence and decide what changes in the workflow.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle has no pre-written workflow. Start with a business outcome, choose work people actually run, map the flow end to end, and simplify it before proposing AI. The goal is a better workflow and a useful learning loop, not a tool demonstration.
keyTalkingPoints: The workflow must be recurring and tied to a business or customer outcome.
Someone in the room must own it.
Map the whole flow, including inputs, decisions, handoffs, permissions, approvals, output, and downstream users.
Improve obvious process friction before adding AI.
A specific recent example beats a general description.
discussionQuestions: What outcome are we trying to improve?
What workflow most influences it, and who experiences the result?
Where does the end-to-end flow lose time, quality, confidence, or customer value?
What is impractical today that AI might make possible?
Where must a person review, approve, or intervene?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the outcome to the end-to-end flow, from the flow to its real bottleneck, and from that bottleneck to one bounded experiment with an owner, reviewer, stop condition, and leading evidence. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Workflow improvement starts with the outcome and follows the whole flow, including downstream effects. A bounded test preserves permissions, a human checkpoint and honest benefit or failure evidence. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Where does the end-to-end workflow lose time, quality, confidence, or customer value?
Would improving one step move the bottleneck downstream?
What should be simplified before AI is added?
What could the team accomplish that is impractical today?
What permissions, monitoring, approval, or human intervention does the test require?
What would a one-week experiment look like?
Where did a peer's one-step AI improvement move the bottleneck downstream?
listenFor: Tool adoption presented as the outcome, a single-task speedup that moves the queue downstream, inaccessible inputs, missing permissions or approvals, an output nobody would notice if it were wrong, and experiments too broad to finish in a week. Also note capability-add opportunities that improve decisions, anticipate risk, or explore more options rather than only saving time.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one end-to-end workflow map and experiment card: trigger, inputs, decisions, handoffs, bottleneck, bounded test, permissions, reviewer and stop condition. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn about the whole workflow? Name one friction to remove, one new capability AI might add, one downstream risk, and the judgment that must stay human.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a small workflow test you can own, or adapt the idea without running it. Any actual test must respect permitted inputs, human checkpoints and stop conditions; observations of benefit, harm or no benefit must not be invented. Approvals and outreach must not be automated. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized observation: time or rework changed, a quality issue caught, a capability explored, or no benefit. You might describe a human correction or a possibility for the team to explore. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A recurring workflow contains repeated handoffs and avoidable rework. Map the friction and choose one small test, keeping approvals and customer outreach with humans.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Workflow improvement starts with recurring friction and a small test whose benefit is still to be observed. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the familiar task, friction and bounded experiment in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Tool availability does not establish workflow benefit or a successful experiment. Look for a small human-owned test with a baseline, safeguards and an honest not-run state.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: tool availability does not establish workflow benefit or a successful experiment. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Work out whether your territory actually covers your number
activities.description: Do the arithmetic between what your territory can realistically produce and what you have been asked to deliver, and quantify the gap.
activities.prompt: Test whether [quota, pipeline by stage/value, renewal base and actual conversion rates] cover my territory target. Show the arithmetic using my rates, not benchmarks. Keep renewals separate and avoid overlap/double-counting. Calculate the new-pipeline gap; derive a latest creation date only from [sales-cycle or milestone timing, if known]. If quota treatment or timing is missing, ask instead of inventing a rule or date.
activities.expectedOutput: A coverage calculation with the arithmetic shown, new business and renewal base kept separate, the remaining gap quantified, and the latest pipeline-creation date only where supported sales-cycle or milestone timing allows it; otherwise an explicit timing question or unknown.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns both the conversion rates and the treatment of renewals. Optimistic conversion produces a plan that looks covered and fails in the second half, and how renewals count toward attainment varies by plan rather than being a universal rule.
activities.requiredContext: Your quota for the year; current pipeline by stage with values; your renewal base; the conversion rates your team actually achieves at each stage; how renewals are treated in your own compensation plan. Include observed sales-cycle or confirmed milestone timing needed for a latest-start calculation, and any renewal/pipeline overlap.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rates your team actually achieves.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it. Without your own conversion rates it will have nothing to calculate from.
3. Check the arithmetic yourself. This is the number you will be held to.
4. Check how renewals count toward your own quota before treating the renewal base as coverage; that varies by plan and the calculation deliberately keeps them separate.

5. If supported sales-cycle or milestone timing is available, note the date by which new pipeline must exist, not the date it must close. Otherwise retain the timing question or unknown; do not invent a date.
activities.whyThisMatters: A territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. Most are never tested against arithmetic until a review tests them, which is the worst moment to find out.

activities.name: Find where the growth is most likely to come from
activities.description: Identify which accounts in your territory have the strongest evidence for growth, so coverage planning is based on signal rather than familiarity.
activities.prompt: Across [account list or territory scope], identify where the available signals support a hypothesis for new pipeline. Consider consumption against commitment, workloads owned but not deployed, renewal timing and recent engagement, without treating any of these alone as customer demand. Rank account hypotheses by strength of evidence rather than account size. For each, show the source signal, customer-outcome hypothesis, decision-changing unknown and next discovery or validation action. Distinguish customer-confirmed need from internal signals and seller inference. Name a relevant FY27 Conversation or connected Conversations only where supported; leave the mapping open otherwise. Flag accounts where evidence is insufficient.
activities.expectedOutput: Accounts ranked for follow-up by the evidence supporting each growth hypothesis, with confirmed needs distinguished from inferred potential, key unknowns, next discovery actions and relevant FY27 Conversation context only where supported.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller checks customer intent before treating a growth hypothesis as a qualified opportunity and decides which follow-up is realistic given their capacity. A ranked list that exceeds the hours in the year is not a plan, and the seller owns that trade-off.
activities.requiredContext: Your assigned account list; consumption and renewal data; your coverage gap from the previous practice.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your assigned accounts.
2. Compare the ranking against your own instinct, and take seriously anywhere they disagree.
3. Note the accounts flagged as having no basis for judgment. Those need research, not a forecast.
4. Pick up to three account hypotheses and name the customer outcome to test, the key unknown and the next discovery action; add relevant FY27 Conversation context only where supported.
5. Compare the potential with the coverage gap without counting an unconfirmed hypothesis as qualified pipeline; name the evidence needed before relying on it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Territory planning defaults to the accounts you already know. The growth is often in the ones you have not looked at, and the evidence for that is usually already sitting in the data.

activities.name: Build the support ask you can defend
activities.description: Turn the coverage gap into a specific, evidenced request for the help you need, rather than a general statement that the number is hard.
activities.prompt: I have a coverage gap and I need to ask for support. Here is what I have: [the coverage gap, ranked opportunities, prior support attempts/results and specific support ask]. Using only what I have supplied, help me turn this into a request a manager could act on: state the ask precisely, tie it to the specific accounts and evidence, show what has already been attempted, and set out what changes if it is not provided. Flag any part of the ask my evidence does not support, and do not invent a consequence I have not described.
activities.expectedOutput: A support request naming the specific ask, the accounts and evidence behind it, what has already been attempted, and the consequence of not getting it, with unevidenced elements flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what consequence to state. Overstating what happens without support costs credibility in the next review, and the seller is the one who will be there for it.
activities.requiredContext: Your coverage gap; your ranked growth opportunities; what support you have already tried to secure and the response; the specific resource, specialist or investment you need.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what you have already tried, and the specific support you need.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Cut anything you cannot evidence. An unevidenced ask weakens the parts that are real.
4. Check the consequence it states is one you would defend in a review.
5. Take it to your territory review or your manager rather than waiting to be asked.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support goes to the people who ask for something specific and evidenced. A general statement that the territory is difficult competes with everyone else saying the same thing.

activities.name: Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong
activities.description: Find the single assumption your territory plan most depends on, and work out what happens if it does not hold.
activities.prompt: Stress-test [territory plan and coverage calculation]. Identify the single assumption carrying most coverage, such as a renewal, large opportunity, conversion rate or consumption ramp. Use the supplied arithmetic to show what changes if it fails; label scenario assumptions and name gaps rather than inventing impact. Identify the earliest evidenced warning signal, its owner role and a practical contingency to reduce dependency. If the evidence cannot identify one dominant assumption, say so.
activities.expectedOutput: The plan's most load-bearing assumption named, the coverage impact if it fails, the earliest warning signal, and a contingency to reduce the dependency.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides how much concentration is acceptable. Some territories are genuinely dependent on one renewal, and the judgment is whether that is a risk to manage or a plan to change.
activities.requiredContext: Your territory plan and coverage calculation; the largest single opportunities and renewals within it; the conversion assumptions you used.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your plan and coverage calculation.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much rests on one deal or one renewal.
4. Work out the earliest signal that the assumption is failing, and schedule a check.
5. Decide now what the contingency is, while there is still time to build one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most territory plans fail on one assumption, not many. Knowing which one, and how early it would show, is the difference between adjusting in month three and explaining in month nine.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. This session tests that claim against arithmetic, while there is still time to do something about the answer.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current fiscal planning and territory-review requirements for your organization. Test the plan against governed quota, pipeline and renewal evidence, preserving dates and metric definitions. Separate actuals, forecasts and assumptions, and name the dependency or support request that changes the plan.
discussionQuestions: Do you know, arithmetically, whether your pipeline covers your number?
What single deal or renewal is your year most dependent on?
What support would actually change your position, and have you asked for it specifically?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out whether your territory actually covers your number'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coverage gap to the specific, evidenced support request each person will make. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Territory planning makes coverage arithmetic and assumptions inspectable. An evidenced support ask informs the manager; it does not authorize staffing or assign capacity. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: What is your uncovered gap, and by when would new pipeline have to exist to close it?
Where is the growth evidence strongest, and does it match where you spend your time?
What is the one assumption your plan cannot survive without?
Which conversion or capacity assumption would a colleague challenge before accepting the coverage plan?
listenFor: Optimistic conversion rates used to make a plan look covered, growth ranked by familiarity rather than evidence, concentration risk nobody has named, and support asks phrased as a general complaint about difficulty.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one territory coverage calculation: supplied target/baseline, explicit conversion assumption, concentration/capacity risk and evidenced support question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the arithmetic tell you that your instinct had not, and what changes because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could check a material coverage assumption and take an evidenced support recommendation to the manager or territory review, respecting staffing and capacity authority. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized manual scenario or leave the gap open; no report is required. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized coverage assumption checked and whether it sharpened the ask or changed the plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A territory plan depends heavily on one uncertain deal or renewal. Compare governed quota and dated pipeline context, distinguishing actuals, forecasts and assumptions before proposing support.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Fiscal planning weighs quota, pipeline and renewal assumptions against concentration, timing and realistic capacity. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the governed baseline and planning assumption in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain. Look for a concentration or timing assumption with a contingency and early check.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

WF-FISCAL-PLAN.keyTakeaway: A useful plan makes its assumptions, trade-offs, owners, and conditions for revision explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain. Manager support can support an appropriate resource or ownership decision without making a new forecast commitment.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help explore a defensible support or contingency question; keep actuals, forecasts and assumptions distinct without requiring a new territory plan.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support an appropriate resource or ownership decision without making a new forecast commitment? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year
activities.description: Separate the deals that can still be fully executed and processed before the period ends from the ones that are already next year's.
activities.prompt: For [territory or account], inspect opportunities closing this fiscal period. Show available approval, signature and outstanding-step evidence, and compare processing timing only with [confirmed cutoff/bookings guidance, if supplied]. State source coverage and what must still happen; don’t predict bookings or guarantee processing dates. Route missing cutoff or bookings-rule questions to Deal Desk/operations.
activities.expectedOutput: Each in-period opportunity with its approval state, what is still outstanding, its signature position, any indication it will miss the processing cutoff, and what still has to happen for it to be capable of booking.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the bookings rule locally and decides what is genuinely closeable. An approval state in the record is a snapshot, and only the person in the deal knows whether the customer will actually sign in time or is simply being polite about the date.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one customer/account; the opportunities you expect to close in the period; their current approval state; what each is waiting on; your Deal Desk or operations contact for the bookings rule that applies to your segment.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, select your authorized patch or an account with possible period-end deals using existing context, or a permitted excerpt arranged by the facilitator. No newly prepared deal list is required; keep unverified booking assumptions explicit.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Confirm the bookings rule that applies to your own segment with Deal Desk or operations rather than assuming it. What has to be true for a deal to book in a period, and by when, is set locally.
4. Separate deals waiting on Microsoft approvals from deals waiting on the customer. Confirm who can act on each and check verified processing runway rather than only the signature date.
5. Decide which deals you are deliberately leaving in the new year, and say so out loud rather than carrying them as hope.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every year some deals get forced into June that were always going to close in July, and are discounted for the privilege. The deals worth pushing are the ones that only need a signature, not the ones that still need a decision.

activities.name: Find the renewals whose expiration timing will cost you the booking
activities.description: Identify renewals whose expiration date sits at the period boundary, where how they are handled decides whether they land in this year or the next.
activities.prompt: For [territory scope or Customer/Account], list the renewals with expiration dates at or near the end of the current fiscal period. For each, tell me the actual expiration date, whether it has been committed as on-time, what is still outstanding to complete it, and what the record shows about customer engagement on it. Flag any renewal where the expiration falls on the final day of the period, so I can confirm any booking/billing-calendar difference with the authoritative operations owner. Tell me what you cannot see rather than assuming it is fine. State a calendar rule only where the current guidance I supply confirms it.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewals at the period boundary with their actual expiration dates, commitment status, outstanding work and customer engagement, with last-day expirations flagged for deliberate handling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the processing runway with the person who owns it. Renewal processing has a real lead time and the deadline that matters is when the work has to arrive, not when the agreement expires.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one customer/account; renewals with expiration dates near the period end; their commitment status; your renewals or operations contact.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose an authorized patch or account with renewals near the period boundary using existing context, or a permitted renewal excerpt arranged by the facilitator. No new portfolio analysis is required to attend.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Flag last-day expirations for an operations check; do not assume a different treatment without current authoritative guidance.
4. Confirm the processing runway with your renewals or operations contact rather than assuming it.
5. Commit the ones that are genuinely on-time and stop describing the others as on-time.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal at the period boundary is the easiest booking to lose and the hardest to explain, because nothing about it looked at risk until it was.

activities.name: Prioritize record corrections against verified fiscal deadlines
activities.description: Find apparent record discrepancies and distinguish corrections with a confirmed fiscal deadline from year-round hygiene or timing that still needs verification.
activities.prompt: For [patch or Customer/Account], inspect the authorized records and agreement evidence available or supplied for apparent discrepancies in agreement, licensing, enrollment, amounts, forecast dates and commitments. State what the record shows, what the authoritative evidence shows and what remains uncertain. Using current correction-window guidance I supply, separate items with a confirmed fiscal-close deadline, year-round hygiene and items whose deadline is unverified. Cite the rule behind a deadline; do not assume a field becomes uneditable at year end. Identify which owner must verify or correct each item. Do not change any record.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidence-backed correction list with confirmed fiscal deadlines, year-round hygiene and unverified timing separated; each discrepancy has an accountable verification/correction owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller verifies the correct position against the agreement before changing anything. A confidently inferred correction is still a guess, and a wrong correction made in the last week of the year is materially harder to undo than a wrong original.
activities.requiredContext: Authorized account/patch and identifiers; authoritative agreement/licensing evidence; current correction-window guidance if available; operations or Deal Desk contacts. Missing guidance leaves the deadline unverified.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose an authorized account or patch and inspect existing executed-agreement or other authoritative evidence, or an approved evidence excerpt arranged by the facilitator. No new Team Member evidence packet is required; stop the discrepancy check if authoritative evidence is unavailable.
2. Confirm current correction-window guidance with operations or Deal Desk.
3. Run the prompt and verify each apparent discrepancy and deadline.
4. Prioritize confirmed deadline-sensitive items by consequence and remaining runway; leave unverified deadlines as questions.
5. The authorized owner approves and makes exact corrections through the usual process, or routes them to the team that can act.
activities.whyThisMatters: Verified correction windows let the seller prioritize material discrepancies without treating an assumed fiscal cutoff as policy.
