resources.description: Detailed reference for Sales Agent components, capabilities, and example prompts.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

resources.title: Use Sales Agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot
resources.description: Official Sales agent overview and example prompts for connected CRM data. Internal sales scenarios and available records can differ.

resources.title: Sales Agent on mobile
resources.description: Announcement and prompt starters for Sales Agent on mobile, available through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app and in Teams and Outlook. Covers pre-meeting account summaries, fast pipeline lookups, and updating MSX from the field behind a confirmation card. Current as of August 2026.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

resources.title: Microsoft Scout FAQ
resources.description: What Scout is, what it can do across files, browser, shell and Microsoft 365, and how autonomous and scheduled work behaves.

resources.title: MCAPS Lobster Pound community
resources.description: Seller community sharing working Scout patterns, including account planning, customer language mining and recurring monitoring.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for a quick single answer that Copilot would handle in the app you are already in, and do not use it for a multi-step task you want done once and handed back, which is Cowork. It sees the same Microsoft 365 content under the same permissions as the others, so reaching for it does not get you more access. Do not use it to bypass a human checkpoint because it can run unattended; anything it produces while running on its own still needs the same review.
stepsToGetStarted: Go to aka.ms/m, the internal Scout hub. Request the access package, complete the agreement, download and install Scout, then sign in with Microsoft 365 and GitHub as instructed. Start with a business outcome rather than a tool command.

primaryAgents.name: Cowork
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Agentic Microsoft 365 experience for longer-running, outcome-focused, multi-source work.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Plans and executes multistep work, invokes skills, and creates deliverables with checkpoints.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When you want to hand off a multi-step piece of work and review it rather than do it. Complex tasks spanning Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 data, documents, presentations and recommendations, where it plans the work, runs the steps and checks in before it finishes.
keyBenefits: Executes multi-step work across Microsoft 365 instead of answering one question at a time. Built for delegation: it plans, invokes skills, works across data sources, and produces deliverables with review checkpoints.

resources.title: Copilot Cowork overview
resources.description: Overview of Cowork tasks, skills and action controls. Optional tool guidance, not a Dynamics 365 Sales skills guide.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

resources.title: What to Use When
resources.description: Routes a request to the best-fit Copilot agent and reserves Cowork for longer multi-output work. Useful early in a role path when tool choice is still forming.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for a quick single answer when Copilot or a specialized agent is sufficient, and for work that should keep running on a schedule after you stop asking, which is Scout.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select Cowork beside Chat. Describe the outcome you want rather than a single question, then review the work at each checkpoint it presents.

primaryAgents.name: ECIF Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Through Sales Agent, ECIF Agent brings program guidance, guided workscope drafts, guided creation/submission of supported investment requests, request-draft editing and delivery-health signals together with account and opportunity context. The full end-to-end conversational investment lifecycle is still evolving.
primaryAgents.whatItIs: Investment guidance and supported workflows surfaced through Sales Agent.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Discover programs and prior investments/yield; search suppliers; create guided AI workscope drafts; create and submit supported investment requests, edit request drafts, link workscopes and select consumption plans; review milestones, delivery health and risk. Compliance hold/release is role-permitted; eligibility, supplier selection and approval remain governed decisions.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Discovering programs or suppliers for an evidenced investment need; preparing guided workscope drafts; creating/submitting supported investment requests or editing request drafts; reviewing available milestones and delivery risk. Confirm request-type coverage and role permissions; this does not imply saved-workscope editing or full Agent MCR.
keyBenefits: Simplifies investment preparation and progression by bringing program guidance, supplier search, guided workscope drafts and supported guided request creation, draft editing and submission into one conversation; helps teams review milestone and delivery-risk evidence. Generated drafts and signals still need human verification.

resources.title: MCAPS Help for ECIF support
resources.description: ECIF support entry point in MCAPS Help. This link does not confer approval or funding authority.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

resources.title: Open ECIF Central
resources.description: Open ECIF Central for workscope and delivery detail. Use Sales Agent for investment guidance and supported request-draft work. Confirm the program-specific submission and approval path with current guidance; Azure Accelerate, Azure Access and CSP need not follow the same route. Use MCAPS Help for access or process blockers.

resources.title: ECIF Agent: current capabilities and limits
resources.description: Current ECIF Agent guidance in Sales Agent: program and supplier discovery, guided workscope drafts, supported request-draft work, delivery-health signals and in-progress features. Use it to distinguish draft types and check capability boundaries; program-specific process guidance still governs.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat the agent as the final authority for policy, eligibility, compliance, funding approval, or supplier selection. Review generated content and required evidence before submission, and use governed ECIF channels for exceptions or approvals.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Sales Agent and ask for ECIF, process or program help in the chat. The current capability guide can help distinguish supported steps from in-progress features. Use reviewed text and analysis in the huddle; any request or record change needs a separate authorized action.

secondaryAgents.name: Microsoft 365 Copilot
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: AI assistant across Microsoft 365 apps and work data.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Draft, summarize, analyze, prepare, and create within familiar Microsoft 365 experiences.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Everyday work grounded in emails, meetings, chats, files and app content, in the app you are already working in. Ask and get: you want the answer or the draft now.
keyBenefits: Reduces time spent drafting, summarizing, and preparing work; uses permitted Microsoft 365 context to keep work grounded.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use as a substitute for a specialized agent when the work requires a specific system or workflow, for a multi-step task you would rather hand off and review, which is Cowork, or for work that should keep running on a schedule, which is Scout.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot from the app launcher or copilot.cloud.microsoft and start in Chat.

activities.name: Prioritize account action for this week
activities.description: Use Sales Agent and available sales context to rank accounts and name one next action for each.
activities.prompt: Across [assigned account list or authorized territory scope], propose up to ten accounts deserving attention this week, fewer if evidence is insufficient. Show each priority driver, active opportunity stage, renewal or whitespace signal, partner context and one seller action, with dated evidence and gaps. Distinguish account actuals from portfolio rollups and missing access. Whitespace is a hypothesis, not customer-confirmed demand. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: A proposed weekly account ranking with dated priority evidence, available stage/renewal/whitespace/partner context, missing inputs and one seller action per account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which account genuinely deserves attention this week. A ranking built from recorded signal cannot see a relationship about to open or close, and cannot know what is realistic in the days actually available.
activities.requiredContext: Your account list; access to opportunity, renewal and whitespace signals; partner coverage for those accounts.
activities.whyThisMatters: Prioritization is a decision about what will not get attention.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Account planning fails when it becomes an inventory. Focus on a short operating plan that helps you decide where attention goes this week.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritization requires saying no. AI can assemble customer, pipeline, renewal, whitespace, partner, and investment signals. You decide which account deserves action and why.
discussionQuestions: Which accounts get your attention by habit rather than evidence? Where is the account plan missing a decision? What signal would change your priority list?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prioritize account action for this week'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from account list discussion to one AE selecting a top account and naming the next action. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the account priority list', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Prioritization improves when account signals change where you spend attention, not when the list grows. Separate supported priorities from assumptions before choosing the next account action. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account deserves attention that it is not getting? Which account gets attention mostly by habit? What evidence would change your top three?
How does another AE distinguish evidence-led priority from an account that gets attention by habit?
listenFor: Planning as annual documentation, prioritization by revenue alone, unclear next actions, missing role coverage, and customer priorities not connected to pipeline.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-account priority table: dated signal, customer priority, role gap, next action and AE judgment. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore an account priority view, with or without AI, and consider whether it suggests a worthwhile next action. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share one priority you checked and whether it clarified the next action. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: Two accounts both appear urgent: one has a recent relationship signal, while the recorded ranking favors the other. Compare the dated evidence and identify the next account action without changing the plan automatically.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Account prioritization connects recorded signals with relationship context to decide where AE attention is useful next. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review how the example's dated priority signal relates to the existing account plan.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Habitual attention is not evidence of account priority. Look for a next account action linked to a recorded signal and relationship context.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: habitual attention is not evidence of account priority. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Schedule account or opportunity checks
activities.description: Run a recurring MSX and interaction-grounded check In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: For [account/opportunity scope], run a one-time, read-only check for material changes, stale engagement, missing next steps and new risks. Show dated sources, gaps and one proposed seller action per issue. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline. Don’t schedule, send messages or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run opportunity review with actual source coverage, signals and proposed seller actions. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides what the scheduled check should be looking for. A check scoped too broadly reports everything and stops being read, and only the person reading it knows which signals would change what they do.
activities.requiredContext: A small named account/opportunity scope; approved source-access confirmation or permitted extracts; previous verified result if one exists; and a human reviewer. Recurrence, if separately chosen, needs explicit approval of scope, reachable sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Read that first result against opportunities you already know. Every flagged item should name a source signal you can check; discard anything it got wrong.
5. Make one correction you own off the back of that read, so the check has earned its place.
6. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
7. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recurring checks should reduce review burden, not create another inbox.

activities.name: Review applied pipeline fixes and resolve judgment items
activities.description: Check supported Auto-Fixes against the real deal, then resolve the hygiene items that still require seller judgment.
activities.expectedOutput: A reviewed hygiene queue distinguishing verified applied fixes, accepted or reverted changes where supported, seller-resolved items, and unresolved corrections routed to their owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE owns record accuracy whether or not they authorized the change. A fix can satisfy the rule and still misdescribe the deal, and the only person who can tell is the one who had the conversation. Reverting is the seller exercising ownership, not overriding the system.
activities.requiredContext: Your authorized MSX opportunities; access to Pipeline Hygiene and supported Auto-Fixes; the enabled rule configuration; verified deal timelines and evidence for any correction.
activitySteps: 1. Open MSX, then Pipeline Hygiene > Auto-Fixes if available to your role. Confirm which supported rules are enabled; do not assume a default configuration.
2. Separate changes already applied from items awaiting your judgment.
3. Compare each applied change with verified deal dates, customer evidence and forecast context.
4. Use the supported accept or revert controls where available. If a correction cannot be made there, use your authorized record-correction process.
5. Resolve surfaced items yourself, confirming the exact correction before changing the record.
6. Discuss a rule-correct change inspected in this activity that did not describe the deal; if none occurred, use the facilitator's illustrative example. Do not expose sensitive account detail.
activities.whyThisMatters: Rule compliance is not deal accuracy. Reviewing applied changes protects the forecast while reserving seller judgment for context the rule cannot see.

activities.name: Keep pipeline hygiene current between reviews
activities.description: Stand up a recurring sweep of your owned pipeline so hygiene problems surface on a schedule instead of the night before a review. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: Check [pipeline/portfolio scope] read-only for past close dates, no activity in 30 days, weak next steps, or unchanged stages with moved close dates. Draft the question/correction for each, ranked by current-period revenue at risk. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline and flag gaps. Don’t change records, schedule checks or send follow-ups.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run baseline or change hygiene list ranked by revenue at risk, with a drafted resolution for each flagged opportunity. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE confirms each flagged item is genuinely stale before updating, and makes every record change themselves rather than delegating the write.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your owned pipeline; your current period close dates; your team's definition of a healthy next step. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Confirm your team's definition of a healthy next step so the check flags the right things.
5. Review the first list and confirm each flagged opportunity is genuinely stale rather than deliberately paused.
6. Make every record change yourself; do not let the check write to MSX.
7. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
8. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: A source-checked change list can make hygiene review more focused without letting an unattended check alter the deal record.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on restoring trust in the pipeline signal before it becomes a forecast argument.
keyTalkingPoints: Bad data creates bad inspection. Stage, close date, next step, customer engagement, and partner attach should reflect reality. AI can flag issues; you verify and decide the correction.
For a chosen MSXI practice, check the relevant report/visual, portfolio filters, period and plan measures; progression needs history, not just a snapshot.
discussionQuestions: Where does your pipeline data most often mislead you? Which field do you trust least? Which opportunity would you hesitate to defend in a review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Ask what the certified business data says'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the individual records the check surfaced to the aggregate gap they add up to, then decide which correction would change the forecast conversation. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Tell the applied fixes apart from the ones waiting on you', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pipeline trust comes from checking material signals and routing corrections to the record owner. An AI explanation is a hypothesis, not a verified stage or forecast change. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Which opportunity would you not want inspected right now? What field, date, or next step might be telling the wrong story? What correction would change the forecast conversation?
What recurring inspection check has a peer used to catch a misleading date or next step before the review?
listenFor: Manual reconciliation, stale dates, close-date optimism, missing customer engagement, and records corrected only right before reviews.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a pipeline inspection row with the metric, baseline, uncertainty and record-owner question. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did inspection reveal about the pipeline or forecast story, and which correction or caveat changes the decision?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could run one pipeline signal-quality check and correct or flag one material issue. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share the type of issue verified, corrected or routed and whether it reduced a misleading pipeline signal. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An opportunity's close date is current, but its next step is generic and its last recorded engagement is old. Check the available source before deciding whether to flag a record correction.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Pipeline quality depends on whether opportunity fields reflect the deal, not just whether the record is complete. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged pipeline gap example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check portfolio filters, period, plan baseline and stage/timing measures in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. For discovery or definitions, start from the goal or metric; a known report name is optional. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A rule-correct field can still misrepresent the deal, and a snapshot does not establish slow progression without movement measures. For the optional pushed-metrics activity, the guide's read-only Insights widget is not evidence of subscriptions, sending preferences or delivery; keep setup on hold unless those features are separately confirmed.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a rule-correct field can still misrepresent the deal. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help the facilitator distinguish a record-quality question from a seller inspection; leave corrections with the opportunity owner. activities.name: Pressure-test the forecast narrative
activities.description: Find the movement, risk or commitment in your forecast narrative that you cannot yet evidence.
activities.prompt: Review [paste or attach the forecast narrative and dated evidence]. For each claim about movement, risk or commitment, state the certified source behind it and whether the judgment is yours or the data's. Identify the two claims most likely to be challenged in inspection and what evidence would settle them.
activities.expectedOutput: A forecast challenge list separating sourced movement from seller judgment, with the evidence needed for the two weakest claims.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which challenged claim to defend and which to concede before inspection. Arguing too hard for a weak claim costs credibility on the strong ones, and only the person who will be in the room knows which is which.
activities.requiredContext: The forecast narrative; the certified data behind each claim; the commitments you have made to your manager.
activities.whyThisMatters: Separating certified movement from seller judgment exposes the forecast claims that need evidence before inspection.

activities.name: Create the forecast follow-through plan
activities.description: Turn the forecast inspection into the specific actions and dates that change the position before the next review.
activities.prompt: Build a forecast follow-through table from [reviewed forecast narrative and at-risk commit evidence: source names or links], leading up to [next forecast call or inspection date]. For each commit or gap driver, show the action, owner, target date and evidence I should check. Preserve recorded owners and dates; mark suggestions proposed and flag unconfirmed commitments or missing evidence. Suggest a check-in rhythm; do not schedule meetings or update forecast records.
activities.expectedOutput: Forecast follow-through table with actions, recorded or proposed owners/dates, evidence the AE should check, unconfirmed commitments and suggested check-in rhythm.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE owns the dates in this plan and confirms them with the people named before it is shared. A follow-through plan built on dates nobody has agreed to reads as commitment and behaves as fiction.
activities.requiredContext: Reviewed forecast narrative and at-risk commit evidence, identified by source names or links; next forecast call or inspection date; recorded owners and dates where available.
activitySteps: 1. Select this practice or another Featured option and identify the reviewed narrative, commit evidence and next inspection date.
2. Generate and inspect the follow-through table; keep missing evidence and proposed actions visible.
3. The AE confirms dates and ownership with the people named before sharing. Scheduling and forecast updates are separate authorized actions.
activities.whyThisMatters: A forecast risk changes only when an accepted action and a dated evidence check can change the position.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A forecast narrative explains why the outlook changed, what remains uncertain and which decision needs attention. Focus on the evidence behind one change rather than a more confident-sounding number.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Connect movement, risk and timing to dated evidence.
2. A draft organizes the story; it cannot own the forecast commitment or remove a caveat.
3. If Cowork follow-through is selected, inspect the table's actions and unconfirmed owners/dates; if the brief is selected, review the draft brief and keep optional seller concerns unverified.
4. If the MSXI comparison is selected, check the report/visual, filters, qualified/committed definitions and comparable weekly measures; missing history is an evidence gap.
5. Explain the remaining human-owned forecast question. These are alternative practices, not a required tool sequence.
discussionQuestions: What changed since the last review? Which commit has the weakest evidence? What question from your manager would be hardest to answer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Analyze certified forecast movement'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from report output to the narrative the AE would actually use in a forecast review. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the forecast narrative', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: A useful forecast narrative exposes the evidence, uncertainty and decision behind the number. Carry unresolved risks into inspection rather than smoothing them out. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
facilitatorQuestions: What changed since last week? Which commit carries the most risk? What would your manager ask that the current narrative cannot answer?
How would another AE challenge your highest-risk commit using dated evidence rather than confidence?
listenFor: Forecast narrative built from memory, risk without evidence, unclear inspection questions, and confusion between confidence and wishful thinking.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a forecast movement row with prior/current dates, changed fact, gap and inspection question. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did inspection reveal about the pipeline or forecast story, and which correction or caveat changes the decision?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could try drafting a forecast narrative for your scope and consider whether to adapt it for an inspection or manager discussion. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share one forecast caveat changed by human review and whether it improved the discussion; omit customer metrics and the full forecast. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A forecast explanation still relies on a next step that a later meeting note calls uncertain. Reconcile the sources and describe what the record owner needs to decide.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A forecast narrative explains changed evidence and uncertainty so the AE can exercise opportunity judgment. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged forecast movement example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check forecast filters, comparable weekly dates and qualified/committed movement measures in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A confident narrative does not establish the commitment. Look for a changed fact, retained caveat and human-owned forecast question. In the selected Cowork practice, a recorded owner/date is not necessarily accepted; an unprovided seller concern must not be invented. Drafting a brief is different from sharing it or changing forecast records.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a confident narrative does not establish the commitment. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

AE-PIPE-2.keyTakeaway: Separate a signal from a verified deal state; record source, scope, and as-of timing before changing the forecast or route.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a confident narrative does not establish the commitment. Manager support can support the evidence clarification needed in the next forecast conversation.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which forecast assumption is worth exploring, without asking the team to defend a live forecast or treating a draft narrative as a commitment. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check forecast filters, comparable weekly dates and qualified/committed movement measures; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. A confident narrative is not a commitment; forecast judgment remains human-owned. If Cowork follow-through is chosen, ask which owner/date still needs agreement; for the brief, distinguish recorded seller judgment from optional unverified concerns. If MSXI is chosen, check the report/view, visual, scope, period and comparison basis: is this a comparable change, a missing snapshot or an unverified seller explanation? Narrow broad questions using report terms. Ask for uncertainty, not confidence; do not require both practices or turn either into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the evidence clarification needed in the next forecast conversation? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.

Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

activities.name: Qualify buying signals into opportunity hypotheses
activities.description: Surface customer outcomes, discovery evidence, and routing needs from approved signals; return a qualified opportunity brief with explicit next-owner handoff.
activities.prompt: For [Customer/Account], review authorized MSX data and any customer-conversation sources actually available or supplied. Identify the customer outcome, buying trigger, discovery evidence, intent confirmed by the customer versus inferred interest, existing opportunity overlap and unsupported signals. Return up to three hypotheses, each with the next discovery conversation or routing recommendation and proposed receiving role; mark owner acceptance unconfirmed. Do not create or advance an opportunity.
activities.expectedOutput: Opportunity hypothesis brief with customer outcomes, sourced discovery signals, existing opportunity overlap, recommended routing or next conversation, evidence gaps, and unsupported signals clearly separated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE verifies that the stated customer outcome and discovery signal are supported, decides whether to route for follow-up or create/advance an opportunity, and owns the next customer conversation; a signal alone is not customer intent.
activities.requiredContext: The account you are working; access to MSX, recent meetings and email for it; your open opportunities so you can spot overlap.
activities.whyThisMatters: A qualified opportunity starts with a trigger and evidence, not the need to fill coverage.

activities.name: Develop whitespace outreach from evidence
activities.description: Use a supplied whitespace and customer-priority snapshot to draft testable opportunity hypotheses and an initial outreach plan.
activities.prompt: Using the account/territory snapshot, solution penetration and customer priorities I supply, identify up to three whitespace hypotheses. For each state evidence, assumptions, known prior declines or duplicate opportunities, a relevant partner role only where supported, a first outreach draft and first-meeting agenda. Treat low penetration as a question, not proof of need. Name missing inputs rather than assuming live MSX access.
activities.expectedOutput: Whitespace opportunity hypotheses with evidence, assumptions, first outreach, partner consideration, and meeting agenda.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether this outreach should go to this customer. Whitespace is an absence in the record rather than a need, and approaching a customer on something they have already declined makes the next approach harder.
activities.requiredContext: Approved account/territory snapshot; solution-penetration evidence; customer-stated priorities; known prior outreach and supported partner context where available.
activities.whyThisMatters: Whitespace only matters when it becomes a customer problem worth testing.

activities.name: Pressure-test the opportunity hypotheses
activities.description: Separate the opportunity signals that are genuinely evidenced from the ones that reflect optimism.
activities.prompt: Review [the opportunity hypotheses and supporting signals]. For each, state the trigger event, the evidence it rests on, and whether a customer has actually indicated intent or the intent is inferred. Identify which would create duplicate or unsupported pipeline, and the one next evidence check that could strengthen or reject each hypothesis. Do not treat that check alone as full opportunity qualification.
activities.expectedOutput: A qualification challenge per hypothesis, with evidence status, duplication risk, and one next evidence check that could strengthen or reject it without implying full opportunity qualification.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether the customer has actually indicated intent or the intent is inferred. Building pipeline from an inferred signal is how forecast credibility is lost, and the distinction is usually visible only to whoever had the conversation.
activities.requiredContext: The opportunity hypotheses; the trigger and evidence behind each; your existing pipeline so you can spot duplication.
activities.whyThisMatters: An inferred buying signal is not customer intent; qualification tests prevent unsupported or duplicate pipeline.

activities.name: Create the opportunity follow-through plan
activities.description: Turn qualified opportunity hypotheses into the first customer action and the date you will know whether it is real.
activities.prompt: Turn [the qualified opportunity hypotheses] into a follow-through plan. For each, define the first customer action, the stakeholder, the date, the response that would confirm it is real, and the point at which you would stop pursuing it. Rank qualitatively by which is most likely to convert, explaining the evidence and uncertainty; say when the material does not support a ranking and do not invent conversion probabilities. Preserve confirmed stakeholders and dates, label proposed ones, and do not imply that a proposed owner has accepted the work. Use the supplied material and flag gaps.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked opportunity follow-through plan with first actions, stakeholders, dates, confirming signals, and stop conditions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE names the stop point before pursuing, not after. An opportunity with no kill criterion stays in pipeline long after it is dead, and defining one later is always harder.
activities.requiredContext: The qualified hypotheses; the stakeholder you would approach for each; your outreach capacity this week.
activities.whyThisMatters: A first customer action and explicit stop condition turn an opportunity hypothesis into a test rather than indefinite pursuit.

activities.name: Watch your accounts for buying signals worth acting on
activities.description: Set up a standing watch across your account list so external and internal signals reach you while they are still actionable. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: For [account list or territory], review available public buying signals—leadership, earnings, initiatives, regulation/funding—alongside internal support, usage and engagement signals. Cite dates/sources, distinguish evidence from inference and explain what would make each opportunity hypothesis credible. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline. Flag access gaps. Run once, read-only; don’t schedule, send or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run signal digest per account with sourced external events, internal activity changes, and an explicit evidence-versus-inference split. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE validates each signal against what they know about the account before acting, and never repeats an unsourced claim to a customer.
activities.requiredContext: Your named account list; access to internal account activity; the priority solution areas for your territory. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose a small named account scope you are authorized to review, or the facilitator's permitted example. Confirm reachable sources or work from facilitator-arranged approved extracts; no newly prepared account list is required.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Check which accounts in the selected scope have reachable internal activity; treat inaccessible coverage as unknown.
5. Check the first digest against one account you know well, and confirm every external claim carries a source.
6. Discard any signal you cannot trace to a source before acting on it.
7. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
8. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Opportunity creation is mostly a timing problem. The trigger events that make an account ready are public or visible internally - the constraint is noticing them while there is still time to act.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The next opportunity is often already visible in customer signals. Focus on finding and testing those signals without creating pipeline noise.
keyTalkingPoints: Whitespace is not just a product gap. A qualified opportunity has a trigger, stakeholder, business problem, next action, and evidence. AI can surface signals; you test whether they are real.
discussionQuestions: Where did your last real opportunity come from? What makes a signal qualified rather than hopeful? Where might you be missing a signal because it sits outside MSX?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Qualify buying signals into opportunity hypotheses'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from signal discovery to one opportunity hypothesis and the first outreach or discovery action. If a Team Member rejects or overrides the draft, ask which evidence or workflow condition it missed and compare the correction. Discuss only permitted details; do not assume this review sends anything to a transcript service. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the opportunity hypotheses', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Buying signals become opportunities only when discovery supports a customer need and a sensible next action. Rejecting a weak hypothesis is useful learning, not failed pipeline creation. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which signal looks promising but not yet qualified? What evidence would make it real? What customer action would test the hypothesis?
What signal did a colleague initially reject, and what customer evidence changed the qualification?
listenFor: Opportunities created to fill coverage, whitespace treated as product absence, duplicate opportunities, and signals without a named stakeholder or trigger.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one opportunity hypothesis: observed signal, stakeholder/trigger, customer validation question, duplicate check and go/hold rationale. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which signal warrants a customer action rather than just a new record, and what evidence would disprove the opportunity?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could qualify one opportunity hypothesis and document the trigger, evidence, next action, and uncertainty. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized signal confirmed or rejected and whether discovery prevented wasted pursuit or clarified customer need. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An account has increased engagement but no clear buying decision. Distinguish a useful follow-up question from evidence strong enough to qualify an opportunity.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Qualifying demand means testing whether a buying signal supports a real customer need and a useful next conversation. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the buying signal in the example and the qualification question it leaves open.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Interest alone is not a qualified opportunity. Look for a sourced signal distinguished from a qualification assumption.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: interest alone is not a qualified opportunity. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. activities.prompt: Prepare a concise sourced brief for an upcoming executive conversation with [customer] and [executive/remit]. Use customer primary sources for public customer facts, credible industry evidence for market context and permitted work content for account-specific facts. Cite material factual claims; separate public findings, work evidence and inference. Flag material conflicts, stale evidence and gaps without filling them. Organize findings around the conversation purpose where known; an exploratory brief need not wait for a precise decision.

activities.humanCheckpoint: AE verifies each citation actually supports the claim, discards anything unsourced, and decides what is appropriate to reference in front of the customer.
activities.requiredContext: Customer name; executive and remit; conversation purpose where known; permitted public and work-source scope. A precise decision is not required for an exploratory brief.
activities.whyThisMatters: An executive notices the difference between a seller who did the research and one who read the account record. activities.name: Decide whether the satisfaction signal changes your ask
activities.description: Test the ask you were planning to make against the customer's current satisfaction and support experience, and change it if the evidence says you should.
activities.prompt: I am going into a conversation with [account name or TPID] and the ask I intend to make is [intended customer ask]. Based on this customer's current satisfaction and support experience, tell me whether that ask is well timed. Name anything in the recent evidence that a customer could reasonably raise in this meeting that I would struggle to answer, and suggest what I should resolve or acknowledge first. If available evidence supports no change, say so plainly rather than inventing a concern. Distinguish that from absent, stale or inaccessible evidence, which leaves timing unconfirmed; state material coverage gaps. Keep CX Vitals and respondent details out of customer-facing drafts. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: A judgment on whether the intended ask is well timed, the issues a customer could raise that you are not ready for, and what to resolve or acknowledge before making the ask.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether to proceed with the ask. The tool can flag a poorly timed ask, but only the AE knows what the relationship can carry and what has already been discussed offline.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its TPID; the specific ask you intend to make; the meeting date.
activitySteps: 1. Write down the ask you intend to make before you run anything. The point is to test it, not to discover it.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt with that ask included.
4. Decide whether to proceed with the ask, soften it, or resolve something first.
5. Prepare an answer for anything the customer could reasonably raise.
6. Never quote the internal satisfaction data in the meeting. It shapes your preparation and stays out of the room.
activities.whyThisMatters: Preparation usually fails at the ask, not the agenda. Walking a growth ask into a customer whose support experience is deteriorating is how a relationship gets set back a quarter.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer conversations are where decisions move. Focus on preparing the position, evidence, objections, and ask before the meeting starts.
keyTalkingPoints: A brief is not a recap. It should state the intended outcome, customer context, evidence, open questions, likely objections, and the ask. You validate tone and relationship nuance.
discussionQuestions: What do you often walk into a meeting still not knowing? What would change if the ask were explicit before the meeting? Which claim would need validation before customer use?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the account and conversation brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from preparation concept to one live meeting brief and the ask the AE will use. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the executive conversation plan', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Customer preparation is useful when grounded claims and a primary or fallback ask help the customer decide. Rehearsal does not replace judgment about what to say or promise. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the meeting move? What claim must be validated? What objection is likely but uncomfortable to prepare for?
What did a peer change after the executive questioned the value claim or meeting ask?
listenFor: Recaps instead of positions, meetings with no intended outcome, generic value language, unsupported claims, and missing fallback asks.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one executive meeting brief: intended decision, supported value claim, caveat, likely objection, primary ask and fallback. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence would make this customer conversation credible, and what decision or question still belongs to a person?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could prepare one customer conversation brief and validate the claims before use. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized claim validated or removed, or an ask sharpened, and whether preparation made the conversation more useful; a meeting result is optional. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An executive conversation has a detailed value story but no explicit decision ask. Use the approved proof point to rehearse one ask and identify a claim that still needs review.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: An executive conversation needs a customer decision ask supported by evidence, not only a polished account story. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example's executive ask, proof point and objection.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A polished briefing can conceal an unclear customer ask. Look for a decision ask that changes after its evidence or objection is tested.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a polished briefing can conceal an unclear customer ask. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Align on the customer decision the conversation should support; encourage challenge to the evidence behind the ask rather than presentation polish.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a polished briefing can conceal an unclear customer ask; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the right role contribution before the real executive conversation? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. activities.name: Generate the Deal Book for a renewal and choose your scenario
activities.description: Compile the returned renewal evidence for one enrollment, then judge which available draft scenario warrants investigation.
activities.prompt: Identify the intended EA/EAS renewal enrollment for [Account Name or TPID]. Alternatively, use PCN [PCN], Master Agreement [Master Agreement] or Enrollment Number [Enrollment Number] as the single reference. Confirm returned identity and expiry details before continuing. Reuse its Deal Book or create one draft. Compare returned renewal/growth scenarios with [customer context], separating purchase history, licensing assumptions and unconfirmed expansion. Recommend a scenario to investigate and what evidence would change it. Cite sources, flag stale/missing data or guidance and name commercial/compliance questions. Do not invent scenarios, approve pricing/compliance, create/change quotes or proposals, submit or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Reviewed existing or draft Deal Book evidence for one confirmed enrollment, a supported renewal/growth scenario to investigate, key assumptions, relevant compliance questions and source/retrieval gaps; no approved terms or transactional proposal/quote.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Check the deal facts and scenario assumptions against their sources. Confirm pricing, exceptions and amendments with the accountable commercial owner.
activities.requiredContext: An authorized renewal enrollment, or an account name, TPID, PCN or Master Agreement for EA/EAS enrollment discovery. Customer context for comparing scenarios; an existing Deal Book if available; access to the relevant Sales Agent/CRM records.
activitySteps: 1. Use an authorized known renewal enrollment, or discover related EA/EAS enrollments from the account, TPID, PCN or Master Agreement. Check identity, agreement type, dates and linked billing enrollments; confirm one enrollment before continuing.
2. Reuse an existing Deal Book where available, or generate one draft. Inspect returned history, renewal/growth assumptions and relevant compliance guidance; note source and retrieval gaps.
3. Choose one scenario to investigate against the customer evidence. Keep unsupported growth suggestions as hypotheses and route commercial or compliance questions to the accountable owner.
activities.whyThisMatters: Verified renewal history narrows the scenario choice; the AE still decides which assumptions fit the customer and which commercial questions need approval.

activities.name: Prepare the EA quote inputs and approval route
activities.description: Translate the selected Deal Book scenario into reviewable EA quote inputs, then identify the approval path before any record creation or submission.
activities.prompt: For Enrollment Number [Enrollment Number], draft EA quote inputs in chat from [selected Deal Book scenario and applicable current approval guidance]. Inspect existing scenario/record evidence; do not start a quote or approval workflow for this drafting step. Show supported price settings, missing fields, validation issues and approval questions with sources. Do not assume discount authority or invent rules. Give reviewed inputs for manual entry if needed; any later quote creation is a separate human-confirmed action.
activities.expectedOutput: Reviewable EA quote inputs with source-versus-required fields, validation gaps and approval routing. An MSX draft quote exists only after separate human confirmation in an available authorized workflow.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE verifies every pricing field before submission, treats the draft as a draft rather than a final quote, and routes discount approval, exceptions, and any material amendment through the accountable owner and the legal approval chain rather than around it.
activities.requiredContext: The enrollment number and the Deal Book scenario you selected. Knowledge of your own empowerment level and who owns approval beyond it. Sales Agent access with your CRM scope connected.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the enrollment number, reviewed Deal Book scenario and current approval guidance.
2. Run the prompt to prepare and inspect the proposed quote fields.
3. Verify every price setting and resolve missing or inconsistent inputs.
4. Confirm approval requirements with the accountable owner.

activities.name: Test whether customer investment would unblock this deal
activities.description: Assess whether customer investment could remove a documented deal barrier; assemble supported business-case/proposal inputs, evidence, assumptions, owner, and the next human decision.
activities.prompt: For Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID], give an investment hypothesis in chat from existing deal-blocker and account-priority evidence; do not start an investment workflow. activities.name: Pressure-test the deal inspection
activities.description: Find the blocker, approval or stakeholder gap that the deal plan assumes is handled but nobody owns.
activities.prompt: Review [seller-validated deal inspection] alongside the agreement, enrollment and renewal context retrieved through Sales Agent. Use the inspection to identify the next customer decision, its exit criteria, whether supporting evidence exists, and which blocker has no named owner. Identify any material assumption affecting the close date and what would confirm it. Name the one with the greatest impact only where the inspection supports comparison; otherwise state that the ranking is uncertain. If no unowned blocker is evidenced, say so. Do not infer the customer decision path or account-team ownership from the financial context alone; flag missing inputs.
activities.expectedOutput: A deal challenge naming the next customer decision, any evidenced unowned blockers, and material close-date assumptions, identifying the largest impact only where comparison is supported.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE names the assumption that would most move the close date. A model can list unowned blockers, but which one actually threatens the date depends on customer dynamics that were never written down.
activities.requiredContext: The seller-validated deal inspection, including the next customer decision, current-stage exit criteria, blockers and known account-team owners, plus the verified agreement, enrollment and renewal context from AE-05-DEAL-01. That financial context supplements but does not replace the inspection.
activities.whyThisMatters: An unowned blocker or unsupported customer decision can invalidate a close date even when the financial context is accurate.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Strategic deals stall when the next decision, blocker, or owner is unnamed. Focus on making the deal inspectable.
keyTalkingPoints: A close date is not a plan. Exit criteria, approvals, commercial dependencies, stakeholder coverage, and customer actions determine whether the deal can move. AI can organize the deal picture; you route decisions to the right owners.
discussionQuestions: What is your deal really waiting on? Which approval, customer action, or role gap is not yet explicit? What should not be decided by AI?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect deal context before customer action'. Choose one Featured practice within the 15-minute slot; other Featured choices are alternatives, not extra live steps. If choosing the Deal Book alternative, use one confirmed renewal enrollment and an existing book where possible; bulk-book setup is not required. Move from the reviewed evidence to the next customer decision and owner question. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test the deal inspection', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live slot, and no Extended follow-up is also valid.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Deal inspection should expose the next decision and its accountable owner, not merely produce a blocker list. A routed ask is not accepted or approved work. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next decision, not the next task? Which blocker has no owner? Which commercial, technical, or partner decision needs another role?
How does another AE secure a decision owner without taking over CE, technical or partner authority?
listenFor: Close date as proxy for plan, approval paths discovered late, role gaps, unsupported deal assumptions, and AI outputs that overstep CE or SME authority.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one deal decision map: next customer decision, commercial/technical/partner blocker, evidence gap, accountable role and checkpoint. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal assumption changed when you inspected the evidence, and who owns the next decision or approval?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a strategic deal's next decision or blocker and consider a question for its accountable owner; no blocker needs to be resolved or routed for the huddle. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized decision routed to its owner and whether it clarified the next step; pending acceptance is valid. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A pursuit looks commercially attractive, yet its next customer decision and approval owner are unclear. Compare the seller-validated inspection with financial context and leave unsupported owners or dates unconfirmed.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Deal progression depends on the next customer decision and the technical or commercial conditions that still need an owner. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the open decision and blocker in the example's seller-validated deal inspection.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A model cannot approve a deal or accept another role's responsibility. Look for a specific blocker and an accountable next decision owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a model cannot approve a deal or accept another role's responsibility. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a model cannot approve a deal or accept another role's responsibility. Manager support can clear the cross-role or approval obstacle without overruling the customer decision.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help separate support the account team can offer from commercial decisions held elsewhere; do not turn the huddle into a deal approval.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals.
