facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on designing an executive briefing experience.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is an EBC plan with desired decisions, contributor functions and decision rights, evidence, preparation milestones and follow-through ownership. In Researcher's plan review, missing participation is a role or decision-right question, not an invented name; known participants or owners remain unconfirmed until evidenced. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What is the one thing the customer should leave the briefing believing?
Who in the room can actually approve the next step?
What is on your briefing preparation list that currently has no owner?
What would make this briefing worth their time rather than ours?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Design the executive briefing experience'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the briefing design to the single decision it is meant to produce and who must be present for that. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate briefing evidence and decisions', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: A briefing earns executive time by advancing a relevant customer decision with the right evidence and contributors. An invitation is not confirmed attendance or a decision guarantee. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: What will the customer do differently after this briefing?
Who in the room can approve that, and are they invited?
Which part of the agenda serves us rather than them?
Which agenda choice did a peer remove to make room for the customer decision?
listenFor: Agendas built around what we want to present, attendee lists without a decision maker, briefings with no ask, and content density that leaves no room for the customer to talk. Also note an experience designed for the meeting rather than for what happens after it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one executive briefing outline: customer decision, required decision-maker role, agenda choice, evidence and follow-through ask. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What makes the briefing worth executive time, and which decision or contributor is still missing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review an executive briefing around a customer decision, check who can make it and draft the reason to attend; report attendance as requested or confirmed, not guaranteed. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized change to the decision, audience or reason to attend and whether it made the briefing more purposeful; pending attendance is acceptable. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A proposed executive briefing contains many sessions but leaves the customer's next decision unclear. Retain one useful contribution and identify its preparation owner or open dependency.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A useful executive briefing is organized around the customer's decision, with contributions and preparation dependencies that support it. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the planned decision ask and the contributor roles in the example briefing.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A briefing agenda does not prove contributor readiness or customer agreement. Look for a narrower decision-focused experience with a named preparation dependency.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a briefing agenda does not prove contributor readiness or customer agreement. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a briefing agenda does not prove contributor readiness or customer agreement. Manager support can coordinate contributor support without making the huddle another briefing planning meeting.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help narrow the briefing to the decision it should enable; support realistic contributor coordination without assuming readiness or agreement.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a briefing agenda does not prove contributor readiness or customer agreement; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to coordinate contributor support without making the huddle another briefing planning meeting? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer

Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager

Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive

roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

activities.name: Rehearse the strategic technical talk track
activities.description: Practice the technical conversation and receive coaching.
activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the upcoming strategic technical conversation with the customer or stakeholder. Use [paste/describe the approved fictional or de-identified technical narrative] and focus on technical outcomes, open decisions, likely objections, evidence, and the technical ask. Pause for my response before coaching me on clarity, listening, evidence, and next step. Do not invent customer facts or commitments. Keep responses fictional; this is rehearsal, not a customer interaction.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which technical claims survive into the conversation. Rehearsal makes an answer fluent, and fluency is easy to mistake for evidence in front of an audience technical enough to test it.

activities.whyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing the talk track is cheaper than improvising it in the room.

activities.name: Find the weak claims before the customer does
activities.description: Audit the talk track claim by claim, separating what is evidenced from what rests on assumption or unshipped roadmap.
activities.prompt: Audit [the talk track and any approved supporting proof] claim by claim. For each claim, state the evidence that supports it, whether that evidence is approved for customer use, and what a technically informed customer would ask for. Flag any claim that rests on assumption, marketing language, or a roadmap item rather than something available today. Record customer-use approval only when the supplied evidence establishes it for the intended audience; otherwise mark it unknown for human confirmation. Do not infer disclosure approval from having the material.
activities.expectedOutput: Claim-by-claim audit separating supported claims, unsupported claims, and roadmap-dependent claims.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS decides which challenges are real and validates any technical claim before it is used with the customer.
activities.requiredContext: Draft talk track, current customer signals, and approved evidence.
activities.whyThisMatters: Executive credibility is lost on one unsupported claim, and roadmap language is the most common source.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on adjusting the technical talk track from customer signals.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a signal-adjusted talk track with opening language, questions, objections, responses, and human review flags. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What did the customer say recently that should change how you talk about this?
Where is your current talk track still answering last quarter's objection?
What signal are you choosing to ignore because it is inconvenient?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Adjust the talk track from current signals'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the customer signal to the specific line in your talk track that has to change because of it. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find the weak claims before the customer does', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Talk tracks improve when actual customer signals change a specific message. Keep what the customer said separate from your interpretation and validate new claims. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: What specifically did the customer say, and what did you infer from it?
Which part of your talk track is now answering a question they stopped asking?
What would you change if you took their last objection at face value?
What change in a customer's wording caused a colleague to change the substance, not just the phrasing?
listenFor: Signals interpreted to confirm what we already planned, talk tracks updated in wording but not in substance, and customer silence read as agreement. Also note adjustments based on one conversation with one person treated as the account's position.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one talk-track revision: quoted synthetic or sanitized signal, separate inference, changed line, caveat and customer validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What customer statement changed the message, and where did you separate the signal from interpretation?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could revisit a talk-track line against an existing customer statement and consider what you would change; no new customer conversation is needed. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized customer signal and a paraphrase of the line it changed, plus whether the revised message was clearer or still needs testing. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A talk track answers an older objection, while an approved recent customer comment points to a different concern. Revise the claim and identify what still needs testing.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A technical talk track should respond to current customer evidence while retaining the limits of its claims. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Compare the example's recent customer signal with the existing short talk track.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Rehearsal must not invent a customer reaction. Look for a talk-track change justified by the actual customer signal.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: rehearsal must not invent a customer reaction. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when rehearsal must not invent a customer reaction. Manager support can make room for the customer evidence that challenges the team's preferred story.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Invite discussion of what should change in the message and why; do not treat a fluent rehearsal as evidence of customer response.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that rehearsal must not invent a customer reaction; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to make room for the customer evidence that challenges the team's preferred story? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for a quick single answer that Copilot would handle in the app you are already in, and do not use it for a multi-step task you want done once and handed back, which is Cowork. It sees the same Microsoft 365 content under the same permissions as the others, so reaching for it does not get you more access. Do not use it to bypass a human checkpoint because it can run unattended; anything it produces while running on its own still needs the same review.
stepsToGetStarted: Go to aka.ms/m, the internal Scout hub. Request the access package, complete the agreement, download and install Scout, then sign in with Microsoft 365 and GitHub as instructed. Start with a business outcome rather than a tool command.

activities.name: Build the v-team commitment board
activities.description: Lay the v-team's commitments out as a board the team can see and work from.
activities.prompt: From [commitment and technical evidence], draft a v-team board for its account/portfolio scope, oldest activity first. Show each commitment’s owner, dependency, last evidenced activity and agreed checkpoint, with outcomes, workloads, technical decisions, risks and roles. Mark missing checkpoints unagreed and proposed dates as proposals; only agreed dates can be overdue. Keep my portfolio view separate from each account’s shareable view to prevent cross-account disclosure. Return paste-ready tables.
activities.expectedOutput: A commitment board with recorded owners, activity dates and agreed checkpoints, with unknowns and proposals clearly marked.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Check owner acceptance and capacity, and keep each account's shared view appropriate to its team.
activities.requiredContext: Approved account/technical commitment evidence across the selected accounts; role/decision context; review date; existing tracking tool if any. Extract recorded activity dates, owners and agreed checkpoints from that evidence rather than retyping each; absent values remain unknown.
activities.whyThisMatters: Twelve commitments written as prose have to be re-read. The same twelve as rows can be sorted.

activities.name: Assess role coverage and handoffs
activities.description: Identify missing role coverage and handoff risk.
activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID] or Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID], assess AE, ATS, SSP, SE, CE, CSA, CSAM, partner and investment coverage for [customer technical decision]. Cite current role and handoff evidence. Flag missing capability, unclear ownership and dependency risks; distinguish recorded assignment from accepted ownership. Identify the next handoff and the question for its receiving owner, rather than inventing acceptance.
activities.expectedOutput: Role coverage and handoff map.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms ownership with the people named, not from the record. A coverage map shows who is assigned rather than who has actually picked it up, and an unclaimed handoff looks identical to a covered one until it fails.
activities.requiredContext: Account or opportunity; current team context; decision to move.
activities.whyThisMatters: You cannot orchestrate a team if the coverage gaps are invisible.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

activities.name: Assess ECIF investment opportunities
activities.description: Identify whether ECIF funding could accelerate technical outcomes.
activities.prompt: For Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID], return an investment/non-funding comparison in chat for [proposed investment or documented barrier]; do not start a funding-request workflow. Assess architecture roadmap, consumption goals and technical outcomes against existing evidence. Cite candidate guidance and prior-investment/yield evidence; explain dependencies, risks and why funding may not help. Keep impact directional/assumption-labelled unless an evidenced model supports it. Name the next ECIF/technical-owner question. Do not determine eligibility, funding or approval, or claim a validated business case.
activities.expectedOutput: Source-backed candidate investment programs and a non-funding alternative, with technical outcomes, available prior-investment evidence, assumption-labeled consumption impact, risks, dependencies and ECIF-owner questions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS and ECIF owner validate eligibility, funding motion, technical feasibility, consumption assumptions, dependencies, and recommendation before action.
activities.requiredContext: Opportunity ID; architecture roadmap; consumption goals; deployment blockers.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment belongs in the v-team discussion when it removes a blocker to the technical strategy.

activities.name: Keep the v-team commitments moving between huddles
activities.description: Set up a recurring check that watches the technical v-team commitments and tells you what has slipped, without you having to go looking. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: Check technical v-team commitments for [account or opportunity] read-only using available meeting, mail and account evidence. Flag no recorded activity, passed agreed dates and quiet customer follow-through; draft the chase and proposed owner. Compare with [previous verified result, if available] to separate new/repeated issues; otherwise establish a baseline. Show source dates/gaps. Don’t schedule, send or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run commitment check that reports slipped, stalled and quiet items with a named chase for each. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS decides whether silence actually means a stall, and owns the judgment about which chases are appropriate given the relationships involved.
activities.requiredContext: The v-team commitments and owners from the commitment board; approved access to your own mail, meetings and account record. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Choose a small named team scope during the activity and inspect its already-authorized commitments, or a permitted commitments excerpt arranged by the facilitator. Confirm reachable sources or use approved supplied extracts; no new commitment list is required.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Check the supplied commitments for recorded owners and dates; leave missing ownership or checkpoints explicit rather than inventing them.
5. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
6. Confirm each flagged commitment is genuinely stalled rather than progressing somewhere you cannot see.
7. Raise slipped items with the owner directly rather than in the group thread.
8. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
9. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical commitments do not fail loudly. They go quiet, and by the time anyone notices the customer has moved on. This is exactly the persistent, between-sessions work that Scout is built for.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on mobilizing the technical v-team around priorities and risks.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a v-team commitment board with owners, dependencies, investment signals, checkpoints, and next actions. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Who on your technical v-team could not state the current priority if asked today?
Which dependency has gone quiet in the last two weeks?
Where does your v-team actually look to see what is outstanding?
What are you carrying yourself that should belong to someone else?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the v-team commitment board'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coordination picture to one specific ask, to one named person, with a date. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Keep the v-team commitments moving between huddles', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: V-team mobilization turns a dependency into a bounded, answerable ask. Confirm accepted ownership and capacity rather than treating the board as agreement. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: If I asked each v-team member the current priority, would I get the same answer?
Which dependency is at risk, and does its owner know?
What are you doing yourself that is really someone else's accountability?
How does another ATS confirm a v-team commitment without absorbing another role's accountability?
listenFor: Priorities that live only in the ATS's head, owners assigned in a document but never agreed in a conversation, dependencies tracked without dates, and the ATS absorbing work because delegating it feels slower. Also note v-team meetings that report status without deciding anything.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one v-team commitment row: technical priority, dependency, proposed accountable role, acceptance needed, date and escalation trigger. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which handoff is still assumed rather than accepted, and what owner, request, or date would make it actionable?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a bounded v-team ask using the existing account board or a small manual note, with the input and proposed date clearly marked. Drafting does not require sending it. Receiving-owner acceptance is required before treating any actual handoff as accepted; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a safe description of a v-team ask and whether it was accepted, clarified or held; note any reduction in handoff ambiguity. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A technical dependency has no recent update and two contributors assume the other owns it. Clarify the proposed next action without assigning an absent colleague.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical v-team coordination makes dependencies and accepted ownership visible rather than relying on a list of contributors. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the example commitment, proposed owner and checkpoint.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: No visible update is not proof that work stopped. Look for a dependency clarified with the accepted receiving owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: no visible update is not proof that work stopped. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ATS-TEAM.keyTakeaway: Cross-role work moves when every dependency has an accepted input, an accountable owner, and a next decision.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when no visible update is not proof that work stopped. Manager support can help unblock a cross-team commitment without replacing its accountable owner.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish an unclear update from a genuinely unowned dependency; do not assign work or dates on behalf of absent contributors.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that no visible update is not proof that work stopped; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help unblock a cross-team commitment without replacing its accountable owner? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Engages early with the opportunity owner to shape executable commercial constructs across Microsoft and partner transaction routes. Navigates negotiation guardrails, coordinates owner-validated policy and licensing questions, routes approvals and exceptions, and hands off approved terms while addressing renewal commercial risk.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes SME&C commercial terms across transaction routes and coordinates approvals and renewals.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

SSP-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
SSP-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
SSP-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

primaryAgents.name: Cowork
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Agentic Microsoft 365 experience for longer-running, outcome-focused, multi-source work.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Plans and executes multistep work, invokes skills, and creates deliverables with checkpoints.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When you want to hand off a multi-step piece of work and review it rather than do it. Complex tasks spanning Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 data, documents, presentations and recommendations, where it plans the work, runs the steps and checks in before it finishes.
keyBenefits: Executes multi-step work across Microsoft 365 instead of answering one question at a time. Built for delegation: it plans, invokes skills, works across data sources, and produces deliverables with review checkpoints.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for a quick single answer when Copilot or a specialized agent is sufficient, and for work that should keep running on a schedule after you stop asking, which is Scout.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select Cowork beside Chat. Describe the outcome you want rather than a single question, then review the work at each checkpoint it presents.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

resources.description: Detailed reference for Sales Agent components, capabilities, and example prompts.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

resources.description: Official Sales agent overview and example prompts for connected CRM data. Internal sales scenarios and available records can differ.

resources.title: Sales Agent on mobile
resources.description: Announcement and prompt starters for Sales Agent on mobile, available through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app and in Teams and Outlook. Covers pre-meeting account summaries, fast pipeline lookups, and updating MSX from the field behind a confirmation card. Current as of August 2026.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for a quick single answer that Copilot would handle in the app you are already in, and do not use it for a multi-step task you want done once and handed back, which is Cowork. It sees the same Microsoft 365 content under the same permissions as the others, so reaching for it does not get you more access. Do not use it to bypass a human checkpoint because it can run unattended; anything it produces while running on its own still needs the same review.
stepsToGetStarted: Go to aka.ms/m, the internal Scout hub. Request the access package, complete the agreement, download and install Scout, then sign in with Microsoft 365 and GitHub as instructed. Start with a business outcome rather than a tool command.

activities.name: Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan
activities.description: Review digital signals and conversation context to prioritize lead follow-up; return source-backed fit, consent status, and the next contact action.
activities.prompt: Using approved lead or attendee context for [solution area], draft a prioritized lead follow-up plan, not a general account or deal review. Favor current, relevant signals; flag context that may be stale, outside the intended scope or uncertain. For each lead, concisely show source, account, likely interest, solution relevance, suggested message, known or proposed owner, and next action. If scope or evidence is unclear, ask for clarification or a supporting document or link. A signal alone is not confirmed customer interest. State consent/contact-history status only where supported; otherwise mark it unknown and identify the check needed before outreach. Do not send outreach.
activities.expectedOutput: Prioritized lead follow-up plan with digital signal source, conversation/contact context, fit, consent status, owner, and next action; unverified signals are flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP validates the digital signal and prior-conversation context, checks consent and contact history, and decides whether to engage; a signal alone is not customer intent.
activities.requiredContext: Approved lead or attendee context, the selected solution area and relevant account or interaction context; recorded consent/contact history where available.
activities.whyThisMatters: A sourced fit assessment and verified contact status make outreach selective rather than treating every digital signal as demand.

activities.name: Identify missed solution-area opportunities
activities.description: Use sales signals to identify solution-area opportunities the SSP may be missing.
activities.prompt: For [solution area] across [active account list or territory scope], identify opportunity signals I may be missing. Show the source signal, likely customer need, possible relevant FY27 Conversation or solution context, clearly labeled as a hypothesis unless customer-confirmed, uncertainty, and the next discovery action. Separate facts from recommendations. State the coverage and gaps in the available evidence. Prioritize hypotheses where supported relevance and timing allow comparison; explain ties or an unsupported ranking, and say when no hypothesis is supported. Activity alone does not establish demand, qualification or consent. Align Stage 1 follow-up with the AE/account team; do not create or advance records or contact anyone.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked opportunity hypotheses with next discovery actions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides whether a signal represents a real opportunity or activity that resembles one. An opportunity created from a weak signal fills pipeline with something somebody has to explain later.
activities.requiredContext: SSP scope; solution area; available MSX and approved customer signals.
activities.whyThisMatters: Unnamed solution opportunities never get an owner.

agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. activities.name: Draft the first contact for the top-priority lead
activities.description: Turn the top-ranked lead into a specific, short first message that connects the signal to a reason for the customer to respond.
activities.prompt: Here is the top lead from my follow-up plan: [the top lead's source signal, account, role and recorded prior interaction]. Draft a first contact message under 100 words that references the specific signal, states one evidence-supported reason this is relevant to their business now, or frames relevance as a respectful question when it is unknown, and asks for one small next step. Give me two versions: one for a business decision maker and one for a technical decision maker. Do not claim knowledge of their environment we do not have, and do not assert a product feature I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: Two short first-contact drafts, one business and one technical, tied to the originating signal.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms consent and outreach appropriateness, verifies every factual statement about the customer, and owns the wording before sending.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized lead plan; the source signal; the contact's role; prior interaction history; consent and outreach appropriateness.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the lead's source signal, account, role and contact context.
2. Draft the messages and check consent, facts and tone.
3. Discuss which version gives the recipient a useful reason to respond.
activities.whyThisMatters: A prioritized list that never becomes a message is just a better-sorted backlog.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan

activities.name: Close the loop on what the follow-up produced
activities.description: Review what happened after follow-up and decide which signals are worth testing again.
activities.prompt: Here are the leads I followed up this week and what happened with each: [the leads, source signals, actions and documented responses or confirmed silence]. Tell me which signal sources produced a response and which did not, what the responses have in common, and which two signal types I should prioritize next week. Be direct about small sample size; do not overstate a pattern from a handful of leads. If the sample cannot support a change, say what further evidence is needed rather than forcing a new priority.
activities.expectedOutput: A short evidence-limited read on source signals and a proposed priority change only where supported, otherwise the next check needed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP judges whether the pattern is real or coincidence given the sample size, and owns the decision to change prioritization.
activities.requiredContext: The leads worked this week; the originating signal for each; the action taken; the response or lack of one.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the leads, source signals and documented outcomes.
2. Compare the responses, silences and size of the sample.
3. Discuss whether the evidence supports a priority change or only another check.
activities.whyThisMatters: Lead follow-up improves only if you find out which signals were worth following.

activities.name: Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer
activities.description: Track the outreach you have sent so the follow-ups that matter are surfaced and drafted rather than remembered.
activities.prompt: Review the outreach in [sent-message/account scope] over the last 30 days and identify every message where I asked for something - a meeting, an introduction, a decision, or information - and did not receive a substantive reply. For each one, tell me how long it has been waiting, how important it looks based on the opportunity involved, and draft a short follow-up in my own voice that adds a new reason to respond rather than simply repeating the ask. Do not send anything. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of unanswered asks with elapsed time and a drafted follow-up for each that adds new value rather than repeating.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP reviews and edits every draft before sending, and removes any follow-up where the silence is itself the answer.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your sent messages; your current lead and opportunity list; your team's follow-up cadence norms.
activitySteps: 1. Choose permitted sent-message evidence and run the prompt.
2. Check one unanswered ask and edit its follow-up to add value.
3. Discuss whether another message is useful or the silence should be respected.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most lost specialist opportunities are not rejected - they are dropped. The follow-up that would have converted was never sent because it was never surfaced.

agents.name: Scout
agents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
agents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Lead and account signals are noisy. Focus on turning them into a focused follow-up plan.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritize relevant lead follow-up rather than a general account or deal review.
Distinguish source signals, inferred interest and confirmed customer intent; keep uncertain or out-of-scope context explicit.
Keep suggested messages and owners provisional, and check contact history and consent before any outreach.
discussionQuestions: Which lead or signal deserves attention first? What evidence makes it real? Who owns the next action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build a prioritized lead follow-up plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from noisy signals to one prioritized follow-up plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Lead prioritization matters when credible demand leads to appropriate, consent-aware follow-up. Activity or a high AI ranking alone does not establish customer intent. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Which signal supports relevance to the selected solution area, and what is only inferred?
What may be stale or outside the intended scope?
Who is the known or proposed follow-up owner, and what should be checked before any outreach?
listenFor: Undifferentiated lead lists, vague ownership, weak message fit, and missing consent/context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a three-lead ranking: source signal, customer relevance, missing context/permission, known or proposed follow-up owner and next question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which signal warrants a customer action rather than just a new record, and what evidence would disprove the opportunity?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore whether a priority lead warrants first contact and adapt a possible follow-up. Contact is not a huddle assignment; any outreach still needs appropriate permission and human judgment. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized lead signal and whether the reviewed follow-up clarified interest or avoided a poor contact; no sent message is required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An attendee engaged with a solution-area event, but there is little evidence of a current need. Compare the source signal and known interaction context, distinguish interest from inference, and choose a useful follow-up question without assuming consent or accepted ownership.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Lead follow-up tests a digital or conversation signal against qualification evidence before pursuit effort is prioritized. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example's lead or attendee context and selected solution area. Note what supports relevance, whether timing changes the interpretation, and which questions remain.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A contact or interest signal is not confirmed customer intent. Look for a prioritized follow-up question and a known owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a contact or interest signal is not confirmed customer intent. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a contact or interest signal is not confirmed customer intent. Manager support can help the team resolve lead ownership without rewarding volume over qualification.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Align on a useful follow-up question, not a requirement to create pipeline; keep contact history and customer intent in view.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a contact or interest signal is not confirmed customer intent; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help the team resolve lead ownership without rewarding volume over qualification? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM
roles.description: Leads partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executive stakeholders and governance around growth priorities. Coordinates partner growth and co-sell efforts, drives course correction through business reviews, and brings technical, sales, and marketing owners together while reserving investment and commercial commitments for authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. Coaches partner sellers and inspects renewal and consumption-commitment opportunities, avoiding duplicate pipeline attribution while keeping customer decisions with account teams and partner records and economics with partners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)
roles.description: A leadership audience focused on strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies. Brings attention to issues requiring strategic intervention and communicates decisions and direction, with action and escalation shaped by each participant's applicable authority rather than a shared management remit.
roles.descriptionSummary: A leadership audience for strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Manages USPSI account priorities, opportunities, forecasts, renewals, and expansion. Inspects pipeline using only certified records and minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or user-supplied excerpts, with source, scope, as-of/freshness dates, and human verification; coordinates account teams while retaining technical, policy, and approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages USPSI accounts and pipeline using certified records and approved, human-verified evidence.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Advances USPSI solution-area prospecting, discovery, proof, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances USPSI solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and decisions using approved evidence.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates USPSI outcome-based success plans, milestones, and accepted owners using approved health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder evidence. Aligns executives and teams, supports adoption and growth planning, and manages delivery risks within organizational requirements while retaining technical architecture approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates USPSI success plans, adoption, milestones, and delivery risks using approved evidence.
