activities.name: Build the outcome-led solution plan
activities.description: Build an outcome-led solution plan from customer priorities, discovery evidence and the customer-specific value assessment; connect relevant FY27 Conversations to solution scope, proof, owners, decisions and gaps, using program, Consumption Plan and Adoption Plan inputs only where supported.
activities.prompt: For [Customer/Account], draft an outcome-led solution plan from [customer priorities and discovery evidence]. Connect supported FY27 Conversations to use cases, workloads and the proof needed for the next decision. Include stakeholders, maturity, solution vision, value narrative, demo/workshop sequence, risks and a 30-day next-decision plan. Separate confirmed needs from assumptions; use program, Consumption Plan or Adoption Plan inputs only where evidenced. Ask about material gaps and leave owner acceptance unconfirmed.
activities.expectedOutput: Outcome-led solution plan separating confirmed needs from assumptions, with relevant FY27 Conversation context where supported, solution scope, customer-specific value, evidence-backed program/Consumption/Adoption Plan inputs, next decisions, proposed owners, proof needs and evidence gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP confirms the plan follows the customer decision and that program and consumption/adoption inputs are supported; unconfirmed dates or commitments stay flagged.
activities.requiredContext: Account; customer-stated priorities and discovery evidence; relevant FY27 Conversation context where established; solution scope; current stage; known stakeholders; approved evidence; what the customer said the problem is. Supply relevant program/Consumption/Adoption Plan inputs if applicable, and flag unavailable ones.
activities.whyThisMatters: The solution plan should connect customer priorities to the scope and proof that clear their next decision, not add activity disconnected from their problem.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

resources.title: Sales Agent on mobile
resources.description: Announcement and prompt starters for Sales Agent on mobile, available through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app and in Teams and Outlook. Covers pre-meeting account summaries, fast pipeline lookups, and updating MSX from the field behind a confirmation card. Current as of August 2026.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Pressure-test the solution strategy
activities.description: Test the plan against customer priorities, competitive alternatives, stakeholders, and decision criteria.
activities.prompt: Review [the outcome-led solution plan and permitted supporting evidence] against customer priorities, competitive alternatives, stakeholder coverage, proof needs, technical/commercial dependencies and decision criteria. Cite material findings, separating customer-confirmed evidence from assumptions and proposed actions. Use authoritative public evidence for product/competitor claims where relevant; flag conflicts and material evidence gaps. Return consequential risks, gaps and next decisions without rewriting the strategy, inventing customer agreement or assigning unconfirmed stakeholders.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidence-linked review of the existing solution strategy, with consequential risks, gaps and next decisions; not an authored replacement strategy.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides which of the plan's weaknesses are worth acting on. A pressure test surfaces more gaps than a pursuit can close, and choosing among them is a judgment about this customer's priorities.
activities.requiredContext: Draft outcome-led solution plan; customer context; stakeholder map; proof and constraints.
activities.whyThisMatters: If the solution strategy will fail, it should fail in review before it fails with the customer.

keyBenefits: Produces source-cited research reports rather than unattributed summaries, combining work content and web research across multiple steps so claims can be traced.

activities.name: Map who actually decides and who is missing
activities.description: Build the real decision map for this solution scope, including the people who can stop it, not only the people who like it.
activities.prompt: Using [solution plan and stakeholder list with evidenced roles/engagement], map who influences, decides and funds the customer decision. Use the plan’s scope, organizational model and governance constraints. Flag missing stakeholders, assumptions about authority and the next validation question; ask only about gaps that would change the map. Don’t treat participation as decision authority.
activities.expectedOutput: A decision map separating stakeholder-stated criteria from hypotheses and confirmation questions, with missing functions supported by the supplied context and the risk each gap creates.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP validates the stakeholder reality against what the account team actually knows, and owns the plan to reach anyone missing.
activities.requiredContext: Solution-selling plan; stakeholders engaged with roles; the solution scope and decision type; the customer's organizational model; known procurement and technical governance constraints; who owns the customer relationship.
activitySteps: 1. List stakeholders engaged so far with role and engagement level.
2. Gather the solution scope, decision type, customer organizational model, and governance constraints.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Identify the highest-risk absence.
5. Decide who introduces you to that person and by when.
activities.whyThisMatters: Solution plans usually fail on a person nobody engaged, not on a fact nobody knew.

activities.name: Convert the plan into dated commitments
activities.description: Reduce the plan to the few actions that will actually happen in the next 30 days, each with a named owner and a date.
activities.prompt: From only [the pressure-tested outcome-led solution plan, named account-team roles and availability], draft the next-30-day actions needed to clear [the next customer decision and timing]. For each, show action, named or recorded owner role, evidenced due date and what it unblocks; distinguish accepted commitments from proposed assignments/dates and flag unknowns. Limit the plan to five actions. If more than five are critical, show the capacity/timing evidence for what is not realistic and the tradeoff I must decide; do not silently drop required controls or force a cut unsupported by evidence. Do not assign unnamed people/teams, make commitments or update the opportunity.
activities.expectedOutput: Five or fewer dated actions with named owners and what each unblocks.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms each owner has actually agreed to the action and the date, rather than being assigned it in a document.
activities.requiredContext: The pressure-tested outcome-led solution plan; the account team and their availability; the next customer decision and its timing.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the pressure-tested plan.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut to five or fewer.
4. Confirm each owner has agreed.
5. Record the dates where the account team will see them.
activities.whyThisMatters: A plan without dates and owners is a description of intentions.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A outcome-led solution plan is useful only if it changes pursuit execution. Focus on building a plan that can be worked.
keyTalkingPoints: Plan around customer-stated outcome, discovery evidence, relevant FY27 Conversation context and solution scope, stakeholders, proof needs, demo or workshop sequence, and next decision.
discussionQuestions: Which solution pursuit needs a clearer plan? What proof or stakeholder coverage is missing?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the outcome-led solution plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from plan structure to one active pursuit. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Map who actually decides and who is missing', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Outcome-led solution plans should expose who decides, what proof matters and where engagement is missing. A stakeholder map is a hypothesis until the account team or customer confirms it. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: What next customer decision makes this pursuit worth specialist time? Where does the plan lack a stakeholder, proof path or dated commitment? What planning check from a colleague would expose that gap earlier?
listenFor: Generic solution plans, missing stakeholder coverage, unclear proof path, and no 30-day plan.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one solution-pursuit plan slice: next decision, stakeholder coverage, minimum proof, dependency, owner and dated action. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could check the decision map for a live pursuit and validate a missing stakeholder or proof requirement with the account owner before outreach. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized decision-maker or proof gap checked and whether it improved the pursuit plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A solution plan lists activities but omits the proof needed for its next customer decision. Review one gap and the stakeholder contribution that could resolve it.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A solution plan links customer outcomes and decisions to the proof and stakeholder contributions the pursuit needs. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the customer outcome and proof gap in the example solution plan.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A populated plan can still lack a customer decision or stakeholder coverage. Look for an outcome-linked plan change with a named validation need.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a populated plan can still lack a customer decision or stakeholder coverage. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

SSP-PLAN.keyTakeaway: Make trade-offs explicit: choose what to advance, defer, or route, and name who owns the next decision.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a populated plan can still lack a customer decision or stakeholder coverage. Manager support can remove a proof or stakeholder coordination obstacle rather than ask for a parallel plan.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help focus on the plan change that would support a real customer decision; do not treat listed activity as stakeholder coverage.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a populated plan can still lack a customer decision or stakeholder coverage; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to remove a proof or stakeholder coordination obstacle rather than ask for a parallel plan? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

SSP-VALUE.roleTopicDescription: Translate the solution into the customer's own priorities, evidence, caveats, and next ask.
SSP-VALUE.wiifm:
A value case grounded in the customer's own work gives champions a more credible basis for internal discussion than generic benefits or unsupported outcome figures.
Microsoft Customer Zero can supply relevant departmental experience for a value discussion; it is not a customer-specific ROI promise.
SSP-VALUE.name: Prove and Communicate Customer Value
SSP-VALUE.description: Connect delivered work to customer-recognized outcomes using appropriately sourced evidence, contribution limits, and a clear audience and decision.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. Supports covered consumption portfolios through milestone readiness, partner and scale-engine handoffs, targeted adoption and technical interventions, attributed value evidence, and expansion hypotheses without assuming blanket customer or partner-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports covered SME&C consumption portfolios with readiness, handoffs, and targeted interventions.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PDM
roles.description: Leads partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executive stakeholders and governance around growth priorities. Coordinates partner growth and co-sell efforts, drives course correction through business reviews, and brings technical, sales, and marketing owners together while reserving investment and commercial commitments for authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: PDM-R
roles.description: Develops a recruitment portfolio from qualification and partnership development through launch, a first transactable listing, and early wins. Mobilizes technical specialists, coordinates validated readiness, and prepares graduation handoffs accepted by accountable owners, with program approvals and graduation criteria retained by authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Recruits EPS partners from qualification to launch, first transactable listings, and early wins.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. Coaches partner sellers and inspects renewal and consumption-commitment opportunities, avoiding duplicate pipeline attribution while keeping customer decisions with account teams and partner records and economics with partners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)
roles.description: A leadership audience focused on strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies. Brings attention to issues requiring strategic intervention and communicates decisions and direction, with action and escalation shaped by each participant's applicable authority rather than a shared management remit.
roles.descriptionSummary: A leadership audience for strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Manages USPSI account priorities, opportunities, forecasts, renewals, and expansion. Inspects pipeline using only certified records and minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or user-supplied excerpts, with source, scope, as-of/freshness dates, and human verification; coordinates account teams while retaining technical, policy, and approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages USPSI accounts and pipeline using certified records and approved, human-verified evidence.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Advances USPSI solution-area prospecting, discovery, proof, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances USPSI solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and decisions using approved evidence.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates USPSI outcome-based success plans, milestones, and accepted owners using approved health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder evidence. Aligns executives and teams, supports adoption and growth planning, and manages delivery risks within organizational requirements while retaining technical architecture approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates USPSI success plans, adoption, milestones, and delivery risks using approved evidence.

SSP-VALUE.whyItMatters: Credible value evidence supports better customer, renewal, and investment decisions without overstating causal impact.
SSP-VALUE.desiredOutcome: Explain solution value in terms customers can recognize and relay, distinguishing applicable evidence from assumptions and removing claims that cannot withstand scrutiny.

activities.prompt: Research [the customer/industry/use-case value-story context] for the stated customer outcome and solution scope. Use customer primary public sources for public customer signals, credible market/comparable-use-case evidence and relevant work evidence for customer-specific priorities or results. Identify relevant proof, risks and counterevidence, citing material claims. Separate facts, inference and proposed value arguments; flag unsupported value/competitor claims and material conflicts or staleness. Comparable outcomes are context, not proof this customer will realize the same value. Keep private account details out of public queries. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Evidence brief for the value narrative.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides which research applies to this customer. Industry evidence describes a population, and this customer may be the case that does not fit it.
activities.requiredContext: Customer; industry; use case; customer outcome and solution scope; relevant FY27 Conversation context where useful; approved source boundaries.

activities.name: Stress-test the assumptions the value claims depend on
activities.description: Expose what each outcome number quietly assumes, and record which assumptions the customer would have to accept.
activities.prompt: Review [value narrative and evidence brief]. For each outcome claim, show its key assumption, who must accept it, available evidence and what happens if adoption is half as fast as projected. Treat the half-as-fast case as an illustrative sensitivity, not a prediction. Quantify it only where the supplied adoption model, horizon, baselines, units and benefit relationship support the calculation; otherwise explain the qualitative risk and missing evidence. Do not assume half speed means double duration or half benefit. Rank claims by vulnerability to failed assumptions where comparison is supported, otherwise state the uncertainty. Don’t add claims or evidence absent from the material.
activities.expectedOutput: An assumption and risk table ranked by how much each claim depends on an unproven assumption.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP decides which assumptions are defensible with this customer, and owns every outcome figure before it reaches them.
activities.requiredContext: The value narrative; the evidence brief; the customer's financial context; adoption expectations already discussed with them.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value narrative and evidence brief.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Find the claim that collapses hardest.
4. Either find proof for its assumption or remove the claim.
5. Discuss the assumption table produced in this practice and the claim that still needs evidence, or record that review question for the normal pursuit workflow.
activities.whyThisMatters: The value claim you cannot defend is the one the customer will ask about.

activitySteps: 1. Bring the rehearsed narrative with weak claims removed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The conversation happens before the story is finished. Focus on turning what you heard into a customer-specific narrative the account would recognize.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer defines value. Use sourced evidence, caveats, use cases, and a clear next ask.
discussionQuestions: What customer priority does this solution map to? Which claim is supported, assumed, or missing evidence?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Tailor the solution value narrative'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from what the customer told you to the value logic and the proof it needs. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the assumptions the value claims depend on', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Customer-specific value depends on defensible assumptions and customer-stated priorities. Removing an unsupported claim can improve trust more than polishing the narrative. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Which customer-stated priority anchors the value claim? What source and assumption support it, and what remains unproved? How would a peer challenge the claim before it reaches the customer?
listenFor: Generic value claims, unsupported ROI, customer priorities inferred rather than sourced, and missing caveats.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one value-claim strip: customer-stated priority, proposed benefit, supplied evidence, assumption, caveat and validation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which outcome can you substantiate for this audience, and what claim or next action still needs validation?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could test the assumptions behind one value claim, and remove any claim you cannot defend. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized claim qualified, retained or dropped and whether checking it made the value story more credible. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A draft value story makes a broad benefit claim that the approved conversation excerpt does not establish. Qualify the claim and identify a useful validation question.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A solution value narrative connects a customer outcome to evidence while making assumptions and validation needs visible. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Compare the approved customer excerpt with the example's caveated value claim.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A persuasive value statement is not validated customer value. Look for a sourced claim separated from its assumption and missing evidence.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a persuasive value statement is not validated customer value. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a persuasive value statement is not validated customer value. Manager support can reinforce honest claim qualification in the next pursuit conversation.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Invite challenge to a persuasive but unsupported benefit claim; keep customer validation distinct from an internally agreed narrative.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

activities.name: Rehearse solution discovery and objection handling
activities.description: Rehearse the solution conversation and receive coaching before customer use.
activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the upcoming meeting type with the customer or stakeholder. Use [paste/describe the approved fictional or de-identified solution conversation plan] and focus on solution discovery, differentiation, proof points, likely objections, next solution decision, and primary ask. Pause for the team member response, then coach clarity, evidence, listening, and next step. Do not invent customer facts or commitments. Keep responses fictional; this is rehearsal, not a customer interaction.
activities.expectedOutput: Interactive role-play, targeted coaching, objections, and improvement list.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP validates facts, claims, commitments, guidance, and decides what to change before customer use.
activities.requiredContext: Approved conversation plan; meeting type; customer context; desired outcome.
activities.whyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing is cheaper than improvising in the room.

activities.name: Find the discovery gap before the meeting, not after
activities.description: Check what you still do not know that would change your recommendation, and build the question that closes it.
activities.prompt: Here is what we currently know about [Customer/Account] for the relevant customer priorities and solution scope: [the known priorities, environment, stakeholders, constraints and prior notes]. Identify what we do not know that would materially change our recommendation, ranked by how much it would change it. For the top three unknowns, write one open question each that could be asked naturally in the upcoming conversation without sounding like a survey. Distinguish what we actually know from what we have assumed. Do not invent unknowns or questions to fill the three-question exercise; if fewer or none are material, state that and explain where the evidence does not support a ranking.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of decision-changing unknowns and three natural questions to close the top ones. If fewer than three material unknowns are supported, make that explicit rather than manufacturing questions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies which items are genuinely known versus assumed by the account team, and chooses which question is worth the meeting time.
activities.requiredContext: Relevant known account and solution context; prior conversation notes; the recommendation you intend to make.
activitySteps: 1. Assemble what is known about the account.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Separate known from assumed.
4. Choose one question to definitely ask.
5. Add it to the conversation plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: The most expensive assumptions are the ones nobody noticed they were making.

activities.name: Turn the conversation into decisions and commitments
activities.description: Convert meeting notes into what changed, what was agreed, and what the customer actually committed to.
activities.prompt: Here are my notes from the customer conversation: [the conversation notes or transcript summary]. Produce three separate lists: what we learned that changes our understanding, what was explicitly agreed and by whom, and what remains open. Then draft a short follow-up note to the customer confirming only what was actually agreed. Do not record something as agreed if the notes only show it was discussed. Flag anything ambiguous rather than resolving it.
activities.expectedOutput: Separated lists of learnings, agreements, and open items, plus a short confirming follow-up note.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Check that each agreement is supported by the meeting notes and confirm the follow-up wording. A draft does not update the customer record.
activities.requiredContext: Meeting notes or transcript summary; who attended; what was asked for; the conversation plan you went in with.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the conversation notes and run the prompt.
2. Check the agreed list against what was actually said and edit the follow-up draft.
3. Discuss any ambiguity before deciding what to use.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deals slip on the gap between what was discussed and what was agreed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A solution conversation moves a customer decision when the evidence addresses a real concern. Focus on the ask, the likely objection and what still needs validation.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Link the conversation to a specific customer decision rather than a list of solution features.
2. Use approved proof points and distinguish a confirmed customer concern from an assumption.
3. Test a primary and fallback ask in rehearsal; a role-play response is not customer agreement.
discussionQuestions: What decision should this conversation advance? What objection is most likely? What proof will you use?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prepare the solution-specific customer conversation'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from preparation to rehearsal or next customer ask. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find the discovery gap before the meeting, not after', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Solution conversations should resolve the unknown most likely to change the recommendation. Use proof and rehearsal to improve the question, not manufacture customer commitment. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
facilitatorQuestions: What decision and fallback ask should this meeting advance? Which objection would expose a gap in discovery? What did a peer change after rehearsing a similar customer conversation?
listenFor: Meetings framed around content rather than customer decision, objections first discovered live, and unclear ask.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a short customer rehearsal: intended decision, discovery question, likely objection, evidence-qualified reply and fallback ask. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Rehearse with a peer; if alone, write both sides and mark the exchange untested, not a validated customer or coaching response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence would make this customer conversation credible, and what decision or question still belongs to a person?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore the unknown most likely to change your recommendation and adapt a discovery question, without arranging or completing a customer conversation. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized discovery question and what its answer changed, or what remains unknown; note whether the conversation became more focused. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A solution conversation has a clear product story but an unresolved customer objection. Rehearse a decision ask with supplied proof, labeling all simulated reactions as rehearsal.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Solution conversations combine discovery, proof and objection handling around a customer decision. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the decision ask, supplied proof and likely objection in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Role-play does not establish a customer's actual response. Look for a revised ask or proof point that survives a grounded objection.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: role-play does not establish a customer's actual response. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when role-play does not establish a customer's actual response. Manager support can support the next customer validation without scoring the seller's rehearsal.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which objection is useful to explore; keep simulated reactions separate from what the customer actually said or agreed.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that role-play does not establish a customer's actual response; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the next customer validation without scoring the seller's rehearsal? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM
roles.description: Leads partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executive stakeholders and governance around growth priorities. Coordinates partner growth and co-sell efforts, drives course correction through business reviews, and brings technical, sales, and marketing owners together while reserving investment and commercial commitments for authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)
roles.description: A leadership audience focused on strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies. Brings attention to issues requiring strategic intervention and communicates decisions and direction, with action and escalation shaped by each participant's applicable authority rather than a shared management remit.
roles.descriptionSummary: A leadership audience for strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies.

Inspects pipeline using only certified records and minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or user-supplied excerpts, with source, scope, as-of/freshness dates, and human verification; coordinates account teams while retaining technical, policy, and approval owners.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Advances USPSI solution-area prospecting, discovery, proof, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances USPSI solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and decisions using approved evidence.

Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries through authoritative sources and approved handling, coordinating decision narratives, approvals, and execution without assuming policy, exception, legal, or compliance approval authority.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for a quick single answer that Copilot would handle in the app you are already in, and do not use it for a multi-step task you want done once and handed back, which is Cowork. It sees the same Microsoft 365 content under the same permissions as the others, so reaching for it does not get you more access. Do not use it to bypass a human checkpoint because it can run unattended; anything it produces while running on its own still needs the same review.
stepsToGetStarted: Go to aka.ms/m, the internal Scout hub. Request the access package, complete the agreement, download and install Scout, then sign in with Microsoft 365 and GitHub as instructed. Start with a business outcome rather than a tool command.

activities.name: Build the specialist, technical, partner, and funding plan
activities.description: Clarify role coverage, dependencies, asks, owners, partner/funding needs, and decision checkpoints.
activities.prompt: Using the opportunity brief, confirmed roles, partner criteria, funding context and constraints I am supplying, create a pursuit orchestration plan for the opportunity with customer outcome, solution scope, required specialist and technical roles, partner need, funding consideration, dependencies, owner for each action, decision checkpoints, and unresolved risks. For each action, state which customer outcome it moves, directly or through a required dependency; drop actions that move none, but do not drop required controls merely because their contribution is indirect. Do not represent funding as approved. Preserve recorded owners and distinguish accepted work from proposed assignments. Mark unknown funding/request authority or partner availability explicitly; do not submit funding requests, assign work or update pursuit records.
activities.expectedOutput: Pursuit orchestration plan with owners and checkpoints, where every action names the customer outcome it supports directly or through a required dependency, required controls are preserved, and actions supporting no outcome have been dropped.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides who genuinely needs to be on the v-team. Every added role dilutes accountability, and an oversized v-team is usually a sign that nobody owns the outcome.
activities.requiredContext: Approved opportunity, customer context, roles, partner criteria, funding context, and constraints.
activities.whyThisMatters: Pursuits stall when handoffs, partner asks, or funding dependencies are assumed rather than owned.

activities.name: Make each ask specific enough to be accepted
activities.description: Turn a role requirement into an ask a busy colleague can say yes to without a meeting to clarify it.
activities.prompt: From [the pursuit orchestration plan], write the individual ask for each role involved. Each ask must state: what specifically is needed, why this pursuit needs that role rather than someone else, what the person receives from me to make it easy, the date it is needed by, and how long it should take. Keep each ask under 80 words. Do not represent funding, approvals, or customer commitments as secured if the plan does not show them as secured.
activities.expectedOutput: One short, specific, dated ask per role, ready to send.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies that no ask overstates funding, approval, or customer commitment status, and owns what is promised in return.
activities.requiredContext: The pursuit orchestration plan; the roles required; what you can supply to each; the customer timeline.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the pursuit plan and draft the role-specific asks.
2. Check each ask's purpose, time needed and promised support.
3. Discuss whether the recipient could accept it; keep acceptance unconfirmed until evidenced.
activities.whyThisMatters: A vague ask gets a polite yes and no calendar time.

activities.name: Catch the checkpoint that quietly slipped
activities.description: Compare the plan against what has actually happened and surface the dependency nobody has mentioned in two weeks.
activities.prompt: Here is [paste or attach the pursuit plan with checkpoints and owners], and here is what has actually happened since [paste or attach the dated updates, meeting notes or status evidence]. Identify every checkpoint that has passed without evidence of completion, every dependency that has gone quiet, and every owner who has not confirmed. Rank by impact on the customer timeline. For the top item, draft the one message that would restart it. Do not assume something is complete because it was not mentioned.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled checkpoints and quiet dependencies, plus one message to restart the highest-impact item.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms an item is genuinely stalled rather than simply undocumented before escalating to an owner.
activities.requiredContext: The orchestration plan with checkpoints and owners, written down even if only informally; recent updates, notes, or status; the customer timeline. If checkpoints and owners do not exist yet, create them before running this activity.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the plan and recent activity. If the plan has no dated checkpoints or owners recorded, write them down first; the activity does not work without them.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Confirm which items are genuinely stalled.
4. Send the restart message for the top one.
5. Reset the checkpoint date.
activities.whyThisMatters: Pursuits rarely stop. They go quiet, and quiet looks like progress until the date arrives.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Pursuits stall at handoffs. Focus on making every role, partner, funding dependency, and checkpoint explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Name the objective, contributors, asks, owners, dates, dependencies, and escalation points.
discussionQuestions: Which handoff is currently assumed rather than owned? Where could partner or funding support change the path?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Bring funding into the pursuit orchestration plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from orchestration principles to one stalled handoff. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Make each ask specific enough to be accepted', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Cross-role orchestration should unblock the customer decision with the smallest necessary accepted contribution. Funding, partner capacity and technical help are not secured merely by requesting them. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which specialist, technical, partner or funding dependency is stalled? What evidence and acceptance does the next owner need? How does a peer make that handoff executable without representing funding as approved?
listenFor: Unnamed owners, handoffs without dates, partner input treated as optional, and funding status overstated.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one specialist/technical/partner/funding handoff row: contribution needed, proposed owner, evidence, acceptance gap and next date. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which handoff is still assumed rather than accepted, and what owner, request, or date would make it actionable?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore the most consequential stalled handoff and draft a bounded, reviewed ask for its contributor; sending it is not required. Do not request work from every role merely to complete the exercise. Receiving-owner acceptance is required before treating any actual handoff as accepted; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized stalled handoff and whether a bounded ask clarified ownership or exposed a gap; no collection of every role request is needed. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A pursuit depends on partner support and a possible investment, but no receiving owner has accepted the handoff. Map the dependency without implying funding approval.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Pursuit orchestration connects specialist, partner and possible funding contributions without assuming they are secured. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the example handoff and its partner or funding dependency.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A coordination plan does not establish partner acceptance or funding. Look for a realistic role-specific ask with an explicit receiving owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a coordination plan does not establish partner acceptance or funding. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Research competitive and industry context
activities.description: Investigate current evidence before positioning.
activities.prompt: Research the competitor and solution area in [the competitive context], within its customer/industry scope and approved public-source boundaries. Compare publicly supportable positions, proof, recent developments, common objections and uncertainty. Use primary competitor/product sources for advertised capabilities and credible industry evidence for market context. Cite material claims; distinguish public facts from positioning inference and flag relevant conflicts or stale evidence. Do not infer confidential competitor information or present market objections as this customer's stated view. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Sourced competitive context brief.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP checks how current the competitive material is. Competitor capability moves quickly, and an out-of-date claim used in front of a customer hands them the advantage.
activities.requiredContext: Competitor; solution area; industry and customer/use-case scope where relevant; approved public-source boundaries and any sanitized background.

activities.name: Build the competitive differentiation brief
activities.description: Use approved win/loss and market context for a proof-backed competitive position.
activities.prompt: Using the approved win/loss report extract, current competitive proof and customer decision context I supply, draft a competitive differentiation brief. Include relevant drivers, up to three customer-relevant differentiators with proof, objection responses, risks and a concise talk track. Cite each claim and source date, separate the report signal from interpretation, and flag weak or missing proof. Do not assume access to MSXI or introduce confidential competitor information.
activities.expectedOutput: Competitive brief with differentiators, proof, objections, and talk track.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides which competitive claims are safe to make. Win-loss material records what was concluded at the time, and a competitor position that has moved since turns a strong brief into an exposed one.
activities.requiredContext: Dated authorized win/loss extract; current approved positioning/proof; customer decision criteria.
activities.whyThisMatters: Competitive conversations are lost by improvisation.

activities.name: Test the differentiator against the customer's real decision criteria
activities.description: Pressure-test each claimed differentiator against what this customer actually said they will decide on, and drop the ones that do not connect.
activities.prompt: You are helping a specialist seller sharpen a competitive position. Here is the customer's stated decision criteria and evaluation process: [the customer-stated criteria, evaluation team and timeline]. Here are the differentiators we plan to lead with: [the proposed differentiators and approved proof]. For each differentiator, state which specific decision criterion it addresses, how directly it addresses it, and what proof the customer would need to accept it. Identify any differentiator that does not map to a stated criterion and recommend dropping or reframing it. Flag any criterion we currently have no answer for. Do not add differentiators that are not in my list.
activities.expectedOutput: A shortened differentiator list mapped to decision criteria, plus a named list of criteria with no current answer.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms the decision criteria are what the customer actually said rather than what the team assumes, and owns the decision to drop a differentiator.
activities.requiredContext: Customer decision criteria and evaluation process; current differentiators and supporting proof; who is on the evaluation team.
activitySteps: 1. Gather the customer's stated decision criteria from meeting notes or MSX.
2. List current differentiators and their proof.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Cut differentiators that do not map to a criterion.
5. Name the gaps you cannot yet answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: A differentiator the customer is not deciding on is noise, however true it is.

activities.name: Rehearse the competitive conversation and build the objection handler
activities.description: Practice the response out loud, then convert what broke into a written objection handler tied to approved proof.
activities.prompt: Role-play a fictional customer technical evaluator who favors [competitor], using [competitive position and approved proof]. Challenge me on price, migration effort and lock-in without softening objections. After three exchanges, draft an objection table with my responses, supporting proof and evidence gaps. Don’t invent proof or treat simulated preferences/reactions as customer facts.
activities.expectedOutput: An objection handler table mapping each objection to a response and the approved proof behind it, with proof gaps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP judges whether the rehearsed language is accurate, appropriate for this customer, and consistent with approved competitive guidance before using it externally.
activities.requiredContext: Competitive position and differentiators; the competitor in play; approved competitive proof sources; known evaluator concerns; customer role you will be speaking to.
activitySteps: 1. Bring an existing approved competitive position/differentiator list and proof, or a permitted rehearsal example.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run a short rehearsal with the agent as the skeptical evaluator.
4. Have it produce the objection handler table.
5. Fill or remove any row where proof is missing.
6. Discuss the objection-handler table produced in this practice, including its unresolved proof gaps; do not require a separately prepared table for attendance.
activities.whyThisMatters: Competitive conversations are lost in the moment, not in the brief.

activities.name: Convert the competitive position into the next customer step
activities.description: Turn the position into a concrete next action in the opportunity rather than a document that stops at the brief.
activities.prompt: Using [the competitive position and customer-stated decision criteria], propose the single next step that would most reduce competitive risk in this opportunity. Give me three options ranked by impact, each with: what it is, who from our side needs to be involved, what the customer gets out of it, and what evidence it would generate for the decision. Then draft the short note I would send to the customer to set it up. Keep the note under 120 words and do not overstate what we have proven.
activities.expectedOutput: One chosen next step with owner and purpose, and a short customer-ready note to set it up.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP owns the choice of next step and the customer-facing wording, and confirms it fits the account team's plan before sending.
activities.requiredContext: Tested competitive position/differentiators and open proof gaps; customer-stated decision criteria; opportunity stage/close plan; known relationship owner and available contributors.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the differentiator list tested in the earlier practice and its open gaps, or a permitted tested example arranged by the facilitator. If neither exists, pause this dependent step rather than assign advance testing to Team Members.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Pick one next step.
4. Adjust the draft note in your own voice.
5. Record the next step in the opportunity.
activities.whyThisMatters: A competitive brief that does not change the next customer interaction has not changed the deal.

activities.name: Build a reusable objection and language library from real calls
activities.description: Mine your own customer conversations for the objections and language that keep recurring, and turn them into something the team can reuse.
activities.prompt: Review [last-quarter meeting transcripts and mail] for [solution area]. Group recurring objections, customer language, competitor claims and stalled conversations by frequency. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Competitive response should be built on customer context and proof, not generic battlecards.
keyTalkingPoints: Use current approved competitive evidence, win/loss context, differentiators, objections, risks, and review flags.
discussionQuestions: Which competitor or alternative is shaping the decision? What proof is strongest and where is it weak?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the competitive differentiation brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from competitor context to one proof-backed response plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test the differentiator against the customer's real decision criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Competitive responses are credible when current approved proof addresses the customer decision criterion. Objection handlers are not permission for unsupported competitor claims. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which competitive claim changes the customer decision, and which dated source supports it? What would make it inapplicable here? How has a colleague tested differentiation against the customer's actual criteria?
listenFor: Stale battlecard claims, unsupported competitor statements, and differentiators not tied to customer priorities.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one competitive response row: customer criterion, proposed differentiator, dated source or unknown, applicability caveat and validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which customer criterion does approved competitive proof address, and what claim should you qualify or avoid?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could adapt an objection handler tied to approved proof and consider where it might help; using it in a live conversation is not required. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized objection and whether approved proof answered it, required a caveat or showed a need for discovery. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A competitor is favored on one customer criterion, while the response relies on a generic claim. Check the approved evidence and retain the limitation if proof is weak.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Competitive differentiation depends on current proof against this customer's criteria, not a generic competitor claim. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the customer criterion and approved competitive evidence in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A competitor assertion is not evidence about this customer's decision. Look for a differentiated claim qualified by its proof and weakest gap.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a competitor assertion is not evidence about this customer's decision. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a competitor assertion is not evidence about this customer's decision. Manager support can support access to approved competitive expertise without inventing customer preference.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help the facilitator keep attention on the customer's decision and evidence limits rather than winning an internal product comparison.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a competitor assertion is not evidence about this customer's decision; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support access to approved competitive expertise without inventing customer preference?
