activities.name: Inspect solution opportunity readiness
activities.description: Identify the decision or blocker preventing progression.
activities.prompt: For Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID], assess readiness for the next customer decision within its evidenced outcome and solution scope. Show recorded stage, stakeholder coverage, proof/demo results, technical/commercial dependencies, partner or funding needs and blockers, citing current sources. Separate recorded status from confirmed customer intent and inferred readiness. Name the single next decision, action and recorded owner or owner role to confirm; turn missing evidence into a question. Do not advance stage, forecast or commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Readiness view with blockers, next decision, actions, and owners.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP judges whether the stage reflects reality. A stage is what somebody recorded, usually optimistically, and the gap between the recorded stage and the real one is the entire point of the inspection.
activities.requiredContext: Opportunity ID; customer outcome and solution scope; relevant FY27 Conversation context if established; current sales context.
activities.whyThisMatters: Readiness inspection is judgment work. The agent proposes; the SSP stays accountable.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Create the solution acceleration action plan
activities.description: Turn enabled opportunity data into prioritized actions.
activities.prompt: In [Report Name], for [solution-area opportunity/portfolio scope] during [review period], prioritize milestone or timing signals using available status and movement measures. Cite the relevant visual, filters and comparison dates. Draft proposed next actions and SSP validation questions; flag missing stakeholder evidence, owners and capacity rather than infer intent, causes or commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Proposed solution-opportunity action plan tied to sourced milestone/timing signals, with gaps and validation questions. Recorded or supplied owners and capacity remain subject to SSP confirmation; no milestone, forecast or customer commitment is changed. Missing report access or movement measures remain gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides which intervention is realistic this week. A plan built from the record proposes what should happen rather than what the account team has capacity to do, and an unrealistic plan quietly becomes no plan.
activities.requiredContext: Report name; permitted solution-area opportunity/portfolio scope and filters; review period and comparison baseline; available milestone, status and timing measures; any confirmed owners and capacity constraints.
activitySteps: 1. Check the right report/view, permitted scope, period, relevant visual and measure definitions, including any comparison baseline.
2. In the available report Copilot Pane, ask the concise business question using the visual's titles and report terms.
3. Compare the answer with the report metrics. Inspect missing measures or unsupported conclusions, and refine the question if needed; optional book prompts can help.
activities.whyThisMatters: The path advances when blockers, owners, and next decisions are explicit.

activities.name: Prepare the conversation that clears the next decision
activities.description: Design the single conversation that would unblock the opportunity, and decide who needs to be in it.
activities.prompt: For the opportunity, the next decision required is [the next customer decision] and the current blocker is [the current blocker and opportunity context]. Design the one conversation that would most likely clear it: who needs to be in the room from both sides, what each person needs to hear, what we must bring as evidence, what we are asking them to decide by the end, and what we do if they say not yet. Keep it to one conversation; do not propose a sequence of three meetings.
activities.expectedOutput: A single conversation design with attendees, evidence needed, the decision being asked for, and a fallback.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP validates that the named blocker is the real one, confirms attendees with the account team, and owns what is asked of the customer.
activities.requiredContext: The readiness view; the next decision required; the current blocker; stakeholder coverage; available evidence and proof.
activitySteps: 1. Supply the next customer decision and the evidence for its blocker.
2. Draft the conversation and check the attendees, proof and fallback.
3. Discuss whether this conversation would clear the real blocker.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most stalled opportunities need one specific conversation, not more activity.

activities.name: State the close plan in the customer's terms
activities.description: Confirm which customer commitments and decision milestones are genuinely agreed; return the shared plan with dependencies and unconfirmed items marked for human closure.
activities.prompt: Rewrite this existing internal close plan for one opportunity [the approved internal close plan] as a draft shared plan from the customer's point of view. Use their supplied stated outcome, decision process and confirmed-versus-assumed dates. Replace our sales stages with their decision milestones, name what they need from us and what we need from them, and end with their stated outcome. Remove internal language and forecast terms. Flag unconfirmed steps, dates and dependencies for SSP review; do not turn portfolio priorities into a close plan or invent missing customer agreements.
activities.expectedOutput: Customer-facing decision plan with customer-confirmed commitment, milestones, dependencies, and any unconfirmed items clearly flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP verifies the customer agreement and whether the person can make the commitment, and separates customer-confirmed milestones from internal forecast language before sharing the plan.
activities.requiredContext: An existing internal close plan for one opportunity, approved for use in this practice; the customer's stated outcome and decision process; confirmed dates versus assumed dates. A portfolio action list is not a substitute.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose an opportunity you own and inspect an already-approved internal close plan if authorized, or a permitted plan excerpt arranged by the facilitator. This is not a request to prepare a plan or a portfolio prioritization report; if no appropriate input exists, discuss the gap manually.
2. Paste it into the prompt and supply the customer's stated outcome, decision process and confirmed-versus-assumed dates, then run it.
3. Remove anything still internal.
4. Confirm which dates and steps the customer has actually agreed to and keep the rest marked unconfirmed.
5. Review and approve the customer-safe draft before sharing it through your usual channel and asking the customer to correct it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A close plan the customer has never seen is a forecast, not a plan.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle focuses on the next decision, not the whole deal.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect milestone readiness, stakeholder gaps, proof, blockers, dependencies, partner/funding needs, and owners.

For a chosen MSXI practice, inspect the relevant visual, permitted scope, review period and milestone/movement measures; the action plan stays provisional until the SSP checks owners, capacity and customer evidence.
discussionQuestions: What is the pursuit actually waiting on? What evidence or owner will clear the next decision?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect solution opportunity readiness'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from readiness inspection to a 14- to 30-day action plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Prepare the conversation that clears the next decision', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Opportunity progress means clearing an evidenced customer decision, not just advancing a record. Separate confirmed milestones from assumptions and validate the next conversation with its owner. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next customer decision, rather than the next internal task? Which evidence gap or missing owner prevents it? What would another specialist change in the next 14 to 30 days without promising a close?
listenFor: Close-date language instead of next decision, unowned blockers, missing proof, and unclear stakeholder gaps.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a solution-readiness card with signal, proof gap, proposed next decision and owner question. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal assumption changed when you inspected the evidence, and who owns the next decision or approval?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could draft or rehearse a conversation around the next decision on a stalled opportunity. Any later use must be appropriate and its ask validated with the owner; a meeting or customer result is not required. Verify claims and commercial or approval boundaries with the accountable owner; AI is advisory. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a safe description of the next decision and whether preparing the conversation clarified a blocker; a closed decision is not required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A live pursuit has a milestone but no clear next decision. Compare its evidence and, if that practice is selected, an approved close plan; do not turn assumed dates into commitments.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Pursuit readiness asks what decision is blocked and which evidence or contribution could move it forward. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged solution-opportunity timing example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check opportunity filters, review period and available milestone/status or movement measures in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A favorable readiness summary does not clear the next customer decision. Look for a blocker-linked next step with evidence and an accountable owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a favorable readiness summary does not clear the next customer decision. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

SSP-DEAL.keyTakeaway: Make the next decision and its prerequisites visible before asking customers, partners, or internal teams to act.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a favorable readiness summary does not clear the next customer decision. Manager support can help remove the role or decision bottleneck without taking over the pursuit.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree whether the blocker is useful for peer exploration; distinguish a possible intervention from a new commitment or required close plan. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check opportunity filters, review period and available milestone/status or movement measures; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations without scoring individuals. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check the report/view, relevant visual, scope, period and source basis before one focused question: Which next action follows from a measured signal, and which still needs the SSP to confirm ownership or customer evidence? Narrow a broad query using the visual's terminology; keep consequential judgment with its accountable human owner and do not turn the practice into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help remove the role or decision bottleneck without taking over the pursuit? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Engages early with the opportunity owner to shape executable commercial constructs across Microsoft and partner transaction routes. Navigates negotiation guardrails, coordinates owner-validated policy and licensing questions, routes approvals and exceptions, and hands off approved terms while addressing renewal commercial risk.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes SME&C commercial terms across transaction routes and coordinates approvals and renewals.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. Supports covered consumption portfolios through milestone readiness, partner and scale-engine handoffs, targeted adoption and technical interventions, attributed value evidence, and expansion hypotheses without assuming blanket customer or partner-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports covered SME&C consumption portfolios with readiness, handoffs, and targeted interventions.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. SE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
SE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
SE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

activities.name: Draft the sourced technical answer matrix
activities.description: Answer technical questions with sources, confidence, assumptions, exceptions and reviewer flags. Formal RFPs and questionnaires route to the proposal process instead.
activities.prompt: Answer [the selected technical questions or permitted question-list link] using approved work evidence for customer facts and current official guidance for product claims. Preserve question order. For each item give the answer, material source citations, qualitative evidence status (supported, partial or unknown), assumptions and reviewer/SME flags. Surface material conflicts, stale sources and unsupported areas rather than guessing. If an item belongs to a formal RFP or questionnaire, route the customer-facing response to the proposal process and answer only the underlying technical question. Do not issue policy, security or roadmap approval.
activities.expectedOutput: A technical answer matrix in original question order, with material citations, qualitative evidence status, assumptions and reviewer/SME or proposal-process flags; unsupported answers remain unresolved.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE routes security, legal and product claims to the SMEs who own them. A sourced answer looks authoritative regardless of whether the source was current, and these are the answer types a customer will hold you to.
activities.requiredContext: Selected technical questions; approved sources.
activities.whyThisMatters: A technical answer is safer when confidence, assumptions, and reviewer needs are visible.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical responses move faster when supported answers, assumptions, qualitative evidence status, exceptions and required reviewers are visible.
keyTalkingPoints: Answer with sources and qualitative evidence status, not just fluency.
Preserve unsupported areas instead of smoothing them over.
Use the response package to route review, not to bypass it.
discussionQuestions: Which technical answer needs evidence before it can be used?
Where do we usually hide uncertainty?
Who must review the response before it goes to the customer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft the sourced technical answer matrix'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from answer drafting to response governance and exception routing. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Route unsupported technical answers for review', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Grounded technical responses distinguish sourced answers, uncertainty and claims needing specialist or formal review. A defensible answer matters more than filling every box. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
facilitatorQuestions: Which answer is most consequential?
What source supports it?
Where should the response show confidence, caveat, exception, or SME-needed flag?
What review habit has a peer used to catch an answer that sounded certain but lacked support?
listenFor: Confident but unsourced answers, hidden uncertainty, overbroad commitments, and missing reviewers.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one answer-matrix row: technical question, supplied authoritative source or unavailable, bounded answer or hold, caveat and SME reviewer. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which answer is supported by its source, and which uncertainty belongs with a specialist or formal reviewer?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a technical response for an upcoming conversation: verify a consequential answer, flag source or uncertainty, and route unsupported claims to technical or formal proposal review. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized answer qualified or routed and whether it prevented an unsupported technical claim. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A technical answer sounds confident, but its source does not cover the customer's constraint. Qualify the answer and route the unsupported part to its technical reviewer.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Architecture validation works best when options, criteria, assumptions, and risks are visible before the technical debate starts.
keyTalkingPoints: Compare options against the agreed decision criteria.
Name the assumptions and validation steps, not just the recommended design.
Use AI to assemble evidence and decision records while keeping architecture judgment human.
discussionQuestions: Which architecture assumption would hurt most if wrong?
What criteria will decide between options?
What validation step should happen before the customer sees the recommendation?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Compare architecture options against decision criteria'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from option comparison to creating the architecture decision record. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate architecture evidence and assumptions', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Architecture recommendations should be tested against customer criteria and the limiting constraint. A generated design remains a proposal until validation supports it. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which option should be compared, and against what criteria?
Which assumption needs validation first?
What would make the architecture recommendation unsafe to share?
Which architecture assumption would another SE ask you to test before sharing the recommendation?
listenFor: Unchallenged assumptions, uncited guidance, missing security or operations review, and options that are not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a two-option architecture record: supplied criterion, known constraint, untested assumption, evidence gap, reviewer and deferred choice. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could design one solution and name the constraint that most limits it. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized architecture assumption checked and whether it changed the recommendation or next validation. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: Two architecture options satisfy different customer criteria, and one relies on an untested assumption. Compare the evidence and identify what could change the recommendation.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Architecture comparison weighs feasible options against customer criteria and shows which assumptions could change the recommendation. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the customer criterion and two architecture options in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: An architecture comparison is not validated production readiness. Look for an explicit tradeoff and the evidence that could change the design.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: an architecture comparison is not validated production readiness. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.prompt: Create a demo or workshop package for the customer decision using the approved scenario and context I supply. Include audience, decision criteria, agenda, demo flow, sample data needs, roles, likely objections, tenant or permission dependencies, fallback plan and explicit next decision. List what must be built or configured first. Use only the supplied run results or logs to identify portions actually run end to end, with their test date, environment and result. Where evidence is absent, mark execution status or date unknown and name the verification needed. A plan is not evidence that a demo has run.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE chooses the appropriate workshop/demo/whiteboard/prototype format and validates technical evidence and limitations in the intended environment; a generated plan or unknown test status is not proof of readiness.
activities.requiredContext: Customer decision; audience; approved scenario; available run logs or test results with test date and environment. If execution evidence is unavailable, say so and keep the affected testing status unknown.
activities.whyThisMatters: A decision-centered plan keeps the demo or workshop from becoming a feature tour.

activities.whyThisMatters: Authoritative proof and known limitations are what make the demo safe to use in a customer decision.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A demo or workshop earns its place when it tests a customer decision. Focus on the scenario and evidence that would change that decision, not the breadth of the product tour.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Name the customer question and the criterion the experience must test.
2. Keep evidence, environment constraints, roles and fallback conditions explicit.
3. Distinguish a plan, a completed run and customer validation; missing logs or permissions are gaps, not proof of success.
discussionQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop make easier?
Which scenario proves the most important customer concern?
Where could environment, permission, or data issues derail the experience?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the decision-centered demo or workshop plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from scenario selection to the demo or workshop plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate demo evidence and known limitations', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Demos and workshops should provide the smallest relevant proof for the customer decision. Cut feature tours that do not test the criterion and keep prerequisites, limits and fallback visible. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop advance?
Which scenario proves that decision?
What could fail because of data, tenant, permission, or environment constraints?
What fallback has a peer used when a demo environment failed without claiming the proof succeeded?
listenFor: Feature tours, unclear audience, unsupported claims, missing fallback plans, and proof not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one demo/workshop storyboard: audience decision, proof scenario, environment prerequisite, known limitation and fallback explanation. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. This is a storyboard or proof contract, not an executed demo, successful test or permission to use an environment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What decision does the scenario test, and what feature or unsupported claim did you cut because it did not help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could revise a demo or workshop scenario to test the customer criterion, checking prerequisites, limits and fallback. Building or running the whole session is not required. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized scenario retained or cut and whether review made the decision clearer; a customer session need not have occurred. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A proposed demo covers many features, but only one scenario tests the customer's decision criterion. Keep that scenario, check any dated run evidence and prerequisites, and mark unexecuted verification unknown.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A decision-centered demo or workshop tests a customer criterion rather than covering the most features. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example scenario, criterion and explicit run-status note.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A demo plan or attractive product tour is not proof of the criterion. Look for a scenario retained or cut for its decision value with execution gaps visible.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a demo plan or attractive product tour is not proof of the criterion. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a demo plan or attractive product tour is not proof of the criterion. Manager support can protect technical review time and support the next actual verification.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Support a narrow, decision-relevant exploration; encourage an honest unknown test status rather than a polished implied success.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a demo plan or attractive product tour is not proof of the criterion; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to protect technical review time and support the next actual verification? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Pressure-test PoC readiness
activities.description: Review a proposed PoC plan for gaps and ambiguity.
activities.prompt: Review [the PoC plan]. State first whether the proof is warranted at all, or whether the customer decision could be made without one. Then identify vague success criteria, unowned dependencies, unrealistic milestones, missing security or data assumptions, weak linkage to the customer decision and unclear exit paths. Say who would run the proof and whether that should be a partner. Return five review questions and the smallest revisions needed.
activities.expectedOutput: Readiness review and revision list.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns the go or no-go call and confirms the required reviewers have seen the plan before it is called ready. A readiness checklist can be entirely green while the one thing that will actually break the proof was never on it, and that thing is usually known to the engineer rather than to the checklist.
activities.requiredContext: Proposed PoC plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: Readiness issues should be found in planning, not after the customer expects a proof.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A PoC is valuable only if it has a bounded hypothesis, success criteria, and an exit decision before work starts.
keyTalkingPoints: Define the smallest useful proof.
Make success, exit, milestones, owners, dependencies, and review gates observable.
Pressure-test readiness before the customer or delivery team absorbs ambiguity.
discussionQuestions: What is the smallest proof that would answer the technical decision?
Which success criterion is too vague?
What should trigger exit, handoff, or no-go?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Scope the smallest useful PoC'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from proof idea to readiness pressure test. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate PoC success and exit criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Proof work is warranted only when it can change a decision. Define observable success, failure and exit before execution; declining unnecessary proof protects time and capacity. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: What is the smallest useful proof?
Which success criterion is measurable?
Which dependency or owner is missing?
How has another SE shrunk a PoC while keeping meaningful success and exit criteria?
listenFor: Vague success criteria, PoCs that duplicate demo work, unowned dependencies, and no exit path.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one PoC scope card: customer doubt, minimum proof, measurable success/negative result, exit condition, dependency and approval gap. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. This is a storyboard or proof contract, not an executed demo, successful test or permission to use an environment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What would proof change, and what would justify no proof, a smaller test or an early stop?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore whether proof would change a decision, including a no-proof option. If real proof is pursued, success criteria, a stop condition and an accountable execution owner must be agreed before it starts. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share the human proceed, revise or no-proof decision and a sanitized criterion that informed it; note avoided effort or a clearer proof boundary. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A proposed PoC may repeat evidence already available. Decide whether proof adds value; if it does, scope one hypothesis, execution owner, success criterion and stop condition.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Proof is useful when it resolves a decision-relevant uncertainty that credible existing evidence cannot already settle. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the proposed hypothesis, success criterion and exit condition in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Proof is not mandatory when credible existing evidence resolves the question. Look for a justified bounded test or an explicit evidence-based no-proof decision.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: proof is not mandatory when credible existing evidence resolves the question. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when proof is not mandatory when credible existing evidence resolves the question. Manager support can help secure an appropriate execution owner only when validation is justified.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help the facilitator keep both a bounded test and an evidence-based no-proof decision available; do not make a PoC the expected outcome.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.

What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief
activities.description: Synthesize approved customer and technical context into a brief that names the customer decision, constraints, evidence gaps, and criteria.
activities.prompt: Use [customer and technical sources plus confirmed attendee list] to draft a discovery brief: business outcome, owner, architecture, constraints, open questions and five questions that advance the decision. Identify who must authorize funding/staffing and who is attending; flag unknowns. Separate customer-agreed decision criteria from proposed criteria, citing evidence and who must confirm each. Don’t turn hypotheses into agreement.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical discovery brief with questions, evidence gaps, the business outcome and its owner, decision-maker coverage, and explicit decision criteria. Each criterion identifies customer-agreed versus proposed status, supporting source where available, and the person who must confirm it or an unresolved ownership gap.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides which questions are appropriate to ask this customer. A technically sound discovery question can be premature or presumptuous given where the relationship is, and discovery is where that costs most. The SE also decides how directly to ask who can approve, since the question is fair to ask and can still land badly depending on who is in the room.
activities.requiredContext: Selected approved customer/technical sources; confirmed meeting attendee list; sourced decision-authority or decision-maker measures where available; any recorded customer-agreed criteria and their evidence.
activities.whyThisMatters: Discovery becomes useful when it produces decision criteria the customer and team can inspect.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Discovery should end with decision criteria, not a second discovery meeting. Today focuses on making the customer decision explicit early.
keyTalkingPoints: Start from the customer decision and work backward to criteria and evidence.
Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and open questions.
Capture what must be validated before architecture, demo, or PoC work begins.
discussionQuestions: Which decision is the customer actually trying to make?
Who has to say yes for this to happen, and were they in the room last time?
What evidence gap would make the next technical step unsafe?
What criteria need to be agreed rather than inferred?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from discovery discussion to building the actual decision-criteria brief. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Map evidence gaps against decision criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical discovery separates customer-agreed criteria from assumptions and identifies who can say yes. Write criteria before the conversation, then revise them as evidence changes. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which discovery question would most change the technical decision?
What evidence is missing or only assumed?
Which criteria must be agreed with the customer?
Which question has a peer used to turn assumed criteria into a customer-confirmed decision?
listenFor: Vague decisions, inferred criteria, missing evidence, and questions that sound impressive but do not advance the decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one discovery-criteria brief: customer decision, confirmed versus assumed criterion, evidence needed, discovery question and confirmation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore discovery criteria and the approval question using existing context; a new customer conversation is not required. Any real discovery should keep proposed criteria distinct from customer-confirmed criteria. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized criterion confirmed or corrected and whether it focused discovery or clarified approval ownership; it need not have been wrong. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A discovery conversation produced feature requests but no agreed technical decision criterion. Prepare one question that distinguishes customer evidence from the team's inference.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical discovery turns requests and constraints into criteria that the customer can confirm. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the discovery question and sourced customer constraint in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: The team's inference is not a customer-confirmed technical criterion. Look for a sharper criterion and a named authority for its confirmation.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: the team's inference is not a customer-confirmed technical criterion. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. activities.whyThisMatters: Technical deal health improves when blockers, proof gaps, and next decisions are visible in one place.

activities.name: Validate the blocker evidence and mitigation path
activities.description: Check that every blocker in the technical risk plan has evidence, an owner, a mitigation and a next decision rather than just a name.
activities.prompt: Review [the technical risk plan and permitted supporting evidence]. For each listed blocker, check evidence, impact, owner, mitigation, checkpoint and next decision. Return the blocker evidence/mitigation review with the next evidence check or owner-role question, not a new risk plan.
activities.expectedOutput: Blocker evidence and mitigation review.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides whether each blocker has a real mitigation or only a named owner. An owner without a mitigation is a way of recording that nothing is being done about it.

activities.whyThisMatters: A blocker without evidence and owner remains an observation, not a plan.

activities.name: Monitor technical blockers across your accounts between reviews
activities.description: Set up a standing watch on the technical signals that predict a stalled deployment, so intervention happens before the review rather than at it. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: For [account list or territory], flag flat/declining deployment or consumption, prolonged technical blockers, support patterns suggesting architectural issues and slipped milestones without new dates. For each, cite evidence, propose a hypothesis and identify the next confirming check—not a confident diagnosis. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline. Flag access gaps. Run once, read-only; don’t schedule, send or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run technical risk list with a stated hypothesis, supporting evidence, and the confirmation step for each item. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SE validates each hypothesis technically before raising it with the customer or the account team, and corrects any signal that reflects a known planned change.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts you support; access to deployment, consumption and support signals; the committed technical milestones. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Review each technical hypothesis and check the evidence actually supports it.
5. Confirm any blocker technically yourself before raising it with the customer.
6. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
7. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical blockers are cheapest to fix early and most expensive to fix at a review. The signal is usually present weeks before anyone names the problem.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical risk should be named while it is still a decision, not after it becomes a customer escalation.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect exit criteria, blockers, proof gaps, objections, dependencies, and handoffs.
Every risk needs evidence, owner, mitigation, checkpoint, and next decision.
Use AI to surface signals, but use your judgment to prioritize them.
discussionQuestions: What technical risk is blocking progression right now?
Which proof gap is being treated as if it were already closed?
Who owns the next technical action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect technical deal health and proof gaps'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from risk naming to action plan and handoff. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the blocker evidence and mitigation path', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Early technical risk management turns evidence into a timely owner conversation, mitigation or accepted handoff. Inference is not a confirmed blocker or escalation rule. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical risk is blocking progression?
What evidence would clear or confirm it?
Who owns the mitigation and next checkpoint?
How does another SE keep an untested proof gap visible in the technical handoff?
listenFor: Risks without owners, proof gaps treated as closed, delivery handoffs without requirements, and blockers framed too broadly.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one technical risk row: blocker, available evidence, untested proof gap, proposed mitigation owner, handoff requirement and next check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could identify one technical risk early enough to be a conversation rather than an escalation. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized concern checked and whether acting early clarified mitigation or avoided a later surprise. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A pursuit treats a proof gap as closed even though a dependency remains unresolved. Review the evidence and identify the technical action that still needs an owner.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical deal health exposes unresolved proof gaps and dependencies before a handoff is treated as ready. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the dated blocker and its known dependency or reviewer in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A technical risk summary does not resolve the cause or approve a workaround. Look for a specific uncertainty with an evidence check and accountable owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a technical risk summary does not resolve the cause or approve a workaround. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

SE-HEALTH.keyTakeaway: A health signal is actionable when its evidence, accountable owner, and next decision are clear.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a technical risk summary does not resolve the cause or approve a workaround. Manager support can help bring the necessary specialist into the risk conversation without escalating speculation.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish a risk description from a resolved technical issue; keep a workaround or receiving acceptance with its accountable owner.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a technical risk summary does not resolve the cause or approve a workaround; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help bring the necessary specialist into the risk conversation without escalating speculation? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. activities.name: Package a reusable technical asset with context
activities.description: Convert successful work into a repeatable, governed asset.
activities.prompt: Using the approved demo, script, architecture, response or checklist and validation evidence I supply, create a reusable asset package with purpose, prerequisites, steps, editable parameters, validation checks, known limitations, owner and example use. For code or configuration, include the supplied repository location and run instructions. Identify actual test results, validation date and environment only where supported by the supplied evidence. Otherwise mark validation status or date unknown and specify the test needed before reuse. Do not treat an approved asset or documented test procedure as evidence that the test was executed.
activities.expectedOutput: Reusable asset package with source location and run instructions where supplied, validation checks, evidence-backed test status/date/environment, and unknowns plus required verification. A documented check is distinguished from an executed test.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SE removes sensitive content, validates technical accuracy and confirms reuse permissions. Verify actual test evidence before representing code or configuration as validated; an unknown status remains a reuse blocker until resolved.
activities.requiredContext: Approved technical asset; owner and reuse permissions; available repository location, run instructions, test results or validation metadata with date and environment. Identify unavailable evidence explicitly rather than inferring validation history.
activities.whyThisMatters: Reuse happens when the asset includes enough context for another SE to trust and adapt it.

activities.name: Create a technical Skill Blueprint for a repeatable SE workflow
activities.description: Describe a repeatable workflow as a draft Skill Blueprint, with implementation and testing still explicit before promotion.
activities.prompt: Create a draft reusable Skill Blueprint for [SE workflow]. Define trigger, inputs, trusted sources, ordered steps, expected output, rules, exclusions, exception behavior, human review and validation checks. Include one representative test case with expected output and pass/fail criteria, plus implementation tasks for the skill owner. Label the result as a draft specification, not an installed or tested skill. A walkthrough of the blueprint is not an execution test; do not invoke or publish an implementation that does not yet exist.
activities.expectedOutput: Draft technical Skill Blueprint with validation checks, representative test case, expected results, walkthrough gaps and implementation owner/tasks. No claim that a skill has been installed, executed or validated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE or skill owner approves the blueprint, implements it in a supported environment, then runs and records representative execution tests. Validate access, outputs, safeguards and repository placement before approving publication or promotion; a blueprint walkthrough alone is not sufficient.
activities.requiredContext: SE workflow; trusted sources and access constraints; representative approved test case and expected outcome; the owner who will implement and validate the skill.
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout and choose one repeatable SE workflow; no installed skill is required for this drafting practice.
2. Replace [SE workflow] in the prompt and supply trusted sources and a representative, approved test case.
3. Run the prompt to generate the draft Skill Blueprint.

4. Review its steps, access assumptions, outputs and safeguards, then walk through the test case against the specification. Record expected results and gaps; do not mark this as an executed skill test.
5. Keep the blueprint as a draft and name the owner who will implement it in a supported skill format and authorized environment.
6. After an implementation is available, the owner runs the representative test, records actual results and resolves gaps. Publish or promote only after the human checkpoint is approved.
activities.whyThisMatters: A blueprint lets the team test repeatability before pretending the skill is production-ready.

activities.name: Sanitize and validate the reusable asset
activities.description: Check a technical asset for sensitive content, accuracy and missing prerequisites before anyone else reuses it.
activities.prompt: Review [the approved sanitized asset] using only permitted non-sensitive evidence. Check residual sensitive content, technical accuracy, prerequisites, limitations, permissions, owner and validation checks before reuse. Cite material technical findings to source evidence or current official guidance where relevant; distinguish tested behavior from assumptions. Flag unresolved sharing restrictions for the human owner rather than declaring the asset cleared. Do not request restricted originals or treat this review as permission to publish.
activities.expectedOutput: Asset readiness and sanitization review.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides what is safe to make reusable and removes customer-identifying and sensitive content before it is published. A sanitization miss in a reusable asset propagates to everyone who reuses it.
activities.requiredContext: Approved sanitized asset; permitted non-sensitive context needed to judge it; team's sharing rules. Confirm permission and sanitization before supplying material to the selected tool; do not upload restricted originals for the tool to sanitize.
activities.whyThisMatters: Reusable assets create risk when sensitive content or unvalidated assumptions travel with them.
