roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Engages early with the opportunity owner to shape executable commercial constructs across Microsoft and partner transaction routes. Navigates negotiation guardrails, coordinates owner-validated policy and licensing questions, routes approvals and exceptions, and hands off approved terms while addressing renewal commercial risk.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes SME&C commercial terms across transaction routes and coordinates approvals and renewals.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. Supports covered consumption portfolios through milestone readiness, partner and scale-engine handoffs, targeted adoption and technical interventions, attributed value evidence, and expansion hypotheses without assuming blanket customer or partner-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports covered SME&C consumption portfolios with readiness, handoffs, and targeted interventions.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM
roles.description: Leads partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executive stakeholders and governance around growth priorities. Coordinates partner growth and co-sell efforts, drives course correction through business reviews, and brings technical, sales, and marketing owners together while reserving investment and commercial commitments for authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: PDM-R

Mobilizes technical specialists, coordinates validated readiness, and prepares graduation handoffs accepted by accountable owners, with program approvals and graduation criteria retained by authorized owners.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. Coaches partner sellers and inspects renewal and consumption-commitment opportunities, avoiding duplicate pipeline attribution while keeping customer decisions with account teams and partner records and economics with partners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)
roles.description: A leadership audience focused on strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies. Brings attention to issues requiring strategic intervention and communicates decisions and direction, with action and escalation shaped by each participant's applicable authority rather than a shared management remit.
roles.descriptionSummary: A leadership audience for strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies.

Inspects pipeline using only certified records and minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or user-supplied excerpts, with source, scope, as-of/freshness dates, and human verification; coordinates account teams while retaining technical, policy, and approval owners.

Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional

Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.

roles.name: Solution Engineer

Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.

roles.name: Commercial Executive

Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries through authoritative sources and approved handling, coordinating decision narratives, approvals, and execution without assuming policy, exception, legal, or compliance approval authority.

CSA-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
CSA-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
CSA-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: Explain why the shared huddle motion matters: we go first as Customer Zero, learn from peers, and build confidence through real work. Orientation establishes the motion for everyone; role-specific practice begins in Week 2.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Review the Orientation HTML and agree a brief opening and handoffs with the facilitator. Locate the baseline survey, readiness checklist, shared Top 5 Agents resources, and access help so questions can be supported.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Introduce the why, reinforce the weekly rhythm, and welcome questions. Help distinguish the future weekly-experience preview from today's Orientation. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A gap in planned usage does not tell us why it exists. Explore the customer and workload context, distinguish possible causes, and decide what to check next. Plan a technical intervention when its cause has been validated.
keyTalkingPoints: Separate observed usage or consumption signals from possible causes; be clear about the measure and period.
Use Cowork to investigate when the cause is unclear, or choose the planning alternative when validated causes are already available.
A report can show movement, but it does not establish a technical cause. Researcher can check public technical plausibility, not private customer facts.
For optional MSXI analysis, check the relevant visual, permitted scope, period and consumption/plan measures; missing comparisons are gaps, not technical causes.
discussionQuestions: Where do consumption or usage signals become technical work for you?
Which shortfall signal is most likely to hide a technical cause?
What evidence would you need before owning an intervention?
suggestedTransitions: Start with 'Investigate risks to planned usage' in Cowork when the situation or cause is still unclear. If validated causes are already supplied, choose 'Plan from validated consumption causes' instead; it is an alternative, not a required second live step. Extended choices are certified-report analysis (where available) and public-guidance evidence critique. Neither requires an MSXI run as a prerequisite.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Summarize what is known, which explanations remain provisional, and the next useful check. Choose a proposed technical action only when the cause and measure warrant it; keep commercial and customer-priority decisions with their accountable owners. Treat an unavailable report or missing comparison as a gap, not evidence that the underlying data is wrong.
facilitatorQuestions: What do we know about the situation, and which missing detail would change the next decision?
Which explanation is evidenced, and which is still a hypothesis?
What check would distinguish technical, adoption-related and other causes?
If using a report, are its scope, period and measures suitable for this question?
listenFor: Relevant supplied context reused; observed signals separated from cause hypotheses; an evidence check that could change the decision; honest access or measure gaps. Proposed owners and dates are not accepted commitments. Public technical guidance does not verify private customer evidence.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Keep the sanitized situation or clearly fictional manual hypothesis/options table when inputs or host access are missing. Only for a chosen MSXI report question, optionally use a starter/book prompt or narrow to the relevant visual; if the route or measures remain unavailable, use an approved excerpt or continue without a measured result. Fictional practice is not a tool result, customer finding, diagnosis or approval. No additional Team Member prework is required.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your interpretation, and which assumption or ownership question needs checking before action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a consumption-gap hypothesis against permitted evidence and confirmed metric definitions, and consider an intervention or owner question. Keep the cause provisional if evidence is incomplete. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized consumption hypothesis checked and whether it changed the diagnosis or intervention owner. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A workload is not reaching planned usage. A project note mentions an integration problem, while a customer note suggests rollout has been delayed. Neither establishes the cause. Compare the explanations and identify one useful evidence check before recommending a technical intervention.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A consumption gap can have technical, adoption or nontechnical causes; the measure alone does not choose the intervention. Start with Cowork to frame the situation and hypotheses, or choose the validated-causes planning alternative when that evidence already exists. Certified figures still require an authorized source; Cowork is not a replacement MSXI data retriever. CSA owns the technical judgment, not commercial approval or overall consumption-plan ownership.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Keep the existing Cowork investigation or validated-causes planning choice as alternatives, not a tool sequence. Arrange a sanitized situation or approved supplied figures. Only if optional MSXI analysis is chosen, check the report/visual, customer filters, period, plan/consumption measures and available report Copilot Pane; the home link alone establishes no access or successful retrieval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Usage variance is not proof of a technical cause; a Cowork hypothesis is not validated analysis. Researcher checks public technical plausibility, not private customer data. For optional report analysis, check the applicable report, scope, period, permissions and measures. Use the report's Copilot panel where available, not Take Action / MSXI Action Agent; do not assume a report run has succeeded.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree whether the example needs hypothesis framing or already has validated causes; choose one Featured alternative. Keep team-member attendance free of new artifact requirements. Agree who can help check technical assumptions or interpret the measures if questions arise.

CSA-PIPE.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when usage variance alone does not prove a technical cause. Manager support can help obtain the right diagnostic expertise rather than impose an unsupported cause.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish competing explanations before discussing a technical action; keep metric definitions and missing evidence visible. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check customer filters, period, consumption definitions and any plan/milestone comparison; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations without scoring individuals. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check the report/view, relevant visual, scope, period and source basis before one focused question: What changed in the measure, and what evidence would distinguish a technical cause from adoption or other causes? Narrow a broad query using the visual's terminology; keep consequential judgment with its accountable human owner and do not turn the practice into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help obtain the right diagnostic expertise rather than impose an unsupported cause? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Prepare the technical advisory conversation
activities.description: Turn approved evidence into a customer-centered plan.
activities.prompt: Prepare me for a technical advisory conversation with [customer/account] about [technical topic or decision]. Find relevant emails, chats, meeting notes and files. Draft a customer advisory plan covering the goals, current technical situation, recommendation and trade-offs, key questions, evidence gaps and next steps. Add a short internal account-team brief identifying the proposed recommendation, alignment needed and decisions outside my authority. Cite material evidence and distinguish confirmed facts, accepted ownership and commitments from proposals. If the customer, topic or intended decision is unclear, ask me to clarify before drafting. Otherwise proceed and flag missing evidence. Do not send messages, schedule follow-up or update records. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: A draft customer advisory plan and a short internal account-team alignment brief.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which tradeoffs to surface, and who has to see the internal brief before the customer meeting. Advisory credibility comes from naming the downside before the customer finds it. The internal brief exists because an account team that hears a recommendation for the first time in front of the customer cannot support it.
activities.requiredContext: Customer/account and the technical topic or decision to discuss. A short note, meeting reference or relevant source link can be added if useful; no new document or meeting invitation is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Preparation for the technical advisory conversation is the step most often skipped and most often decisive.

activities.name: Rehearse the architecture recommendation
activities.description: Role-play and coach a technical advisory conversation.
activities.prompt: Use [paste/describe the approved fictional or de-identified advisory plan] to role-play with the customer/stakeholder. Simulate realistic architecture, readiness, security, operational, cost and implementation questions. Coach clarity, evidence, listening, tradeoffs and next step. Identify claims needing SME review. activities.whyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing the architecture recommendation is cheaper than improvising it in the room.

activities.name: Design the advisory adoption plan
activities.description: Convert the advisory recommendation into the actions, owners and checkpoints the customer would need to actually adopt it.
activities.prompt: Using only [the agreed advisory recommendation and delivery dependencies], draft a sequenced customer adoption plan. For each action, show recorded customer and Microsoft owners, the dependency most likely to stall it, checkpoint dates and progress evidence. Preserve confirmed responsibilities/dates; label suggested ones proposed and acceptance unknown when not evidenced. If delivery coverage changes the next step, use known global delivery or field delivery context or ask. Do not assign work, schedule checkpoints or implement changes.
activities.expectedOutput: An adoption plan for the advisory recommendation with paired customer and Microsoft owners, dependencies, and checkpoints.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA names the dependency most likely to stall adoption. Adoption plans fail on the customer side far more often than the technical side, and only someone who knows the customer operating reality can predict where.
activities.requiredContext: Agreed advisory recommendation; known customer/Microsoft owner roles and delivery dependencies; existing checkpoint dates where available. Global delivery or field delivery coverage, only if it changes the next action.
activities.whyThisMatters: A recommendation becomes adoptable when customer and Microsoft owners accept the dependencies and checkpoints it requires.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A useful advisory brief makes the intended decision and supporting evidence clear. Focus on one recommendation and the questions that could change it.
keyTalkingPoints: A brief is not a summary. It is a position plus the questions that would change it.
The intended outcome is the part most preparation leaves out, and it changes how the meeting runs.
Anticipated objections are cheaper than recovered ones.
discussionQuestions: Which upcoming conversation needs a recommendation, not just a summary?
What evidence would make the advisory position credible?
What customer decision should the conversation advance?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prepare the technical advisory conversation'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from generic preparation to one upcoming conversation and its intended customer decision. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the evidence behind the advisory recommendation', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical advice connects a grounded recommendation and alternatives to the customer decision. Internal alignment does not establish customer agreement. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: What technical decision should the advisory conversation advance? Which recommendation can you defend from current evidence, and what is missing? What objection did a peer use to improve the ask or fallback?
listenFor: Preparation that summarizes but does not decide; evidence gaps; customer facts needing review; and advisory recommendations without a named decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one advisory brief: customer decision, evidence-qualified recommendation, missing fact, likely objection, intended ask and fallback. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence would make this customer conversation credible, and what decision or question still belongs to a person?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could prepare one advisory conversation around the decision you need, not the content you have. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized recommendation or ask sharpened and whether review made the advisory conversation more useful. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A technical advisory brief summarizes the situation without recommending a next decision. Use the approved evidence to frame one recommendation and the question that could change it.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical advisory work connects evidence and alternatives to a recommendation and an explicit customer decision. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the recommendation, alternatives and constraints in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: An advisory draft is not customer acceptance. For the selected Cowork advisory activity, retain both linked jobs: the customer advisory plan and internal account-team alignment brief. The recommendation is the CSA's proposed position; missing team agreement stays visible. Global delivery or field delivery coverage matters only if it changes the next action.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: an advisory draft does not establish customer acceptance. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when an advisory draft does not establish customer acceptance. Manager support can support the next technical clarification without substituting the manager's architecture choice.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which tradeoff is useful to explore; a confident advisory rehearsal is not customer acceptance.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that an advisory draft does not establish customer acceptance; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the next technical clarification without substituting the manager's architecture choice? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most production designs are inherited rather than chosen. Focus on landing on one recommended direction, naming who has to approve it, and saying plainly what would prove it wrong.
keyTalkingPoints: Design and proof are one motion. A design the customer cannot see is a document.
Success criteria set before the work are the only ones that count.
AI accelerates the assembly. The architecture judgment stays human.
discussionQuestions: Which architecture option is still being treated as obvious?
What decision criteria would change the recommendation?
What evidence would you need before supporting this design?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Compare production architecture options'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from architecture principles to one live architecture decision with explicit criteria. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the architecture evidence before the design is shared', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Production architecture is a proposed direction, not a readiness declaration. Test constraints and cross-environment dependencies before reviewers or customers rely on it. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which production architecture options should be compared against the customer's criteria? Which security, operations or resilience claim still needs validation? What assumption would a peer challenge before recommending a design?
listenFor: Untested assumptions; option comparisons without decision criteria; public guidance used without applicability review; and controls, governance, or resilience claims needing SME validation.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a two-option production architecture comparison: explicit criteria, security/operations/resilience constraint, supporting evidence, unknown and validation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a production architecture direction against a customer constraint and critical dependency; identify needed validation instead of declaring the draft production-ready. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized production dependency validated or open and whether it changed the design or prevented premature readiness claims. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An inherited production design assumes a constraint that may no longer hold. Compare options and identify the evidence and owner needed before changing direction.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Production architecture decisions test options against this customer's criteria and validation needs. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the architecture option, production criterion and validation gap in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A proposed design is not confirmed technical readiness. In a selected Cowork architecture practice, preserve the decision package, diagram and required-review status; in validation practice, a proof plan is not an executed test. Keep source conflicts, material owner gaps and outstanding reviews visible. Coverage is global delivery or field delivery only where it changes the next action.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a proposed design is not confirmed technical readiness. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A design that has not been argued against has not really been validated. Focus on the proof, and about being clear which readiness call is yours and which belongs to somebody else.
keyTalkingPoints: Design and proof are one motion. A design the customer cannot see is a document.
Success criteria set before the work are the only ones that count.
AI accelerates the assembly. The architecture judgment stays human.
discussionQuestions: Which dependency could make the design fail in production?
What proof is small enough to validate the decision?
Who owns the next technical decision after validation?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Validate the evidence behind the technical decision path'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use the supplied prior technical decision path and approved evidence to review one assumed decision, owner or slip risk. For the alternative Featured validation-path intervention, the facilitator or manager arranges an existing permitted validation plan and reviewed gaps as shared inputs. Review them during the activity; if they are unavailable, use a sanitized case or select another eligible practice rather than assign Team Members advance preparation. Do not run both Featured alternatives sequentially live. Investment-readiness Extended work applies only when proposed or funded scope is relevant, never as funding approval. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Design the architecture intervention plan', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Readiness follows proportionate validation of the design and its critical dependencies. Keep technical proof distinct from delivery ownership and respect agreed stop conditions. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Which decision in the prior technical path is being assumed rather than owned and scheduled? What gap in the supplied evidence could change readiness? How would a peer define the smallest proof without expanding funded scope or treating funding as approval?
listenFor: Validation scoped too broadly; unowned prerequisites; proof criteria written after work begins; and investment-funded scope that may not be deliverable as designed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one prior-design decision-path review: decision point, supplied evidence or unavailable, proposed owner/date, slip impact and smallest settling proof. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could define the validation path for one design, including what would tell you to stop. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized validation criterion checked and whether it clarified readiness, a hold or a delivery-owner question. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A readiness claim rests on a validation plan with an unresolved proof gap. Review the supplied evidence and distinguish the next technical decision from any optional investment question.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Readiness judgment distinguishes validation plans from executed evidence and the conditions still unresolved. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example validation plan and its stated evidence gaps; do not assume the preceding practice was completed.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Absence of a validation result cannot be filled with a hypothetical pass. Look for a readiness decision that distinguishes tested evidence from remaining conditions.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: absence of a validation result cannot be filled with a hypothetical pass. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Build a technical health evidence brief
activities.description: Review customer technical health and adoption evidence for risks and possible restart signals; hand off source gaps and potential interventions for CSA judgment.
activities.prompt: Using the approved customer technical sources I am attaching, build a technical health brief. Separate verified evidence from assumptions. Summarize architecture and delivery state, material technical risks, optimization opportunities, open commitments, dependencies and missing evidence. Before ranking anything, say which parts of this customer's estate these sources do not cover, which risks would not appear in them at all, and who would know about those. Then end with the three issues that most deserve CSA attention and why. Include adoption and consumption coverage where supplied. Flag a possible restart conversation only as an evidence-backed human follow-up question, not as a confirmed trigger.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical health brief with adoption and consumption coverage, customer-health risks, possible restart signals, and source/coverage gaps before priority issues are named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA interprets technical health and adoption evidence in customer context and validates any possible restart signal; no risk, value, or trigger is treated as confirmed solely because a source recorded it.
activities.requiredContext: Approved customer technical sources; review period and customer outcome; adoption/consumption evidence where available.
activities.whyThisMatters: Source coverage gaps matter as much as the top risks; a complete-looking health brief can omit an entire part of the customer estate.

activities.name: Prioritize a technical risk response
activities.description: Analyze enabled certified data relevant to technical health.
activities.prompt: In [Report Name], for [customer scope] during [period], show material consumption, usage or adoption changes using the relevant visual's measures. Cite filters, measure definitions and comparable dates; flag missing comparisons. Separate observed signals from technical-review questions; do not infer health scores, intent or technical causes from usage alone.
activities.expectedOutput: Sourced consumption, usage or adoption signals with dates, definitions and comparison gaps, plus technical-review priorities for CSA validation. No diagnosis or health score is inferred; unavailable report access or measures remain named gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA decides what is technically significant. A metric can move sharply and mean nothing, and chasing statistical noise is how technical credibility gets spent on non-problems.
activities.requiredContext: Report name; permitted customer scope and filters; reporting period and comparison baseline; available consumption, usage or adoption measures; delivery context (global delivery or field delivery coverage).
activitySteps: 1. Check the right report/view, permitted scope, period, relevant visual and measure definitions, including any comparison baseline.
2. In the available report Copilot Pane, ask the concise business question using the visual's titles and report terms.
3. Compare the answer with the report metrics. Inspect missing measures or unsupported conclusions, and refine the question if needed; optional book prompts can help.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deciding a technical risk response is really deciding what you will not do. Say it out loud.

activities.name: Watch consumption and health signals between reviews
activities.description: Set up a standing check on the accounts you carry, so a health or consumption change reaches you when it happens rather than at the next review. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: Check technical health for [account list or territory]: consumption against plan, new deployment/adoption blockers and previously flagged risks. Show dated evidence, what it cannot establish and one next technical question per issue. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise establish a baseline. Flag source gaps. Run once, read-only; don’t schedule, send or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run health check separating new movement from unchanged risk, with the next technical question for each. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CSA confirms the technical reading of each signal and decides which movement is significant enough to act on.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts you carry; approved consumption, usage and support data; the risks currently on your register. Your delivery context, whether global delivery or field delivery coverage, since it changes which next action is right. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. Review the first output and separate genuinely new movement from risk you already knew about.
5. Validate each technical hypothesis yourself before raising it with the customer or the account team.
6. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
7. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Risk found early is a conversation and the same risk found late is an escalation. Between reviews is exactly where that gap opens, and it is where an always-on agent earns its place.

activities.name: Validate the technical health evidence
activities.description: Separate what the health signals actually evidence from what the team has been assuming, before a risk is escalated.
activities.prompt: Review [the technical health assessment and its permitted source evidence]. For each risk, cite the signal supporting it, its currency and what is inference rather than observation. Identify material conflicting evidence or gaps and the next evidence needed to confirm the risk. Distinguish technically supported risk from an unverified diagnosis or customer sentiment; unavailable evidence does not mean healthy or unhealthy. Return the technical health evidence map, retaining the assessment's risks rather than manufacturing new ones.
activities.expectedOutput: A technical health evidence map separating observed signal from inference, with the confirmation needed for each weak item.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which risk evidence would survive a customer challenge. Telemetry can support a risk the customer own operations team will immediately contradict, and losing that exchange costs the advisory relationship.
activities.requiredContext: Existing technical-health assessment and the dated evidence behind its risks.
activities.whyThisMatters: Customer-visible risk should rest on current telemetry or corroborated evidence, not a plausible technical interpretation.

activities.name: Design the technical risk intervention plan
activities.description: Turn the prioritized technical risks into sequenced interventions with owners and checkpoints that show whether they worked.
activities.prompt: Using only [the prioritized technical risks and delivery constraints], draft a sequenced intervention plan: technical action, recorded owner, blocking dependency, checkpoint date and success evidence per risk. Rate customer impact qualitatively from the evidence and sequence by which risk becomes customer-visible soonest; say when the evidence cannot support a ranking. Distinguish documented escalation conditions from proposals for my CSA review; identify the known internal reviewer before customer communication or flag the gap. Preserve accepted responsibilities/dates and mark suggestions or missing confirmation explicit. If coverage changes the next step, use known global delivery or field delivery context or ask. Do not invent escalation thresholds, notify anyone or execute changes.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced technical intervention plan with owners, dependencies, checkpoint dates and success evidence per risk, each carrying a customer-impact rating, an escalation threshold and the internal audience that needs to know.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA sequences by which risk becomes customer-visible soonest, owns that ordering, and sets the escalation threshold rather than leaving it implicit. A technically correct sequence that lets the customer discover a problem first turns a managed intervention into an escalation. A risk held past its threshold stops being managed and becomes absorbed.
activities.requiredContext: Validated technical risk list and delivery constraints; known delivery/customer owners; existing checkpoints and escalation/communication route where documented. Global delivery or field delivery coverage, only if it changes the next action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sequenced mitigations and explicit escalation thresholds keep a technical risk from becoming a customer surprise.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Risk you find this week is a conversation. The same risk found by the customer is an escalation. Focus on finding it earlier.
keyTalkingPoints: A health score can tell you something is wrong. It rarely tells you what to do.
Every risk needs an owner and a date or it is an observation.
AI is good at surfacing signal. Prioritizing it is judgment.
For a chosen MSXI practice, check the relevant visual, permitted scope, period and comparable usage/consumption measures; do not assume a health score or technical diagnosis is available.
discussionQuestions: Which technical risk is visible now but not yet owned?
What is evidence, and what is interpretation?
What intervention could prevent this from becoming customer-visible?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build a technical health evidence brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from health signal to one risk, its evidence, owner, and next intervention. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the technical health evidence', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical health combines recorded evidence with customer and team signals. Investigate what data misses without treating a missing metric as proof of risk. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical-health signal is a symptom rather than a cause? What evidence makes the risk real, and who can intervene? How does another CSA separate technical action from CSAM, support, delivery or commercial ownership?
listenFor: Health scores treated as causes; risks without owners or dates; technical blockers becoming customer-visible; and actions that require CSAM, support, delivery, or commercial alignment.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a technical-health row with dated signal, cause hypothesis, customer consequence and accountable-role question. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a technical-health question that recorded data may miss and consider which owner could clarify it; no new risk or owner contact needs to result. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized human signal checked and whether it corrected the health interpretation or clarified the risk owner. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A technical health signal is concerning but its explanation is still an interpretation. Verify the source and propose a proportionate intervention question.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical health review tests whether a signal is consequential in customer context before choosing a risk response. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged technical-health signal example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check customer filters, period and comparable consumption/usage or adoption measures in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A health indicator is not a diagnosis or proof of urgency. Look for a prioritized risk with a verifiable source and proportionate next check.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a health indicator is not a diagnosis or proof of urgency. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

CSA-HEALTH.keyTakeaway: A health signal is actionable when its evidence, accountable owner, and next decision are clear.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a health indicator is not a diagnosis or proof of urgency. Manager support can help resolve the expertise or ownership obstacle to the chosen intervention.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Encourage a proportionate next check; do not turn a metric movement into an unsupported diagnosis or urgency claim. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, help the facilitator check customer filters, period and comparable consumption/usage or adoption measures; keep a missing report, route or measure as a gap rather than a participant access test.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations without scoring individuals. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check the report/view, relevant visual, scope, period and source basis before one focused question: Which signal is supported by the visual, and what separate technical evidence is needed before calling it a risk? Narrow a broad query using the visual's terminology; keep consequential judgment with its accountable human owner and do not turn the practice into a commitment or readiness test.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help resolve the expertise or ownership obstacle to the chosen intervention? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Build the optimization evidence base
activities.description: Analyze enabled usage, cost and consumption evidence from the certified report.
activities.prompt: In [Report Name], for [customer scope] during [period], summarize available usage, consumption and cost changes using the relevant visual's measures. activities.expectedOutput: Optimization evidence summary with available measures, comparable periods and source limits; resource-level evidence and savings validation gaps remain explicit. Unavailable report access or cost measures do not become savings estimates.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms what each measure actually counts before acting on it. Optimization metrics are defined differently across services, and acting on a misread one produces a saving that never appears.
activities.requiredContext: Report name; permitted customer scope and filters; reporting period and comparison baseline; available usage, consumption and cost measures; delivery context (global delivery or field delivery coverage).
activitySteps: 1. Check the right report/view, permitted scope, period, relevant visual and measure definitions, including any comparison baseline.
2. In the available report Copilot Pane, ask the concise business question using the visual's titles and report terms.
3. Compare the answer with the report metrics. Inspect missing measures or unsupported conclusions, and refine the question if needed; optional book prompts can help.
activities.whyThisMatters: Certified cost and usage patterns identify optimization questions; they do not establish a deployable saving without resource-level validation.

activities.name: Create the FinOps and optimization recommendation
activities.description: Produce a bounded optimization recommendation.
activities.prompt: Using only [approved customer/workload optimization evidence and architecture context], draft an optimization recommendation: current state and outcome; options with supported technical/financial effects and tradeoffs; dependencies, risks, milestones and human reviews. Mark claims requiring resource-level Azure validation and distinguish deployed-resource-validated savings from provisional estimates; do not infer savings from consumption alone or put unsupported savings in customer-facing claims. For each provisional figure, preserve its recorded confirmation owner/date or mark either unknown and state the check needed; never invent one. Record any contractual or MACC implication as approved with authority/date evidence, not yet approved or unknown; approval is not inferred from a report. Do not invent customer intent or implement changes. If coverage affects the next action, use known global delivery or field delivery context or ask.
activities.expectedOutput: Optimization recommendation separating resource-validated savings from provisional claims, with recorded confirmation owners/dates or explicit gaps. Contractual/MACC implications include approval authority/date evidence, not-yet-approved or unknown status; no inferred savings, approval or customer intent.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the saving is achievable in this customer's environment and does not put a provisional figure in front of the customer as a saving. Optimization recommendations are generated from consumption patterns rather than from the deployed resources, so anything that needs resource-level access goes to the customer only after somebody with that access has confirmed it. Name who that is and by when, or leave the figure out of the recommendation.
activities.requiredContext: Approved optimization evidence; architecture context, outcome and constraints; resource-level validation evidence where available; known figure-confirmation owner/date and contractual/MACC approval records, if any. Global delivery or field delivery coverage, only if it changes the next action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Separating provisional savings from validated effects protects customer finance decisions and exposes contractual review needs.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A saving nobody can verify is a claim. Focus on the cost evidence you can actually stand behind, and who has to approve it.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer defines value. Our job is to evidence it in their terms.
Causality is easy to claim and hard to support. Say what the data supports.
A value story nobody hears is not value realized.
For a chosen MSXI practice, check the relevant visual, permitted scope, period and cost/usage measures; resource-level validation is still needed before any savings claim.
discussionQuestions: Which technical progress has not yet been translated into customer value?
Which cost, consumption, or optimization signal is credible enough to use?
What claim would you refuse to make without stronger evidence?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the optimization evidence base'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the signal to one bounded recommendation or technical value narrative. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the cost and optimization evidence', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: FinOps recommendations need comparable measures and resource-level confirmation before savings can be presented as achievable. Provisional estimates do not authorize customer changes or commercial commitments. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Which optimization option has a defensible baseline and cost evidence? What performance, resilience or operational trade-off could outweigh the benefit? How would a peer challenge the savings assumption before it becomes a recommendation?
listenFor: Invented savings; correlation presented as causality; optimization divorced from architecture tradeoffs; and value claims not tied to supported outcomes.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the available MSXI Pane cannot resolve the chosen report question, optionally use a role starter or the current report's book of prompts, or ask for a narrower question aligned to the visual. If access, routing or measures remain unavailable, stop the data claim and use an approved sanitized excerpt or a clearly labeled fictional case to rehearse a FinOps option card with baseline/period, cost evidence or gap, trade-off and reviewer. Keep evidence, assumptions and gaps separate; fictional practice establishes no live result, commitment or approval, and requires no additional Team Member prework.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which saving depends on an unverified resource or metric assumption, and who can confirm it before customer use?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could test an optimization against its cost basis and trade-offs. Ask someone with resource-level access to confirm achievable savings before customer use; otherwise withhold the figure. Implementation or commercial decisions require the authorized owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized savings assumption confirmed, corrected or withheld after resource-owner review and whether it prevented a misleading recommendation. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An optimization recommendation quotes an expected saving without enough supporting context. Review the evidence and caveats before asking the accountable owner to consider a change.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Optimization recommendations connect a cost baseline and feasible change to a qualified estimate of benefit. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the facilitator-arranged optimization evidence example. If the related MSXI practice is chosen, check customer filters, period, comparable cost/usage measures and resource-level evidence gaps in the relevant report/view and available Copilot Pane; the home link alone confirms neither access nor the report route. Use the report's visual labels for a focused question. Keep missing fields or comparisons visible; no new Team Member artifact is required.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Estimated savings are not realized savings or approved changes. Qualify recommendations by scope, measurement basis and feasibility. Claims requiring deployed-resource validation remain provisional; consumption trends alone do not confirm savings. Unknown confirmation owners/dates stay unknown, and contractual/MACC implications need authority/date approval evidence before customer use or change.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: estimated savings are not realized savings or approved changes. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Create the technical progress and value narrative
activities.description: Connect landing-zone, adoption/change, and technical-progress evidence to customer-visible value; return a sourced narrative with gaps, expansion possibilities, or restart signals marked for human validation.
activities.prompt: Using only [approved architecture, delivery, adoption, consumption, optimization and risk materials] for [customer, review period and audience], draft two linked outputs. Customer value narrative: progress tied to supported outcomes, risks and decisions, recorded commitments/owners and proposed next technical actions. Internal delivery/governance readout: milestone status, missing proof and recorded evidence owners or ownership gaps, risks needing a decision and next intervention. Separate measured evidence from interpretation; flag unsupported value and unaccepted responsibilities. Include landing-zone and adoption/change evidence only where relevant and supplied. Keep expansion/restart questions separate from realized outcomes; signals do not establish customer intent. If coverage changes the next step, use known global delivery or field delivery context or ask. Do not share drafts, accept handoffs or change delivery records.
activities.expectedOutput: Linked customer-facing value narrative and internal governance readout: evidenced progress/outcomes, commitment status, missing proof/ownership gaps and proposed next actions; expansion/restart questions remain hypotheses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA validates the link between technical progress, landing-zone/adoption/change evidence, and claimed customer value; unsupported progress, expansion, or restart triggers remain unasserted.
activities.requiredContext: Approved review sources; customer, audience and review period; relevant landing-zone/adoption-change evidence where available. Global delivery or field delivery coverage, only if it changes the next action.
activities.whyThisMatters: Separate customer value and internal governance views keep supported outcomes clear without exposing unapproved internal interpretation.

activities.name: Validate the evidence behind the customer value story
activities.description: Check that the value story is built on measured outcomes rather than activity, before the customer's finance function does it for you.
activities.prompt: Review [the technical value narrative, measurement basis and permitted supporting evidence]. For each claimed outcome, cite whether it is measured or projected, its baseline and any change in measurement basis since commitment. Separate delivered value from activity completed; flag unsupported attribution, material conflicts and figures needing finance/measurement-owner review. A missing source leaves the claim unverified, not false, and evidence of activity does not establish customer-recognized value. Return the value-claim review and corrections or proof questions, not a rewritten narrative.
activities.expectedOutput: A value-claim review separating measured from projected outcomes, with baseline integrity and finance-review risk per claim.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA separates delivered value from activity completed. Activity is easy to evidence and is not what was committed, and a value story built on it fails at the first executive question.
activities.requiredContext: Draft value narrative, agreed outcomes and the measurement baseline used.
activities.whyThisMatters: Completed activity is not delivered value; the customer outcome claim needs a stable baseline and actual measurement.

activities.name: Design the value-translation intervention plan
activities.description: Close the gap between the value you have delivered and the value the customer can see, with named owners and evidence.
activities.prompt: Using only [the validated value narrative, its evidence gaps, intended customer stakeholders and next-review context], draft a value-evidence plan. Distinguish evidence that can be obtained before the review from what remains unresolved, using known constraints rather than invented feasibility. Keep customer recognition separate from analysis; do not assign work or send the narrative.
activities.expectedOutput: A value evidence plan naming the missing proof, its producer, the date, and the stakeholder it must convince.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA identifies which gaps can be closed before the next review and which cannot, and says so. A value gap discovered by the customer is worse than one disclosed early with a plan attached.
activities.requiredContext: Validated value narrative and gaps; intended customer stakeholders; upcoming review and known evidence-production constraints/owners.
activities.whyThisMatters: A value gap needs a proof producer and review date, or the next customer discussion will repeat the unsupported claim.
