What early intervention threshold has a peer used before a technical risk became an escalation?
listenFor: Risks ranked by score rather than by consequence, interventions with no named owner, escalation thresholds that were never defined, and risks the team has normalized because they have lived with them. Also note signals from conversations that never made it into the system data.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one risk intervention row: consequential risk, evidence, earliest signal, proposed owner, next action and escalation threshold needing confirmation. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore an evidenced technical risk and a proposed intervention for its owner. Any actual escalation must use applicable confirmed guidance; if none is confirmed, keep the policy gap explicit and seek owner agreement before treating a review trigger as established. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized risk and whether its owner confirmed an intervention or review trigger; note any faster clarification or evidence gap. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: Recorded health looks stable while an approved human signal suggests a technical risk. Compare the evidence and consider intervention, monitoring or escalation under verified guidance.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Technical health review compares recorded signals with customer context to choose a proportionate next check. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the dated health signal and open intervention question in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A dashboard signal does not identify its cause or justify every intervention. Look for a proportionate risk response supported by the source and scope.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a dashboard signal does not identify its cause or justify every intervention. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a dashboard signal does not identify its cause or justify every intervention. Manager support can help the technical owner obtain missing expertise without evaluating people.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Encourage discussion of monitoring, intervention or escalation according to the evidence; leave diagnosis and accepted ownership explicit.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a dashboard signal does not identify its cause or justify every intervention; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Define the investment-funded technical scope and decision criteria
activities.description: Bound what the investment is technically meant to prove, including the assumptions, dependencies and explicit out-of-scope items.
activities.prompt: For Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID], use [customer problem and proposed investment] to define the bounded technical scope: intended outcome, architecture assumptions, observable decision criteria, dependencies, material risks and out-of-scope work. Cite confirmed customer requirements and distinguish them from proposed scope or assumptions. Name the technical question and owner role that must be resolved next. Do not infer eligibility or funding approval.
activities.expectedOutput: Bounded technical scope and decision-criteria brief.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides what counts as a technical outcome the investment can be judged against. A scope that reads well and names no observable result gets funded and then argued about at closure, when the evidence no longer exists to settle it.
activities.requiredContext: Customer problem, opportunity context, proposed investment
activities.whyThisMatters: Clear technical scope prevents investment-funded work from expanding beyond the proof it was meant to produce.

activities.name: Pressure-test investment scope against failure modes
activities.description: Stress the proposed technical scope for the assumptions and failure modes that would undermine the investment.
activities.prompt: Using [paste or attach the draft technical scope and architecture assumptions], identify the assumptions that would most damage the outcome if wrong, the failure modes that would surface during delivery, and the evidence that would confirm or rule out each one.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE names the assumption that would most damage the outcome if wrong. Failure modes are easy to list and unequally weighted, and only the engineer knows which one actually breaks the delivery.

activities.whyThisMatters: Failure modes found during scoping are cheaper than failure modes found during delivery.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE states which technical decisions must not change without returning to them. Delivery roles reasonably optimize what they are handed, and an unmarked constraint is the first thing optimized away.
activities.requiredContext: Approved scope, technical evidence package, success measures
activities.whyThisMatters: A handoff protects the technical decisions that should not change without re-engaging the SE.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment-funded proof work needs scope, success measures, failure-mode awareness, and handoff boundaries before execution begins.
keyTalkingPoints: You own the technical clarity, not eligibility, policy, commercial, or approval decisions.
Success measures must be observable.
Delivery handoff should state what is decided, what remains open, and when SE must be re-engaged.
discussionQuestions: What technical problem is the investment meant to prove or unblock?
Which success measure is observable enough?
What failure mode would make the investment underdeliver?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Define the investment-funded technical scope and decision criteria'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from investment idea to bounded technical proof package. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Funded proof should test the customer doubt with verifiable measures and a bounded exit. Technical scoping does not approve investment, resources or delivery commitments. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical scope boundary matters most?
Which success measure proves the investment helped?
What failure mode or handoff gap needs to be closed before review?
Which success or failure criterion would a peer challenge without taking over investment approval?
listenFor: Eligibility or approval decisions implied by the SE, vague proof measures, hidden open questions, and delivery handoffs without re-engagement triggers.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one funded technical proof card: in/out scope, decision criterion, success/failure measure, dependency, delivery handoff and re-engagement trigger. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What would justify or disqualify the investment, and what must the accountable owner verify before committing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could define what one investment-funded proof must demonstrate, in measures someone else could verify. Eligibility, funding and resource commitments remain with authorized owners; a draft is not approval. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized success or failure criterion clarified and whether it kept proof proportionate; not-run and approval-pending are valid. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A proposed funded proof has broad ambitions but vague success measures. Review one verifiable criterion, delivery constraint and handoff boundary without claiming the proof was run.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A funded technical scope still needs observable success measures, delivery constraints and a bounded proof question. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the proposed scope and observable success criteria in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Investment sponsorship does not establish proof readiness or approval. Look for a bounded proof with a known dependency and a separate governed decision.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: investment sponsorship does not establish proof readiness or approval. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

SE-INVEST.keyTakeaway: A prepared investment case is not an eligibility or funding decision; make evidence, gaps, and authority visible at each gate.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when investment sponsorship does not establish proof readiness or approval. Manager support can help clarify the accountable proof and investment owners without committing resources for them.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help keep proof design distinct from funding approval and execution; encourage a clear condition that could stop or change the scope.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that investment sponsorship does not establish proof readiness or approval; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help clarify the accountable proof and investment owners without committing resources for them? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID] and [one labeled Enrollment Number or Agreement Number], assess [proposed investment: type, activities, timing and amount/range if known] in a read-only chat brief using existing contract records and applicable current guidance. Do not initiate a pre-approval, DealBook or investment workflow. Cover term, commercial structure, exception and precedent risks. Distinguish confirmed facts, approved positions, proposed but unapproved positions and unknowns; cite the contract and authority basis. Flag missing, conflicting or stale evidence and name the next question for the recorded owner or owner role. Do not imply funding or exception approval.
activities.expectedOutput: Commercial structure assessment with precedent risks, exception questions, and cited guidance.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE owns the precedent judgment and cites the authoritative guidance rather than paraphrasing it. Investment structures get compared across customers, and one unusual shape becomes the argument for the next.
activities.requiredContext: Account name or TPID; proposed investment type, activities, timing and amount/range if known; one labeled Enrollment Number or Agreement Number; available term/commercial context and known applicable guidance or approval references.
activities.whyThisMatters: Working through the commercial shape of the investment forces a position, and a position is what the decision needs.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

activities.name: Track the approval path and unblock the next decision
activities.description: Follow an in-flight investment request through approval and identify what is actually holding it.
activities.prompt: For [investment request name or approved request reference], return a read-only status brief in chat from its existing authoritative tracker. Do not start a request-edit or approval workflow. Show approval stage, supplied evidence, outstanding items, recorded owner and next decision with source/date. Distinguish unavailable or conflicting status from a confirmed block; name the evidence question and owner role. Do not report approval as granted without authoritative evidence or change the request.
activities.expectedOutput: Approval-path status with blocking item, owner, evidence needed, and next decision.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE confirms approval state against the authoritative record before reporting it. Reporting an approval that has not landed causes the account team to commit to a customer date on the strength of it.
activities.requiredContext: Investment request name or approved matching reference; available dated tracker status and submitted evidence; known policy constraints, approval stage and owner context.
activitySteps: 1. Ask Sales Agent for authorized request status where available, or supply a permitted status extract.
2. Compare the summary with the submitted package.

3. Verify request stage, current owner and approval evidence in the authoritative tracker for that request route; MSX Deal Assistance applies where that is the submission route. ECIF Central supplies workscope/delivery detail, not a substitute approval.
4. Identify the evidenced blocking item and questions still unresolved.
5. Review and route the missing-evidence request yourself.
activities.whyThisMatters: Comparing a dated authoritative tracker view with the submitted evidence helps locate the blocker and responsible decision path.

agents.whatItIs: Investment guidance and supported workflows surfaced through Sales Agent.

Confirm request-type coverage and role permissions; this does not imply saved-workscope editing or full Agent MCR.

Generated drafts and signals still need human verification.

activities.name: Find where the approval is actually stuck
activities.description: Work out which approval a request is waiting on, who holds it, and what would move it, rather than waiting for it to surface.
activities.prompt: Analyze [dated request-tracker status, submitted package and current approval guidance] in chat to identify the approval or evidence item holding the request. Do not progress the request or open an approval workflow. Separate a confirmed block from a delay of unknown significance. Cite the approver requirement where established; otherwise give the owner question. Recommend one legitimate next action, its owner and needed evidence without claiming approval or bypassing an approver.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear read on whether the request is progressing or stalled, the specific blocker, its owner, and one action to unblock it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CE owns the judgment about whether a delay is normal or a genuine block, and never routes around an approver or represents an approval that has not been given.
activities.requiredContext: Request name or matching reference and dated tracker status; the submitted package or permitted extract; known approver requirements and applicable approval-guidance references if available.
activitySteps: 1. Open the request's authoritative tracker: use MSX Deal Assistance only for that route; ECIF workscope detail is not approval status. Use MCAPS Help for access issues.
2. Run the prompt with the dated status and inspect the reported blocker.
3. Discuss which evidence or owner question would move the decision.
activities.whyThisMatters: A dated approval snapshot and the specific missing evidence make an owner conversation more useful than another general status request.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Track the approval path and unblock the next decision

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence, and clean handoffs. Focus on the commercial and policy link in that chain.
keyTalkingPoints: Eligibility, funding, exception, and approval remain human decisions. Your contribution is to surface commercial and policy dependencies, cite authoritative guidance, and route questions to the right owner.
discussionQuestions: Which commercial dependency would slow this investment later? Which decision is genuinely yours? Which question must be routed to an authoritative owner?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Identify commercial and policy dependencies for the investment'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the investment lifecycle to the CE-owned dependency and the next governed action. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Investment commercial structure requires explicit agreement, policy and approval dependencies. Precedent or a routed question cannot replace the authorized decision. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commercial or policy dependency blocks the investment path? What evidence does its authorized owner need? How would a peer keep a proposed exception, eligibility assessment and actual approval distinct?
listenFor: Eligibility, funding, or approval implied rather than decided; exception ownership unclear; handoffs without named owners; and questions that need authoritative guidance.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one investment dependency row: commercial/policy question, evidence, proposed exception, authorized owner, approval gap and next governed action. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What would justify or disqualify the investment, and what must the accountable owner verify before committing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could map the approval dependencies for one investment and find where it is actually waiting. Eligibility, funding and resource commitments remain with authorized owners; a draft is not approval. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized investment dependency located and whether its owner clarified the blocker or held the case. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A proposed investment fits the customer need but raises an unresolved agreement or policy question. Map the dependency and decision owner without granting an exception in the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: An investment can fit a customer need while still depending on unresolved commercial, agreement or policy decisions. CE clarifies commercial options and routes; only the designated authority can approve terms, exceptions or funding.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the proposed investment and open commercial dependency in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A favorable business case cannot establish funding or exception authority. Look for a commercial dependency clearly assigned to its governed owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a favorable business case cannot establish funding or exception authority. Confirm who can explain the commercial judgment and governed approval boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

CE-INVEST.keyTakeaway: A prepared investment case is not an eligibility or funding decision; make evidence, gaps, and authority visible at each gate.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a favorable business case cannot establish funding or exception authority. Manager support can support the commercial or policy escalation without taking the investment decision.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Agree which dependency the team can clarify; do not turn a favorable business case into an exception or funding decision.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a favorable business case cannot establish funding or exception authority; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the commercial or policy escalation without taking the investment decision? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Surface delivery risk before it reaches the customer
activities.description: Review in-flight investment delivery for the technical risks that would become customer-visible.
activities.prompt: Using approved delivery status, milestone evidence and any available ECIF Agent delivery-health signals for the engagement, identify technical risks, unmet prerequisites and dependency slippage that could become customer-visible. Distinguish recorded signals from technical interpretation and unknown coverage. State evidence, confirmed owner and the intervention available now; route any milestone-change or compliance action to its authorized owner outside the huddle.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical delivery-risk brief with evidence, owners and interventions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA states the intervention available now rather than only the risk. Surfacing a delivery risk without an available action moves it to the customer attention without moving it toward resolution.
activities.requiredContext: Approved delivery status, milestone evidence, customer prerequisites; your delivery context, whether global delivery or field delivery coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
activitySteps: 1. Ask ECIF Agent through Sales Agent for available milestone and delivery-health signals within authorized scope; use approved delivery evidence if lookup is unavailable.
2. Check signal coverage and source freshness, then review dependency slippage and unmet prerequisites; no signal does not establish healthy delivery.
3. Verify milestone detail in ECIF Central where needed.
4. Name evidence, confirmed owner and an available intervention for each risk.

5. Raise urgent risks to the delivery owner. Any milestone change or role-permitted compliance action is a separate governed action outside the huddle; do not initiate Agent MCR or configure notifications.
activities.whyThisMatters: A technical delivery risk becomes actionable when its evidence, responsible owner and available intervention are explicit.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Focus on your part of that chain.
keyTalkingPoints: Every role owns one link. The chain breaks at the handoff.
Eligibility, funding and approval are human decisions. AI assembles the evidence.
An investment request without named open questions hides them rather than resolving them.
discussionQuestions: Where could investment-funded scope become undeliverable?
Which prerequisite, dependency, or owner must be confirmed before delivery starts?
What technical outcome evidence will be needed later?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Validate delivery readiness and technical dependencies'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the investment lifecycle to the CSA's delivery-readiness or outcome-evidence action on a live or sanitized case. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Funded delivery readiness requires confirmed prerequisites, accepted ownership and outcome evidence. Planned investment does not imply delivery capacity or approval. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which prerequisite or handoff could make the investment-funded delivery fail? What milestone status is verified against a dated authoritative record? How would a peer define measurable outcome evidence while leaving funding and approval with their owners?
listenFor: Funding or approval inferred from summaries; delivery status not checked against the authoritative record; unowned prerequisites; and technical outcomes that cannot be measured later.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one investment-delivery gate: prerequisite, recorded milestone status or unknown, technical owner, measurable outcome and approval question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What would justify or disqualify the investment, and what must the accountable owner verify before committing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could validate delivery readiness for one investment and name the dependency most likely to slip. Eligibility, funding and resource commitments remain with authorized owners; a draft is not approval. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized delivery dependency checked and whether it changed readiness, a hold or the evidence plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An investment-funded scope is proposed for delivery, but a technical dependency and checkpoint owner are unconfirmed. Review the readiness gap before anyone claims execution is ready.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Investment-funded delivery still depends on technical prerequisites, outcome measures and accepted ownership. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the approved scope and delivery dependencies in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Funded scope does not prove delivery readiness or acceptance. Look for an explicit readiness gate with outcome measures and accountable owners.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: funded scope does not prove delivery readiness or acceptance. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

CSA-INVEST.keyTakeaway: A prepared investment case is not an eligibility or funding decision; make evidence, gaps, and authority visible at each gate.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when funded scope does not prove delivery readiness or acceptance. Manager support can help coordinate technical and delivery owners without approving missing gates.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help expose an unconfirmed prerequisite or checkpoint owner; funding does not establish delivery readiness or customer acceptance.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that funded scope does not prove delivery readiness or acceptance; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help coordinate technical and delivery owners without approving missing gates? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment should be governed through the success plan, not treated as a separate administrative process.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment execution needs confirmed owners, milestones, handoffs and outcome evidence. Use available delivery-health signals to focus owner review; missing signals are gaps, not evidence of healthy delivery. You govern the operating rhythm and realization story, not funding or approval.
discussionQuestions: Is the investment on this account connected to the success plan, or running beside it?
Who owns delivery, and when did you last confirm status with them rather than assume it?
What evidence would the realization review need that you do not have yet?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Connect the investment to the success plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the investment rhythm to the one checkpoint you will run this month and the evidence it produces. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Track investment delivery risks and handoffs', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Investment execution should be checked against confirmed delivery status and outcomes. A progress report is not realized value, and unknown status must stay visible. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: How does this investment show up in the success plan?
Which delivery status did you confirm rather than assume?
What evidence will the realization review need, and who is producing it?
How does another CSAM bring investment realization into the success plan rather than a parallel process?
listenFor: Investment running as a parallel process rather than part of the success plan, delivery status inferred from silence, realization evidence identified only when the review is booked, and the CSAM answering eligibility or approval questions that belong elsewhere.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one investment success-plan checkpoint: agreed outcome, verified/unknown delivery state, evidence producer, review date and realization gap. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed when you confirmed status, and what evidence separates investment progress from realized value?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could run one investment checkpoint and confirm a delivery status rather than assuming it. Eligibility, funding and resource commitments remain with authorized owners; a draft is not approval. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized status confirmation and whether it changed the checkpoint or value-evidence request. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An investment milestone is described as on track, but its delivery owner has not confirmed status. Compare approved success-plan context and identify the next checkpoint question.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Investment follow-through links funded work to the success plan and evidence the customer would recognize. CSAM connects customer priorities, milestones and stakeholders; technical approval remains with the appropriate technical owner.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the investment objective and success-plan checkpoint in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Delivery of funded work does not by itself prove realized customer value. Look for a checkpoint with outcome evidence and an explicit unproven claim.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: delivery of funded work does not by itself prove realized customer value. Confirm who can explain the customer-success outcomes and stakeholder orchestration boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Check whether the support actually moved the priority
activities.description: Review what changed after partner or specialist involvement, so the next request is based on evidence rather than habit.
activities.prompt: Gather what has happened on [Customer/Account] since [last-review date] from my recent meetings, notes, chats, and files, and summarize it against this original capability gap and ask: [paste or attach the original capability gap and support ask]. Then assess whether the gap is now closed, partially closed, or unchanged, and what evidence supports that judgment. If it is unchanged, compare possible explanations such as brief, fit, timing or a misdiagnosed gap; state supporting evidence and the check needed, leaving the cause unknown where not established. If you cannot find enough recent activity to judge, say so rather than inferring. Be direct.
activities.expectedOutput: Evidence-backed comparison of the original gap with recent progress, with unresolved causes and specific confirming questions rather than a forced diagnosis.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS owns the assessment of a colleague's or partner's contribution and decides how, or whether, it is shared.
activities.requiredContext: The original capability gap and the ask made; the date support began; access to recent meetings, notes, and files, or a manual summary if access is unavailable; the current state of the technical priority.
activitySteps: 1. Restate the original gap and ask.
2. Let the agent gather recent activity, or supply it manually if the agent cannot reach the sources.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Decide whether to continue, change the ask, or stop.
5. Record the lesson for the next request.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support gets added by habit unless someone checks whether the last one worked.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on aligning partner and specialist support to technical priorities.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is a partner and specialist alignment plan with expertise gaps, owners, timing, and the next decision. AI can assemble approved evidence and draft options; you remain accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Where is technical expertise the constraint, rather than time or priority?
When you last brought in a specialist, did it change the outcome?
What would a partner need from you to arrive useful rather than catching up?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Identify partner and specialist capability gaps'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the feature gap to one specific, dated ask with the briefing that makes it answerable. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Partner and specialist support should address the actual gap: expertise, capacity or direction. Give an answerable brief and confirm who can accept the work, especially across external boundaries. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Is the gap feature, capacity, or clarity? They need different answers.
What exactly would you ask this partner or specialist to do?
What will you send them so they arrive useful rather than catching up?
How does a colleague distinguish a capability gap from a capacity or unclear-ask problem?
listenFor: Support requested by habit rather than by need, asks vague enough that anyone could decline them politely, briefings promised verbally and never sent, and customer-sensitive detail heading to an external partner without a classification step.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one support ask: capability/capacity/clarity gap, bounded task, briefing inputs, confidentiality boundary, proposed receiver and response date. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Does the gap need expertise, capacity or clearer direction, and what must the recipient confirm before acceptance?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could draft an answerable partner or specialist ask and consider what briefing would support it; no request needs to be sent for the huddle. Receiving-owner acceptance is required before treating any actual handoff as accepted; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized support ask and whether the recipient could respond or identified a scope gap. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A technical priority is blocked, but the proposed support request does not name the expertise needed. Clarify the gap and briefing before assuming a partner or specialist can contribute.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A specialist or partner request needs a specific expertise gap and a suitable briefing, not just a name on the plan. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the evidenced capability gap and intended recipient in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A proposed partner or specialist has not accepted the work. Look for a scoped expertise request with explicit evidence and acceptance gaps.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a proposed partner or specialist has not accepted the work. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. activities.name: Check request completeness before governed submission
activities.description: Review one prepared investment request and confirm its current submission route, with later submission performed by the authorized human owner.
activities.prompt: Return a completeness/route brief in chat from [investment package, opportunity linkage and current route-specific guidance]; do not start a request/submission workflow for this review. Check customer outcome, justification, supported ROI, workscope reference, applicable supplier detail and required consumption-plan evidence. Identify the program/location/business-model route; distinguish Azure Accelerate, Azure Access, non-Azure ECIF and CSP rather than assuming Navigator for every Azure offer. Cite guidance, name missing inputs/owners and unresolved route questions. Eligibility, funding, approval and later submission remain governed owner decisions.
activities.expectedOutput: A source-checked completeness and route brief with missing inputs and accountable owners. Later submission and tracker status are recorded only if the authorized human has actually submitted the reviewed package.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP verifies the business justification and actual route, then the authorized owner approves the exact submission package. Eligibility, supplier selection, policy, funding and final approval stay with their governed owners.
activities.requiredContext: Prepared request, MSX opportunity identifier, applicable workscope and consumption-plan evidence, current route-specific guidance, authorized submitter and required human reviewers.
activitySteps: Tool/access: Open Sales Agent and ask for ECIF/investment help; do not assume automatic routing. Use authorized inputs, or approved supplied evidence if lookup is unavailable. Draft/analyze only; human request edits, submission and record changes remain outside the huddle.
1. Confirm the selected program's applicable route and your authority with the process owner using current guidance.
2. Review the prepared package for completeness, keeping request drafts and workscope text distinct.
3. Verify findings and identify the owner of each missing item.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment requests slow down when inputs, owners, or open questions are hidden. Focus on readiness.
keyTalkingPoints: Separate facts from assumptions and name missing inputs, contributors, process questions and the next owner. Review available or proposed workscope text without creating or changing records. Keep workscope text distinct from a request draft; supported request-draft edits happen later, by an authorized owner. Readiness review is not eligibility or approval.
discussionQuestions: Which request input is missing? Who owns it? What should not be represented as approved?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Assess investment fit and request readiness'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from request readiness to next governed action. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Investment requests advance through evidence completeness and authoritative status checks. A drafted or submitted case is neither eligible funding nor approval. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which investment-request input is evidenced and which is missing? Who supplies it and who decides eligibility or approval? What did a colleague learn about a handoff that delayed a previous request?
listenFor: Eligibility or funding implied rather than confirmed, hidden open questions, and contributor inputs without owners.

activities.name: Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks

activities.prompt: I run this recurring workflow: [describe the workflow, trigger, cadence and consumers]. Here is a recent example of it going badly: [one recent failure example]. Break the workflow into its actual steps. For each step, identify what input it needs, what decision it requires, and who owns it. Then tell me which two or three steps most likely cost time or quality, and why you think so. Ask me for anything you need rather than assuming it. Do not propose tools yet.

activities.requiredContext: A recurring workflow you personally run; a recent concrete example; who owns each step; what inputs the workflow depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Describe the workflow and one recent example.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Correct the step map where the model got your work wrong; that correction is where the learning is.
5. Agree as a group which step leaks the most.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most workflow friction is invisible to the person living with it, because they have already adapted to it.

activities.name: Design one bounded experiment you can finish this week
activities.description: Turn the real end-to-end bottleneck into a one-week test tied to an outcome, with explicit permissions, human review, leading evidence, and a capability or improvement worth learning about.
activities.prompt: Here is the business outcome and end-to-end workflow I want to improve: [paste the outcome and workflow map]. Here is the bottleneck: [bottleneck step and its observed consequence]. Design a one-week experiment. Specify the exact input, action, output, permissions, reviewer, stop condition, human accountability, downstream effect to watch, and leading evidence across time, quality, risk, customer value, or capability added. Keep it small enough to run in under an hour total. Suggest a best-fit tool only after the test is clear. If the scope is too large, narrow it rather than proposing a bigger plan.
activities.expectedOutput: A bounded experiment card with outcome, input, action, output, permissions, reviewer, stop condition, downstream effect, and leading evidence of efficiency, quality, risk reduction, customer value, or capability added.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide whether the experiment is genuinely small enough to finish, and you own the judgment about what output is safe to use in real work.
activities.requiredContext: The business outcome; end-to-end workflow map; selected bottleneck; accessible data and systems; required permissions or approvals; downstream users; and an available human reviewer.
activitySteps: 1. Take the step your group identified.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut the experiment down until it fits in an hour.
4. Name your reviewer and your stop condition out loud.
5. Put it in your calendar before you leave the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A fast task is not transformation if it moves the bottleneck downstream. A bounded test should improve the whole workflow or prove a capability the team could not reasonably use before.

Do not claim the experiment succeeded if the evidence is incomplete.

2. Run the prompt using only that supplied information.

4. The workflow owner decides whether to stop, adjust, or continue.
5. Record the decision, next action, owner, and evidence to bring back.
activities.whyThisMatters: Designing a test is not enough; the team needs to learn from the evidence and decide what changes in the workflow.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle has no pre-written workflow. Start with a business outcome, choose work people actually run, map the flow end to end, and simplify it before proposing AI. The goal is a better workflow and a useful learning loop, not a tool demonstration.
keyTalkingPoints: The workflow must be recurring and tied to a business or customer outcome.
Someone in the room must own it.
Map the whole flow, including inputs, decisions, handoffs, permissions, approvals, output, and downstream users.
Improve obvious process friction before adding AI.
A specific recent example beats a general description.
discussionQuestions: What outcome are we trying to improve?
What workflow most influences it, and who experiences the result?
Where does the end-to-end flow lose time, quality, confidence, or customer value?
What is impractical today that AI might make possible?
Where must a person review, approve, or intervene?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the outcome to the end-to-end flow, from the flow to its real bottleneck, and from that bottleneck to one bounded experiment with an owner, reviewer, stop condition, and leading evidence. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Workflow improvement starts with the outcome and follows the whole flow, including downstream effects. A bounded test preserves permissions, a human checkpoint and honest benefit or failure evidence. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Where does the end-to-end workflow lose time, quality, confidence, or customer value?
Would improving one step move the bottleneck downstream?
What should be simplified before AI is added?
What could the team accomplish that is impractical today?
What permissions, monitoring, approval, or human intervention does the test require?
What would a one-week experiment look like?
Where did a peer's one-step AI improvement move the bottleneck downstream?
listenFor: Tool adoption presented as the outcome, a single-task speedup that moves the queue downstream, inaccessible inputs, missing permissions or approvals, an output nobody would notice if it were wrong, and experiments too broad to finish in a week. Also note capability-add opportunities that improve decisions, anticipate risk, or explore more options rather than only saving time.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one end-to-end workflow map and experiment card: trigger, inputs, decisions, handoffs, bottleneck, bounded test, permissions, reviewer and stop condition. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn about the whole workflow? Name one friction to remove, one new capability AI might add, one downstream risk, and the judgment that must stay human.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a small workflow test you can own, or adapt the idea without running it. Any actual test must respect permitted inputs, human checkpoints and stop conditions; observations of benefit, harm or no benefit must not be invented. Approvals and outreach must not be automated. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized observation: time or rework changed, a quality issue caught, a capability explored, or no benefit. You might describe a human correction or a possibility for the team to explore. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A recurring workflow contains repeated handoffs and avoidable rework. Map the friction and choose one small test, keeping approvals and customer outreach with humans.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Workflow improvement starts with recurring friction and a small test whose benefit is still to be observed. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the familiar task, friction and bounded experiment in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Tool availability does not establish workflow benefit or a successful experiment. Look for a small human-owned test with a baseline, safeguards and an honest not-run state.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: tool availability does not establish workflow benefit or a successful experiment. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Find out what this customer actually owns
activities.description: Retrieve the agreements, enrollments, and license estate for one of your own accounts, so you know what the customer already has before you talk to them.
activities.prompt: Show existing agreements and enrollments for [Account Name or TPID] in chat, with type/status. For the agreement I select next, show license estate grouped by SKU. This is read-only fact retrieval; do not start a DealBook, pre-approval or other commercial creation workflow. Cite sources and name missing data rather than estimate it. Do not infer entitlements that the records do not establish.
activities.expectedOutput: A list of agreements and enrollments for the account, plus license estate grouped by SKU for one agreement.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You confirm the retrieved data matches the account you meant, and treat entitlement and licensing detail as information to verify with the deal owner before making any customer-facing commitment.
activities.requiredContext: Account name or TPID for the account-level list; select the specific agreement for license-estate detail. Access to Sales Agent with your CRM scope connected.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account you work on during the activity, using already-authorized context, or use a permitted shared example arranged by the facilitator; no new account material is required.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt with the account name or TPID.
4. Pick one agreement from what comes back and ask for the license estate grouped by SKU.
5. Note anything you did not know.
6. Note anything you had assumed that turned out to be different.
activities.whyThisMatters: Verified ownership and licensing context prevent customer conversations from starting with an unsupported assumption about what was purchased.

activities.name: See what is expiring and what that means for your work
activities.description: Surface upcoming renewals and consumption trend for your account, then work out what it changes for your own role rather than for the deal owner's.
activities.prompt: Return renewal facts in chat for [Account Name or TPID]: upcoming renewals, expiry dates, existing agreement details and month-over-month ACR over [review period]. Inspect existing records only; do not start a pre-approval or other commercial workflow. Cite sources/dates, distinguish recorded terms and measured consumption from unavailable data and do not estimate gaps. Do not recommend a renewal strategy; I will decide my role's action before the nearest expiry.
activities.expectedOutput: Upcoming renewals with expiry dates, agreement detail, and consumption trend, plus one action your own role owns ahead of that date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide what the timing means for your own work, and leave renewal strategy, pricing, and commercial approach to the account owner and Commercial Executive.
activities.requiredContext: Authorized account name or TPID from an existing permitted source, or the earlier lookup if used; your own role's commitments on that account.
activitySteps: 1. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
2. Run the prompt for your account.
3. Note the nearest expiry date.
4. Work backwards: what does your role need to have done before that date?
5. Name the one thing you would otherwise have found out too late.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal date is a deadline for every role touching the account, not only for the person who owns the deal.

activities.name: Draw the line between what you can answer and what you should hand off
activities.description: Sort the deal questions you get asked into ones you can now answer yourself and ones that belong to the deal owner, so you stop escalating retrievable facts and stop answering commercial questions you should not.
activities.prompt: Sort [deal-related questions I have been asked] into factual retrieval versus commercial, pricing, policy or approval decisions. For each retrievable question, give a prompt with its relevant labelled account, Opportunity ID, Enrollment Number or Agreement Number input, not every identifier. Do not answer the commercial decisions. Identify their accountable person only from [supplied contacts]; otherwise give the owner role and a confirmation question.
activities.expectedOutput: Your questions sorted into retrievable and decision-requiring, with a prompt for the first group and an owner for the second.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You own the judgment about where the line sits on your accounts, and confirm that anything commercial, pricing, policy, or approval related routes to the accountable owner rather than being answered from retrieved data.
activities.requiredContext: Real questions you have been asked. Knowledge of who owns commercial decisions on your accounts.
activitySteps: 1. List the deal questions you have been asked in the last month.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Check the split against your own judgment.
4. Choose one potentially retrievable question and check what evidence and access would be needed to answer it.
5. Pick one you should always route, and confirm who owns it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Two failures cost time: escalating a question you could have answered, and answering one you should have escalated.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Deal making features live inside Sales Agent. There is no separate agent to select: when you ask Sales a deal-related question, those features answer. This session is not about learning to run deals. It is about being able to find deal facts for your own accounts, whatever your role, instead of waiting for someone to send them to you.
keyTalkingPoints: Deal-related capabilities are accessed through Sales Agent; confirm the supported scenario and your access before using them. Use approved TPID, agreement or enrollment identifiers to ground a lookup, and verify the returned source and date. Keep one deal per thread so context remains inspectable. Looking up permitted deal facts does not authorize commercial decisions, approvals or material amendments.
discussionQuestions: When did you last need agreement, licensing, or renewal information and have to ask someone for it?
How long did that take, and what did you do while waiting?
What have you assumed about a customer's entitlements that you have never actually verified?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find out what this customer actually owns'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the lookup you ran to the single fact that changes how you would open your next conversation with that customer. No Extended follow-up is listed for this placement.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Retrieved deal facts can improve account work, but entitlement, renewal and usage need source and scope checks. Commercial interpretation stays with the deal owner and CE. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
facilitatorQuestions: What did the lookup return that you did not already know?
What did you previously assume about this customer's estate that turned out to be wrong or unverified?
Where does this stop being your call and become the deal owner's?
How does a peer verify a retrieved deal fact without treating it as approved pricing or taking the deal owner's decision?
listenFor: Vague prompts producing vague answers, which is the most common reason people conclude deal making does not work. A first response being treated as final on a complex deal, when the guidance is to re-run and verify against current data. Several unrelated deals being worked in one chat thread. Someone treating a retrieved figure as approved pricing or a commitment, or stepping past retrieval into structuring a deal that belongs to the AE or Commercial Executive. Also note the opposite: someone escalating a question they could now answer themselves.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one deal-fact lookup plan: entitlement/agreement question, dated available fact or unknown, source owner and boundary requiring AE/CE handoff. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal assumption changed when you inspected the evidence, and who owns the next decision or approval?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could verify a retrieved agreement, entitlement or renewal fact against a permitted source and intended account before a customer conversation. If access is unavailable, ask the source owner or use a sanitized example; route commercial questions to the deal owner or CE. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized retrieval fact or gap and whether checking it improved preparation or avoided unnecessary escalation; omit the prompt response and agreement details. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A teammate needs an entitlement fact before a conversation but has only an uncertain identifier. Verify the intended account and permitted lookup, or record the access gap instead of guessing.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Entitlement lookup supports a work question only when the account and agreement scope are correct. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the permitted account example and intended agreement or enrollment identifier.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A retrieved fact may refer to the wrong account or be unavailable. Look for an account-scoped fact checked against its source with gaps retained.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a retrieved fact may refer to the wrong account or be unavailable. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ALL-DEAL.keyTakeaway: Make the next decision and its prerequisites visible before asking customers, partners, or internal teams to act.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a retrieved fact may refer to the wrong account or be unavailable. Manager support can help resolve identifier or access questions through the accountable owner.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish a retrieved fact from licensing or commercial advice; retain an access gap instead of asking the group to guess.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a retrieved fact may refer to the wrong account or be unavailable; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help resolve identifier or access questions through the accountable owner? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

AE-HEALTH.wiifm: Earlier awareness of dissatisfaction gives the account team room to protect customer trust and coordinate support before concerns become a surprise executive escalation.
