AE-HEALTH.description: Interpret customer, technical, and delivery signals, identify material risk or satisfaction gaps, and agree the intervention, owner, and evidence needed to assess progress.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. Coaches partner sellers and inspects renewal and consumption-commitment opportunities, avoiding duplicate pipeline attribution while keeping customer decisions with account teams and partner records and economics with partners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)
roles.description: A leadership audience focused on strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies. Brings attention to issues requiring strategic intervention and communicates decisions and direction, with action and escalation shaped by each participant's applicable authority rather than a shared management remit.
roles.descriptionSummary: A leadership audience for strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Read what the customer's satisfaction data already says
activities.description: Pull the satisfaction, support and relationship signals for one account and separate what the data shows from what you assumed.
activities.prompt: Give me a CX health summary for [account name or TPID]. Show OSAT, DSAT and VSAT with their trend over the last four fiscal months, the ATQ and RM scores, and the most recent verbatims. Tell me which metric moved most and when it moved only where the source definitions, scales and periods support comparison; otherwise explain why a largest movement cannot be established. For each requested metric, name missing coverage and undefined source labels rather than omitting it or inventing an expansion. Use source definitions and sample/coverage metadata where available, and flag gaps. Keep CX Vitals and respondent details out of customer-facing drafts.
activities.expectedOutput: A satisfaction summary for one account with OSAT, DSAT, VSAT, ATQ and RM trends, recent verbatims, the largest metric movement only where comparable, otherwise an explicit comparison gap, and any metric with no coverage named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether the data matches the relationship they actually have. Where the score and the lived relationship disagree, that gap is the finding, and the AE names which one they trust and why.
activities.requiredContext: One account you own and its TPID; your own current read on how that customer feels; Sales Agent access.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account you own during the activity and check its TPID using already-authorized context, or use a permitted TPID-mapped example arranged by the facilitator. CX Vitals covers only TPID-mapped accounts; if mapping or access is missing, discuss the evidence gap manually rather than require advance setup.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Open Sales Agent and run the prompt if the mapped-account evidence and authorized access are available; otherwise use the permitted example or manual evidence-gap fallback in step 1.
4. Compare what the data shows against what you believed about this account before you ran it.
5. Note any metric returned as no data, and treat that as unknown rather than healthy.
6. Keep the output internal. CX Vitals content is Microsoft internal and must not be shared with the customer.
activities.whyThisMatters: You already have a satisfaction signal on most accounts. Not looking at it is a choice, and it is usually the reason a deteriorating account becomes a surprise.

activities.name: Rank your portfolio by where satisfaction is deteriorating
activities.description: Compare satisfaction across the accounts you own so attention goes to the steepest decline rather than the loudest customer.
activities.prompt: Rank accounts in [account list or territory scope] by OSAT, lowest first, and separately show me the accounts whose OSAT has declined most over the last two quarters. Flag any account scoring below 3.5. For each flagged account, show the DSAT drivers and the most negative recent verbatims. Do not compare my accounts against another seller's portfolio. Treat 3.5 as the stated screening threshold for this exercise, not a policy or automatic escalation rule. Include sample size and as-of date where available. Keep CX Vitals and respondent details out of customer-facing drafts.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked views of satisfaction level and decline, with sub-3.5 screening flags, available sample sizes and supporting feedback.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Check the trend and sample size against known customer issues before deciding which finding needs attention.
activities.requiredContext: Your owned account list mapped to TPIDs; any known open escalations so you can discount what is already being handled.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt within your authorized account scope; do not compare other sellers' accounts.
2. Compare low scores with steep declines and check whether an issue is already being addressed.
3. Discuss which finding needs a confirming check.
activities.whyThisMatters: Comparing absolute score, direction of change and sample size helps distinguish known low satisfaction from a new deterioration that needs investigation.

activities.name: Turn the satisfaction finding into an owned intervention
activities.description: Turn one satisfaction finding into a proposed response with the right people and a clear next check.
activities.prompt: For [Customer/Account], I need to act on a declining satisfaction signal. Using the CX evidence, help me draft an intervention plan: what the evidence suggests is wrong, which of those causes I can address and which belong to support or delivery, and the specific next action with an owner and date. Check whether the evidence already warrants escalation through the established route; if not, state what further change would trigger it. Separate what the data evidences from what is my inference. Keep CX Vitals and respondent details out of customer-facing drafts.
activities.expectedOutput: A proposed response separating observed dissatisfaction, possible causes, actions and questions about ownership or escalation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Confirm the possible cause with the account team before acting; a satisfaction score alone does not explain it.
activities.requiredContext: The satisfaction evidence for one account; who owns support and delivery for that customer; your escalation route.
activitySteps: 1. Use existing satisfaction evidence for an authorized account or a permitted shared case; completing a previous practice is not required.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Split the causes into ones you own and ones that belong to support, delivery or the CSU; confirm possible causes before acting.
5. Confirm the person and date for each action; keep unconfirmed assignments or dates explicit rather than inventing agreement.
6. Confirm the established escalation route and applicable threshold. If the evidence already warrants escalation, use that route rather than waiting for the situation to worsen.
activities.whyThisMatters: A satisfaction signal is useful when it leads to a proportionate confirming check and, where warranted, an owned response; the score alone does not establish cause or the right intervention.

activities.name: Mine the verbatims for what the score hides
activities.description: Read what customers actually wrote rather than the number it rolled up into, and find the theme the score cannot show.
activities.prompt: Show me all recent verbatims for [account name or TPID] and group them by theme. For each theme, tell me how many comments support it, whether it is getting better or worse over time, and whether it points at product, support, delivery or relationship. Quote the customer's own words rather than paraphrasing. Do not infer a theme from a single comment. Keep CX Vitals and respondent details out of customer-facing drafts.
activities.expectedOutput: Verbatim themes with supporting comment counts, direction of travel, the function each points at, and the customer's own wording preserved.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which themes are real signal and which are one unhappy individual. A single strong comment is not a pattern. The AE is also accountable for the boundary: verbatims inform the questions you ask, and never appear in anything the customer sees.
activities.requiredContext: One account with verbatim coverage; the themes you already believe are true so you can test them.
activitySteps: 1. Use an account where the score alone has not explained the situation.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Read the actual quotes before reading the themes.
5. Discard any theme resting on a single comment.
6. Use the customer's own vocabulary in your next conversation rather than translating it into internal terms, but never quote a verbatim directly or reveal that you have their survey responses.
activities.whyThisMatters: The number tells you something is wrong. The verbatims tell you what. Only one of those is useful in the next customer conversation.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Read what the customer's satisfaction data already says

activities.description: Compare satisfaction movement across your accounts and choose which change to investigate.
activities.prompt: Across [account list or territory scope], show me current OSAT with its trend, any account scoring below 3.5, where the most negative recent verbatims sit, and where the support experience measured by ATQ is getting worse. Rank by size of recent movement rather than absolute score. Do not compare my accounts against another seller's portfolio. Use 3.5 only as this exercise's screening threshold; do not infer a policy breach or automatic escalation. Keep CX Vitals and respondent details out of customer-facing drafts.
activities.expectedOutput: A portfolio satisfaction sweep ranked by recent movement, with sub-3.5 accounts, negative verbatims and worsening support experience identified, plus a dated record to compare against next time.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which movements are real. A single survey response can move a score on a small account without anything having changed, and the AE owns that judgment rather than the ranking.
activities.requiredContext: Your owned account list with TPIDs; the note or record from your previous sweep if you have one; the review rhythm this should feed.
activitySteps: 1. Choose the authorized, TPID-mapped accounts covered by the check.

2. If a verified earlier result is available, compare like-for-like dated results, noting coverage gaps and small samples. Otherwise record a dated current baseline; do not invent a previous result or a change between runs.
3. Discuss one evidenced change or current finding and the next question to investigate.
activities.whyThisMatters: Comparing a dated result with a verified prior result can expose changing customer perception; absent data or an absent prior baseline is unknown, not improvement.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most accounts already carry a satisfaction signal the seller has never looked at. Focus on reading it, deciding whether it matches the relationship you think you have, and acting while the conversation is still yours to lead.
keyTalkingPoints: Use available CX Vitals in Sales Agent as internal, read-only evidence for the identified account. Confirm scope with its TPID, verify freshness and distinguish the score from account-team interpretation. Do not copy internal signals into customer-facing material.
discussionQuestions: Which account are you most confident about, and when did you last check that confidence against data?
Where would a satisfaction score and your own read of the relationship disagree?
Who tells you first today when a customer becomes unhappy?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Read what the customer's satisfaction data already says'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the account picture to the single account each person will act on this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Mine the verbatims for what the score hides', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Satisfaction trends prompt investigation and owned intervention, not automatic customer conclusions. Compare the data with relationship evidence before acting. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Where did the data disagree with your own read, and which one do you trust?
Which of the causes you found do you actually own, and which belong to support or delivery?
What would have to get worse before you escalate this?
What evidence would a colleague use to challenge both the satisfaction score and the account team's intuition?
listenFor: Sellers treating a score as a diagnosis rather than a symptom, accounts written off as fine without evidence, surprise at what verbatims say, and anyone about to take an internal metric into a customer conversation.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one satisfaction evidence card: customer signal, alternative explanation, source/date, intervention owner and escalation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the data tell you about a customer that you did not already know, and what will you do differently because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a CX health summary for an account you are uncertain about and consider whether any intervention is warranted. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized mismatch between signal and expectation and whether checking it improved the intervention or exposed an uncertain cause. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An account feels healthy to the AE, while a dated satisfaction signal suggests friction. Compare the approved evidence and identify a proportionate next customer-outcome question.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Account health brings relationship judgment together with dated satisfaction evidence; missing feedback remains unknown. AE owns the account plan and opportunity judgment; technical, commercial and delivery decisions stay with their accountable roles.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the account identifier and satisfaction signal in the example before discussing a discrepancy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Missing satisfaction data means unknown, not healthy. Look for a discrepancy between relationship judgment and source evidence.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: missing satisfaction data means unknown, not healthy. Confirm who can explain the account and opportunity ownership boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

activities.name: Find out what you actually inherited
activities.description: Assemble the history, relationships, open work and unresolved risk on an account you are taking on, before you speak to anyone.
activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID], prepare an inherited-context brief: customer-stated priorities, open opportunities/stages, commitments and milestones, support/delivery escalations, stakeholders and recorded relationship owners, and unresolved or overdue items. Cite available sources and dates. Distinguish customer statements from record entries or interpretation; name thin, stale, conflicting or unavailable context and the questions only the outgoing seller can settle. Missing risk evidence does not establish a healthy account. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: An inherited-context brief covering priorities, open opportunities, commitments, escalations and stakeholders, with the thin or stale parts of the record explicitly named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what the silence means. An account with no recorded risk is not a healthy account, it is an unwritten one, and the incoming seller must treat an empty field as unknown rather than as good news.
activities.requiredContext: The customer/account you are inheriting or handing over; access to MSX for that account; the name of the outgoing or incoming seller.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account you are inheriting or handing over during the activity from already-authorized context, or use a permitted transition example arranged by the facilitator. No new handoff packet is required to attend.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the record says from what it does not say. The gaps matter more than the summary.
5. Write down the three questions only the outgoing seller can answer.
6. Do not contact the customer yet. The internal handoff comes first.
activities.whyThisMatters: You inherit whatever the last person wrote down, and most of what mattered was never written down. Finding that out before the customer meeting is the difference between a handover and a restart.

activities.name: Run the internal handoff conversation properly
activities.description: Turn the gaps you found into the specific questions for the outgoing seller, and capture the answers where the next person will find them.
activities.prompt: Here is what I found on the inherited account and here is what is missing: the supplied gaps. Help me prepare the internal handoff conversation with the outgoing seller. Draft the specific questions I should ask about relationships, unwritten history, sensitivities, commitments made verbally, and anything that would embarrass me in front of this customer. Prioritize the questions whose answers exist only in that person's head. Give me questions to confirm who will notify the customer and how; do not assume that notification is already agreed.
activities.expectedOutput: A prioritized outgoing-seller question list. After the human handoff conversation, reviewed answers and the confirmed customer-notification plan are captured through the authorized process.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what is safe to record. Some relationship context is candid and belongs in a conversation rather than a permanent field, and the seller owns that line rather than transcribing everything.
activities.requiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and its gaps; time with the outgoing seller; access to update the account record in MSX.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the inherited-context brief and its evidence gaps.
2. Run the prompt to prepare the outgoing-seller questions.
3. Hold the internal handoff conversation and capture answers, separating customer statements from seller interpretation.
4. Confirm who will introduce the incoming owner to the customer and the notification approach.
5. Review what is appropriate for a permanent record, then update it yourself through the authorized process; discuss sensitive relationship context separately.
activities.whyThisMatters: The handoff conversation is the only chance to collect what was never written down. Held badly, the next transition starts from the same empty record.

activities.name: Prepare the customer conversation that earns the relationship
activities.description: Plan the introduction so the customer hears continuity and a reason to invest in a new relationship, not an administrative notification.
activities.prompt: I am being introduced to [Account Name or TPID] as their new [role], using my inherited-context brief. Help me prepare the first conversation. I want to show I already understand their priorities and open commitments, ask what the record cannot tell me, and give them a reason to invest in this relationship. Draft the opening, the three questions worth their time, and how I acknowledge anything that has gone wrong recently without over-promising. Do not invent history I have not confirmed.
activities.expectedOutput: A first-conversation plan with an opening that demonstrates continuity, three questions the record could not answer, and a considered position on any recent problem.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to acknowledge. Raising a known problem you cannot yet fix builds credibility only if you also say what happens next, and the seller judges whether that is ready.
activities.requiredContext: Account Name or TPID; your inherited-context brief and the handoff answers; the outgoing seller's introduction plan; the customer stakeholders you will meet.
activitySteps: 1. Use the context and the answers from the internal handoff.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Cut anything you cannot personally stand behind. Confidence about details you have not verified is what damages a first meeting.
5. Agree with the outgoing seller how the introduction is made.
6. Hold the introduction and record its actual status and follow-through owner through your usual approved process.
activities.whyThisMatters: The customer did not choose this change and is measuring whether it costs them. The first conversation is where they decide whether to invest in you or wait you out.

activities.name: Pressure-test what you are handing over
activities.description: Look at an account you are handing on and find what only exists in your own head, before it is lost.
activities.prompt: I am handing over [Customer/Account]. Ask me if the scope is unclear. First, based on what is recorded in MSX, tell me what an incoming seller would and would not understand about this account. Then interview me: ask me up to six questions, one at a time, designed to surface what I know that is not written anywhere, covering informal relationships, the history behind a decision, sensitivities, verbal commitments and who actually influences outcomes. Do not guess my answers. After I have answered, organize what I told you into what belongs in the record and what is better said in conversation.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on what the record fails to convey, plus your own tacit knowledge drawn out through questioning and sorted into what to record and what to say in person.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The outgoing seller decides which commitments must be written down. A verbal commitment that dies with the handover becomes the incoming seller's credibility problem and the customer's evidence that Microsoft does not remember.
activities.requiredContext: An account you are handing over; your own knowledge of its unwritten history; access to update the record.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account you are handing over, or one you know well.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt. It will read the record first, then ask you questions; answer them as you go.
4. Be specific in your answers. The value of this is entirely in what you say, not what the tool retrieves.
5. Record the parts it identifies as belonging in the system, and plan to say the rest in conversation.
6. Check whether any verbal commitment you mentioned is captured anywhere.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every seller who inherited a thin account was handed it by someone who knew more than they recorded. This is where that stops being someone else's problem.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find out what you actually inherited

activities.name: Own the ninety days after the introduction
activities.description: Convert what the customer said in the first meeting into commitments with dates, so the transition is judged on follow-through rather than on the meeting.
activities.prompt: Turn [first customer-conversation notes] into a ninety-day follow-through plan: commitments made, customer requests, work needing another Microsoft role and evidence of delivery expected by the ninety-day point. Preserve confirmed commitments and dates; label proposed actions, dates and owner roles, with acceptance unconfirmed. Flag promises not supported by my authority or available resources and the question needed before relying on them. Do not invent commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A ninety-day follow-through plan with commitments, owners, dates, and any unconfirmed promise flagged for resolution.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms every commitment is one they can actually keep. A transition is judged on whether the first promise was kept, and an unkept one costs more than the original change did.
activities.requiredContext: Your notes from the first customer conversation; the commitments you made; the Microsoft roles who would own anything outside your control.
activitySteps: 1. Open your notes from the first customer conversation.
2. Paste those notes into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it.
3. Check every commitment it identifies. Deal with anything you promised without meaning to.
4. Put dates against each item and name owners for anything that is not yours.
5. Put a date on the ninety-day point now, while it still feels urgent.
activities.whyThisMatters: Transitions are not judged by the introduction meeting. They are judged ninety days later, on whether the thing you said you would do happened.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Prepare the customer conversation that earns the relationship

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every seller in this room has inherited an account with nothing useful written down, and every seller has handed one over. Focus on the transition you are in the middle of right now, on either side of it.
keyTalkingPoints: Verify current transition timing and completion requirements for the applicable segment and geography with authoritative guidance. Make contacts, the current plan, open commitments and the customer conversation usable to the receiving seller. Record actual acceptance and unresolved gaps; populated fields alone do not prove a completed transition.
discussionQuestions: What is the worst account you have ever inherited, and what specifically was missing?
What do you know about your accounts that exists nowhere in MSX?
When a customer is handed a new seller, what does it actually cost them?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find out what you actually inherited'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from what the record is missing to the one conversation each person needs to have this week, internal or customer-facing. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Pressure-test what you are handing over', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Account continuity depends on tacit context reaching the next owner with accepted responsibility. Record updates support transition but cannot replace the right conversation. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: What did the record fail to tell you that you needed?
What do you know that would be lost if you handed this account over tomorrow?
What would this customer say if you asked them how the last transition went?
What unwritten commitment has a peer receiver needed to avoid making the customer start over?
listenFor: Transitions treated as administration rather than as a customer experience, records closed before the customer meeting happened, verbal commitments nobody has captured, and sellers assuming an empty risk field means there is no risk.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one transition brief: inherited fact, unwritten commitment, customer continuity risk, outgoing/receiving-role question and proposed next conversation. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you find missing from an account record that you assumed would be there, and what will you write down differently because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore what permitted tacit account context would help a transition owner and what conversation or acceptance would still be needed; updating the record or completing a transition is not required. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized manual scenario or leave the gap open; no report is required. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized continuity gap captured and whether it reduced repeated questions or improved transition. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An inherited account has operational records but lacks context about an open customer concern. Identify what can be captured safely and what the transition owner still needs to clarify.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Account transition combines recorded information with safe transfer of the context an incoming owner cannot infer. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the account-transition example and known continuity questions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: An internal handoff is not permission to contact the customer immediately. Look for a gap between the record and tacit context with the right outgoing owner.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: an internal handoff is not permission to contact the customer immediately. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ALL-TRANSITION.keyTakeaway: A handoff is complete when the receiving owner accepts the work and knows the decision, evidence, boundaries, and next step.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when an internal handoff is not permission to contact the customer immediately. Manager support can help arrange outgoing and receiving-owner time before the customer experiences the transition.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help clarify what the outgoing owner still needs to explain; an internal handoff does not itself authorize immediate customer outreach.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that an internal handoff is not permission to contact the customer immediately; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help arrange outgoing and receiving-owner time before the customer experiences the transition? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

ALL-HANDOFF.roleTopicName: Make the Handoff Land Where It Is Received
ALL-HANDOFF.roleTopicDescription: Prepare, run and close a handoff between roles so the receiving team can act on it the same day rather than reconstructing it.
ALL-HANDOFF.wiifm: A usable handoff reduces reconstruction and preventable delays, making it easier for colleagues to continue customer work without relying on your unwritten knowledge.
ALL-HANDOFF.name: Transfer Work with Accepted Ownership
ALL-HANDOFF.description: Transfer a decision, route, or work item to an accountable receiver with the context, intent, evidence, constraints, acceptance criteria, and re-entry path needed to continue.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Engages early with the opportunity owner to shape executable commercial constructs across Microsoft and partner transaction routes. Navigates negotiation guardrails, coordinates owner-validated policy and licensing questions, routes approvals and exceptions, and hands off approved terms while addressing renewal commercial risk.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes SME&C commercial terms across transaction routes and coordinates approvals and renewals.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. Supports covered consumption portfolios through milestone readiness, partner and scale-engine handoffs, targeted adoption and technical interventions, attributed value evidence, and expansion hypotheses without assuming blanket customer or partner-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports covered SME&C consumption portfolios with readiness, handoffs, and targeted interventions.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: All Roles
roles.description: An audience for shared Enterprise content supporting recurring cross-role workflows, not an individual job. Emphasizes evidence reuse, output review, and accepted handoffs across roles while retaining existing decision authority and avoiding new ownership assignments.
roles.descriptionSummary: An audience for shared Enterprise cross-role workflows, evidence reuse, and accepted handoffs.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM-R
roles.description: Develops a recruitment portfolio from qualification and partnership development through launch, a first transactable listing, and early wins. Mobilizes technical specialists, coordinates validated readiness, and prepares graduation handoffs accepted by accountable owners, with program approvals and graduation criteria retained by authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Recruits EPS partners from qualification to launch, first transactable listings, and early wins.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. Coaches partner sellers and inspects renewal and consumption-commitment opportunities, avoiding duplicate pipeline attribution while keeping customer decisions with account teams and partner records and economics with partners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: All Roles
roles.description: An audience for shared SME&C cross-role workflows, not a formal job. Supports evidence-based coordination and accepted handoffs among account, specialist, technical, partner, and success roles while retaining current authority and existing ownership boundaries.
roles.descriptionSummary: An audience for SME&C workflows, evidence-based cross-role coordination, and accepted handoffs.

ALL-HANDOFF.todayObjective: Test a cross-role opportunity or milestone handoff from the receiver's perspective, examining qualification evidence, missing context, stalled transfers, and the acceptance conversation.
ALL-HANDOFF.whyItMatters: Explicit ownership and preserved context prevent dropped decisions, repeated discovery, and unauthorized assumptions across role or team boundaries.
ALL-HANDOFF.desiredOutcome: Send and recover cross-role handoffs with sufficient verified context and explicit receiver acceptance, recognizing that a completed transfer record alone does not establish ownership.

activities.name: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role
activities.description: Check that an opportunity being handed on has the qualification evidence the receiving role needs, before you transfer it rather than after they reject it.
activities.prompt: For Opportunity ID [Opportunity ID], review [qualification evidence and receiving-team criteria] for specialist handoff. Identify gaps in the customer outcome, business/technical decision makers, evidenced budget/timing, blockers and mitigations, and the linked milestone's supported value/date or explicitly applicable non-monetary measure. Apply only the supplied criteria. Separate facts from assertions; for each material gap name the evidence needed and owner-role question. Do not invent values, declare receiver acceptance or advance records.
activities.expectedOutput: A gap list against the qualification the receiving role needs, covering outcome, decision makers, budget, timing, blockers and milestone completeness.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what is genuinely known versus assumed. Handing over an assumption dressed as a qualified fact is worse than handing over an acknowledged gap, because the receiving role will act on it.
activities.requiredContext: One opportunity being transferred, with its ID; the milestone attached to it; the qualification criteria your team applies.
activitySteps: 1. Choose one opportunity you are about to hand over, or one you recently received.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Treat every gap as work to do before the transfer, not after.
5. Verify the date and applicable value or outcome measure from evidence; flag unknowns rather than entering an artificial non-zero value.
6. If you received this handoff, send the gap list back rather than rebuilding it silently.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most handoffs are rejected or quietly rebuilt because the receiving role cannot act on what arrived. The gap was always visible before the transfer; nobody looked.

activities.name: Write the handoff so the next role does not have to ask
activities.description: Capture qualification, customer context and relevant unwritten detail in the record so the next role can use it before and after the handoff conversation.
activities.prompt: Using the supplied opportunity gap list and customer notes, help me write handoff notes for the receiving role identified there. Cover what the customer is trying to achieve and in their own words where I have them, what has been agreed and what has not, who influences the decision and how, what I have already tried, and what I would warn the receiving person about. Write it so someone who has never spoken to this customer could pick it up. Flag anything I have written that is my opinion rather than something the customer said. Ground decision roles and influence in the supplied evidence; mark unknown authority rather than inventing it. Keep consequential delivery warnings, but omit unnecessary personal or confidential relationship judgments and flag material needing sender/audience review before recording. Drafted notes do not establish receiver acceptance.
activities.expectedOutput: Handoff notes covering customer outcome, agreed and unagreed items, decision influence, what has been tried, and warnings, with opinion separated from evidence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what belongs in a permanent record. Candid relationship context may be better said than written, and the sender owns that judgment rather than transcribing everything.
activities.requiredContext: Your gap list; what the customer has said in their own words; the receiving role and who specifically will take it.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the gap list you produced in the previous practice.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the customer actually said from your interpretation of it, and label both.
5. Put the notes in the record, not in a chat message. Chat is not where the next person will look.
6. Hold the handoff conversation as well. The notes make the conversation shorter, not unnecessary.
activities.whyThisMatters: The handoff conversation happens once and is forgotten. The record is what the receiving role actually works from, and what the person after them inherits.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role

activities.name: Find the handoffs that stalled in the gap between roles
activities.description: Look across your opportunities and milestones for transfers that were started and never completed, where ownership is ambiguous and nothing is moving.
activities.prompt: Across [my authorized opportunity/milestone portfolio scope], identify transfers needing an ownership check: changed owners without follow-through, past-due milestones, engagement without subsequent activity, or unclear next-action ownership. Use dated source evidence and [team transfer windows, if known]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore the transfer-window field and continue without assuming a timing rule. Rank by time static only where comparable. Separate recorded transfer from receiver acceptance and missing visibility from a confirmed stall. Name the sender/receiver confirmation question and next owner action. Do not change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled or incomplete transfers with time static, and the ownership ambiguity named for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms actual ownership with the other role directly. A record showing a transfer completed is not evidence that anyone picked it up.
activities.requiredContext: Your opportunities and milestones; the expected transfer windows your team works to, only if known; the roles you routinely hand off to.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your own opportunities and milestones.
2. For each result, establish who actually believes they own it. It is often nobody, and sometimes two people.
3. Pick the one that has been static longest and resolve ownership today.
4. Check whether the customer is waiting on any of these. That changes the priority.
5. Record the owner in the system rather than agreeing it verbally.
activities.whyThisMatters: Work does not usually stall inside a role. It stalls in the space between two, where both parties believe the other has it.

activities.name: Rehearse receiving a handoff you were given badly
activities.description: Practice the conversation that recovers a thin handoff without damaging the relationship with the role that sent it.
activities.prompt: I have received a handoff for [fictional or de-identified opportunity scenario] and it is thin. Play the role of the person who sent it. Keep the entire exchange explicitly simulated, not evidence about an actual colleague. I will ask for what I need. Push back the way a busy colleague would, including being defensive if I imply they did it badly. Afterwards, tell me which of my questions got the most useful information, where I put them on the defensive unnecessarily, and how to ask for the missing context without making it a complaint.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed recovery conversation with coaching on which questions produced information and where the approach created defensiveness.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The receiving role decides how hard to push. The relationship with that colleague outlasts this opportunity, and a handoff recovered at the cost of a working relationship is a poor trade.
activities.requiredContext: A fictional or de-identified thin-handoff opportunity scenario; the missing business context, customer outcome and simulated sending/receiving roles for rehearsal.
activitySteps: 1. Choose a fictional or de-identified thin-handoff scenario and the business information still needed.
2. Supply the scenario, customer outcome and simulated sender/receiver roles to the prompt; keep the exchange explicitly simulated.
3. Rehearse asking for the missing information.
4. Review which questions helped and where the wording caused avoidable defensiveness.
5. Rewrite the opening around the customer outcome in the scenario.
6. Discuss what you would change in a later real handoff conversation. Any real follow-up is separate and optional; the simulation is not evidence about an actual colleague.
activities.whyThisMatters: Nobody sends a bad handoff deliberately. Getting what you need without making it an accusation is the skill that keeps the next one better.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Write the handoff so the next role does not have to ask

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A handoff stalls when the sender considers it complete but the receiver cannot act. Focus on one live transfer: the decision, usable evidence and acceptance still needed.
keyTalkingPoints: Confirm the applicable current handoff requirements and timing with the accountable owners. A handoff is complete only when the receiving role can act and acceptance is recorded. Include the customer outcome, usable evidence, open decisions and next checkpoint; do not substitute an ownership-field change for acceptance.
discussionQuestions: What is the least useful handoff you have ever received, and what was missing?
When you hand something over, what do you assume the other person already knows?
How would you know today if a handoff you sent had gone nowhere?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the gap analysis to the one handoff each person will prepare, repair or chase this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Rehearse receiving a handoff you were given badly', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Handoffs succeed when the receiver can use qualification evidence and accepts the next action. Completeness reduces ambiguity, not legitimate questions or conversation. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Could the receiving role act on what you sent, without asking you anything?
Where in your own list has a transfer stalled with nobody owning it?
What do you know about this opportunity that is written nowhere?
What missing field has a peer receiver needed before they could accept a handoff?
listenFor: Handoffs described as notifications, ownership that changed without anyone accepting it, milestones carrying placeholder values or dates, and sellers rebuilding a thin handoff silently rather than sending it back.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or approved context is unavailable, use a sanitized supplied example or a clearly labeled synthetic case. On paper, complete one handoff acceptance check: required context, milestone evidence, proposed receiver, missing field and draft return reason. Mark evidence, assumptions and unknowns. Treat the receiver and acceptance state as proposed until confirmed; record the access gap and who must validate the handoff before use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you assume the receiving role already knew, and what will you write down next time instead of assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a handoff from the receiving role's perspective and identify a consequential missing input. Any actual transfer requires explicit receiving-owner acceptance; follow-up questions remain welcome. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized missing input clarified and whether the receiver could act or identified a remaining gap. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An opportunity transfer contains documents but not the next decision or evidence gap. Review what the receiving role needs and seek acceptance rather than assume it.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: An effective opportunity handoff carries the decision and evidence the receiving role needs, not just documents. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the example handoff and unresolved receiving-role question.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A transferred record does not convey tacit context or recipient acceptance. Look for a receiving-role question that exposes the continuity gap. The starting prompt or required inputs still need product-owner clarification; do not fill the gap with an invented capability.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a transferred record does not convey tacit context or recipient acceptance. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ALL-HANDOFF.keyTakeaway: A handoff is complete when the receiving owner accepts the work and knows the decision, evidence, boundaries, and next step.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a transferred record does not convey tacit context or recipient acceptance. Manager support can help secure sending and receiving-owner attention before a customer transition.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help the facilitator explore the continuity gap without assuming the receiver accepted the work or that a record transfer settled it.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a transferred record does not convey tacit context or recipient acceptance; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help secure sending and receiving-owner attention before a customer transition? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

ATS-CONSUME.roleTopicName: Build the Consumption Plan the Customer Will Follow
ATS-CONSUME.roleTopicDescription: Turn a customer commitment into a sequenced consumption plan with owned milestones, dependencies and evidence that deployment is real.
ATS-CONSUME.wiifm: A realistic consumption path gives the v-team work it can execute and helps customers avoid committed spend remaining disconnected from deployed, used workloads.
ATS-CONSUME.name: Activate Delivery and Realize Usage
ATS-CONSUME.description: Plan and govern delivery, activation, support, and consumption so that an agreed solution can reach intended use; surface readiness gaps and route blockers to the authorized owner.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. Supports covered consumption portfolios through milestone readiness, partner and scale-engine handoffs, targeted adoption and technical interventions, attributed value evidence, and expansion hypotheses without assuming blanket customer or partner-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports covered SME&C consumption portfolios with readiness, handoffs, and targeted interventions.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Advances USPSI solution-area prospecting, discovery, proof, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances USPSI solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and decisions using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates USPSI outcome-based success plans, milestones, and accepted owners using approved health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder evidence. Aligns executives and teams, supports adoption and growth planning, and manages delivery risks within organizational requirements while retaining technical architecture approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates USPSI success plans, adoption, milestones, and delivery risks using approved evidence.

ATS-CONSUME.todayObjective: Examine the gap between customer commitment, deployment, and usage to test the milestone sequence, dependency-backed dates, and ownership behind the technical consumption plan.
ATS-CONSUME.whyItMatters: Connecting delivery and adoption work to intended usage helps teams resolve friction without claiming that deployment alone proves value.
ATS-CONSUME.desiredOutcome: Shape and revise technical consumption plans from agreed baselines and confirmed dependencies, recognizing when deployment progress does not yet establish usage or customer adoption.

activities.name: Establish what the customer committed to and what they have actually deployed
activities.description: Set the honest baseline for a consumption plan by separating what was committed, what is deployed, and what is only forecast.
activities.prompt: For TPID [TPID], show the current consumption commitment and remaining term, workloads deployed and consuming, and planned work not started. Use measured consumption over [review period] to show the current run-rate gap against the commitment, with units, dates and source coverage. Label each workload figure measured or projected, and distinguish recorded commitment from modeled trajectory. Name unavailable deployment/consumption evidence and the owner question needed to agree the baseline; do not estimate gaps in the data.
activities.expectedOutput: A consumption baseline separating committed, deployed, planned and forecast, with the gap quantified and measured figures distinguished from projected.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms the baseline with the account team before planning from it. A disputed baseline invalidates every milestone built on top of it, and the dispute always surfaces later than it should.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its consumption commitment; access to current consumption data; the commitment term and how much of it remains.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an authorized account with a consumption commitment during the activity, or a permitted commitment-and-baseline example arranged by the facilitator. No new consumption analysis is required to attend.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate measured consumption from projected consumption everywhere it appears.
5. Calculate the gap honestly, including the time remaining to close it.
6. Do not build the plan yet. Get agreement on the baseline first, because a plan built on a disputed number will be relitigated.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most consumption plans fail because they were built on an optimistic starting number nobody agreed to. The argument you avoid now happens in a review instead.

activities.name: Sequence the milestones that close the consumption gap
activities.description: Break the gap between commitment and current usage into milestones with owners, dependencies and dates that hold.
activities.prompt: Using [agreed consumption baseline, customer-confirmed outcome and commitment], propose a dependency-ordered milestone sequence to close the gap. If that basis changed or is unconfirmed, ask before optimizing. Show workload, customer/Microsoft responsibilities, blocking dependency, evidence of progress and a date supported by owner estimates. Distinguish proposed owners/dates from accepted commitments and capacity. Identify the milestone carrying most of the gap only from comparable incremental values without double counting; otherwise name the attribution gap. Do not invent values, feasibility or durations.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced milestone plan with paired owners, blocking dependencies, dependency-aware dates, progress evidence, and the milestone carrying most of the gap identified where supported by comparable evidence, otherwise an explicit attribution gap.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms each date with the person who owns the dependency. A plan full of dates nobody has agreed to is the most common form of consumption planning, and the least useful.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed consumption baseline; the technical dependencies you know about; the Microsoft and customer roles who could own each milestone.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the agreed baseline.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Test every date against the dependency named beneath it. A date without a resolved dependency is a wish.
5. Assign a named owner on both the Microsoft and customer side. A team is not an owner.
6. Record the milestones where the v-team will actually see them.
activities.whyThisMatters: A consumption plan without owned milestones is a forecast. The milestone is the unit of work someone can actually be held to.

activities.name: Find the milestone that is quietly slipping
activities.description: Check the consumption plan against what has actually happened, and surface the milestones that have stopped moving before they become a shortfall.
activities.prompt: Review [the consumption plan and dated progress evidence] against what has actually happened since it was built. Identify milestones with no evidence of progress, dates that have passed without being reset or explained, dependencies that were assumed resolved and are not, and any workload where the deployment has started but usage has not followed. For each, tell me what the evidence shows and what I would need to confirm before raising it.
activities.expectedOutput: A slip analysis distinguishing late milestones from stalled ones, with unresolved dependencies and deployment-without-usage cases identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides whether a slip is technical, commercial or customer-driven before assigning it. Routing a customer-priority problem to a technical owner wastes a cycle and the deadline does not move.
activities.requiredContext: The current consumption plan with its milestones and dates; recent consumption and deployment data; what you know about customer-side changes.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the consumption plan and the current consumption data.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Separate a milestone that is late from one that has stopped. They need different interventions.
4. Check whether deployment without usage is a technical issue or an adoption one, because the owner differs.
5. Raise the largest slip with the account team before the next review, not in it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Consumption shortfalls are visible in the milestone plan months before they are visible in the number. By the time the number moves, the runway to fix it has gone.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Sequence the milestones that close the consumption gap

activities.name: Test whether deployment is actually turning into usage
activities.description: Look past deployment milestones to whether people are using what was deployed, since a deployed workload nobody uses will not renew.
activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID] over [review period], compare deployed workloads with actual usage. Identify completed deployments with flat or declining usage, narrow rather than spreading adoption, and patterns suggesting deployment succeeded but adoption did not follow. Cite comparable deployment/usage evidence and name missing coverage. Separate technical from organizational adoption gaps where evidenced; identify what needs customer investigation. Do not assume a deliberate phased rollout is an adoption failure.
activities.expectedOutput: A deployment-versus-usage comparison identifying flat or concentrated usage and separating technical from organizational adoption gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms with the customer team before concluding adoption has failed. Low usage can reflect a deliberate phased rollout, and treating a plan as a failure damages credibility.
activities.requiredContext: An account with completed deployment milestones; usage data for those workloads; who owns adoption on the customer side.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account where deployment milestones have completed.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate technical adoption problems from organizational ones.
5. Identify who owns adoption on the customer side; it is rarely the person who owned deployment.
6. Raise flat usage as a finding, not as a criticism of the deployment.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deployment is the milestone Microsoft measures; usage is the one the customer renews on. They are not the same, and the gap between them is invisible unless you look.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Establish what the customer committed to and what they have actually deployed
