facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A customer commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. Focus on the plan that converts one into the other, and about being honest where that plan has stopped being real.
keyTalkingPoints: The ATS owns the technical plan behind the consumption number. Milestones without a named owner and a dependency-aware date are forecasts, not plans. Deployment and usage are different measures, and only one of them renews.
discussionQuestions: Which of your accounts has committed spend that is not converting, and do you know technically why?
Which milestone dates in your current plan would you personally bet on?
Where has something been deployed that nobody is actually using?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Establish what the customer committed to and what they have actually deployed'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the baseline to the single milestone each ATS will resequence or re-own this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test whether deployment is actually turning into usage', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Consumption plans are credible when milestone dates rest on confirmed dependencies and accepted ownership. Proposed dates should change when evidence no longer supports them. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Is your baseline a number the account team would agree with?
Which milestone carries most of the gap, and who actually owns it?
Where has deployment completed without usage following?
How does another ATS tell deployment completion from consumption progress when resequencing milestones?
listenFor: Baselines nobody has agreed, dates set without checking the dependency beneath them, teams named as owners instead of people, and deployment milestones being treated as evidence of adoption.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one consumption milestone sequence: customer commitment, baseline or unknown, dependency, owner, deployment state and usage evidence needed. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which date in your plan turned out to rest on an unconfirmed dependency, and what did you do about it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could confirm a milestone dependency with its owner and ask the plan owner to validate or revise the proposed date; do not commit timing for someone else. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized dependency checked and whether owner confirmation changed sequence or timing; actual customer dates are unnecessary. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A consumption commitment appears in the plan, yet deployment and usage lag. Check one technical dependency and proposed date with its owner, keeping unsupported timing unconfirmed.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Consumption planning connects commitments and milestones to measured usage and the dependencies behind the dates. ATS connects technical strategy and readiness to the account decision; accountable specialists retain their domain approval.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example commitment, plan milestone and measured-usage baseline.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A commitment or deployment date does not prove actual usage. Look for a plan dependency checked against actual consumption and ownership.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a commitment or deployment date does not prove actual usage. Confirm who can explain the technical account strategy boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ATS-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a commitment or deployment date does not prove actual usage. Manager support can support agreement on the baseline before asking for a new recovery plan.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help separate technical dependencies from commercial or customer-priority issues; avoid treating a proposed date as an accepted commitment.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a commitment or deployment date does not prove actual usage; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support agreement on the baseline before asking for a new recovery plan? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

ALL-SPONSOR.roleTopicName: Find Out Whether Your Executive Relationships Are Real

ALL-SPONSOR.wiifm: Understanding which relationships can support a real decision helps protect customer trust and exposes dependency on a sponsor before a change disrupts the account.
ALL-SPONSOR.name: Prepare and Lead Customer Engagement
ALL-SPONSOR.description: Plan and lead customer-facing engagement around a clear outcome, relevant stakeholders, evidence, questions, and the decision or relationship action needed.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: All Roles
roles.description: An audience for shared Enterprise content supporting recurring cross-role workflows, not an individual job. Emphasizes evidence reuse, output review, and accepted handoffs across roles while retaining existing decision authority and avoiding new ownership assignments.
roles.descriptionSummary: An audience for shared Enterprise cross-role workflows, evidence reuse, and accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Manages USPSI account priorities, opportunities, forecasts, renewals, and expansion. Inspects pipeline using only certified records and minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or user-supplied excerpts, with source, scope, as-of/freshness dates, and human verification; coordinates account teams while retaining technical, policy, and approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages USPSI accounts and pipeline using certified records and approved, human-verified evidence.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Advances USPSI solution-area prospecting, discovery, proof, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances USPSI solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and decisions using approved evidence.

roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

activities.name: Find out which recorded sponsors are still actually engaged
activities.description: Check the senior relationships your account depends on against real engagement, and find the ones that have gone quiet without anyone noticing.
activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID] over [review period], inspect senior stakeholders recorded as sponsors, executive contacts or decision makers, not the full contact list. Show each person's last evidenced engagement, with me or another Microsoft colleague, and changes in frequency. Identify regularly engaged senior people missing from the sponsor record. Cite source/date and distinguish observed engagement from inferred sponsorship; name coverage gaps and the question that would settle whether sponsorship still exists.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each recorded sponsor covering last genuine engagement, who at Microsoft holds it, and whether it is declining, plus any unrecorded senior contact now engaging.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what absence means. A sponsor who has not been in a meeting may still be engaged through a colleague, and the seller judges that rather than the activity data.
activities.requiredContext: One customer/account; the senior stakeholders currently recorded as sponsors or decision makers; the outcomes the account depends on them for.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an authorized account during the activity, ideally one you feel confident about, or a permitted sponsor-map example arranged by the facilitator. No new stakeholder research is required to attend.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Look first at recorded sponsors with no recent engagement. That is the dangerous category.
5. Note whether the engagement that does exist is yours or a colleague's, because a relationship held by someone else is not yours to rely on.
6. Look last at unrecorded senior contacts. You may be misreading who holds influence.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsorship decays quietly. The person your account depends on may have changed role or priority months ago, and the account plan will keep listing them as your sponsor until someone checks.

activities.name: Separate real sponsorship from polite interest
activities.description: Apply an honest test to each senior relationship, distinguishing executives who would act on your behalf from those who merely take the meeting.
activities.prompt: Here are the senior stakeholders on [Customer/Account] and what I know about each: [the senior-stakeholder list and evidenced actions]. Help me test each one honestly. For each, tell me what evidence exists that they would spend their own political capital for this, what evidence suggests they are merely being courteous, and what I would need to see to be confident either way. Be direct where the evidence is thin. Do not soften a weak relationship into a strong one.
activities.expectedOutput: An honest assessment of each senior relationship separating evidenced sponsorship from courtesy, with the evidence gap named for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns the honesty of the input. An overstated relationship produces a confident assessment of something that does not exist, which is worse than no assessment.
activities.requiredContext: The senior stakeholders on the account; what each has actually done rather than said; the outcomes the account depends on them for.
activitySteps: 1. List each senior stakeholder and what they have actually done, not what they have said.
2. Paste that into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest in what you supply. This exercise is worthless if you overstate the relationship.
4. Identify the single relationship the account most depends on.
5. If no relationship passes the test, that is the finding, and it is worth knowing now.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most accounts believe they have executive sponsorship. Far fewer have someone who would spend their own credibility to unblock something. The difference only becomes visible under pressure.

activities.name: Design the investment that earns sponsorship
activities.description: Plan what you will give an executive relationship over the coming quarter, so sponsorship is earned before it is needed rather than requested when it is.
activities.prompt: I want to deepen the relationship with the executive identified in [approved relationship notes or name/role] at [Customer/Account] over the next quarter. Here is what I know about their priorities and what I can genuinely offer, whether access, insight, introductions or influence: [their evidenced priorities and what I can genuinely offer]. Using only what I have supplied, help me sequence the investment across the quarter: what to lead with, what earns the right to the next conversation, and what would signal the relationship is strengthening. Do not suggest anything I have not told you I can actually provide, and do not give me generic executive engagement advice.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced quarter of relationship investment built only on what you can genuinely provide, with what to lead with, what earns the next conversation, and the signals that sponsorship is strengthening.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what can actually be offered and delivered. Sponsorship built on something you cannot provide costs more than the relationship you were trying to build.
activities.requiredContext: The executive and their role; what the record and your own knowledge show about their priorities; what you can genuinely offer, meaning access, insight, introductions or influence you actually control.
activitySteps: 1. Write down what this executive appears to care about, and separately what you can genuinely offer them.
2. Paste both into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Discard anything that would be true of any executive at any company. That is the test of whether it is useful.
4. Sequence it across the quarter rather than planning a single meeting; sponsorship is built over time.
5. Put a date on the first step. An intention to deepen a relationship is not a plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: Executive relationships deepen through usefulness delivered over time, not through contact frequency or a single well-prepared meeting. The investment has to start from what they need and what you can actually give.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate real sponsorship from polite interest

activities.name: Work out what happens when your sponsor leaves
activities.description: Establish how much of an account rests on one person, and what would survive if that person moved on.
activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID], stress-test [senior relationships and what each enables] against losing each person. Show what could stop, the supported single-person dependency and any evidenced alternative relationship. Separate known influence from assumptions; do not invent another person's authority or willingness. Identify which relationship to strengthen, why, and the next validation question before relying on it as cover.
activities.expectedOutput: An exposure read per key relationship covering what would stop working, who could carry it, the degree of single-person dependency, and the relationship to build as insurance.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller judges how much concentration is tolerable. Some accounts genuinely run through one executive, and the decision is whether to accept that risk or invest in reducing it.
activities.requiredContext: One customer/account; the senior people you rely on and what each one enables; who else at the customer operates at that level.
activitySteps: 1. List the senior people you rely on and what each one actually enables, from renewals to unblocking decisions.
2. Paste that into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much depends on one person. Most accounts depend on more than the seller admits.
4. Identify the second relationship you would need if the first one ended.
5. Start building that relationship now, while it is insurance rather than emergency.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsors leave, get promoted and change priorities, and the account discovers its dependency at the worst moment. The insurance relationship has to be built before it is needed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every account plan claims executive sponsorship. Far fewer accounts have someone senior who would actually spend their own credibility to unblock something. Focus on finding out which kind you have.
keyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps age quietly; the person you are counting on may have changed role or priority. Sponsorship is built over quarters and cannot be assembled in the week you need it. An executive relationship you only use when you need something is not sponsorship.
discussionQuestions: Who on your biggest account would take your call today, and when did you last test that?
Which senior relationship are you assuming is stronger than it is?
When did a sponsor last change without you noticing?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find out which recorded sponsors are still actually engaged'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the tested map to the one relationship each person will act on, and what they will offer. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Work out what happens when your sponsor leaves', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Executive relationships need engagement evidence, not contact lists or presumed sponsorship. A useful contribution tests the relationship without demanding endorsement. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which recorded sponsor has not actually engaged recently?
Which relationship would hold under pressure, and what is your evidence?
What could you offer that this executive cannot easily get elsewhere?
What behavior would convince a peer that sponsorship is more than polite engagement?
listenFor: Sponsorship asserted without evidence, relationships described by meeting frequency rather than by what the person has done, engagement plans that would suit any executive at any company, and sellers softening a weak relationship rather than naming it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one sponsor evidence row: senior stakeholder role, observed action, unsupported sponsorship claim, offered value and next relationship test. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which relationship turned out to be thinner than you assumed, and what will you do about it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore an existing executive-relationship assumption and consider what a relevant contribution might be; no contact, reply or endorsement is required. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized engagement lesson and whether it changed the plan; a single reply or silence does not prove sponsorship. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: An account map labels an executive as a sponsor, but recent engagement evidence is sparse. Consider a useful contribution and keep the sponsorship claim qualified.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Executive sponsorship depends on current engagement and the relationship actually held by the relevant colleague. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the sponsor map and dated engagement evidence in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A colleague's executive relationship is not automatically the seller's access. Look for a sponsorship assumption qualified by who actually engaged and when.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a colleague's executive relationship is not automatically the seller's access. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a colleague's executive relationship is not automatically the seller's access. Manager support can help the team validate the relationship respectfully rather than count contacts.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Invite a careful distinction between polite interest and sponsorship; do not imply that one colleague's relationship gives everyone customer access.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a colleague's executive relationship is not automatically the seller's access; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help the team validate the relationship respectfully rather than count contacts? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Work out whether your territory actually covers your number
activities.description: Do the arithmetic between what your territory can realistically produce and what you have been asked to deliver, and quantify the gap.
activities.prompt: Test whether [quota, pipeline by stage/value, renewal base and actual conversion rates] cover my territory target. Show the arithmetic using my rates, not benchmarks. Keep renewals separate and avoid overlap/double-counting. Calculate the new-pipeline gap; derive a latest creation date only from [sales-cycle or milestone timing, if known]. If quota treatment or timing is missing, ask instead of inventing a rule or date.
activities.expectedOutput: A coverage calculation with the arithmetic shown, new business and renewal base kept separate, the remaining gap quantified, and the latest pipeline-creation date only where supported sales-cycle or milestone timing allows it; otherwise an explicit timing question or unknown.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns both the conversion rates and the treatment of renewals. Optimistic conversion produces a plan that looks covered and fails in the second half, and how renewals count toward attainment varies by plan rather than being a universal rule.
activities.requiredContext: Your quota for the year; current pipeline by stage with values; your renewal base; the conversion rates your team actually achieves at each stage; how renewals are treated in your own compensation plan. Include observed sales-cycle or confirmed milestone timing needed for a latest-start calculation, and any renewal/pipeline overlap.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rates your team actually achieves.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it. Without your own conversion rates it will have nothing to calculate from.
3. Check the arithmetic yourself. This is the number you will be held to.
4. Check how renewals count toward your own quota before treating the renewal base as coverage; that varies by plan and the calculation deliberately keeps them separate.

5. If supported sales-cycle or milestone timing is available, note the date by which new pipeline must exist, not the date it must close. Otherwise retain the timing question or unknown; do not invent a date.
activities.whyThisMatters: A territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. Most are never tested against arithmetic until a review tests them, which is the worst moment to find out.

activities.name: Find where the growth is most likely to come from
activities.description: Identify which accounts in your territory have the strongest evidence for growth, so coverage planning is based on signal rather than familiarity.
activities.prompt: Across [account list or territory scope], identify where the available signals support a hypothesis for new pipeline. Consider consumption against commitment, workloads owned but not deployed, renewal timing and recent engagement, without treating any of these alone as customer demand. Rank account hypotheses by strength of evidence rather than account size. For each, show the source signal, customer-outcome hypothesis, decision-changing unknown and next discovery or validation action. Distinguish customer-confirmed need from internal signals and seller inference. Name a relevant FY27 Conversation or connected Conversations only where supported; leave the mapping open otherwise. Flag accounts where evidence is insufficient.
activities.expectedOutput: Accounts ranked for follow-up by the evidence supporting each growth hypothesis, with confirmed needs distinguished from inferred potential, key unknowns, next discovery actions and relevant FY27 Conversation context only where supported.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller checks customer intent before treating a growth hypothesis as a qualified opportunity and decides which follow-up is realistic given their capacity. A ranked list that exceeds the hours in the year is not a plan, and the seller owns that trade-off.
activities.requiredContext: Your assigned account list; consumption and renewal data; your coverage gap from the previous practice.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your assigned accounts.
2. Compare the ranking against your own instinct, and take seriously anywhere they disagree.
3. Note the accounts flagged as having no basis for judgment. Those need research, not a forecast.
4. Pick up to three account hypotheses and name the customer outcome to test, the key unknown and the next discovery action; add relevant FY27 Conversation context only where supported.
5. Compare the potential with the coverage gap without counting an unconfirmed hypothesis as qualified pipeline; name the evidence needed before relying on it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Territory planning defaults to the accounts you already know. The growth is often in the ones you have not looked at, and the evidence for that is usually already sitting in the data.

activities.name: Build the support ask you can defend
activities.description: Turn the coverage gap into a specific, evidenced request for the help you need, rather than a general statement that the number is hard.
activities.prompt: I have a coverage gap and I need to ask for support. Here is what I have: [the coverage gap, ranked opportunities, prior support attempts/results and specific support ask]. Using only what I have supplied, help me turn this into a request a manager could act on: state the ask precisely, tie it to the specific accounts and evidence, show what has already been attempted, and set out what changes if it is not provided. Flag any part of the ask my evidence does not support, and do not invent a consequence I have not described.
activities.expectedOutput: A support request naming the specific ask, the accounts and evidence behind it, what has already been attempted, and the consequence of not getting it, with unevidenced elements flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what consequence to state. Overstating what happens without support costs credibility in the next review, and the seller is the one who will be there for it.
activities.requiredContext: Your coverage gap; your ranked growth opportunities; what support you have already tried to secure and the response; the specific resource, specialist or investment you need.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what you have already tried, and the specific support you need.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Cut anything you cannot evidence. An unevidenced ask weakens the parts that are real.
4. Check the consequence it states is one you would defend in a review.
5. Take it to your territory review or your manager rather than waiting to be asked.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support goes to the people who ask for something specific and evidenced. A general statement that the territory is difficult competes with everyone else saying the same thing.

activities.name: Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong
activities.description: Find the single assumption your territory plan most depends on, and work out what happens if it does not hold.
activities.prompt: Stress-test [territory plan and coverage calculation]. Identify the single assumption carrying most coverage, such as a renewal, large opportunity, conversion rate or consumption ramp. Use the supplied arithmetic to show what changes if it fails; label scenario assumptions and name gaps rather than inventing impact. Identify the earliest evidenced warning signal, its owner role and a practical contingency to reduce dependency. If the evidence cannot identify one dominant assumption, say so.
activities.expectedOutput: The plan's most load-bearing assumption named, the coverage impact if it fails, the earliest warning signal, and a contingency to reduce the dependency.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides how much concentration is acceptable. Some territories are genuinely dependent on one renewal, and the judgment is whether that is a risk to manage or a plan to change.
activities.requiredContext: Your territory plan and coverage calculation; the largest single opportunities and renewals within it; the conversion assumptions you used.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your plan and coverage calculation.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much rests on one deal or one renewal.
4. Work out the earliest signal that the assumption is failing, and schedule a check.
5. Decide now what the contingency is, while there is still time to build one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most territory plans fail on one assumption, not many. Knowing which one, and how early it would show, is the difference between adjusting in month three and explaining in month nine.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. This session tests that claim against arithmetic, while there is still time to do something about the answer.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current fiscal planning and territory-review requirements for your organization. Test the plan against governed quota, pipeline and renewal evidence, preserving dates and metric definitions. Separate actuals, forecasts and assumptions, and name the dependency or support request that changes the plan.
discussionQuestions: Do you know, arithmetically, whether your pipeline covers your number?
What single deal or renewal is your year most dependent on?
What support would actually change your position, and have you asked for it specifically?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out whether your territory actually covers your number'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coverage gap to the specific, evidenced support request each person will make. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Territory planning makes coverage arithmetic and assumptions inspectable. An evidenced support ask informs the manager; it does not authorize staffing or assign capacity. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: What is your uncovered gap, and by when would new pipeline have to exist to close it?
Where is the growth evidence strongest, and does it match where you spend your time?
What is the one assumption your plan cannot survive without?
Which conversion or capacity assumption would a colleague challenge before accepting the coverage plan?
listenFor: Optimistic conversion rates used to make a plan look covered, growth ranked by familiarity rather than evidence, concentration risk nobody has named, and support asks phrased as a general complaint about difficulty.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one territory coverage calculation: supplied target/baseline, explicit conversion assumption, concentration/capacity risk and evidenced support question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the arithmetic tell you that your instinct had not, and what changes because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could check a material coverage assumption and take an evidenced support recommendation to the manager or territory review, respecting staffing and capacity authority. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized manual scenario or leave the gap open; no report is required. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized coverage assumption checked and whether it sharpened the ask or changed the plan. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A territory plan depends heavily on one uncertain deal or renewal. Compare governed quota and dated pipeline context, distinguishing actuals, forecasts and assumptions before proposing support.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Fiscal planning weighs quota, pipeline and renewal assumptions against concentration, timing and realistic capacity. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the governed baseline and planning assumption in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain. Look for a concentration or timing assumption with a contingency and early check.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ALL-FYPLAN.keyTakeaway: A useful plan makes its assumptions, trade-offs, owners, and conditions for revision explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain. Manager support can support an appropriate resource or ownership decision without making a new forecast commitment.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help explore a defensible support or contingency question; keep actuals, forecasts and assumptions distinct without requiring a new territory plan.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a coverage calculation does not make a contingent deal certain; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support an appropriate resource or ownership decision without making a new forecast commitment? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

ALL-ASSET.roleTopicName: Make Your Best Work Reusable by Someone Else
ALL-ASSET.roleTopicDescription: Take something you built that worked, and package it so a colleague can find it, trust it and adapt it without asking you.
ALL-ASSET.wiifm: Making useful work easier to find and adapt reduces repeated effort across the team while protecting colleagues from hidden assumptions and unsafe customer-detail reuse.
ALL-ASSET.name: Capture and Reuse Proven Work
ALL-ASSET.description: Capture a reusable artifact or learning with provenance, applicability limits, permissions, and enough context for another role to find and adapt it.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

activities.name: Find the thing you have already built that others keep needing
activities.description: Identify which of your own recent work is being asked for repeatedly, and would save colleagues the most time if it were reusable.
activities.prompt: Look across my own mail, meetings and chats from the last quarter and help me find what I have built that others could reuse. Start by telling me which of those sources you can actually reach, and skip anything you cannot rather than guessing at it. Then look for material I have sent to more than one person, questions colleagues have asked me more than once, and work I appear to have rebuilt rather than reused. Rank by how often it comes up, and for each tell me what evidence suggests it is repeatedly needed rather than a one-off.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of your own work that appears repeatedly needed, with the evidence for each, the account-specific items filtered out, and a statement of which sources could not be reached.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what is genuinely transferable. Something that worked because of a specific relationship or a specific customer situation may not survive being generalized, and packaging it anyway wastes everyone's time.
activities.requiredContext: Microsoft 365 Copilot with access to your own mail, meetings and chats; the material you have produced in the last quarter.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt. It works on your own recent activity, so there is nothing to fill in.
2. Check what it says it could not reach. A source it cannot see is a blind spot in the ranking, not an empty one.
3. Look for the thing you have sent to several people, not the thing you are proudest of.
4. Discard anything so account-specific it would not transfer.
5. Pick the one that would save a colleague the most time, and check whether something similar already exists before you package yours.
activities.whyThisMatters: The best candidate for reuse is rarely the work you are proudest of. It is the thing you keep sending to people, which is exactly the thing you stop noticing.

activities.name: Strip out what makes it yours and unusable
activities.description: Remove the customer detail, assumed context and personal shorthand that would stop a colleague using your work or make it unsafe to share.
activities.prompt: Here is something I want to make reusable: [the approved material to assess for reuse]. Review it and tell me what would stop a colleague using it. Identify customer-identifying detail that must be removed, context I have assumed the reader already has, shorthand or internal references that would not be understood, and anything that was true only for my specific situation. Then tell me what is genuinely reusable underneath. Be direct if the answer is that very little of it transfers.
activities.expectedOutput: A list of what blocks reuse covering customer-identifying detail, assumed context, unexplained shorthand and situation-specific content, plus what genuinely transfers.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller is accountable for the customer-identifying detail. An automated pass will miss context that only the person who wrote it recognizes as identifying, and a leaked customer specific in a shared asset is a real incident.
activities.requiredContext: The material you want to make reusable; your team's rules on what may be shared internally; the customers referenced in it.
activitySteps: 1. Take the asset you selected.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Remove every piece of customer-identifying detail it finds, and check yourself as well.
4. Fill in the context you had assumed rather than deleting the part that needs it.
5. If very little transfers, accept that and pick something else. A thin asset costs the next person more than no asset.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most shared assets are unusable because they carry the author's context invisibly. The person who wrote it cannot see what is missing, because to them nothing is.

activities.name: Write what the next person needs to trust it
activities.description: Add the purpose, prerequisites, limitations and ownership that let a colleague judge whether your asset fits their situation.
activities.prompt: Draft a short reuse guide for [sanitized asset]: its job, suitable/unsuitable situations, prerequisites, adaptation points, limits and support contact. Use what the asset actually establishes. If important limits or failure conditions are unclear, ask up to five short questions, one at a time, rather than guessing; then draft something a colleague would actually read. Name a support contact only where supplied and accepted; otherwise mark it to confirm rather than inventing a person or implying maintenance acceptance. The draft does not establish reuse validation or sharing rights; any real storage or sharing follows the human's authorized process.
activities.expectedOutput: A draft reuse guide covering purpose, fit, prerequisites, adaptation points and honest limitations, with an accepted support or maintenance contact where supplied or an explicit confirmation gap. Storage, sharing rights and reuse validation are not established by the draft.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what the asset cannot do. An honest limitation is what makes it trustworthy, and only the person who built it knows where it breaks.
activities.requiredContext: Your sanitized asset; the situations where it does and does not apply; where your team actually looks for shared material.
activitySteps: 1. Take your sanitized asset.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Answer its questions honestly. The limitations are the part it cannot read off the asset, and they are the part that matters.
4. Confirm the support or maintenance contact only where supplied and accepted; otherwise leave it to confirm.
5. Any actual storage or sharing is optional and follows your authorized process after rights and reuse review.
activities.whyThisMatters: Assets go unused because nobody can tell whether they fit. The wrapper is the whole difference between a file in a folder and something a colleague will actually pick up.

activities.name: Draft a reusable skill specification from a repeated prompt
activities.description: Decide whether a repeated prompt is safe to generalize, then specify the parameters, access limits, human checkpoint and tests a skill owner would need.
activities.prompt: Turn [repeated prompt and when I use it] into a draft reusable skill specification. Include its purpose, trigger, inputs, steps, outputs, permissions, human checkpoints and failure behavior. Identify what needs validation and what should stay manual. Don’t install or activate anything, and don’t claim the skill or source connections exist.
activities.expectedOutput: A decision on safe generalization and a draft skill specification with parameters, access boundaries, failure modes, human checkpoint, representative test and implementation owner; no installed or tested skill is claimed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides whether the prompt is safe to generalize. A prompt that works because of what the author knows about their own accounts becomes dangerous when someone runs it without that knowledge.
activities.requiredContext: A prompt you run repeatedly; the situations you use it in; what data access it depends on; the colleague who would test it.
activitySteps: 1. Choose a repeated prompt and describe its actual workflow.
2. Run the specification prompt using permitted, sanitized context.
3. Verify account parameters, access assumptions, failure modes and the human checkpoint.
4. Walk through one representative test case and record gaps; do not claim a skill has run.
5. Name the implementation owner. Test an actual implementation with recorded results before approving wider publication.
activities.whyThisMatters: The prompt you have retyped four times is a skill waiting to be written. Most never get written because nobody notices they are repeating themselves.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Everyone in this room has rebuilt something a colleague had already solved, and everyone has had their own work rebuilt by someone else. Focus on breaking that cycle with one thing you have already made.
keyTalkingPoints: The best reuse candidate is the thing you keep sending to people, not the thing you are proudest of. An asset without prerequisites and limitations will be used once and abandoned. An asset nobody owns is one nobody trusts.
discussionQuestions: What have you sent to more than one colleague in the last month?
What have you rebuilt that you suspect someone else had already done?
What would you need to see before you trusted a colleague's asset enough to use it with a customer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Find the thing you have already built that others keep needing'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the chosen asset to what each person must write down before anyone else could use it. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Turn a repeated prompt into a reusable skill', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Reusable work needs purpose, provenance, limits and permission to share. Findability helps peers learn, but publication is a separate human decision, not a huddle requirement. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: What in your asset only makes sense because of what you already know?
What would you have to tell someone before they could safely use it?
What does it genuinely not do?
What prerequisite did another person discover only after trying to reuse an apparently finished asset?
listenFor: Assets chosen because the author is proud of them rather than because they are repeatedly needed, customer detail nobody has noticed, limitations left unstated, and material about to be stored where only its author would look.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one reusable-prompt or asset card: purpose, required context, sanitized inputs, limitations, provenance, rights gap and reviewer. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep reuse/publication on hold until rights, sanitization and actual validation are reviewed; no repository access is required for the draft.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you have to explain about your own work that you had never noticed you were assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review an existing reuse candidate for purpose, provenance, prerequisites and limits. Ask rights and publication owners whether sharing is permitted; keep it a private draft if approval is missing. Publication is not required before the next huddle. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized reuse lesson or permission gap and whether it clarified when the method is useful; do not bring or publish the asset itself. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A colleague wants to reuse a proven work product but lacks its source context and permission limits. Review one small candidate and keep it private if publication approval is missing.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Reusable work needs its source context, limits and intended audience so another person can judge whether it fits. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Understand the example work product's provenance, audience and reuse constraints.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Something that worked once may be unsafe or unhelpful in another setting. Look for a reuse candidate with its limits, reviewer and maintenance need visible.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: something that worked once may be unsafe or unhelpful in another setting. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help keep reuse optional and appropriately reviewed; a useful work product need not be published or shared beyond its permitted audience.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that something that worked once may be unsafe or unhelpful in another setting; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support a practical reviewer and maintainer without requiring a new published artifact? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

activities.name: Check whether committed milestones are actually progressing
activities.description: Test each committed milestone against evidence of real delivery progress, rather than against its status field.
activities.prompt: For [Account Name or TPID], inspect the committed milestones I own. Show dated delivery, deployment/consumption and customer-engagement evidence of progress, distinguishing it from status-only updates. Flag overdue dates and dates approaching in the next month without supporting evidence. State which relevant sources are unavailable; those milestones remain unknown, not stalled. Identify the next delivery-owner question for unsupported progress. Do not change milestone status or dates.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each committed milestone separating evidenced progress from status-only updates and from milestones the agent could not see, with unsupported approaching dates flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM verifies with the delivery team before treating a milestone as stalled, and treats anything the agent could not see as unknown rather than as bad news. Delivery work often runs ahead of what is recorded, and raising a false alarm costs credibility with the people you need.
activities.requiredContext: One customer/account; the committed milestones you own; access to delivery and consumption activity for that account.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an authorized account with committed milestones you own during the activity, or a permitted milestone example arranged by the facilitator. Work from existing context; no new milestone update is required to attend.

3. Read what it says it could not reach first. Unknown and stalled are not the same thing, and acting on the difference is the whole point.
4. Separate genuine progress from a status field somebody updated.
5. Check the dates approaching in the next month first; those are still recoverable, then pick the milestone with the weakest evidence and find out what is actually happening.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone status is a claim, not evidence. The ones that fail were usually failing quietly for weeks while the status said otherwise.

activities.name: Diagnose why a milestone stopped and route it correctly
activities.description: Establish what is actually blocking a stalled milestone and get it to the person who can move it, rather than escalating in the wrong direction.
activities.prompt: A committed milestone may have stalled. First distinguish a confirmed stall from insufficient progress evidence; if status is unknown, identify the delivery-owner check before diagnosing a cause. Here is what I know: [the milestone, dates, actual progress and known blocker]. Help me work out what is most likely blocking it: a technical dependency, a customer-side resource or decision, a Microsoft delivery constraint, or a commercial issue. Allow multiple contributing blockers. For each possibility, tell me what evidence would confirm or rule it out, and which role or function would own it at Microsoft and at the customer. Name the role rather than a person, since you cannot know either org chart; I will map the role to a name. Do not guess at a cause the evidence does not support.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked set of supported possible causes, including combinations, with confirming or disconfirming evidence and the candidate owning roles at Microsoft and the customer; where status or cause is not established, an explicit evidence gap. Actual person mapping and the cause to act on are confirmed by the CSAM before routing.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms the cause before routing. Every misrouted milestone costs a cycle, and the commitment date does not move to accommodate the mistake.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled milestone with its dates; what has and has not happened; any blocker you already know about; your Microsoft and customer contacts for that workload.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the milestone with the weakest evidence from the previous practice and distinguish missing visibility from a confirmed stall before diagnosing it.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Rule out causes before acting on one. Routing a customer-side problem to a technical owner loses a week.
4. Map each named role to an actual person yourself, and confirm the likely cause with someone closer to the work.
5. Hand it to that person with the evidence attached, not just the problem.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone can have several contributing blockers, or simply lack current progress evidence. Confirming the status and cause before routing avoids sending the problem to the wrong owner.

activities.name: Test whether completed milestones produced real usage
activities.description: Check that milestones marked complete actually resulted in the customer using what was delivered.
activities.prompt: For [Customer/Account], look at the milestones marked complete in the last two quarters and compare them against actual usage of what was delivered. Here is the intended rollout scope as far as I know it: [the intended rollout scope, marking unknowns]. Tell me first which usage data you can actually reach. Then identify anything marked complete where usage is flat, where usage started and then declined, or where adoption sits with a much smaller group than was intended. Tell me what the data supports and what would need checking with the customer before I draw a conclusion.
activities.expectedOutput: A comparison of completed milestones against real usage, identifying flat, declining or narrowly concentrated adoption, with what needs customer confirmation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms the intended rollout before calling adoption a failure. A deliberately phased deployment looks identical to a failed one in the data.
activities.requiredContext: An account with recently completed milestones; usage data for the delivered workloads; the customer's intended rollout scope, or an honest statement of where you do not know it.
activitySteps: 1. Bring an account with milestones completed in the last two quarters.
2. Supply your account and intended rollout scope as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Distinguish a phased rollout from an adoption failure before reacting. If you did not know the intended scope, that is the first thing to go and find out.
4. Identify who owns adoption on the customer side; it is rarely whoever owned the deployment.
5. Raise flat usage as a finding to work on together, not as a criticism of the delivery.
activities.whyThisMatters: Completed delivery is not adoption; verified rollout scope and usage expose value gaps before they undermine renewal confidence.

activities.name: Prepare the conversation that unblocks a customer-side delay
activities.description: Plan how to raise a milestone stalled on the customer's side without turning it into a complaint about them.
activities.prompt: Prepare a customer conversation from [stalled milestone/blocker, intended customer outcome, known roles and support I am authorized to offer]. Frame the delay as a shared problem: practical support, the specific customer ask and evidenced impact or clearly labelled possible risk if nothing moves. Leave unsupported consequences open and proposed support unpromised. Identify the confirmation needed before any commitment. Keep this customer-safe, not a chase for a Microsoft number; do not invent resources or funding.
activities.expectedOutput: A conversation plan framing the delay as a shared problem, with what you will offer, the specific ask, and the consequence expressed in the customer's terms.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides how hard to push. A milestone date that matters to Microsoft may not matter to the customer, and pressing on Microsoft's timeline damages the relationship the renewal depends on.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled milestone and its customer-side blocker; who at the customer is involved; what you are genuinely authorized to offer; the customer outcome the milestone supports.
activitySteps: 1. Supply an existing customer-side delay, its impact and what you can genuinely offer.
2. Draft the conversation and check the ask and consequences in the customer's terms.
3. Discuss who can move the blocker and what needs confirming.
activities.whyThisMatters: When a customer-side blocker is confirmed, a shared-outcome conversation can help resolve it without sounding like Microsoft is chasing its own number.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You inherit milestones the customer has committed to, and you are measured on whether they complete. Focus on finding the ones that are quietly not going to land, while there is still time.
keyTalkingPoints: A milestone status is a claim, not evidence. Committed milestones transfer to customer success to be driven to completion, which means to real usage rather than to a completion flag. Most stalls sit on the customer side, and those conversations go badly when they sound like Microsoft chasing its own number.
discussionQuestions: Which of your committed milestones would you actually bet on landing?
When a milestone stalls, how long does it usually take you to find out?
Which completed milestone do you suspect nobody is using?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Check whether committed milestones are actually progressing'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the milestone review to the single stalled milestone each person will diagnose and route this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Prepare the conversation that unblocks a customer-side delay', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Committed milestones require delivery and usage evidence, not optimistic status. Investigate the actual stall and route the confirmed cause to an owner able to act. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
facilitatorQuestions: Which milestone has a status but no evidence behind it?
What is actually blocking the one that stopped, and who owns that?
Where has something completed without anyone using it?
How does a peer distinguish a genuine stalled milestone from a deliberately phased rollout?
listenFor: Status fields treated as evidence, causes guessed at rather than confirmed, milestones escalated to the wrong owner, and phased rollouts being mistaken for failed adoption.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one milestone diagnosis: status versus evidence, stalled dependency, phased-rollout alternative, accountable role and usage check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which milestone turned out to be stalled for a different reason than you assumed, and what did that change?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore what evidence would clarify an unsupported committed milestone, without needing to resolve the stall or contact its owner. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized difference between assumed and confirmed blocker and whether it changed the owner conversation. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A committed milestone is reported as progressing, but available usage evidence is thin. Check what is actually happening before choosing a support or customer conversation.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Milestone review tests recorded progress against delivery and usage evidence before choosing the next support conversation. CSAM connects customer priorities, milestones and stakeholders; technical approval remains with the appropriate technical owner.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the committed milestone, dates and available delivery or usage evidence in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: An updated status field is not evidence of realized progress. Look for a genuine delay separated from missing evidence and an accountable follow-up.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: an updated status field is not evidence of realized progress. Confirm who can explain the customer-success outcomes and stakeholder orchestration boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

CSAM-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when an updated status field is not evidence of realized progress. Manager support can help clarify delivery or adoption ownership without treating unknown as failure.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Encourage the team to separate a genuine delay from missing evidence or a planned rollout; avoid treating an agent's visibility gap as bad news.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that an updated status field is not evidence of realized progress; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help clarify delivery or adoption ownership without treating unknown as failure? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires
activities.description: Check each uncommitted milestone against the criteria a commitment is supposed to satisfy, and identify which criteria are not yet met.
activities.prompt: Review uncommitted milestones for [account]. For sponsor, agreed outcome, value, date and budget, separate evidenced, asserted and absent information. For feasibility, resources and delivery model, show only whether confirmation is recorded and by whom; technical validation belongs to the Solution Engineer. Rank by proximity to genuine commitment, cite accessible sources and flag gaps. Populated fields alone aren’t evidence of agreement.
activities.expectedOutput: Each uncommitted milestone scored against the commitment criteria, with sponsor, value, date and budget separated into evidenced, asserted and absent, the technical criteria reported only as recorded or not and by whom, a readiness ranking, and the unreachable sources named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides what counts as evidence of sponsorship, and routes the technical criteria rather than judging them. A named contact in a field is not a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, and a feasibility box ticked by nobody in particular is not confirmed feasibility.
activities.requiredContext: One customer/account; the uncommitted milestones you own; the sponsor, value, date and budget position on each as far as you know it.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an authorized account with an uncommitted milestone you own during the activity, or a permitted shared example arranged by the facilitator. No newly prepared milestone case is required.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Separate a populated field from an evidenced one. Most milestones fail on evidence, not on data entry.
4. Take the closest milestone to commitment, not the largest one.
5. Split the missing criteria into the ones you close and the ones your SE closes, and send the technical half to them today rather than carrying it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone gets committed once. Everything after that is measured against it, so the cost of committing an unready one lands months later on someone who did not make the call.

activities.name: Build the case the sponsor has to agree to
activities.description: Turn the milestone into the outcome, value and commitment a named sponsor would actually put their name to.
activities.prompt: I need a sponsor to commit to a milestone. Here is what I have: [the milestone, outcome, known sponsor priorities and proposed value/date]. Help me build the case in the sponsor's terms rather than in ours: what outcome they are being asked to own, what they get, what they have to put in including budget and their own people, and what happens to their outcome if the date slips. Tell me which parts of this I have not actually given you, and ask me for them rather than filling them in yourself.
activities.expectedOutput: A sponsor-facing case stating the outcome they would own, what they receive, what they must contribute, and the consequence to their outcome if the date moves, with the gaps you still need to fill named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP judges whether this person can actually commit. Agreement from someone without budget or authority reads identically in the record and fails identically later.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and the outcome it produces; the named sponsor and what they are measured on; the value and date you intend to propose; what the customer would need to contribute.
activitySteps: 1. Supply an existing milestone, sponsor priorities and proposed value/date.
2. Build the case and check the outcome, contribution asked for and missing evidence.
3. Discuss whether the ask is proportionate and the sponsor can actually commit.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsorship is the criterion most often recorded and least often true. The test is not whether they are supportive; it is whether they would defend the date to their own leadership.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires
