activities.name: Pressure-test the value and the date before you commit to them
activities.description: Challenge the value and date on a milestone against the evidence behind them, before they become a commitment you are measured on.
activities.prompt: Challenge [milestone, proposed value/date and their basis] commercially. Which scope, adoption and timing assumptions are evidenced? Test the date against customer budget, approvals, procurement, decision cadence and contractual/fiscal constraints—not technical delivery sequencing. Show how the proposal depends on the weakest assumption without inventing a replacement number. Leave technical validation to the Solution Engineer.
activities.expectedOutput: The commercial assumptions the value and date rest on, which are evidenced and which are not, the approval, budget and customer-timing dependencies on the date, and what both would become if the weakest assumption failed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP owns the number and knows to get the delivery sequence from the SE rather than from a model. The decision to commit a value and a date in front of a customer and a forecast is not one to take on a commercial read alone.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone with its proposed value and date; how you arrived at each; the scope and adoption assumptions behind the value; the budget, approval and customer decision timing the date depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value and date you intend to commit to, and how you arrived at each.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Look for the assumption carrying the most of the number. There is usually one.
4. Get the technical side of the date from your SE rather than from the model. A commercial date that ignores the delivery sequence is half a commitment.
5. Record what the commitment depends on alongside it, so the reason is still there when someone asks in a quarter.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recording the evidenced commercial and technical assumptions lets the account team challenge the estimate before it becomes a commitment.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires

activities.name: Find the uncommitted milestones that are never going to commit
activities.description: Identify uncommitted milestones that have stopped moving and should be closed or reset rather than carried.
activities.prompt: For [account], flag uncommitted milestones with repeatedly moved dates but no changed basis, or no logged activity. Show the recorded sponsor and contact-record date, without guessing whether they still hold the role. Explain what supports resetting or closing each milestone and what evidence is missing. Don’t recommend closure from missing data alone.
activities.expectedOutput: The uncommitted milestones with repeated date moves or no logged activity, the recorded sponsor and how stale that record is, what the record does and does not show, and a reset-or-close recommendation with the evidence still needed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides what to close. Closing a milestone removes it from the picture everyone else is working from, and a quiet customer is not the same as a dead opportunity.
activities.requiredContext: One customer/account; your uncommitted milestones with their date history; the recorded sponsor on each; what you know yourself about recent customer engagement.
activitySteps: 1. Use the same account and its uncommitted milestones.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Check the recorded sponsors yourself. A stale contact record looks identical to a current one, and the agent cannot tell them apart.
4. Check each candidate before acting. A milestone can be quiet because the customer is quiet, not because it is dead.
5. Reset the ones with a real basis and a stale date, close the ones without, and say why in the record. A closed milestone with a reason is reusable evidence; one without is just a gap.
activities.whyThisMatters: Uncommitted milestones that nobody will close make the consumption picture look healthier than it is, and the sponsor who left is usually discovered by the person who inherits the milestone rather than the one who carried it.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A milestone commitment gives others a date and outcome to plan against. Focus on checking the evidence before committing, and making unresolved dependencies explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: A milestone is ready to commit when there is a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, an agreed value and date, confirmed feasibility, available customer and delivery resources, an available budget and a chosen delivery model. A populated field is not evidence. Once the milestone is committed it transfers to customer success to be driven to completion, so what you commit becomes someone else's number to defend.
discussionQuestions: Which of your uncommitted milestones would you personally defend the date on?
When a milestone gets committed early, what usually forces it?
Which committed milestone in your patch was committed before it was ready, and what did that cost?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the readiness read to the single milestone each person will either take to a sponsor or deliberately hold. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Find the uncommitted milestones that are never going to commit', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Uncommitted milestones advance only when customer and technical evidence support the criteria. Holding is valid; AI cannot create sponsorship, budget or commitment. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commitment criteria are populated on your milestone but not actually evidenced?
Would your sponsor defend this date to their own leadership?
Which single assumption is carrying most of your value?
What evidence would another specialist require before defending the proposed value and date to the sponsor?
listenFor: A named contact being treated as an agreed sponsor, values built from scope assumptions nobody has tested, dates set from when the number is needed rather than when the work can be done, and milestones being carried rather than closed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one commitment-readiness card: proposed sponsor/value/date, evidence behind each, untested assumption and sponsor validation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which commitment criterion did you find you had been treating as met without evidence?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could verify the weakest commitment criterion, then recommend advance, hold or stop to the milestone owner. Only the authorized person updates the record or records customer commitment. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized criterion checked and whether the human decision was advance, hold or stop; movement is not compulsory. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A proposed milestone has an attractive date but weak sponsorship or recorded technical confirmation. Verify the criterion and leave actual commitment recording to the authorized person.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Moving a milestone toward commitment needs supported sponsorship, value, timing and technical confirmation. SSP shapes the solution pursuit and value case; SE, commercial and receiving roles retain their own evidence and approval decisions.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the uncommitted milestone, value assumption and proposed date in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: A populated commitment field is not evidence that the customer can commit. Look for a missing commercial or technical criterion assigned to the right role.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: a populated commitment field is not evidence that the customer can commit. Confirm who can explain the solution pursuit and customer commitment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

SSP-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when a populated commitment field is not evidence that the customer can commit. Manager support can support the SSP and SE handoff before anyone represents the milestone as committed.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help the facilitator distinguish a named contact from a sponsor able to commit; route technical criteria to the appropriate technical role.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that a populated commitment field is not evidence that the customer can commit; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support the SSP and SE handoff before anyone represents the milestone as committed? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

SE-CONSUME.roleTopicName: Confirm the Technical Basis Before a Milestone Is Committed
SE-CONSUME.roleTopicDescription: Establish whether the technical path, the dependencies and the delivery model behind a milestone will hold before anyone commits to its date.
SE-CONSUME.wiifm: A candid technical readiness position helps account teams avoid committing customers to dates based on borrowed patterns, overstated pilot results, or unsecured resources.
SE-CONSUME.name: Activate Delivery and Realize Usage
SE-CONSUME.description: Plan and govern delivery, activation, support, and consumption so that an agreed solution can reach intended use; surface readiness gaps and route blockers to the authorized owner.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings permitted sales data and supported record actions into the flow of work, including on mobile. Deal Agent can assemble renewal facts and Deal Books from supported source systems; verify freshness, completeness, and current scenario availability. Review each proposed MSX write and your authority before confirming it.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed
activities.description: Establish which parts of the technical path behind a milestone are proven and which are still assumptions carrying the date.
activities.prompt: Here is a milestone we are considering committing to: [the milestone, workload, target approach and actual proof so far]. Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed. For each assumption, tell me what would prove or disprove it, the supplied owner estimate of effort to establish it, or unknown if absent, and what breaks if it turns out to be false. Then tell me which single assumption carries the most of the date. Do not treat something we have done at another customer as confirmed here; say what would make it transferable.
activities.expectedOutput: Confirmed facts, open technical assumptions, confirming tests, known effort estimates and consequences of failure, highlighting the assumption most affecting the date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides what counts as proven in this environment. A pattern that worked elsewhere is a hypothesis here, and the difference is invisible in the record once the milestone is committed.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and its workload; the target architecture or approach; what has already been proven and where; the customer's environment constraints as far as you know them.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose an uncommitted milestone with an uncertain technical dependency from already-authorized context, or a permitted example arranged by the facilitator. No advance technical analysis is required to attend.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Check that it has not quietly promoted a pattern from another customer into a confirmed fact here.
4. Take the assumption carrying the most of the date and work out what would settle it.
5. Say plainly which assumptions remain open. That sentence is what protects the date.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical commitments fail on the assumption nobody wrote down. Naming them before the commitment is the only point at which naming them is cheap.

activities.name: Name the dependencies and resources the date actually needs
activities.description: Work out what the customer and Microsoft must each provide for the milestone to land, and where those are not yet secured.
activities.prompt: Assess [milestone, proposed date, technical approach and reviewed assumptions]. Separate customer prerequisites (people, access, data, decisions), Microsoft/partner resources and delivery-model dependencies. Mark each secured, requested, not yet raised or unknown from the evidence supplied; discussion is not commitment. Identify the dependency most threatening the date only where sequencing and owner estimates support that conclusion. Otherwise ask for the missing timing or resource confirmation. Do not assume capacity or invent durations.
activities.expectedOutput: The dependencies split into customer, Microsoft or partner, and delivery model, each marked secured, requested or not yet raised, with the dependency that decides the date identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE confirms what the customer has actually agreed to provide rather than what was discussed. Assumed customer resource is the most common reason a technically sound milestone misses its date.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and its technical approach; the open assumptions; what the customer has agreed to provide; the intended delivery model; which partner or Microsoft resources are involved.
activitySteps: 1. Supply an existing milestone case, open assumptions and known resource commitments.
2. Run the prompt and check what the customer has actually agreed to provide.
3. Discuss the dependency carrying the date and who needs to confirm it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone date depends on secured customer resources, environment access and delivery ownership as well as technical feasibility.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed

activities.name: Turn the proof result into a commit or hold recommendation
activities.description: Convert what a proof of concept or pilot actually showed into a clear recommendation on whether the milestone can be committed.
activities.prompt: Here is what our proof of concept or pilot actually produced: [the actual test scope, results, untested areas and differences from production]. Turn this into a recommendation on whether the milestone can be committed. Tell me what the result genuinely supports, what it does not support because it was not tested, and what would behave differently at production scale or under production conditions. Then give me the recommendation, either commit, commit with a named condition, or hold, with the reason in one sentence I could say out loud to the account team. Do not extrapolate beyond what was tested.
activities.expectedOutput: What the proof result supports and what it does not, what would differ at production scale, and a commit, commit-with-condition or hold recommendation with a one-sentence reason.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns the recommendation. A proof result is routinely reported as broader than it was, and the person who ran it is the only one who can say where the boundary is.
activities.requiredContext: The proof of concept or pilot scope and results; what was explicitly not tested; how the test conditions differed from production; the milestone the result is meant to support.
activitySteps: 1. Bring a proof of concept or pilot result behind an uncommitted milestone.
2. Paste what was tested and what was not into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Pay attention to what it says was not tested. That is the part the account team will hear as proven.
4. Take a position. Commit, commit with a stated condition, or hold.
5. Give the account team the one-sentence reason as well as the recommendation, so it survives being repeated.
activities.whyThisMatters: A narrow proof supports only the conditions tested; recording its limits protects the milestone from overbroad retelling.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed

activities.name: Work the date backwards from the technical path
activities.description: Build the sequence of technical work a milestone date implies and find where it has no room to absorb a delay.
activities.prompt: Here is a milestone date being proposed and the technical work behind it: [the proposed date, technical work and dependencies from an existing reviewed case or the earlier option]. Work backwards from the date. Lay out what has to happen in what order, what can run in parallel and what genuinely cannot, and where a delay in one step consumes the whole margin. Tell me which step has the least certainty and the most consequence. Do not invent how long anything takes; where you need a duration, ask me for it.
activities.expectedOutput: A backwards-planned sequence from the proposed date showing order, genuine parallelism, where the margin is consumed, and the step with the least certainty and most consequence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE supplies the durations and owns the sequence. The model can structure the dependencies but has no basis for estimating how long work takes in this customer's environment.
activities.requiredContext: The proposed milestone date; the technical work required; the dependencies and who owns each; your own estimate of how long each step takes.
activitySteps: 1. Supply a proposed date, technical work and dependencies from an existing case.
2. Work backwards using accountable duration estimates; leave unknown durations as questions.
3. Discuss the least-certain step and how much delay the sequence can absorb.
activities.whyThisMatters: A date is usually set from when it is needed rather than from when the work can be done. Laying the sequence out is how that gets discussed while it can still change.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Name the dependencies and resources the date actually needs

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You are usually the person in the room who knows whether the date is achievable. Focus on the window where saying so still changes the outcome rather than explaining the miss.
keyTalkingPoints: Feasibility, resources and the delivery model are part of what makes a milestone committable, and they are the part most often assumed. A pattern that worked at another customer is a hypothesis here, not a proven fact. A proof of concept proves what it tested and nothing else, and it gets retold as broader than it was.
discussionQuestions: Which milestone in your patch has a date nobody has worked backwards from?
What is the last thing you assumed the customer would provide and they did not?
Where has a pilot result been repeated back to you as more than it actually showed?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the confirmed-versus-assumed split to the one dependency each person will secure or escalate before the date is committed. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Work the date backwards from the technical path', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical milestone dates distinguish confirmed proof from assumptions about dependencies and capacity. Honest open conditions are more useful than unsupported dates. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
facilitatorQuestions: Which part of your technical basis is confirmed here, as opposed to confirmed somewhere else?
What does the customer have to provide, and has anyone actually asked them?
What did your proof deliberately not test?
Which dependency would another SE require confirmed before recommending commit rather than hold?
listenFor: Patterns from other customers being treated as confirmed, customer-side resource being assumed rather than secured, proof results described more broadly than their scope, and durations being guessed rather than supplied.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one technical commit/hold recommendation: confirmed basis, unconfirmed customer resource, proof scope/limits, duration gap and dependency owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which assumption were you carrying as a fact until you had to write it down?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could examine an assumption behind a milestone date and consider what would settle it. An unresolved assumption must remain explicit rather than be presented to the account team as fact. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized assumption tested and whether it changed date confidence or clarified the technical hold. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A milestone date assumes a customer dependency will be ready, while proof only covers a narrower case. Review what has actually been demonstrated and leave the open condition visible.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: A milestone recommendation separates what is proven in this environment from assumptions carrying its proposed date. SE tests customer technical criteria; plans, hypotheses and rehearsals do not establish an executed test or customer acceptance.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the milestone hypothesis and uncertain technical dependency in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Evidence from another customer cannot confirm this customer's delivery date. Look for a confirmed technical fact separated from the assumption carrying the date.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: evidence from another customer cannot confirm this customer's delivery date. Confirm who can explain the technical discovery, proof and decision evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

SE-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: Usage follows when delivery readiness, customer action, ownership, and blocker resolution are explicit.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when evidence from another customer cannot confirm this customer's delivery date. Manager support can help arrange the smallest authoritative technical check without promising the commitment.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help surface customer resources or conditions still unconfirmed; leave the commit-or-hold recommendation with the technical owner.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that evidence from another customer cannot confirm this customer's delivery date; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help arrange the smallest authoritative technical check without promising the commitment? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year
activities.description: Separate the deals that can still be fully executed and processed before the period ends from the ones that are already next year's.
activities.prompt: For [territory or account], inspect opportunities closing this fiscal period. Show available approval, signature and outstanding-step evidence, and compare processing timing only with [confirmed cutoff/bookings guidance, if supplied]. State source coverage and what must still happen; don’t predict bookings or guarantee processing dates. Route missing cutoff or bookings-rule questions to Deal Desk/operations.
activities.expectedOutput: Each in-period opportunity with its approval state, what is still outstanding, its signature position, any indication it will miss the processing cutoff, and what still has to happen for it to be capable of booking.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the bookings rule locally and decides what is genuinely closeable. An approval state in the record is a snapshot, and only the person in the deal knows whether the customer will actually sign in time or is simply being polite about the date.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one customer/account; the opportunities you expect to close in the period; their current approval state; what each is waiting on; your Deal Desk or operations contact for the bookings rule that applies to your segment.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, select your authorized patch or an account with possible period-end deals using existing context, or a permitted excerpt arranged by the facilitator. No newly prepared deal list is required; keep unverified booking assumptions explicit.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Confirm the bookings rule that applies to your own segment with Deal Desk or operations rather than assuming it. What has to be true for a deal to book in a period, and by when, is set locally.
4. Separate deals waiting on Microsoft approvals from deals waiting on the customer. Confirm who can act on each and check verified processing runway rather than only the signature date.
5. Decide which deals you are deliberately leaving in the new year, and say so out loud rather than carrying them as hope.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every year some deals get forced into June that were always going to close in July, and are discounted for the privilege. The deals worth pushing are the ones that only need a signature, not the ones that still need a decision.

activities.name: Find the renewals whose expiration timing will cost you the booking
activities.description: Identify renewals whose expiration date sits at the period boundary, where how they are handled decides whether they land in this year or the next.
activities.prompt: For [territory scope or Customer/Account], list the renewals with expiration dates at or near the end of the current fiscal period. For each, tell me the actual expiration date, whether it has been committed as on-time, what is still outstanding to complete it, and what the record shows about customer engagement on it. Flag any renewal where the expiration falls on the final day of the period, so I can confirm any booking/billing-calendar difference with the authoritative operations owner. Tell me what you cannot see rather than assuming it is fine. State a calendar rule only where the current guidance I supply confirms it.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewals at the period boundary with their actual expiration dates, commitment status, outstanding work and customer engagement, with last-day expirations flagged for deliberate handling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the processing runway with the person who owns it. Renewal processing has a real lead time and the deadline that matters is when the work has to arrive, not when the agreement expires.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one customer/account; renewals with expiration dates near the period end; their commitment status; your renewals or operations contact.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose an authorized patch or account with renewals near the period boundary using existing context, or a permitted renewal excerpt arranged by the facilitator. No new portfolio analysis is required to attend.
2. Supply your case details as inputs to the prompt, then run it.
3. Flag last-day expirations for an operations check; do not assume a different treatment without current authoritative guidance.
4. Confirm the processing runway with your renewals or operations contact rather than assuming it.
5. Commit the ones that are genuinely on-time and stop describing the others as on-time.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal at the period boundary is the easiest booking to lose and the hardest to explain, because nothing about it looked at risk until it was.

activities.name: Prioritize record corrections against verified fiscal deadlines
activities.description: Find apparent record discrepancies and distinguish corrections with a confirmed fiscal deadline from year-round hygiene or timing that still needs verification.
activities.prompt: For [patch or Customer/Account], inspect the authorized records and agreement evidence available or supplied for apparent discrepancies in agreement, licensing, enrollment, amounts, forecast dates and commitments. State what the record shows, what the authoritative evidence shows and what remains uncertain. Using current correction-window guidance I supply, separate items with a confirmed fiscal-close deadline, year-round hygiene and items whose deadline is unverified. Cite the rule behind a deadline; do not assume a field becomes uneditable at year end. Identify which owner must verify or correct each item. Do not change any record.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidence-backed correction list with confirmed fiscal deadlines, year-round hygiene and unverified timing separated; each discrepancy has an accountable verification/correction owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller verifies the correct position against the agreement before changing anything. A confidently inferred correction is still a guess, and a wrong correction made in the last week of the year is materially harder to undo than a wrong original.
activities.requiredContext: Authorized account/patch and identifiers; authoritative agreement/licensing evidence; current correction-window guidance if available; operations or Deal Desk contacts. Missing guidance leaves the deadline unverified.
activitySteps: 1. During the activity, choose an authorized account or patch and inspect existing executed-agreement or other authoritative evidence, or an approved evidence excerpt arranged by the facilitator. No new Team Member evidence packet is required; stop the discrepancy check if authoritative evidence is unavailable.
2. Confirm current correction-window guidance with operations or Deal Desk.
3. Run the prompt and verify each apparent discrepancy and deadline.
4. Prioritize confirmed deadline-sensitive items by consequence and remaining runway; leave unverified deadlines as questions.
5. The authorized owner approves and makes exact corrections through the usual process, or routes them to the team that can act.
activities.whyThisMatters: Verified correction windows let the seller prioritize material discrepancies without treating an assumed fiscal cutoff as policy.

activities.name: Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented
activities.description: Sort your year-end pressure into work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar and work that belongs on the customer's own timeline.
activities.prompt: Sort [year-end urgent items, believed deadlines and their sources] into work genuinely fixed to fiscal close by a system, approval chain or booking rule, versus work pulled forward from the customer’s own decision, contract or delivery timeline. For the latter, show the cost of forcing it early. Ask about unsourced deadlines instead of assuming they exist.
activities.expectedOutput: Your year-end work sorted into genuinely fiscal-dated and customer-dated, the cost of forcing each item that is being pulled forward, and an owner and date for the items that are genuinely fixed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to force. Some work is worth pulling forward even at a cost, and that is a judgment about the customer relationship and the number, not one a model can make.
activities.requiredContext: Your own list of what you are treating as year-end urgent; where you believe each deadline comes from; the customer decision or contract timing behind each item.
activitySteps: 1. Write down everything you are treating as urgent because of year end, and where you think each deadline comes from.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about the ones where the only deadline is that it is June.
4. For anything you are pulling forward, decide whether the cost of forcing it is worth it. Often it is; the point is to decide rather than to drift.
5. Take the genuinely fiscal-dated items and make sure each one has an owner and a date that is earlier than the cutoff.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of what feels like a June deadline is a deal on its own clock being pulled forward. Doing that deliberately is fine. Doing it because the month feels urgent is how good deals get discounted and customers get pushed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Year end generates a lot of urgency and only some of it is real. This session separates the part that is genuinely fixed by the calendar from the part that only feels that way, and acts on the first while there is still room.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the current local systems-close calendar and authoritative booking, billing and approval guidance; historical dates do not establish current deadlines. Work backward from the applicable cutoff and allow the confirmed processing runway. Verify period-end renewal handling with the responsible owner. Check any ECIF or milestone calendar for its region and motion rather than treating it as a worldwide rule.
discussionQuestions: Which of the things you are rushing right now would still be urgent if it were March?
What did you find out too late at the last year end?
Which deal did you pull forward last year, and what did it cost to do it?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use the chosen result to identify one evidenced close-period action or deliberate carry-forward decision; do not require both a full deal review and record repair live. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Fiscal close depends on verified cutoffs, customer reality and authorized record ownership. Calendar pressure cannot justify forced period timing or unsupported commitments. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your in-period deals is waiting on Microsoft, and which is waiting on the customer?
What could you correct today that stops being correctable after close?
Which of your urgent items has a deadline you could actually point to?
How does a peer distinguish a real processing deadline from urgency inferred only from the fiscal calendar?
listenFor: Signature dates being treated as booking dates with no processing runway, renewals at the period boundary assumed to be fine, corrections being deferred to the week when every queue is longest, and deadlines whose only source is that it is June.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one fiscal-close workback: processing deadline requiring current confirmation, customer/Microsoft dependency, correctable record and carry-forward rationale. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your year-end deadlines turned out to have no source other than the month it is?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could examine an applicable close cutoff or a record/timing assumption at risk. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized cutoff or timing assumption checked and whether it prevented a rushed correction or unsupported year-end commitment. facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: Several deals are labeled urgent, but only one has a verified close-process cutoff. Inspect that dependency without pulling forward the customer's decision or inventing a deadline.

facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Artificial urgency is not evidence of a fiscal deadline. Look for a verified cutoff separated from hope and an owner for the processing question.

discussionQuestions: Where do partner and Microsoft stage/date views disagree?
What is customer-confirmed versus partner-reported?
What correction belongs in each system?

facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pipeline inspection reconciles contradictions and customer evidence before forecast changes. Partner stage is not verified Microsoft forecast state. preparationChecklist: Bring one partner-associated opportunity, dated partner stage/forecast evidence, the corresponding MSX record and unresolved differences. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on choosing the small number of covered accounts where DCSA time changes the result.
keyTalkingPoints: Limited to DCSA-covered or explicitly approved swarm accounts; do not imply account-by-account DCSA coverage.
Current execution: Use accessible consumption, usage, milestone, delivery, and support views; exact availability must be role-validated.
Fallback: Collect a dated exception list from current owners where data cannot be aggregated and label inaccessible evidence.
System of record: Current committed-milestone/consumption record for portfolio action; source systems remain authoritative for telemetry and support.
Optional AI boundary: AI may group supplied movements; DCSA determines cause, materiality, and intervention.
discussionQuestions: Which covered account needs intervention now?
What movement is real after dates and definitions are reconciled?
Which cause still needs owner validation?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Explain material movement before acting'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect one decision-changing evidence gap in the selected artifact, then compare a peer's approach and name the accountable next action. Drafts do not prove acceptance, approval or a completed system update. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Design an intervention with a carrier', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Consumption attention follows material change and evidenced cause. Keep hypotheses distinct and route work outside DCSA ownership. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one covered-account exception, dated usage/consumption/milestone evidence, the relevant baseline and known intervention owner. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.
facilitatorQuestions: Which material consumption or milestone movement changes the covered-portfolio plan? What evidence distinguishes the plausible causes? How does a peer choose DCSA intervention versus routing to another accountable role?
listenFor: Work starting without the stated trigger, partner involvement treated as universal, an unaccepted owner presented as coverage, AI output presented as system evidence, or Digital Cloud Solution Architect absorbing a decision outside this role boundary.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one material portfolio exception: comparable baseline/period, plausible cause, distinguishing evidence and DCSA-intervene versus route judgment. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which change was material, and what remained a hypothesis after source checking?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could inspect a material consumption change, check its cause and propose intervention or routing to its owner; a full portfolio rebuild is unnecessary. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. If inputs are unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized hypothesis corrected and whether it helped target intervention. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on recommending an architecture the customer can decide on and the selected implementer can execute.
keyTalkingPoints: Partner review is required only when a partner is the expected implementer; use the applicable customer, FastTrack, Factory, or Microsoft delivery owner otherwise.
Current execution: Use current authoritative product/security/architecture guidance and customer-validated constraints.
Fallback: Document the options and request a named expert review when required evidence or specialist authority is missing.
System of record: The technical decision record and approved architecture repository; customer source remains authoritative for environment facts.
Optional AI boundary: Researcher may locate current cited guidance; DSE validates applicability and owns the recommendation.
discussionQuestions: Which criterion decides between the options?
What evidence challenges the recommendation?
Who must confirm feasibility for the actual implementation route?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Expose assumptions and architecture options'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect one decision-changing evidence gap in the selected artifact, then compare a peer's approach and name the accountable next action. Drafts do not prove acceptance, approval or a completed system update. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Record the architecture recommendation and risk', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Technical options trace choices to customer criteria, alternatives and buildability evidence. Design recommendation is not implementation commitment. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
preparationChecklist: Bring one accepted technical criterion, architecture options, approved customer constraints and current supporting technical guidance. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.
facilitatorQuestions: Which architecture option best meets the supplied criteria, and which assumption could overturn it? What must the implementer validate for buildability? What limit would another DSE keep visible in the recommendation?
listenFor: Work starting without the stated trigger, partner involvement treated as universal, an unaccepted owner presented as coverage, AI output presented as system evidence, or Digital Solution Engineer absorbing a decision outside this role boundary.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a two-option architecture card: assumption, customer criterion, implementer buildability question, evidence gap and conditional recommendation. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which trade-off or buildability assumption changed the recommended option?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could compare an option with an alternative against a deciding criterion and seek technical or implementation-owner review of its limiting assumption. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. If inputs are unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized trade-off clarified and whether it improved the recommendation or exposed an implementation gap. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

DSE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
DSE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
DSE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

primaryAgents.name: Cowork
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Agentic Microsoft 365 experience for longer-running, outcome-focused, multi-source work.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Plans and executes multistep work, invokes skills, and creates deliverables with checkpoints.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When you want to hand off a multi-step piece of work and review it rather than do it. Complex tasks spanning Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 data, documents, presentations and recommendations, where it plans the work, runs the steps and checks in before it finishes.
keyBenefits: Executes multi-step work across Microsoft 365 instead of answering one question at a time. Built for delegation: it plans, invokes skills, works across data sources, and produces deliverables with review checkpoints.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for a quick single answer when Copilot or a specialized agent is sufficient, and for work that should keep running on a schedule after you stop asking, which is Scout.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select Cowork beside Chat. Describe the outcome you want rather than a single question, then review the work at each checkpoint it presents.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX. It brings relevant alerts, prospecting signals and pipeline context together. Preview is opened across SME&C without separate installation or opt-in; useful data depends on role and assigned records. Managers use separate reporting. Germany and Austria await Works Council approval.
secondaryAgents.whatItIs: SME&C Seller surface within Sales Agent
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. For SME&C individual contributors using MSX, preview does not require separate installation or opt-in. Relevant data is currently concentrated in AE, Specialist and CASA workflows involving Sales Accelerator signals or owned opportunities; do not infer that every role has useful records or that CASA means DCSA. If relevant signal data is absent, use Sales Accelerator or the source system that assigned the queue. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.
secondaryAgents.accessLinkLabel: Open Sales Agent, use Sales Home

resources.title: Sales Home (SME&C Hub)
resources.description: The SME&C seller surface inside Sales Agent. Covers My View, Prospecting and Pipeline today, with Campaign, Planning, Renewal and Realization & Usage on the roadmap. Sales Home is part of Sales Agent rather than a separate product, and works alongside chat rather than replacing it. In preview for SME&C individual contributors since late July 2026; it does not replace MSX. The SME&C individual-contributor preview needs no separate installation or opt-in; useful data varies by role and assigned MSX records. Managers use separate reporting. Germany and Austria await Works Council approval.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Sales Home is only for SME&C individual contributors using MSX, not non-SME&C audiences or managers; managers use separate reporting. Germany and Austria are fast-follow pending Works Council approval. Do not assume useful data for every SME&C role or map CASA to a role without confirmation. Renewal, Campaign, Planning, Realization and Deal Agent integration are roadmap, not available today, so do not build an activity that depends on them.
stepsToGetStarted: Opens Sales Agent. Sales Home is the seller surface inside it - My View for alerts and quota attainment, Prospecting for signals, account research, contacts and outreach, and Pipeline for opportunities, forecast comments, close plans and deal risks. It is not a separate product and has no separate link. No separate installation, opt-in or user enablement is required for the SME&C preview. Use relevant records only; an empty view is not proof of missing provisioning. Germany and Austria await Works Council approval; managers use separate reporting.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Draft, summarize, analyze, prepare, and create within familiar Microsoft 365 experiences.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Everyday work grounded in emails, meetings, chats, files and app content, in the app you are already working in. Ask and get: you want the answer or the draft now.
keyBenefits: Reduces time spent drafting, summarizing, and preparing work; uses permitted Microsoft 365 context to keep work grounded.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX. It brings relevant alerts, prospecting signals and pipeline context together. Preview is opened across SME&C without separate installation or opt-in; useful data depends on role and assigned records. Managers use separate reporting. agents.whatItIs: SME&C Seller surface within Sales Agent
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. For SME&C individual contributors using MSX, preview does not require separate installation or opt-in. Relevant data is currently concentrated in AE, Specialist and CASA workflows involving Sales Accelerator signals or owned opportunities; do not infer that every role has useful records or that CASA means DCSA. If relevant signal data is absent, use Sales Accelerator or the source system that assigned the queue. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Write customer-decision criteria
activities.description: Define what the solution must demonstrate and who accepts it.
activities.prompt: Using only [problem statement, discovery notes and constraints/non-functional requirements], propose a plan and pause for review. Then draft a source-linked criteria matrix: customer need, constraint, evidence gaps, proposed criterion, test method, threshold and acceptance owner. Mark unsourced thresholds and owners for confirmation. Prioritize criteria and open questions in chat; don’t run tests, change records or treat draft criteria as customer agreement. Flag unavailable sources or Cowork access.
activities.expectedOutput: Prioritized criteria with evidence method, threshold, and acceptance owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: DSE authors technical criteria; customer acceptance must be explicit.
activities.requiredContext: Already-enabled Cowork authorized for the supplied materials; DSE-DISC-01 output, approved problem statement, dated discovery notes, constraints, non-functional requirements, risk tolerance and decision participants. Thresholds and acceptance owners require supplied evidence or explicit to-confirm labels. No private-system retrieval or technical execution. Manual or M365 Copilot fallback is not Cowork execution.
activities.bestFitJob: Define what the solution must demonstrate and who accepts it.
activitySteps: 1. Complete DSE-DISC-01 and select the approved problem statement, discovery notes and dated constraint/non-functional-requirement evidence.
2. Open already-enabled, authorized Cowork. Review the proposed source-to-criteria plan before synthesis.
3. Reconcile the inputs into a traceability matrix, preserving contradictions, source dates and missing evidence. Leave unsourced thresholds and acceptance owners to confirm.
4. Draft and prioritize customer-decision criteria with evidence methods; DSE validates technical authorship and does not infer customer acceptance or run a test.
5. Keep the packet and open questions in chat as a draft. No files, sending, scheduling, record update, approval or assignment is authorized.

Access/fallback: No second tool, connector or private-system access is required. If Cowork is unavailable, mark the practice not run and prepare the same output manually or in already-authorized M365 Copilot; do not label the fallback Cowork execution. Clearly label synthetic inputs and outputs.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on avoiding repeated discovery while establishing criteria precise enough to design and prove against.
keyTalkingPoints: Engage when a qualified opportunity requires architecture, security/compliance, proof, or technical-risk judgment; do not apply DSE to every opportunity.
Current execution: Use customer-provided facts, prior discovery, architecture/estate records, and current authoritative technical guidance.
Fallback: Run a focused discovery session and explicitly label unavailable estate/configuration evidence.
System of record: The agreed technical decision record for criteria; source systems remain authoritative for estate and requirements.
Optional AI boundary: An approved assistant may organize supplied notes. It must not infer customer configuration or agree criteria.
discussionQuestions: Which customer decision criteria are still inferred?
What prior discovery can be reused?
Which configuration or estate fact remains unavailable?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Reconcile discovery already completed'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect one decision-changing evidence gap in the selected artifact, then compare a peer's approach and name the accountable next action. Drafts do not prove acceptance, approval or a completed system update. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Close or assign critical evidence gaps', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Discovery makes customer criteria and gaps explicit before design. Proposed criteria remain assumptions until confirmed. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
preparationChecklist: Bring one qualified technical problem, approved prior discovery, customer criteria, known constraints and available estate evidence. Label source, scope and date; record access or evidence gaps. Use only approved material and tools.
facilitatorQuestions: What discovery has already been completed and by whom? Which customer-accepted criterion would settle the technical question? How would a peer close one decisive evidence gap without repeating all the discovery?
listenFor: Work starting without the stated trigger, partner involvement treated as universal, an unaccepted owner presented as coverage, AI output presented as system evidence, or Digital Solution Engineer absorbing a decision outside this role boundary.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one discovery ledger and criterion: prior finding, source/date, confirmed versus assumed state, customer decision, evidence method and acceptance owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which criterion changed after customer or decision-owner validation?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could validate a decision-changing criterion or assumption and identify the next proof gap with the technical decision owner. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. If inputs are unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized criterion checked and whether it reduced discovery rework. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

DSE-PROOF.todayObjective: Test whether existing evidence can settle the customer's technical doubt and, when it cannot, judge the smallest proof scope with meaningful acceptance and exit conditions.
DSE-PROOF.whyItMatters: A traceable path from problem to validated proof helps teams recommend solutions responsibly and move customer decisions without overstating evidence.
DSE-PROOF.desiredOutcome: Choose between reuse, adaptation, and new technical proof based on transferable evidence, keeping the work bounded to a customer decision and its acknowledged limitations.
