facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The investment routes that matter most in this segment run through partners. Focus on using them deliberately.
keyTalkingPoints: Choose the investment route before assembling a request. Check current route-specific guidance and the accountable owner for eligibility, thresholds, funding and partner requirements; historical examples are not current policy. Confirm the partner obligations, evidence, incentives and accepted owner for the selected route. AI may organize the evidence but cannot establish eligibility or approval.
discussionQuestions: Which partner-led routes do you actually use?
When did a partner-led program last produce nothing, and why?
Does the partner know what the program requires of them?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Check what this partner has already signed up to'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the route to the specific obligation the partner has agreed to and the date. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Get the partner to agree to their half', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Partner-led investment needs understood obligations and feasible participation. Nomination is not partner acceptance or approved funding. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
preparationChecklist: Bring one partner and one opportunity where investment could help.
facilitatorQuestions: What does this route require the partner to do?
What does the partner get out of it?
Who is tracking whether they do it?
What evidence has a peer used that a partner accepted its program obligations?
listenFor: Partner obligations being assumed rather than agreed, programs nominated and never started, the partner's incentive being taken for granted, and PSS carrying activity that the program expects the partner to carry.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one partner-program obligation row: proposed route, required partner action, incentive assumption, acceptance evidence or unknown and tracking owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. activities.name: Tell a funding barrier from a decision barrier
activities.description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
activities.prompt: Use supplied material only. For the account identified in [paste/attach approved account and barrier evidence], show what is recorded that would bear on whether investment could help: the open opportunities and their stage, any recorded blocker or objection, the existing agreement and its type, what is deployed against it, whether a partner is associated, and any recorded activity in the last six months. Report what is recorded and do not assess whether investment is appropriate.
activities.expectedOutput: The account's recorded position with the barrier stated, and your own read on whether it is one funding removes.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE decides whether the barrier is one money removes. Validate the customer explanation: decision uncertainty and cost can coexist, and a recorded blocker alone does not prove investment is the right lever.
activities.requiredContext: One account with a barrier that funding might remove, with authorized dated account or opportunity evidence and any required agreement, partner, usage, support or policy extracts supplied by their owners. Sales Agent is optional and must already be authorized for the material; otherwise review manually. The broader SME&C Sales Home preview does not establish access to required external records or integrations.
activities.bestFitJob: Tell a funding barrier from a decision barrier
activitySteps: 1. Use Sales Agent only if already available and authorized for these supplied materials; otherwise review the same evidence manually. Supply the account or opportunity facts with the existing bounded prompt; do not assume a live data connection.
2. Separate what the record shows from what you have been told. Name disagreements.
3. Form your own view of the barrier before reading another assessment.
4. Prepare the evidence question for whoever owns the request rather than acting on it.

Access/fallback: The existing launch and mapping identify Sales Agent as the optional host for supplied-evidence analysis, not proof that Sales Home retrieves the external records this investment review requires. Have authorized owners supply required agreement, usage, support, partner-program, pricing or policy details. Manual review is sufficient; no Deal Agent or renewal integration is assumed.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment is a lever for a specific class of barrier. Offering it against the wrong one trains the customer to wait for it.

activities.name: Check the route sources before the selected handoff
activities.description: Organize the route-specific evidence and unanswered requirements for the request owner before preparing an investment handoff.
activities.prompt: Using only [dated account-barrier evidence and authoritative route guidance], compare applicable direct, partner-led and voucher routes. Draft a source-check table with requirements/questions, supporting evidence, gaps and request-owner questions; mark unestablished routes unconfirmed. Don’t recommend a route, determine eligibility/funding amounts, promise availability or prepare a submission. If guidance conflicts or is missing, flag the gap instead of inventing requirements. Propose owners only; routing doesn’t establish acceptance.
activities.expectedOutput: A route-specific source-check table separating available evidence, missing requirements and questions for the request owner, without an eligibility or funding determination.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE checks source currency and applicability and keeps eligibility, amounts, availability, approval and submission with the authorized request owner. The table is evidence organization, not confirmation that a route is available.
activities.requiredContext: One account barrier, any existing barrier-recognition findings, and supplied current authoritative guidance for each applicable route. Name missing guidance and its owner. Use sanitized supplied evidence when live material is unavailable.
activities.bestFitJob: Check the route sources before the selected handoff
activitySteps: 1. Select this as an alternative live practice when the useful next decision is what route evidence the request owner still needs; use existing barrier findings if available.

2. The facilitator or manager arranges current authoritative guidance for the applicable direct, partner-led or voucher route; review that supplied guidance during the activity. If it is unavailable, record the source question and pause the route comparison rather than ask Team Members to obtain it in advance. Do not assume all three routes apply or funding is available.
3. Compare the supplied requirements and evidence manually, or use Microsoft 365 Copilot only if already authorized for these materials. No portal access or connector is assumed.
4. Check every requirement against its cited guidance; separate available evidence, missing requirements, questions and conflicting sources for the request owner.
5. If the optional DAE-INV-02 handoff is later selected, carry this source-check table into it first. Keep the handoff unsent. This does not make three live practices mandatory.
activities.whyThisMatters: An owner can act on a sourced question. An unsupported route assumption can become an investment promise before anyone has checked the requirements.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment reaches your role even though you do not own the request. Focus on the part that is yours.
keyTalkingPoints: Recognize the customer barrier and route it to the investment owner rather than treating recognition as permission to submit. Verify current route-specific eligibility, funding and partner requirements with authoritative guidance. Compare direct, partner-led and voucher routes where applicable. AI may organize evidence but cannot establish eligibility or approval.
discussionQuestions: Where have you seen investment help, and where have you seen it wasted?
What does your role actually contribute to an investment decision?
Who owns the request once you have raised it?
suggestedTransitions: Choose one live practice: 'Tell a funding barrier from a decision barrier', or 'Check the route sources before the selected handoff' when the useful question is route evidence. These are alternatives, not two mandatory steps. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Route it to whoever owns the request'. If the route source-check was selected, finish it before that unsent handoff and carry forward its missing evidence and owner questions. Do not make all three practices mandatory or infer eligibility from recognition.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Investment recognition distinguishes a removable account barrier from an unresolved customer decision and routes useful evidence to the request owner. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one situation where customer investment is or was in play.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the barrier, precisely?
What is yours to decide here and what is not?
What would you need to see to be confident?
What customer barrier did a peer decide not to solve with investment, and why?
listenFor: Investment proposed as a discount by another name, barriers that are really timing, and DAEs building requests themselves rather than routing them.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one investment-recognition card: evidenced account barrier, why funding may help, remaining customer decision and request-owner handoff. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What could investment remove, and what customer decision would remain even with funding?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could check an investment hypothesis against an account barrier and route the evidence question to the request owner without promising eligibility or funds. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. activities.name: Decide what would count as proof
activities.description: Define observable technical success, negative-result, exit, and review-evidence criteria for the proposed work.
activities.prompt: Use supplied material only. A customer investment would fund this technical work: [paste/attach the technical work and customer concern]. Define what it would need to demonstrate for the customer's doubt to be resolved: the observable success criteria, what would constitute a clear negative result, the exit criteria that end the work either way, and the evidence a reviewer would need afterwards. Do not assume the investment is approved and do not estimate cost or duration.
activities.expectedOutput: What the funded work would have to demonstrate, expressed as things somebody could observe happening.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides how much the funded work must prove before the customer would act on the result. Proving too little leaves the doubt intact and the funding spent; proving too much turns a bounded piece of work into a project, and where that line sits depends on what this specific customer said they doubted.
activities.requiredContext: One proposed piece of technical work, the stated customer doubt, authorized technical evidence and the DSE/customer acceptance owner. Use supplied qualitative criteria; numeric thresholds require actual owner approval. Optional Sales Home account context is not needed to define technical proof and supplies no technical-design authority.
activities.bestFitJob: Decide what would count as proof
activitySteps: 1. Supply proposed technical work, stated customer doubt and authorized technical evidence; Sales Home may provide relevant MSX account context, not a technical proof-design authority.
2. Separate evidenced technical facts from briefed claims; identify observable evidence needed to test the stated customer doubt.
3. Form your own view before reading anyone else's assessment.
4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.

Access/fallback: Sales Home is a preview experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX; no separate installation or opt-in is required. Relevant data varies by role; Germany and Austria await Works Council approval. Use authorized dated account/opportunity extracts; required agreement, usage, support, partner-program, pricing or policy detail must be supplied by its authorized owner. No Deal Agent/renewal roadmap integration is assumed. If relevant records are unavailable, review the same supplied evidence manually or in one already authorized general assistant.
activities.whyThisMatters: Funded technical work is assessed at closure against whatever criteria existed at the start. If none did, the assessment becomes a matter of opinion and the next request is harder.

activities.name: Write the criteria down before the work is funded
activities.description: Record the technical success and exit criteria in a form a reviewer can assess against afterwards.
activities.prompt: Use supplied material only. I have defined what an investment-funded piece of technical work must demonstrate. Here are my criteria: [paste or attach my observable proof and exit criteria]. Write them up for the investment request: what will be demonstrated, how each will be observed, what would constitute a clear negative result, and the point at which the work stops either way. Mark anything I have written that could not actually be observed. Do not add criteria I have not stated and do not estimate effort or duration.
activities.expectedOutput: Success and exit criteria written for the request, with anything unobservable marked before it is submitted.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE owns which criteria survive into the request. Preserve agreed success, negative-result and exit criteria with their evidence method; any change requires relevant technical-owner and customer review rather than assumed approval.
activities.requiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
activities.bestFitJob: Write the criteria down before the work is funded
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and supply the relevant case details as inputs.
2. Check that what you could not determine is as visible as what you found. Silence on a gap reads as a clear result.
3. Say what your role would still have to do. Missing technical responsibilities may block execution and need owner clarification.
4. Prepare an unsent technical-criteria handoff for DSE and request-owner review.

Access/fallback: Use the named assistant only if already available and authorized for these supplied materials; otherwise prepare the same bounded output manually. No second tool, connector or private-system access is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Criteria that live only in your head are renegotiated at closure by people who were not there. Written into the request, they set the terms of the assessment before anyone has a stake in the answer.

activities.name: Plan how the technical proof will produce its evidence
activities.description: Turn the approved proof criteria into a bounded execution plan that identifies method, evidence sources, responsibilities, and the stop point.
activities.prompt: Use only the proof criteria and technical context I provide. Do not invent customer commitments, cost, duration, or evidence access. activities.expectedOutput: A bounded proof plan mapping each agreed criterion to an evidence method, artifact or measurement, responsible owner, reviewer, dependency, and decision point, with unresolved items visible.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE verifies technical feasibility and that the evidence method genuinely tests the customer's stated doubt. The accountable request owner decides whether to submit or approve the plan.
activities.requiredContext: The written success, negative, and exit criteria; proposed technical work; known technical constraints and dependencies; and the human technical owner and reviewer.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the criteria and request write-up from the prior activities.
2. Run the prompt using the supplied technical context.
3. Confirm the evidence method and responsibilities with the technical owner.
4. Flag criteria that cannot be observed or dependencies that are unresolved.
5. Route the execution plan to the request owner; do not imply that investment or work is approved.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment reaches your role even though you do not own the request. Focus on the part that is yours.
keyTalkingPoints: Separate investment routing from technical proof. The request owner confirms the route and current requirements; you make the proposed technical question, success evidence and delivery dependencies explicit. Confirm criteria before work starts. AI may organize evidence but cannot establish eligibility, technical success or approval.
discussionQuestions: Where have you seen investment help, and where have you seen it wasted?
What does your role actually contribute to an investment decision?
Who owns the request once you have raised it?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Decide what would count as proof'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the assessment to the one thing each person routes or confirms this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Write the criteria down before the work is funded', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Funded proof should settle the customer doubt with the smallest verifiable test, including a meaningful negative result and exit. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring one situation where customer investment is or was in play.
facilitatorQuestions: What customer doubt must the funded technical proof settle? Which observable success, negative-result and exit criteria bound it? How would another DSE shrink the proof without changing the investment owner's decision?
listenFor: Success criteria nobody could observe, scope that expands to fill the funding, and exit criteria being omitted entirely.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one technical proof contract: customer doubt, falsifiable success/negative result, minimum scope, evidence method and exit condition. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. This is a storyboard or proof contract, not an executed demo, successful test or permission to use an environment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What observed result would change the decision, and what would justify stopping proof?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could define a bounded success or failure criterion and ask the technical owner to validate scope and evidence method; do not approve execution or funds. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. Funding, terms, eligibility and approvals remain with authorized owners. If inputs are unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized proof criterion clarified and whether it avoided unnecessary work or exposed an untestable claim. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.name: Check the environment, not the opportunity
activities.description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
activities.prompt: Use supplied material only. An investment-funded engagement is proposed for the account identified in [paste/attach the proposed technical work and approved account evidence]. Show me what is recorded about the account that bears on whether it could absorb this: the workloads deployed and what usage is recorded against them, any open or recently resolved support issues, whether a partner is associated, and the recorded technical activity in the last six months. Report what is recorded and do not assess readiness.
activities.expectedOutput: Recorded technical facts and gaps, plus a separately labeled, human-reviewed judgment about delivery dependencies.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which customer-side dependency would genuinely block delivery. Every engagement depends on something the customer must provide, and the judgment is which of those this particular customer will actually struggle with - the record shows what they have, not what they can take on.
activities.requiredContext: One proposed investment-funded engagement and the account it would run on. Supply authorized dated account/opportunity and required agreement, partner, usage, support or policy extracts. Sales Home is a preview experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX; no separate installation or opt-in is required. Relevant data varies by role; Germany and Austria await Works Council approval. Supplied evidence and manual review suffice. No Deal Agent/renewal integration is assumed.
activities.bestFitJob: Check the environment, not the opportunity
activitySteps: 1. Review the supplied account environment and deployment evidence; do not assume Sales Home retrieves these records. The guided-surface fit for this activity needs source-owner confirmation.
2. Separate what the record shows from what you have been told. On a non-unified account the record is thinner, so the difference matters more.
3. Form your own view before reading anyone else's assessment.
4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.

Access/fallback: Sales Home is a preview experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX; no separate installation or opt-in is required. Relevant data varies by role; Germany and Austria await Works Council approval. Use authorized dated account/opportunity extracts; required agreement, usage, support, partner-program, pricing or policy detail must be supplied by its authorized owner. No Deal Agent/renewal roadmap integration is assumed. If relevant records are unavailable, review the same supplied evidence manually or in one already authorized general assistant.
activities.whyThisMatters: Funded technical work needs customer-side prerequisites and capacity. Authorized environment evidence identifies questions to validate; it does not prove readiness or consumption outcome.

activities.name: Name the dependency that would stop it
activities.description: Set out the customer-side dependencies that would block funded delivery, and who would have to resolve each.
activities.prompt: Use supplied material only. I have assessed whether a customer could absorb investment-funded technical work. Here is what I found: [paste or attach the customer-readiness findings and evidence]. Set out the customer-side dependencies that would have to be in place before the work could start or complete: what each is, who on the customer or partner side would have to provide it, and what happens to the engagement if it is not there. Separate the ones I have confirmed from the ones I am assuming. Do not assess whether the investment should proceed.
activities.expectedOutput: The customer-side dependencies that would block delivery, separated into those confirmed and those assumed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA distinguishes a dependency the customer has been told about from one they have agreed to. Preserve actual acceptance evidence and open questions; a write-up or named contact alone is not agreement.
activities.requiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
activities.bestFitJob: Name the dependency that would stop it
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and supply the relevant case details as inputs.
2. Check that what you could not determine is as visible as what you found. Silence on a gap reads as a clear result.
3. Say what your role would still have to do. Missing customer-side responsibilities may block delivery and need owner confirmation.
4. Prepare an unsent dependency handoff for DCSA and request-owner review.

Access/fallback: Use the named assistant only if already available and authorized for these supplied materials; otherwise prepare the same bounded output manually. No second tool, connector or private-system access is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Customer-side dependencies can block sound technical work. Naming required evidence and actual owner acceptance exposes risks without predicting how a future stall will be attributed.

activities.name: Turn customer dependencies into a readiness gate
activities.description: Translate the identified customer-side dependencies into an ordered readiness check with a named owner and evidence required before funded work can begin.
activities.prompt: Use only the dependency findings and approved context I provide. Do not decide whether investment is approved, declare the work ready, or make a customer commitment. Organize each confirmed or assumed dependency by sequence, responsible customer or partner owner, evidence needed to confirm it, and consequence if it is not met. Identify dependencies that block starting work, dependencies that can be resolved during delivery, and unresolved assumptions. If sequencing or ownership is unknown, flag the gap rather than inventing it.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced readiness gate listing dependencies, owner, confirmation evidence, blocker status, and unresolved assumptions, without an approval or readiness decision.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA confirms dependencies with the customer or partner owner and routes the gate to the role that owns the investment decision. Only the authorized owner decides readiness or approval.
activities.requiredContext: The proposed funded work, the recorded environment review, identified customer-side dependencies, known customer or partner owners, and the accountable investment or delivery owner.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the dependency findings from the environment and dependency review.
2. Run the prompt using only confirmed or approved supplied context.
3. Check each owner and readiness evidence with the accountable human.
4. Mark unresolved dependencies and assumptions explicitly.
5. Route the readiness gate to the investment or delivery owner; do not represent the work as approved or ready.

Access/fallback: Use the named assistant only if already available and authorized for these supplied materials; otherwise prepare the same bounded output manually. No second tool, connector or private-system access is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Identifying dependencies is useful only if the delivery owner can see their order, proof, and unresolved blockers before funded work is scheduled.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment reaches your role even though you do not own the request. Focus on the part that is yours.
keyTalkingPoints: Connect proposed funded work to an observable adoption or consumption outcome. Verify delivery capacity and customer dependencies instead of assuming that approval makes execution feasible. The request owner confirms current eligibility, funding and route requirements. AI may organize evidence but cannot establish eligibility, delivery readiness or approval.
discussionQuestions: Where have you seen investment help, and where have you seen it wasted?
What does your role actually contribute to an investment decision?
Who owns the request once you have raised it?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Check the environment, not the opportunity'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the assessment to the one thing each person routes or confirms this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Name the dependency that would stop it', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Absorption readiness requires accepted dependencies, not just a technically eligible environment. Coverage without dedicated support cannot imply customer or partner capacity. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one situation where customer investment is or was in play.
facilitatorQuestions: Which customer-environment prerequisite is actually confirmed? What customer or partner dependency is unaccepted, especially without dedicated support coverage? How would another DCSA record a readiness hold without implying funding approval?
listenFor: Prerequisites the customer has been told about but not agreed to, partner delivery capacity being assumed, and readiness judged from the opportunity rather than the environment.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one customer-environment readiness gate: technical prerequisite, customer/partner dependency, acceptance evidence or unknown, proposed owner and hold reason. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which recorded-ready prerequisite was not accepted by the customer or delivery partner?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could check the customer dependency most likely to block funded work and seek owner confirmation; recommend hold if readiness or support ownership is unclear. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. Funding, terms, eligibility and approvals remain with authorized owners. If inputs are unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized prerequisite checked and whether it changed readiness or prevented an unsupported delivery assumption. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.name: Test whether the structure survives without the investment
activities.description: Check whether a commercial structure you are building depends on funding that has not been approved.
activities.prompt: Use supplied material only. For the account identified in [paste/attach the deal structure and agreement evidence], I am structuring a deal where customer investment is expected to form part of it. Show what is recorded: the existing agreement and its type, the products and quantities involved, any amendment or exception already recorded, the deal stage and value, and whether a partner is associated. Report what is recorded. Do not assess the investment, do not determine eligibility, and do not comment on approval.
activities.expectedOutput: The structure described with and without the investment, and any dependency on an unapproved decision made explicit.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides whether a structure that depends on unapproved investment should be presented at all. Make conditional terms and unresolved approvals explicit; the comparison creates no investment decision or customer commitment.
activities.requiredContext: One deal you are structuring where customer investment is expected to be part of it. Supply authorized dated account/opportunity and required agreement, partner, usage, support or policy extracts. Sales Home is a preview experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX; no separate installation or opt-in is required. Relevant data varies by role; Germany and Austria await Works Council approval. Supplied evidence and manual review suffice. No Deal Agent/renewal integration is assumed.
activities.bestFitJob: Test whether the structure survives without the investment
activitySteps: 1. Review the supplied account agreement and commercial-structure evidence; do not assume Sales Home retrieves these records. The guided-surface fit for this activity needs source-owner confirmation.
2. Describe the structure twice: once assuming the investment arrives and once assuming it does not.
3. If the second version does not work, the structure depends on a decision you do not own. Say so now rather than at approval.
4. Route any eligibility or investment question to the role that owns it rather than answering it.

Access/fallback: Sales Home is a preview experience within Sales Agent for SME&C individual contributors using MSX; no separate installation or opt-in is required. Relevant data varies by role; Germany and Austria await Works Council approval. Use authorized dated account/opportunity extracts; required agreement, usage, support, partner-program, pricing or policy detail must be supplied by its authorized owner. No Deal Agent/renewal roadmap integration is assumed. If relevant records are unavailable, review the same supplied evidence manually or in one already authorized general assistant.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment decisions sit outside the CE's authority in this segment, but the commercial consequence of one not arriving lands entirely on the structure. That exposure is worth seeing before the customer does.

activities.name: Compare authorized structures with and without approved investment
activities.description: Compare the current commercial structure with only the alternatives already authorized by the accountable commercial owner, making the effect of an unapproved investment decision explicit.
activities.prompt: Use only the commercial structure, approved terms, and alternatives I provide. Do not invent pricing, discounts, offers, precedent, or investment eligibility. Compare the current structure with each supplied authorized alternative, both with and without the investment being approved. Show which assumptions or terms change, what remains unresolved, and which option depends on an unapproved decision. If no authorized alternative is supplied, say that the comparison cannot be completed and list the information needed from the accountable commercial owner.
activities.expectedOutput: A side-by-side comparison of the current structure and supplied authorized alternatives with and without approved investment, with assumptions, dependencies, and unresolved approvals identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE confirms that each option and term is authorized and commercially accurate. Investment eligibility and approval remain with their designated owners.
activities.requiredContext: The current commercial structure, approved terms and options supplied by the commercial owner, the known investment decision status, and any applicable approval guidance.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the current structure and only the alternatives confirmed as authorized for consideration.
2. Run the prompt with the investment approval status clearly stated.
3. Verify every term against the approved source and separate facts from assumptions.
4. Route unresolved terms or eligibility questions to their accountable owners.
5. Do not present an unapproved alternative to a customer.

Access/fallback: Use the named assistant only if already available and authorized for these supplied materials; otherwise prepare the same bounded output manually. No second tool, connector or private-system access is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: A structure that only works if unapproved investment arrives is exposed; comparing authorized alternatives makes that dependency visible before a commitment is made.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment may affect a deal you structure even when another role owns the request. Focus on one commercial dependency and the authoritative owner who must resolve it.
keyTalkingPoints: Keep this an awareness discussion about commercial dependencies, not an investment-submission tutorial. Confirm how the proposed investment affects the structure, what remains viable if it is declined, and which authoritative owner must decide. Use current route-specific guidance; do not infer eligibility, funding, precedent or approval.
discussionQuestions: When has an investment changed a structure you built?
What would you want to know before structuring around one?
Who would you ask?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test whether the structure survives without the investment'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the discussion to the single question each person would raise next time. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Compare authorized structures with and without approved investment', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commercial structure must expose unapproved investment dependencies. Funding does not bypass agreement, precedent or approval authority. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
preparationChecklist: Think of one deal where investment was involved.
facilitatorQuestions: What would change about the structure if the investment did not come?
What precedent does this set?
Whose decision is the investment itself?
How would another CE test the commercial construct if proposed investment is declined?
listenFor: CEs taking on investment requests that belong elsewhere, structures that only work if investment is approved, and precedent implications going unnoticed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a two-scenario commercial comparison: construct without investment, conditional construct with approved investment, precedent question and authorized decision owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep commercial, funding, staffing and publication authority with the authorized humans; a proposed owner is not an accepted assignment.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What would change if investment were declined, and who can authorize the alternative?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If investment affects a relevant deal, you could explore the construct without funding and identify a structure or policy question for its authorized owner; discussing a sanitized case or taking no next step is also valid. If you choose Microsoft 365 Copilot, use it only for permitted drafting or analysis; manual exploration is also a choice. Humans validate sources, accept work and control record changes or messages. Funding, terms, eligibility and approvals remain with authorized owners. If inputs are unavailable, you could explore a sanitized example or leave the gap open. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized funding dependency exposed and whether it preserved an alternative or clarified a hold. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.name: Find the closes you cannot account for
activities.description: List recent closed-won opportunities in your book and separate the ones you closed from the ones that closed some other way.
activities.prompt: Show me the opportunities in [account list or territory scope] that were marked closed won with a close date in [review period, e.g. last 30 days]. For each, show the account, the value, the close date, the products or SKU lines attached, and the recorded close reason or status if one is set. Report what is recorded. Do not assess whether any close was correct. State unavailable fields and material source-coverage limits. Distinguish no matching records from inability to retrieve them; do not present a partial result as complete.
activities.expectedOutput: Recent closed-won opportunities with the ones the seller cannot account for identified, or an explicit statement that there were none.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides which closes they can account for. A closed record can be well-formed and still describe something that did not happen, and the check is whether the value, products and date match what was actually sold.
activities.requiredContext: Your own opportunities and the date range you want to review.
activities.bestFitJob: See which of your deals closed without you closing them
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with a short recent period. Keep it small enough to read in one sitting.
2. Go down the list and mark the ones you do not remember closing. You are working from your own memory of the deal here, not from a field.
3. For each one you marked, ask whether you can account for the value, the products and the date. Mark anything you cannot.
4. Take the marked ones forward. If there are none, say so - that is a result worth the room hearing.
activities.whyThisMatters: A closed record carries your number whether or not you set it. A wrong one raises no error and blocks nothing, so it survives until somebody has to explain it.

activities.name: Work out what to do about the one you cannot explain
activities.description: Take a closed record you cannot account for and decide whether to accept it, correct it, or raise it.
activities.prompt: Here is a closed-won opportunity I cannot fully account for: [the closed-won record with account, value, date, close reason and products]. Here is what I know was actually happening on that account: [my account knowledge: sold, signed, delivered and still open]. Lay out where the record and my account knowledge agree, where they disagree, and what would settle each disagreement. Do not tell me whether the close was correct.
activities.expectedOutput: Evidence-limited comparison of where the supplied closed-won record and seller account knowledge agree/disagree, with the evidence needed to settle each disagreement. The seller separately decides accepted, corrected, routed or held disposition.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides whether the record matches what was sold, and whether the correction is theirs to make or somebody else's. Account knowledge is one input rather than the deciding one, and a correction made without the contract in front of you replaces one wrong record with another.
activities.requiredContext: One closed record you could not account for, and what you know was happening on that account.
activities.bestFitJob: Decide what to do about a close you cannot account for
activitySteps: 1. Use the permitted questioned-close record extract or reference and your account-knowledge context in the approved surface; do not paste restricted content.
2. Compare the disagreements and identify what evidence could settle each.
3. The seller decides whether the close is supported, a correction is within their authority, another owner must act or more evidence is needed. Cowork's comparison does not decide the disposition.
4. If you decide a correction is warranted and are authorized, review the exact correction and use the separate approved record process; do not ask Cowork to execute it from this comparison.
5. Record the permitted evidence checked, unresolved question and responsible owner or role so the next person can continue without treating routing as correction or acceptance.
activities.whyThisMatters: A wrong close is easy to leave alone because nothing breaks. It shows up later as revenue that cannot be explained or a customer conversation that starts from a false position.

activities.name: Check what happened after the disposition
activities.description: After a questioned close has been dispositioned, compare the authorized resulting record or receiving-owner response with the evidence behind that disposition.
activities.prompt: Using only [questioned close, checked evidence, prior checked-close disposition and later authorized record extract or receiving-owner response], compare the intended disposition with what later evidence establishes. Draft a source-dated table of confirmed/corrected facts, merely routed/unresolved items and remaining checks. Preserve recorded owners and mark proposed owners or acceptance unconfirmed. Do not infer Auto-Close provenance, revenue matching, completed corrections or acceptance from routing notes. Without later evidence, report unresolved, not verified. Do not retrieve other records or execute actions.
activities.expectedOutput: A post-disposition verification row distinguishing confirmed/corrected evidence, merely routed work and unresolved checks, with owner acceptance recorded only when evidenced.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller verifies the actual later evidence and decides whether trust or ownership has improved. The assistant cannot certify the close, infer acceptance, or authorize corrections.
activities.requiredContext: Prior checked-close disposition and supporting evidence; any authorized dated post-disposition record extract or receiving-owner response. Later evidence may be unavailable; its absence leaves the check unresolved.
activities.bestFitJob: Check what happened after the disposition
activitySteps: 1. After ALL-CLOSEDWON-02, bring its disposition and checked evidence plus any authorized later record or owner response. Keep restricted details in approved systems.
2. If Cowork is already authorized for these materials, supply only those extracts and run the comparison prompt; otherwise compare them manually. No connector or integration is required.
3. Separate what the later evidence confirms or shows was corrected from what was only routed and what remains unresolved. Do not repeat the original diagnosis as a result.
4. Have the seller check whether the result supports trust in the record and whether ownership was actually accepted. A proposed next check remains a proposal.
5. Prepare an anonymized bring-back summary with the remaining evidence check, if any. Do not edit a record or send a follow-up as part of this practice.
activities.whyThisMatters: A sensible disposition is not proof it took effect. The next check tests whether the record can now be trusted and whether the next owner actually took responsibility.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A closed-won record carries your number whether or not you were the one who set it. Closes arrive through your own work, through automation, and through other people acting on the account. Focus on reading your own recent closes and deciding which ones you can stand behind.
keyTalkingPoints: A wrong close raises no error and blocks nothing. It stays in the book until somebody has to explain it, and by then the context has gone.
The test is not whether the record is well-formed. It is whether the value, the products and the date describe what was actually sold.
Your account knowledge is the input here, not the verdict. A correction made without the contract in front of you replaces one wrong record with another.
Finding nothing is a real result. Say so in the room rather than treating the exercise as having failed.
discussionQuestions: When did you last read your own closed-won list rather than your open pipeline?
If a close in your book were wrong, how would you find out?
Which part of a closed record would you struggle to explain in a review?
suggestedTransitions: Choose one live Featured practice appropriate to the evidence: start with 'Find the closes you cannot account for', or work a known questioned record through its disposition. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Check what happened after the disposition', only after ALL-CLOSEDWON-02. Bring later evidence or an explicit unresolved gap; routing alone is not verification. Keep the live huddle to one selected practice.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Closed-book inspection reconciles recorded outcomes with what happened. Accept, correct, route or hold based on evidence and ownership, not pressure to find an error. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
facilitatorQuestions: Which close in your list did you not recognise straight away?
What in that record does not match what you remember selling?
Is this one yours to correct, or does it need somebody else?
What check would a peer use to notice an unexplained close even when the total looks right?
listenFor: Sellers scrolling past records they do not recognise because the totals look right. “that must have been the partner” or “that came from the team” offered as an explanation rather than as something to check. Reluctance to raise a close that flatters the number, and the assumption that a well-formed record is a correct one.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one close-verification row: record identifier in the example, stated close fact, unexplained discrepancy, evidence needed and correction owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you find in your own closed book that you had not looked at before? What would have to be true for you to notice it sooner next time?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore an unexplained closed-won record and consider accept, correct within authority, route or hold for an evidence check; no discrepancy or record change is required. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized manual scenario or leave the gap open; no report is required. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized discrepancy or confirmed record and whether its disposition improved trust or clarified ownership. If you choose to share an Extended follow-up, distinguish later confirmed/corrected evidence from merely routed work and unresolved checks; name the remaining check without assuming owner acceptance. A brief verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share the gap or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A recent closed-won record is difficult to explain from the available account context. Compare approved facts and choose a disposition without assuming an automated close is accurate.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Closed-won review compares recorded facts with authoritative evidence before choosing a discrepancy's disposition. Sending, receiving, account, technical and commercial roles retain separate responsibilities; a shared example does not transfer authority.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the closed-won record, source evidence and possible disposition in the example.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Routing a discrepancy does not prove that it was corrected. Look for a source-backed disposition separated from a later verified result.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: routing a discrepancy does not prove that it was corrected. Confirm who can explain the cross-role workflow judgment boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

ALL-CLOSEDWON.keyTakeaway: Separate a signal from a verified deal state; record source, scope, and as-of timing before changing the forecast or route.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when routing a discrepancy does not prove that it was corrected. Manager support can help the authorized record owner close the evidence gap without inventing a correction.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish a source-backed question from an assumed correction; do not turn discussion of a record into a seller evaluation.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that routing a discrepancy does not prove that it was corrected; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to help the authorized record owner close the evidence gap without inventing a correction? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

activities.name: Watch the satisfaction signals across a live delivery
activities.description: Gather the delivery signals that show how the customer is experiencing the work. In-huddle practice is one reviewed read-only result; recurrence is optional after approval.
activities.prompt: For [customer/account or engagement], check delivery-experience signals read-only: open issues/age, escalations, missed or moved dates, response times and unanswered questions. Reflect the supplied delivery coverage. Compare with [previous verified result, if available]; otherwise draft a baseline. Show dated changes, source coverage and gaps, separating records from inference. Run once; don’t schedule, send messages or change records.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated first-run satisfaction signal watch showing what changed since the last check, separating evidence from inference. Recurrence is a proposed configuration, or a manual repeat plan if unsupported; a scheduled result exists only after separate human approval and an actual later run.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which signals reflect the customer's experience rather than internal process noise. A record with no open issues can still describe a customer who has stopped telling us about them.
activities.requiredContext: Delivery status, open issues, escalation history, milestone dates; your delivery context, whether global delivery or field delivery coverage, since it changes which next action is right. A small named scope, source-access confirmation or permitted extracts, previous verified result if one exists, and a human reviewer. Recurrence needs explicit approval of scope, sources, cadence and output location; no CRM, telemetry or support connector is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the small named scope and sources this tool can actually access, or supply permitted extracts.
2. Run the prompt once, read-only; on the first run create a dated baseline.
3. Review actual source coverage and findings before any scheduling.
4. If recurrence is useful, approve its exact scope, reachable sources, cadence, output location and reviewer before enabling it where supported; otherwise use a manual repeat review.
5. Later, verify the first actual recurring or manually repeated result before relying on it. Any message, record correction or commitment is a separate human-reviewed action.
activities.whyThisMatters: The signals are usually already in the record. The work is looking before the survey does.

activities.name: Rank the satisfaction risks by what the customer would say
activities.description: Turn the signals into a ranked view of what this customer would raise if asked today.
activities.prompt: Using [the permitted dated delivery signals identifying the customer/engagement], rank what this customer would most likely raise if asked about their experience today. For each item give the specific moment behind it, who owns it, and whether it is still fixable within this delivery. Separate what is evidenced from what is inferred.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked satisfaction risks with owner and a fixable or not-fixable call.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms each ranked item traces to a specific moment. A risk with no moment behind it is a feeling, and it will not survive the conversation with the account team.
activities.requiredContext: Satisfaction signal summary; delivery timeline; known action owners; delivery context (global delivery or field delivery coverage).
activities.whyThisMatters: Ranking by what the customer would say, rather than by what is easiest to fix, is what makes this worth doing.

activities.name: Build the satisfaction recovery action
activities.description: Turn the top satisfaction risk into an action with an owner and a date.
activities.prompt: For [delivery-experience concern and supporting context], suggest one practical recovery action. Describe the customer-visible change, dependencies, proposed owner and realistic timing. Draft what we could say, but do not send it or treat the proposal as an accepted commitment. Keep timing provisional unless the supplied constraints support it; flag missing owner acceptance or delivery evidence instead of inventing feasibility.
activities.expectedOutput: One proposed recovery action with customer-visible change, dependencies and suggested ownership/timing.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Confirm the concern with the relevant people and check that the proposed recovery can be delivered before making a commitment.
activities.requiredContext: A delivery-experience concern, supporting context and any known delivery constraints.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an evidenced delivery-experience concern.
2. Review a proposed recovery action.
3. Discuss whether the customer would notice the change and who must agree before it is promised.
activities.whyThisMatters: A customer-visible, deliverable recovery action addresses the experience problem; a change in survey score is not guaranteed.

activities.name: Check the risk against what the record supports
activities.description: Test the satisfaction read against the evidence before taking it to the account team.
activities.prompt: Review [the satisfaction assessment and permitted supporting delivery record]. For each claim, cite where the record supports it, partly supports it or cannot establish it. Identify assertions without evidence, material counterevidence and what the record cannot show either way. Distinguish observed delivery experience from inferred satisfaction; a missing record is not proof of dissatisfaction or its absence. Return the evidence check and any next confirmation needed, without inventing customer sentiment.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA decides what to take forward. Raising an unsupported satisfaction claim with the account team costs credibility on the ones that were real.
activities.requiredContext: Existing satisfaction assessment and the delivery records supporting it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Satisfaction claims get challenged. Checking them first is what lets you hold the position.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Satisfaction is decided during the delivery, not at the survey. Focus on reading it early enough to act.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer already knows how they feel. The survey only tells us.
Responsiveness, clarity and expectation-setting move scores as much as technical outcomes do.
A satisfaction risk you cannot evidence is a feeling. Name what you saw.
discussionQuestions: Where in a current delivery would the customer say we are harder to work with than we need to be?
Which satisfaction signal have you noticed and not acted on?
What would this customer say if they were asked today rather than at the end?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Watch the satisfaction signals across a live delivery'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the general idea of satisfaction to one live delivery and the specific moment that would show up in the score. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Check the risk against what the record supports', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Delivery satisfaction improves when an evidenced concern leads to timely owned response, not a survey risk guessed from an AI summary. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
facilitatorQuestions: Which delivery are you least confident about, and what is the evidence rather than the feeling?
What would the customer say we did slowly or explained badly?
Which satisfaction risk is yours to fix and which belongs to another role?
What specific delivery moment would a peer use to test a satisfaction risk without attributing motives to a contact?
listenFor: Satisfaction inferred from the absence of complaints; technical success treated as the whole of the customer experience; risks named without a specific moment behind them; and anything the CSA plans to absorb that belongs to the CSAM or to delivery.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one delivery satisfaction-risk row: observed customer experience, evidence/date, alternative cause, CSA-owned fix and correct handoff role. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a satisfaction concern on a live delivery against customer and delivery evidence; personally act within your ownership or route it. If evidence is unavailable, you could explore a sanitized manual scenario or leave the gap open; no report is required. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized concern confirmed or revised and whether the response improved clarity or follow-through. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.
facilitatorGuide.exampleScenario: Illustrative scenario: A delivery appears technically on track while approved feedback reveals avoidable customer friction. Compare the evidence and consider an action within the delivery owner's remit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Customer satisfaction review compares a delivery episode with permitted feedback, including concerns not visible in technical status. CSA works within the relevant technical domain; diagnosis, execution, customer acceptance and commercial approval are separate judgments.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the example delivery episode, customer feedback and unresolved issue.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Satisfaction cannot be inferred solely from a technically completed task. Look for a customer concern distinguished from the team's preferred explanation.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to surface the distinction: satisfaction cannot be inferred solely from a technically completed task. Confirm who can explain the technical decisions and delivery evidence boundary if challenged. Keep confidential context minimized and the example facilitator-arranged; attendance must not depend on a new Team Member artifact.

CSA-VSAT.keyTakeaway: A health signal is actionable when its evidence, accountable owner, and next decision are clear.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: This topic matters when satisfaction cannot be inferred solely from a technically completed task. Manager support can support a recovery conversation without blaming the customer or delivery team.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Help distinguish the customer's concern from the team's preferred explanation; focus on an action within the delivery owner's remit.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Invite different interpretations of the evidence without scoring individuals. Reinforce that satisfaction cannot be inferred solely from a technically completed task; keep the consequential judgment with its accountable human owner. Ask for the uncertainty rather than pressure for a confident answer.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions: In the next existing 1:1 or account/team review, what changed in our ability to support a recovery conversation without blaming the customer or delivery team? What remains blocked, who owns that decision, and what manager support is still useful? Treat an untested action as untested rather than demand a success story.

CSA-TECHLEAD.roleTopicName: Become the Technical Advisor the Customer Asks For
CSA-TECHLEAD.roleTopicDescription: Work out what this customer's roadmap will need you to be credible on next, compare that honestly against what you can speak to today, and close one gap.
CSA-TECHLEAD.wiifm: Customer-led expertise choices help you remain useful as the roadmap evolves without trying to master everything or delaying work that needs another specialist.
CSA-TECHLEAD.name: Discover, Shape, and Validate a Solution
CSA-TECHLEAD.description: Clarify the customer problem and decision criteria, shape an appropriate technical approach, validate it against evidence and constraints, and communicate what the proof does and does not establish.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

CSA-TECHLEAD.todayObjective: Compare the customer's upcoming technical decisions with what you can credibly advise on today, distinguishing a gap worth closing from an appropriate specialist handoff.
CSA-TECHLEAD.whyItMatters: A traceable path from problem to validated proof helps teams recommend solutions responsibly and move customer decisions without overstating evidence.
CSA-TECHLEAD.desiredOutcome: Direct ongoing advisory development toward evidenced customer needs, acknowledging expertise limits and choosing when to deepen your judgment versus bringing in specialist support.

activities.name: Map what the customer's direction will demand of you
activities.description: Work out which technical topics this customer's roadmap will require you to be credible on.
activities.prompt: For [customer], use their stated technical direction, current estate and announced priorities to identify advisory topics for the next two to four quarters. Use customer primary sources for public statements and relevant work evidence for estate or plans; cite material claims and label anticipated needs as inference unless confirmed. Rank topics by how soon advice may be needed and how central they are to the customer's direction, not Microsoft's roadmap. Flag evidence gaps and material changes. Use delivery coverage only where it changes the next action; keep private estate details out of public queries. Additional context: [add a short note or relevant source link]; if this placeholder is unchanged, ignore this field and continue.
activities.expectedOutput: A source-linked advisory-topic ranking for the next two to four quarters, using timing and centrality to customer direction, with confirmed versus anticipated needs and material gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms this reflects the customer's direction rather than Microsoft's product roadmap. The two are not the same, and only one of them determines what the customer asks you.
activities.requiredContext: Customer technical direction, current estate, announced priorities; your delivery context, whether global delivery or field delivery coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
activities.whyThisMatters: The list of things worth knowing is set by the customer. Starting anywhere else is how good effort gets spent on the wrong topic.

activities.name: Compare that against what you can defend today
activities.description: Set the customer's coming demands against what you could hold a conversation on now.
activities.prompt: Take [the ranked customer technical-topic list]. For each, help me separate what I could hold an advisory conversation on today, what I could speak to but not defend under challenge, and what I would have to route to a specialist. Ask me what I need to answer honestly rather than assuming.
activities.expectedOutput: Honest gap map across can defend, can discuss, and must route.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA answers this honestly rather than aspirationally. A gap map that flatters you produces a plan that closes nothing.
activities.requiredContext: Ranked customer technical topics and your own assessment of what you can explain or defend.
activities.whyThisMatters: An honest distinction between discussable and defensible topics focuses development while preserving appropriate specialist routing.

activities.name: Find where you were the bottleneck
activities.description: Look back at where a question had to go to someone else, and what that cost.
activities.prompt: Looking across [engagement/work portfolio scope] and its available dated evidence, identify where a technical question had to be routed to someone else, where a decision waited on an answer I could not give, and where I deferred a topic more than once. Group them by topic and show which ones recur.
activities.expectedOutput: Recurring topics where you were the routing point rather than the answer.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which routing was appropriate and which was a gap. Bringing in a specialist is often the right call, and treating every handoff as a personal shortfall points the plan at the wrong thing.
activities.requiredContext: Small engagement scope and review period; use accessible work history or permitted extracts.
activities.whyThisMatters: The gaps that cost the most are the ones that recur. They are visible in your own history if you look.
