PLC-USPSI-CE-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on the team’s progress over the past eight weeks, identify the AI habits to keep building, and agree how to continue learning through team huddles.
PLC-USPSI-CE-W09.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
PLC-USPSI-CE-W09.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Reserve the final five-minute Close & Survey block for participants to complete their own Impact Survey through the approved link. Priorities and the continuing structure should already be agreed in Recap & What's Next.
2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Look back on experience from the first eight weeks without assuming everyone completed every huddle. This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion: keep sharing, explore workflows that matter, and build on what works.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the shared Transition HTML, not the ordinary AI-in-Action practice format. Share recent experience and journey-wide reflection; the facilitator or manager briefly explains why practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue. Then agree the ongoing huddle rhythm and a Week 10 topic, and close with feedback. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
discussionQuestions: Since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well or did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?

Looking back across the journey: Moments that mattered—what changed in how you think about or use AI, and what are you doing differently? Habits worth continuing—which habits and peer learning should we keep building? Make it our own—what has worked about our huddles, what would we change, and what should ongoing huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep a team-owned rhythm, and which topic will we use for Week 10?
suggestedTransitions: Open with the purpose (2 minutes). Use Share Your Experience (15 minutes) for both the since-last-huddle check-in and the journey-wide reflection. The facilitator or manager then presents Sustain (3 minutes): practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Move to What’s Next (8 minutes) to agree the ongoing rhythm and a Week 10 topic using All Topics or Huddle in a Box as appropriate. Close & Feedback (2 minutes) welcomes questions and points to the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the habits worth continuing, the team's ongoing huddle rhythm, and the agreed Week 10 topic. Use Close & Feedback for questions and the Team Member Impact Survey invitation. Participants who already completed the survey do not need to repeat it; this is the beginning of Sustain, not the end of the motion.
facilitatorQuestions: Share Your Experience—since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well, and what did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?
Looking back across the journey:
Moments that mattered: What experience changed how you think about or use AI? What are you doing differently today that you were not doing at the beginning?
Habits worth continuing: Which AI habits are becoming part of everyday work? What have you learned from one another that you want to keep building?
Make it our own: What has worked about our huddles, and what would we change? What should our ongoing team huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep learning together, and which topic will we choose for Week 10?
Close & Feedback: What questions, comments, or ideas would you like to share before we close?
listenFor: Listen for concrete changes, honest uncertainty, habits worth continuing, peer learning, and support needs. Include people with mixed experience or access gaps without assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Seek a shared Week 10 topic, not a tool quota or a ranking of participants.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If app, topic-library, customization, or survey links are unavailable, continue the team discussion and agree a Week 10 topic without a live build or download. Raise the access gap through the approved support route. Do not invent personal impact evidence or generate survey answers.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What has changed in how we think about and use AI, which habits should continue, and where would more practice or support help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Agree how the team will keep learning through huddles and choose a Week 10 topic. Existing All Topics content or Huddle in a Box are options described in the supplied HTML, not required live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; each person supplies their own feedback.
bringBackEvidence: Keep bringing useful experiences, questions, and friction into the existing team rhythm. No new individual report, artifact, or survey-completion proof is required. Distinguish an observed benefit from an untested idea and keep human judgment explicit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Help the team move from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Reflect on the first eight weeks, identify useful habits and remaining support needs, agree how huddles will continue, and choose a topic for Week 10. This is a shared team review, not account planning or technical strategy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the shared Transition HTML and its five-part agenda. With the manager, agree who opens the session, facilitates reflection, presents the brief Sustain explanation, and guides the Week 10 planning. Locate the All Topics, Huddle in a Box, and Impact Survey links before the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Follow the shared 30-minute agenda: Overview 2; Share Your Experience 15; Sustain 3; What’s Next 8; Close & Feedback 2. Sustain is a short facilitator/manager explanation of why ongoing practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue—not another open discussion or AI-practice block. Do not require a success story, a new artifact, or live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to draw out experiences and friction, reinforce why huddles continue, and help the team choose its Week 10 topic and continuing rhythm. Keep the same shared Team Review content across audiences; do not substitute a role-specific planning exercise.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: Help the team own its transition from guided Activation to Sustain: recognize learning, keep useful habits, agree how huddles continue, and choose a Week 10 topic. This shared review is not an account-priority or technical-strategy session.

managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Make space for wins, dead ends, and friction without rating people or assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. PLC-USPSI-CSA-W01.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
PLC-USPSI-CSA-W01.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
PLC-USPSI-CSA-W01.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot from the app launcher or copilot.cloud.microsoft and start in Chat.

activities.name: Analyze consumption trajectory and shortfall drivers
activities.description: Ask what certified consumption data says. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt: Use only approved user-provided report excerpts and plan or milestone records, with source, scope, and as-of/freshness date. Identify missing records instead of assuming access. For [customer/agency] and the period identified in the supplied records, analyze the documented consumption trajectory and compare it with the supplied plan or milestone view. Break down the largest changes by available dimension, identify evidence-supported contributors to potential shortfall, show supporting metrics, and state what the records cannot answer. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Consumption trajectory analysis.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms what the consumption figure actually counts. Similarly named measures include different workloads, and a shortfall diagnosed from the wrong measure sends the intervention to the wrong place.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. User-provided approved report snapshot or excerpt, source, scope, and as-of date; customer and period; delivery context, including global, field, or SME&C coverage.
activities.whyThisMatters: Working through consumption trajectory and shortfall drivers forces a position, and a position is what the decision needs.

activities.name: Design a technical shortfall intervention
activities.description: Connect customer context to intervention planning.
activities.prompt: For [customer/agency], use [consumption analysis and context] to identify evidenced technical blockers, milestones, stakeholders and dependencies. Suggest intervention options, proposed owners, touchpoints and next evidence checks. If the analysis doesn’t explain the shortfall, flag what would establish the cause rather than guessing it. Ask about delivery coverage only if material; don’t make commitments. Use supplied material only; don’t search, connect or take actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Intervention options with evidence, owners and gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the cause before selecting the intervention. Consumption shortfalls have several plausible technical explanations, and the intervention for the wrong one consumes the window the right one needed.

activities.whyThisMatters: Settling a technical shortfall intervention before the work starts is the only version of that decision that holds.

activities.name: Design the consumption intervention plan
activities.description: Build the intervention that changes the consumption trajectory, with the owner and the checkpoint that will show whether it moved.
activities.prompt: Turn the evidenced consumption causes into an intervention plan. For each, define the action, who owns it on both sides, the dependency that could block it, the date you would expect to see movement, and the telemetry that would confirm it. Separate the causes you can act on technically from the commercial or customer-driven ones, and route those to the role that owns them rather than carrying them. Rank by the size of the gap each one closes. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked consumption intervention plan with owners, blocking dependencies, expected movement dates and confirming telemetry, with non-technical causes routed to their owners.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the customer-side owner exists before the intervention plan is used, and does not take ownership of the consumption plan itself. Consumption interventions depend on customer action, and a plan with an unconfirmed owner on the other side simply does not start. The CSA owns the technical milestones that feed the plan, not the plan.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. The validated consumption causes; the deployment and architecture levers available; the customer owners for each dependency. Your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
activities.whyThisMatters: A technical intervention needs customer ownership and a measurable signal, not ownership of the entire consumption plan.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most of us have at some point defended a number we were not fully sure about. Focus on fixing the signal, not the spreadsheet.
keyTalkingPoints: A gap is usually three problems wearing one label: not enough, not moving, or dated wrong.
Certified data settles arguments opinion cannot.
Correction is judgment work. Recommendations are proposals; you decide.
discussionQuestions: Where do consumption or usage signals become technical work for you?
Which shortfall signal is most likely to hide a technical cause?
What evidence would you need before owning an intervention?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Analyze consumption trajectory and shortfall drivers'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the report signal to one technical cause or blocker that can be validated this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the consumption gap analysis', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Consumption diagnosis separates technical causes from other drivers using confirmed measure definitions. Choose an owned intervention and keep unsupported causes provisional. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring one approved, user-supplied consumption or usage report excerpt with source, scope and as-of date, plus the technical context it does not show.
facilitatorQuestions: Which consumption movement matters enough to investigate, and what baseline and period make it comparable? What technical cause is evidenced rather than inferred? How does another CSA choose an intervention that can actually test that cause?
listenFor: Report signals separated from technical cause; assumptions about customer intent; missing owners; and interventions that require architecture or workload context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one consumption exception row: baseline/period, movement, possible technical cause, distinguishing evidence, intervention owner and next check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which consumption signal changed your interpretation, and what technical risk or owner must be checked before acting?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a consumption-gap hypothesis against permitted evidence and confirmed metric definitions, and consider an intervention or owner question. Keep the cause provisional if evidence is incomplete. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized consumption hypothesis checked and whether it changed the diagnosis or intervention owner. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A useful advisory brief makes the intended decision and supporting evidence clear. Focus on one recommendation and the questions that could change it.
keyTalkingPoints: A brief is not a summary. It is a position plus the questions that would change it.
The intended outcome is the part most preparation leaves out, and it changes how the meeting runs.
Anticipated objections are cheaper than recovered ones.
discussionQuestions: Which upcoming conversation needs a recommendation, not just a summary?
What evidence would make the advisory position credible?
What customer decision should the conversation advance?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Prepare the technical advisory conversation'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from generic preparation to one upcoming conversation and its intended customer decision. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the evidence behind the advisory recommendation', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Technical advice connects a grounded recommendation and alternatives to the customer decision. Internal alignment does not establish customer agreement. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming technical advisory conversation, the intended decision, and the approved sources you would trust for preparation.
facilitatorQuestions: What technical decision should the advisory conversation advance? Which recommendation can you defend from current evidence, and what is missing? What objection did a peer use to improve the ask or fallback?
listenFor: Preparation that summarizes but does not decide; evidence gaps; customer facts needing review; and advisory recommendations without a named decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one advisory brief: customer decision, evidence-qualified recommendation, missing fact, likely objection, intended ask and fallback. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence would make this customer conversation credible, and what decision or question still belongs to a person?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could prepare one advisory conversation around the decision you need, not the content you have. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized recommendation or ask sharpened and whether review made the advisory conversation more useful. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most production designs are inherited rather than chosen. Focus on landing on one recommended direction, naming who has to approve it, and saying plainly what would prove it wrong.
keyTalkingPoints: Design and proof are one motion. A design the customer cannot see is a document.
Success criteria set before the work are the only ones that count.
AI accelerates the assembly. The architecture judgment stays human.
discussionQuestions: Which architecture option is still being treated as obvious?
What decision criteria would change the recommendation?
What evidence would you need before supporting this design?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Compare production architecture options'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from architecture principles to one live architecture decision with explicit criteria. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the architecture evidence before the design is shared', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Production architecture is a proposed direction, not a readiness declaration. Test constraints and cross-environment dependencies before reviewers or customers rely on it. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one architecture decision or design assumption, the known constraints, and the evidence you would use to compare options.
facilitatorQuestions: Which production architecture options should be compared against the customer's criteria? Which security, operations or resilience claim still needs validation? What assumption would a peer challenge before recommending a design?
listenFor: Untested assumptions; option comparisons without decision criteria; public guidance used without applicability review; and controls, governance, or resilience claims needing SME validation.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build a two-option production architecture comparison: explicit criteria, security/operations/resilience constraint, supporting evidence, unknown and validation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a production architecture direction against a customer constraint and critical dependency; identify needed validation instead of declaring the draft production-ready. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized production dependency validated or open and whether it changed the design or prevented premature readiness claims. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A design that has not been argued against has not really been validated. Focus on the proof, and about being clear which readiness call is yours and which belongs to somebody else.
keyTalkingPoints: Design and proof are one motion. A design the customer cannot see is a document.
Success criteria set before the work are the only ones that count.
AI accelerates the assembly. The architecture judgment stays human.
discussionQuestions: Which dependency could make the design fail in production?
What proof is small enough to validate the decision?
Who owns the next technical decision after validation?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Validate the evidence behind the technical decision path'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use the supplied prior technical decision path and approved evidence to review one assumed decision, owner or slip risk. For the alternative Featured validation-path intervention, the facilitator or manager arranges an existing permitted validation plan and reviewed gaps as shared inputs. Review them during the activity; if they are unavailable, use a sanitized case or select another eligible practice rather than assign Team Members advance preparation. Do not run both Featured alternatives sequentially live. Investment-readiness Extended work applies only when proposed or funded scope is relevant, never as funding approval. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Design the architecture intervention plan', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Readiness follows proportionate validation of the design and its critical dependencies. Keep technical proof distinct from delivery ownership and respect agreed stop conditions. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
preparationChecklist: Bring the approved technical decision path, validation plan and supporting evidence from the prior design huddle, with known owners, constraints and open proof gaps. These support the Featured evidence review and validation-path plan without requiring funding. Bring approved case or proposed investment scope only if choosing an investment-specific Extended practice.
facilitatorQuestions: Which decision in the prior technical path is being assumed rather than owned and scheduled? What gap in the supplied evidence could change readiness? How would a peer define the smallest proof without expanding funded scope or treating funding as approval?
listenFor: Validation scoped too broadly; unowned prerequisites; proof criteria written after work begins; and investment-funded scope that may not be deliverable as designed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one prior-design decision-path review: decision point, supplied evidence or unavailable, proposed owner/date, slip impact and smallest settling proof. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could define the validation path for one design, including what would tell you to stop. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized validation criterion checked and whether it clarified readiness, a hold or a delivery-owner question. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activitySteps: 1. Supply approved business case, baseline and current outcome evidence with dates/definitions.
2. Confirm comparability and any usage-to-outcome model.

5. Have accountable technical/financial owners verify customer claims and agree any next human checkpoint separately.

activities.whyThisMatters: Comparing actual outcomes with the original baseline prevents usage growth becoming an unsupported value claim.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Value without evidence tends to read as opinion. Focus on the evidence, and who needs to hear it, inside as well as outside.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer defines value. Our job is to evidence it in their terms.
Causality is easy to claim and hard to support. Say what the data supports.
A value story nobody hears is not value realized.
discussionQuestions: What value story would the customer actually recognize?
Which evidence supports the story, and which part is still only expected?
What next technical action would make the value more real?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Create the technical progress and value narrative'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from value language to the evidence package and next technical action. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the evidence behind the customer value story', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Technical value connects progress to customer-recognized outcomes without overstating attribution. Internal alignment and customer claims need the same evidence and limits. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring one technical review, business review, or value-realization example and the evidence behind it.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical progress claim can the customer trace to an agreed outcome? What source proves realization rather than deployment or usage alone? How would a peer state the limitation and the next technical action in the review?
listenFor: Progress not connected to agreed outcomes; unsupported realization claims; missing source links; and follow-through that lacks owners.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or approved context is unavailable, use a sanitized supplied example or a clearly labeled synthetic case. On paper, draft one technical-value claim with the agreed outcome, observed progress, source/date, realization limit, reviewer and next technical action. Mark evidence, assumptions and unknowns; the draft does not establish realized value or customer agreement. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient. Any later AI run must use project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot and approved supplied inputs.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which outcome can you substantiate for this audience, and what claim or next action still needs validation?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could evidence one technical outcome in terms the customer would use themselves, and name what the account team needs to see internally. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized outcome phrasing or attribution caveat improved and whether it made the value discussion more credible. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

PLC-USPSI-CSA-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on the team’s progress over the past eight weeks, identify the AI habits to keep building, and agree how to continue learning through team huddles.
PLC-USPSI-CSA-W09.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
PLC-USPSI-CSA-W09.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Reserve the final five-minute Close & Survey block for participants to complete their own Impact Survey through the approved link. Priorities and the continuing structure should already be agreed in Recap & What's Next.
2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Look back on experience from the first eight weeks without assuming everyone completed every huddle. This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion: keep sharing, explore workflows that matter, and build on what works.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the shared Transition HTML, not the ordinary AI-in-Action practice format. Share recent experience and journey-wide reflection; the facilitator or manager briefly explains why practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue. Then agree the ongoing huddle rhythm and a Week 10 topic, and close with feedback. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
discussionQuestions: Since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well or did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?

Looking back across the journey: Moments that mattered—what changed in how you think about or use AI, and what are you doing differently? Habits worth continuing—which habits and peer learning should we keep building? Make it our own—what has worked about our huddles, what would we change, and what should ongoing huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep a team-owned rhythm, and which topic will we use for Week 10?
suggestedTransitions: Open with the purpose (2 minutes). Use Share Your Experience (15 minutes) for both the since-last-huddle check-in and the journey-wide reflection. The facilitator or manager then presents Sustain (3 minutes): practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Move to What’s Next (8 minutes) to agree the ongoing rhythm and a Week 10 topic using All Topics or Huddle in a Box as appropriate. Close & Feedback (2 minutes) welcomes questions and points to the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the habits worth continuing, the team's ongoing huddle rhythm, and the agreed Week 10 topic. Use Close & Feedback for questions and the Team Member Impact Survey invitation. Participants who already completed the survey do not need to repeat it; this is the beginning of Sustain, not the end of the motion.
facilitatorQuestions: Share Your Experience—since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well, and what did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?
Looking back across the journey:
Moments that mattered: What experience changed how you think about or use AI? What are you doing differently today that you were not doing at the beginning?
Habits worth continuing: Which AI habits are becoming part of everyday work? What have you learned from one another that you want to keep building?
Make it our own: What has worked about our huddles, and what would we change? What should our ongoing team huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep learning together, and which topic will we choose for Week 10?
Close & Feedback: What questions, comments, or ideas would you like to share before we close?
listenFor: Listen for concrete changes, honest uncertainty, habits worth continuing, peer learning, and support needs. Include people with mixed experience or access gaps without assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Seek a shared Week 10 topic, not a tool quota or a ranking of participants.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If app, topic-library, customization, or survey links are unavailable, continue the team discussion and agree a Week 10 topic without a live build or download. Raise the access gap through the approved support route. Do not invent personal impact evidence or generate survey answers.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What has changed in how we think about and use AI, which habits should continue, and where would more practice or support help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Agree how the team will keep learning through huddles and choose a Week 10 topic. Existing All Topics content or Huddle in a Box are options described in the supplied HTML, not required live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; each person supplies their own feedback.
bringBackEvidence: Keep bringing useful experiences, questions, and friction into the existing team rhythm. No new individual report, artifact, or survey-completion proof is required. Distinguish an observed benefit from an untested idea and keep human judgment explicit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Help the team move from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Reflect on the first eight weeks, identify useful habits and remaining support needs, agree how huddles will continue, and choose a topic for Week 10. This is a shared team review, not account planning or technical strategy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the shared Transition HTML and its five-part agenda. With the manager, agree who opens the session, facilitates reflection, presents the brief Sustain explanation, and guides the Week 10 planning. Locate the All Topics, Huddle in a Box, and Impact Survey links before the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Follow the shared 30-minute agenda: Overview 2; Share Your Experience 15; Sustain 3; What’s Next 8; Close & Feedback 2. Sustain is a short facilitator/manager explanation of why ongoing practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue—not another open discussion or AI-practice block. Do not require a success story, a new artifact, or live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to draw out experiences and friction, reinforce why huddles continue, and help the team choose its Week 10 topic and continuing rhythm. Keep the same shared Team Review content across audiences; do not substitute a role-specific planning exercise.

PLC-USPSI-CSAM-W01.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PTS

roles.name: PSA

roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM

roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales

roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)

activities.name: Draft the outcome-anchored success-plan view
activities.description: Draft or refresh the CSP around customer outcomes, milestones, owners, risks and review points. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt: From [customer priorities, meeting excerpts, delivery updates and existing CSP if available] for [customer/agency], draft an outcome-led Success Plan view: measures, milestones, owners, dependencies, risks, review points and evidence. Distinguish customer-stated priorities from system entries and suggestions. For dates or sequencing missing from records, identify a maintained location/owner only if supplied; otherwise ask for confirmation. Leave unsupported parts incomplete. Use supplied material only; don’t search, connect or take actions.
activities.expectedOutput: A human-reviewed, outcome-anchored success-plan view with evidence gaps; each priority labeled as customer-stated or present in a specified approved source record; and a named record location and human owner for items not captured in the source records. If evidence is insufficient, an unfilled planning structure and material confirmation questions only.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides which outcomes the customer would recognize as their own, and does not treat a recorded priority as a confirmed one. A success plan built from Microsoft's view of the account describes what we intend to deliver, which is not the same as what the customer is trying to achieve. Planning around a priority nobody has said out loud costs the quarter it takes to find out.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Customer priorities, existing CSP or notes, recent customer meetings, delivery milestones and known risks; and what the customer has said in their own words, which may not match the recorded priority.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most success-plan toil is assembling scattered signals. The CSAM should spend judgment on the outcome and commitment.

activities.description: Compare documented progress at a human-owned checkpoint, without automatic tracking or mailbox access.
activities.prompt: Compare current/prior success-plan snapshots, dated progress evidence and prior exceptions I supply. activitySteps: 1. Supply dated prior/current plan excerpts, progress evidence and prior exceptions if available.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Success planning is not documentation. It is how the customer and Microsoft agree what progress means.
keyTalkingPoints: A plan should name outcomes, milestones, owners, risks and review points. AI can draft and inspect the plan, but you validate the customer priority and commitment.
discussionQuestions: When did your success plan last change because the customer's priorities changed?
Which milestone in it would the customer not recognize as theirs?
What is in the plan because it is genuinely the outcome, and what is there because it was easy to measure?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft the outcome-anchored success-plan view'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the plan as it stands to the single outcome you will make observable this week. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Create the CSDR-ready success-plan narrative', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Governable success plans link confirmed outcomes to observable measures and accountable milestones. Simplify stale detail with the plan owner, not by dropping real obligations. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
preparationChecklist: Bring one active customer priority, its current CSP or success-plan notes and the latest review or action list.
facilitatorQuestions: Which outcome in your plan is stated in the customer's words rather than ours?
Which milestone has drifted without anyone deciding to move it?
What would you remove from the plan today to make it governable?
How does another CSAM test that the customer recognizes and accepts the stated outcome?
listenFor: Plans built around Microsoft milestones rather than customer outcomes, measures chosen because they are available rather than meaningful, owners who have never agreed to their commitment, and plans so long that nobody governs them. Also note drift being reported rather than decided.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one customer-success-plan row: customer-recognized outcome, measure, milestone, proposed owner, dependency and review point. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed your priority or plan, and which assumption needs checking before the next action?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could make a success-plan outcome more observable and propose simplification if useful. Confirm changes with the plan owner rather than remove obligations to shorten the plan. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized outcome made more observable or plan item clarified and whether it made review easier to govern. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.name: Rank customer health risks and drivers
activities.description: Create a ranked view of health risk across usage, support, sentiment, delivery and stakeholder signals. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt: Compare [dated health, usage, support, delivery, sentiment and stakeholder excerpts] across the cloud environments they cover. Keep contradictions visible with source/date and confirmation questions; don’t infer health for uncovered environments. Draft up to five evidenced risks with impact and confirmed—or explicitly proposed—owners, mitigations and checkpoints. Separate observed drivers from cause hypotheses; a score isn’t a diagnosis. Use supplied material only; don’t search, connect or take actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Up to five sample-bounded health-risk priorities with observed versus hypothesized drivers, source coverage, unresolved conflicts, known versus proposed actions and confirmation questions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM checks how old the signal is, and decides which three to five risks this customer could act on now. Health data lags the situation it describes, and intervening on last month's picture spends the credibility you will need for the real problem. Making the cut is part of the work, not a formatting choice, and it is the CSAM who decides what stays on the list.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Customer health signals, usage or consumption data, support trends, delivery milestones, sentiment and stakeholder notes. If relevant signals span multiple cloud environments, include approved source records from each environment with source, scope, and as-of date; the human reviewer checks coverage and identifies gaps.
activities.whyThisMatters: Health scores rarely tell you what to do. This turns signals into action.
