facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Focus on moving from signal review to intervention. Scores help, but action changes the customer trajectory.
keyTalkingPoints: Health work spans adoption, usage, support, delivery, sentiment and stakeholder change. You must separate noise from the risk that matters most right now.
discussionQuestions: Which customer worries you for reasons the health score does not capture?
What did someone say in a recent conversation that has not made it into any system?
Which risk have you been watching rather than acting on, and why?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Rank customer health risks and drivers'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the ranked health view to one intervention with an owner, a due date, and an escalation threshold. If a participant rejects or overrides the draft, ask which evidence or workflow condition it missed and compare the correction. Discuss only permitted details; do not assume this review sends anything to a transcript service. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Prepare the customer-safe health message', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Customer health judgment identifies actionable causes rather than collecting scores. Confirm a feasible intervention and established escalation guidance or an agreed review trigger. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
preparationChecklist: Bring one approved, user-supplied health, adoption, support or delivery-risk excerpt with source and as-of date, plus the known owner and open question. Record unavailable inputs; do not assume connected health or advisory access.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the driver behind the score, not the score itself?
Which signal came from a person rather than a system, and did it survive into the record?
Who owns the intervention, and by when does it have to start to matter?
What conversation-based signal did a peer find that the health score missed?
listenFor: Health scores treated as the diagnosis rather than the symptom, risks the team has normalized, interventions without owners, and conversation-based signals that never reached the data. Also note the customer's own view of their health being absent from the discussion.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one customer-health row: score/signal, evidenced driver, customer view, intervention, proposed owner/date and escalation question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review the most material actionable risk, verify its driver and ask its owner about a feasible intervention. Use confirmed escalation guidance or agree a review trigger; do not invent a policy threshold or require a minimum-size risk list. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized risk driver checked and whether the owner confirmed an intervention or held it; no risk-list quota is needed. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.whyThisMatters: Stakeholder changes can break adoption, value proof and renewal confidence before metrics show it.

activities.name: Rehearse the executive conversation
activities.description: Role-play the executive stakeholder against your approved brief to expose weak evidence, vague asks and unowned risk.
activities.prompt: Using only the supplied approved executive alignment brief and known decision authority, act as a hypothetical executive. Do not invent an executive position or customer facts. Then give evidence-based coaching, distinguish a requested decision from an agreed commitment, and propose a revised ask for CSAM review. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM checks what the rehearsal invented. Practicing a conversation smooths it, and the smoothing quietly adds detail that sounds established but was never verified with the customer.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Approved executive alignment brief.
activities.whyThisMatters: A ten-minute rehearsal is cheaper than discovering the weak ask in the room.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Executive alignment is where customer success becomes visible to the people who can sponsor, unblock or redirect it.
keyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps should show influence, decision rights, relationship health and the next ask. AI can assemble signals; you decide the message and timing.
discussionQuestions: Who is the most senior person at this customer you have never spoken to directly?
Which stakeholder could stop this work, and do you know what they care about?
When an executive last engaged, what did they actually want from us?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the stakeholder and influence map'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the stakeholder map to the one relationship you will build this month and the reason they would take the meeting. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Rehearse the executive conversation', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Executive alignment rests on observed priorities, relationship coverage and a useful ask. Inferred influence or sponsorship needs confirmation before guiding engagement. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming executive or sponsor conversation, current stakeholder context and an approved organizational sketch if available. If the map is missing, identify one relationship or decision-rights gap rather than trying to build the entire organization in the huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: Which stakeholder can stop this, and what do they need to believe?
Where is your coverage a title on a map rather than a relationship?
What would you ask the executive for if you had fifteen minutes tomorrow?
What behavior has another CSAM used as evidence that executive sponsorship is real?
listenFor: Stakeholder maps built from org charts rather than observed behavior, executive relationships that exist only through an intermediary, engagement plans with no ask, and blockers identified without a plan to reach them. Also note assuming a quiet stakeholder is a supportive one.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one stakeholder map entry: decision influence, observed behavior, relationship gap, executive ask and engagement owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which priority or sponsorship assumption needs confirmation, and how would that change engagement?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a stakeholder-priority or relationship gap and adapt an engagement question. Any actual contact remains a personal, authorized decision; no meeting is required and customer agreement is not implied. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to approved supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized stakeholder assumption checked and whether it changed the introduction, question or next engagement. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.name: Create the v-team orchestration brief
activities.description: Synthesize current workstreams, owners, handoffs, decisions and blockers. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt: From [workstream, meeting, delivery, support and CRM excerpts] for [customer/agency], draft a workstream brief with owners, dependencies, blockers and next steps. Against [last-review date, or unknown], separate evidenced progress, record-only changes, no recorded change and unknown movement. Due dates don’t prove progress, and stale records don’t prove inactivity. Flag missing plan links, unaccepted handoffs, source gaps and specialist/partner activity without a recorded CSAM touchpoint. Treat a later modified/activity date without progress evidence as record-only change; missing or imprecise dates, including the review date, mean unknown movement. Use supplied material only; don’t search, connect or take actions.
activities.expectedOutput: V-team orchestration brief listing every active workstream, marking each as showing confirmed progress, as record changed with progress unconfirmed, as no recorded change since the last review, or as movement unknown where there is no comparable date, with handoffs, and any workstream where a specialist or partner appears engaged with no CSAM touchpoint recorded.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides what is still worth doing, and treats the brief as a picture that moves rather than a model that holds. Orchestration briefs accumulate actions that made sense when they were added, and carrying them forward unexamined is how a v-team stops reading the brief. The work is coordinated in conversations, so the brief is only ever as current as the last one.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. User-provided approved account records, workstream notes, delivery updates, and support context, with source, scope, and as-of date; only the minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or excerpts with their last-modified or last-activity date; and the date you last reviewed the account. A human verifies the source records and decides. Do not include restricted customer or personal data unless policy permits. A human verifies every source record and claim, makes all decisions, and performs any authorized updates; Microsoft 365 Copilot does not make record changes.
activitySteps: 1. A human provides the minimum necessary approved workstream and touchpoint records, including CRM/MSX-derived fields or excerpts only when needed, with source, scope, and as-of date. This workflow uses only supplied inputs and makes no source-record changes; a human verifies and decides.
2. Export or copy only approved, permitted fields into a dated snapshot so the brief uses fixed inputs.
3. Supply that snapshot alongside meeting notes, delivery updates, and support context; otherwise review them manually.
4. Check every cited source against the materials actually supplied.

5. Distinguish confirmed progress, record changes with progress unconfirmed, no recorded change since the last review, and unknown status. Treat no recorded change as a prompt to ask the owner, not as a finding about them. Separately follow up where a partner appears engaged but no touchpoint is recorded.

If Copilot is unavailable or not permitted, complete the same bounded review manually from approved sanitized evidence or a fictional example; never bypass restrictions. Sending, publication, implementation or record updates are separate authorized human actions.
activities.whyThisMatters: CSAMs create leverage by making the system visible instead of carrying every detail personally.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Orchestration is making the customer-success system observable enough to run.
keyTalkingPoints: Handoffs need an input, owner and date. Escalation is not a failure when it is used to unblock the system and protect customer outcomes.
discussionQuestions: Where does work currently stop between Microsoft, the partner, and the customer?
Who believes they own something that someone else also believes they own?
Which handoff have you personally been compensating for?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Create the v-team orchestration brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the coordination map to the one handoff you will make explicit, with both sides named. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Build the weekly customer-success action plan', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Customer-success orchestration makes both sides of the handoff explicit and accepted. A date or listed owner is not agreement until the parties confirm it. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one workstream involving Microsoft, customer, partner, support or delivery handoffs.
facilitatorQuestions: Where exactly does work stop between the three parties?
Who thinks they own that step, and have you asked them?
What are you personally absorbing because the handoff does not work?
How does a colleague make both sides accept a handoff instead of personally compensating for it?
listenFor: The CSAM compensating for a broken handoff rather than fixing it, ownership assumed across company boundaries, partner commitments with no date, and coordination meetings that report rather than decide. Also note the customer's own team being left out of the orchestration picture.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one three-party handoff row: customer/Microsoft/partner contribution, transfer input, proposed receiver, acceptance gap and date. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which handoff is still assumed rather than accepted, and what owner, request, or date would make it actionable?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore where a handoff needs clearer agreement from both sides; no handoff has to be completed for the huddle. Receiving-owner acceptance is required before treating any actual handoff as accepted; do not commit their capacity or send messages automatically. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized handoff gap clarified and whether both sides accepted the next step or need a specific input. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Adoption activity does not automatically become customer value. Focus on proving and accelerating value realization.
keyTalkingPoints: Adoption plans should link underused features, customer priorities, behavior-change actions, milestones and value evidence. AI can draft the plan and value narrative; you validate truth and relevance.
discussionQuestions: What value has this customer actually realized that you could prove today?
Where is adoption stalled, and do you know why or are you guessing?
What would the customer say they got, if asked without us in the room?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Identify adoption friction and next activation actions'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the value picture to one claim you will evidence, and one adoption barrier you will actually diagnose. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Draft the sponsor value update', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Adoption and value are different claims: investigate barriers and verify entitlement and usage before acting. Customer statements and measures have limits that must stay visible. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one workload or solution where adoption progress, friction or value proof needs to be clarified, and the recent customer conversation where the reason was discussed, if there was one.
facilitatorQuestions: What value can you evidence today, and what are you asserting?
Where adoption stalled, do you know the cause or are you inferring it?
Would the customer describe the value the same way you just did?
What evidence would another CSAM require before describing usage as customer value?
listenFor: Value claimed from usage figures alone, adoption barriers guessed rather than investigated, realized value described in Microsoft terms rather than customer outcomes, and proof that would not survive a procurement conversation. Also note value stories that have never been said back to the customer.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one adoption/value row: friction hypothesis, distinguishing evidence, customer outcome, claimed value, caveat and activation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which adoption cause is evidenced rather than guessed, and what supports the customer-recognized value claim?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could check a customer-recognized value claim or adoption barrier using permitted data or conversation. Verify unused-entitlement hypotheses with the owner; finding an unused entitlement is not required. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized adoption barrier or value claim checked and whether it improved intervention or avoided an unsupported entitlement claim. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Renewal readiness starts before the renewal motion. Focus on seeing risk and growth conditions early.
keyTalkingPoints: Consumption, MACC or usage trajectory, adoption gaps, value evidence, support health and stakeholder signals all shape renewal confidence.
discussionQuestions: Which renewal are you least confident about, and what specifically drives that?
What consumption signal would you want to see six months before a renewal conversation?
Where is growth genuinely available versus where are you hoping?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the renewal and growth readiness view'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the forecast to the one early signal you will start tracking, and who you will align it with. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Stress-test the expansion hypothesis', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Consumption trajectory, evidenced value and readiness shape renewal and growth hypotheses. Early signals help inspection; they are not forecast or expansion commitments. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
preparationChecklist: Bring one account with renewal, consumption, usage or expansion relevance in the near planning horizon.
facilitatorQuestions: What is your forecast based on, and how far ahead does the signal reach?
Which growth opportunity is supported by consumption evidence?
What would you need to know now to avoid a surprise at renewal?
How does a peer distinguish customer growth intent from consumption headroom?
listenFor: Forecasts driven by relationship confidence rather than consumption evidence, growth assumed from headroom rather than intent, renewal risk surfacing late because nobody looked early, and commercial ownership blurring between CSAM and CE. Also note consumption trends read without seasonality.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one renewal/growth readiness row: dated consumption signal, seasonality/intent uncertainty, renewal event, value proof and AE/CE alignment question. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What evidence changes the renewal or expansion approach, and which customer or owner decision must follow?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore an early consumption signal and what it might help the account owner understand; starting a tracker or sending a handoff is not required. Verify evidence; commercial terms, forecast commitment and approval stay with accountable owners. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized early signal checked and whether it changed an evidence request or renewal action. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

Include what happened, current impact, what Microsoft is doing, what we need from the customer, next update timing and what remains under investigation. Avoid blame and unsupported commitments. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Customer-safe escalation update.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms support is aligned and the approval path is cleared before anything goes out. An escalation message that contradicts what support has already told the customer turns one problem into two.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Validated escalation brief, customer stakeholder and approved communication position.
activities.whyThisMatters: The wrong update can create more risk than the issue itself.

activities.name: Build the recovery action register
activities.description: Use Microsoft 365 Copilot only with a supplied, validated escalation brief, if permitted and available, or complete the drafting manually; prepare a recovery action register for human approval. Do not assume access to external records or make record changes; an authorized human verifies and updates records as appropriate.
activities.prompt: Using the validated escalation brief and approved owner context I supply, draft a recovery action register with action, owner, customer impact, dependency, due date, escalation threshold and evidence source. Extract confirmed details from the supplied material. Mark absent owners, dates or thresholds unconfirmed and identify who needs to resolve them; do not invent commitments or retrieve incident details from an assumed live connection. Do not update a tracking system or notify anyone. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Draft recovery action register with evidence sources, confirmed versus unconfirmed commitments, and gaps requiring owner confirmation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms each owner knows they own it. A recovery register full of people who have not been told is a list rather than a plan, and recovery is exactly when that distinction shows.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Validated supplied escalation brief, approved owner context, agreed dates/escalation thresholds and source dates; any missing excerpts must be permitted for this use and supplied by their owner.
activitySteps: 1. Use only the validated escalation brief, approved owner context, and agreed dates or thresholds provided by the user.
2. Draft the recovery action register manually or with Microsoft 365 Copilot using only those supplied inputs, if permitted and available.
3. Review source evidence and resolve unconfirmed owners, dates, and thresholds with accountable people.
4. Confirm owners accept the actions and approve the register.
5. Record approved actions through the current authorized process; these instructions do not update a system or notify anyone.

If Copilot is unavailable or not permitted, complete the same bounded review manually from approved sanitized evidence or a fictional example; never bypass restrictions. Sending, publication, implementation or record updates are separate authorized human actions.
activities.whyThisMatters: Escalations repeat when recovery actions do not become governed follow-through.

activities.name: Rehearse the escalation conversation before you have it
activities.description: Practise telling a customer something has gone wrong, before the call.
activities.prompt: Using the supplied validated escalation brief, approved communication position and commitment limits, role-play a frustrated customer. Ask one hypothetical question at a time and wait for my reply; ask for a date not yet supported. After three exchanges identify overcommitment, softened confirmed impact or unapproved cause. Produce a corrected statement of knowns, unknowns and the agreed next update without inventing facts or dates. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed escalation conversation, the objections raised, and coaching on where you over-committed or softened the impact.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides what can be said about cause and timing before the facts are settled. Rehearsal makes an answer fluent, and a fluent answer about an unresolved incident is easy to hear as a commitment.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. activities.whyThisMatters: How an escalation is handled shapes the relationship long after the incident closes. Rehearsing it is cheaper than improvising it while they are angry.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Escalations test trust. Focus on moving from scattered status to a grounded recovery plan.
keyTalkingPoints: A useful brief names customer impact, current status, owner, decision needed, next action and update cadence. AI can consolidate threads; you validate tone, accuracy and accountability.
discussionQuestions: What issue are you currently managing that should probably already be escalated?
What is holding you back: evidence, ownership, or the conversation itself?
When an escalation last worked well, what made it work?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Create the escalation and recovery brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from the delivery risk to a recovery plan with an owner, a customer message, and a defined exit condition. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Build the recovery action register', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Recovery plans need feasible delivery commitments, clear communication and work returned to its accountable owner. Escalation does not make an unaccepted date achievable. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
preparationChecklist: Bring one live or recent delivery risk, incident, support issue or overdue commitment, and be ready to say which parts of it you have ended up doing yourself. For the recovery-register practice, supply the validated escalation brief and approved owner context, including any agreed dates or escalation thresholds; unresolved details stay unconfirmed.
facilitatorQuestions: What threshold would have told you to escalate this a month ago?
What does the recovery plan commit us to, and can we deliver it?
What will you tell the customer, and when?
What recovery commitment has a peer had to narrow to what delivery could actually support?
listenFor: Escalation delayed to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, recovery plans that promise more than delivery can support, customer communication planned after the internal fix rather than alongside it, and escalations raised without a defined exit. Also note the same issue recurring without anyone treating the pattern.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one recovery brief: risk, escalation trigger needing confirmation, feasible recovery action, customer-safe draft message, owner and exit condition. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which recovery commitment can delivery support, and which absorbed task should return to its accountable owner?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a delivery issue with its owner, confirm feasible recovery and agree escalation or resolution. Humans review customer communication and proposed ownership transfers. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized recovery assumption or ownership gap corrected and whether it made communication or delivery action more realistic. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

PLC-USPSI-CSAM-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on the team’s progress over the past eight weeks, identify the AI habits to keep building, and agree how to continue learning through team huddles.
PLC-USPSI-CSAM-W09.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
PLC-USPSI-CSAM-W09.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Reserve the final five-minute Close & Survey block for participants to complete their own Impact Survey through the approved link. Priorities and the continuing structure should already be agreed in Recap & What's Next.
2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Look back on experience from the first eight weeks without assuming everyone completed every huddle. This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion: keep sharing, explore workflows that matter, and build on what works.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the shared Transition HTML, not the ordinary AI-in-Action practice format. Share recent experience and journey-wide reflection; the facilitator or manager briefly explains why practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue. Then agree the ongoing huddle rhythm and a Week 10 topic, and close with feedback. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
discussionQuestions: Since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well or did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?

Looking back across the journey: Moments that mattered—what changed in how you think about or use AI, and what are you doing differently? Habits worth continuing—which habits and peer learning should we keep building? Make it our own—what has worked about our huddles, what would we change, and what should ongoing huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep a team-owned rhythm, and which topic will we use for Week 10?
suggestedTransitions: Open with the purpose (2 minutes). Use Share Your Experience (15 minutes) for both the since-last-huddle check-in and the journey-wide reflection. The facilitator or manager then presents Sustain (3 minutes): practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Move to What’s Next (8 minutes) to agree the ongoing rhythm and a Week 10 topic using All Topics or Huddle in a Box as appropriate. Close & Feedback (2 minutes) welcomes questions and points to the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the habits worth continuing, the team's ongoing huddle rhythm, and the agreed Week 10 topic. Use Close & Feedback for questions and the Team Member Impact Survey invitation. Participants who already completed the survey do not need to repeat it; this is the beginning of Sustain, not the end of the motion.
facilitatorQuestions: Share Your Experience—since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well, and what did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?
Looking back across the journey:
Moments that mattered: What experience changed how you think about or use AI? What are you doing differently today that you were not doing at the beginning?
Habits worth continuing: Which AI habits are becoming part of everyday work? What have you learned from one another that you want to keep building?
Make it our own: What has worked about our huddles, and what would we change? What should our ongoing team huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep learning together, and which topic will we choose for Week 10?
Close & Feedback: What questions, comments, or ideas would you like to share before we close?
listenFor: Listen for concrete changes, honest uncertainty, habits worth continuing, peer learning, and support needs. Include people with mixed experience or access gaps without assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Seek a shared Week 10 topic, not a tool quota or a ranking of participants.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If app, topic-library, customization, or survey links are unavailable, continue the team discussion and agree a Week 10 topic without a live build or download. Raise the access gap through the approved support route. Do not invent personal impact evidence or generate survey answers.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What has changed in how we think about and use AI, which habits should continue, and where would more practice or support help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Agree how the team will keep learning through huddles and choose a Week 10 topic. Existing All Topics content or Huddle in a Box are options described in the supplied HTML, not required live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; each person supplies their own feedback.
bringBackEvidence: Keep bringing useful experiences, questions, and friction into the existing team rhythm. No new individual report, artifact, or survey-completion proof is required. Distinguish an observed benefit from an untested idea and keep human judgment explicit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Help the team move from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Reflect on the first eight weeks, identify useful habits and remaining support needs, agree how huddles will continue, and choose a topic for Week 10. This is a shared team review, not account planning or technical strategy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the shared Transition HTML and its five-part agenda. With the manager, agree who opens the session, facilitates reflection, presents the brief Sustain explanation, and guides the Week 10 planning. Locate the All Topics, Huddle in a Box, and Impact Survey links before the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Follow the shared 30-minute agenda: Overview 2; Share Your Experience 15; Sustain 3; What’s Next 8; Close & Feedback 2. Sustain is a short facilitator/manager explanation of why ongoing practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue—not another open discussion or AI-practice block. Do not require a success story, a new artifact, or live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to draw out experiences and friction, reinforce why huddles continue, and help the team choose its Week 10 topic and continuing rhythm. Keep the same shared Team Review content across audiences; do not substitute a role-specific planning exercise.

managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Make space for wins, dead ends, and friction without rating people or assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Engages early with the opportunity owner to shape executable commercial constructs across Microsoft and partner transaction routes. Navigates negotiation guardrails, coordinates owner-validated policy and licensing questions, routes approvals and exceptions, and hands off approved terms while addressing renewal commercial risk.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes SME&C commercial terms across transaction routes and coordinates approvals and renewals.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. Supports covered consumption portfolios through milestone readiness, partner and scale-engine handoffs, targeted adoption and technical interventions, attributed value evidence, and expansion hypotheses without assuming blanket customer or partner-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports covered SME&C consumption portfolios with readiness, handoffs, and targeted interventions.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Plans solution-area sales with pinned SME&C partners, qualifying partner-originated demand using Microsoft-verifiable facts. Reconciles partner pipeline and forecasts, coordinates deal clinics, checks readiness before handoff, connects closed deals to delivery, and reviews performance and expansion opportunities.
roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.name: Sales Manager
roles.description: Guides team account coverage and priorities, coaching with evidence appropriate to each role's accountability. Coordinates accepted handoffs, addresses customer value, renewal, and delivery risks, aligns capacity within the manager's remit, and escalates decisions to accountable owners when needed.
roles.descriptionSummary: Guides Enterprise team coverage and priorities, coaches by role, and coordinates accepted handoffs.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM
roles.description: Leads partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executive stakeholders and governance around growth priorities. Coordinates partner growth and co-sell efforts, drives course correction through business reviews, and brings technical, sales, and marketing owners together while reserving investment and commercial commitments for authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: PDM-R
roles.description: Develops a recruitment portfolio from qualification and partnership development through launch, a first transactable listing, and early wins. Mobilizes technical specialists, coordinates validated readiness, and prepares graduation handoffs accepted by accountable owners, with program approvals and graduation criteria retained by authorized owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Recruits EPS partners from qualification to launch, first transactable listings, and early wins.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. Coaches partner sellers and inspects renewal and consumption-commitment opportunities, avoiding duplicate pipeline attribution while keeping customer decisions with account teams and partner records and economics with partners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Drives EPS partner territory sales through referrals, shared pipeline, and marketplace sell-through.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. Recommends investments, coordinates approved claims, localization, activation, and qualified sales handoffs, and optimizes performance with attribution limits and reusable learning in view, leaving funding approvals with program owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS partner marketing plans, campaigns, approved claims, and qualified sales handoffs.

roles.name: Leader (M2/M3, OU/Division, or Leadership Team)
roles.description: A leadership audience focused on strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies. Brings attention to issues requiring strategic intervention and communicates decisions and direction, with action and escalation shaped by each participant's applicable authority rather than a shared management remit.
roles.descriptionSummary: A leadership audience for strategic priorities, outcome inspection, and cross-team dependencies.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Manages USPSI account priorities, opportunities, forecasts, renewals, and expansion. Inspects pipeline using only certified records and minimum necessary approved CRM/MSX fields or user-supplied excerpts, with source, scope, as-of/freshness dates, and human verification; coordinates account teams while retaining technical, policy, and approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages USPSI accounts and pipeline using certified records and approved, human-verified evidence.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Advances USPSI solution-area prospecting, discovery, proof, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning using approved evidence and handling information according to organizational requirements. Coordinates account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances USPSI solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and decisions using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.name: Commercial Executive

Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries through authoritative sources and approved handling, coordinating decision narratives, approvals, and execution without assuming policy, exception, legal, or compliance approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads USPSI commercial strategy and negotiation within authoritative policy and approval boundaries.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates USPSI outcome-based success plans, milestones, and accepted owners using approved health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder evidence. Aligns executives and teams, supports adoption and growth planning, and manages delivery risks within organizational requirements while retaining technical architecture approval owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates USPSI success plans, adoption, milestones, and delivery risks using approved evidence.

roles.name: All ATU
roles.description: Shared huddle content for AE, ATS, and CE roles to explore account strategy, customer planning, and coordinated execution. Compare account, technical, and commercial perspectives on customer decisions and handoffs while keeping each role's responsibilities clear.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shared account team workflows for account strategy, customer planning, and coordinated execution across AE, ATS, and CE roles.

roles.name: All STU
roles.description: Shared huddle content for SSP and SE roles to explore discovery, solution development, and coordinated handoffs. Compare customer outcomes, technical criteria, and evidence for the next decision, including what sending and receiving roles need from one another.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shared solution team workflows for discovery, solution development, and coordinated handoffs across SSP and SE roles.

roles.name: All CSU
roles.description: Shared huddle content for CSAM and CSA roles to explore customer-success planning, adoption, and coordinated execution. Connect customer outcomes with delivery, usage, and technical evidence, and clarify decisions and handoffs across the success team.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shared customer success workflows for customer-success planning, adoption, and coordinated execution across CSAM and CSA roles.

roles.name: Services Account Executive (SAE)
roles.description: Co-architect a Services strategy from customer execution and value gaps, with continuity through delivery and value realization. ATU leads account discovery; SAE customer/commercial strategy does not own project delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Execution/value gaps, Services strategy and commercial continuity.

PLC-SMEC-DAE-W09.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
PLC-SMEC-DAE-W09.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.

2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
