PLC-EPS-PSS-W09.keyTakeaway: This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion. Keep sharing, explore workflows that matter to the team, and build on what works.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: Help the team own its transition from guided Activation to Sustain: recognize learning, keep useful habits, agree how huddles continue, and choose a Week 10 topic. This shared review is not an account-priority or technical-strategy session.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Review the Week 9 Team Review HTML and agree light handoffs with the facilitator before meeting. Be ready to support reflection, the continuing team rhythm, and choosing a Week 10 topic. Confirm the supplied Impact Survey link is available without asking for personal responses.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Make space for wins, dead ends, and friction without rating people or assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Agree who will present the brief Sustain explanation: practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Help the team agree its continuing rhythm and a Week 10 topic. Follow the shared five-part agenda rather than adding a live tool exercise.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions:
What habits and support needs should we carry into our existing team rhythm?
Have we agreed how huddles will continue and which topic we will use in Week 10?
If the Impact Survey is still outstanding, do people know where to find it without repeating an already completed response?

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Account Executive
roles.description: Manages SME&C territory coverage across direct and accepted partner-led routes, identifying uncovered gaps and prioritizing evidence-based prospecting. Leads customer outcome conversations, coordinates partner-led deals and forecasts, routes work to appropriate scale engines, and plans portfolio renewals and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Manages SME&C territory coverage, customer outcomes, partner-led deals, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Engages early with the opportunity owner to shape executable commercial constructs across Microsoft and partner transaction routes. Navigates negotiation guardrails, coordinates owner-validated policy and licensing questions, routes approvals and exceptions, and hands off approved terms while addressing renewal commercial risk.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes SME&C commercial terms across transaction routes and coordinates approvals and renewals.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: Digital Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Assesses SME&C handoffs against coverage, sold outcomes, technical decisions, and accepted owners. roles.name: Partner Solution Sales

roles.descriptionSummary: Plans SME&C sales with pinned partners, qualifies demand, and connects deals to delivery and growth.

roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA

roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM

roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: PDM-R
roles.description: Develops a recruitment portfolio from qualification and partnership development through launch, a first transactable listing, and early wins. roles.descriptionSummary: Recruits EPS partners from qualification to launch, first transactable listings, and early wins.

roles.name: Partner Solution Sales
roles.description: Drives partner territory sales execution through quality referrals, shared pipeline qualification, and coordinated marketplace sell-through. PLC-EPS-PTS-W01.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
PLC-EPS-PTS-W01.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
PLC-EPS-PTS-W01.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Review the Orientation HTML and agree a brief opening and handoffs with the facilitator. Locate the baseline survey, readiness checklist, shared Top 5 Agents resources, and access help so questions can be supported.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Introduce the why, reinforce the weekly rhythm, and welcome questions. Help distinguish the future weekly-experience preview from today's Orientation. Support readiness and access questions without inspecting individual tool usage, survey answers, or performance.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions:
Does the team understand the motion and what to expect in the first role-specific huddle in Week 2?
What readiness question or access blocker needs support through our existing channels?

primaryAgents.name: Cowork
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Agentic Microsoft 365 experience for longer-running, outcome-focused, multi-source work.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Plans and executes multistep work, invokes skills, and creates deliverables with checkpoints.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When you want to hand off a multi-step piece of work and review it rather than do it. Complex tasks spanning Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 data, documents, presentations and recommendations, where it plans the work, runs the steps and checks in before it finishes.
keyBenefits: Executes multi-step work across Microsoft 365 instead of answering one question at a time. Built for delegation: it plans, invokes skills, works across data sources, and produces deliverables with review checkpoints.

resources.title: Copilot Cowork overview
resources.description: Overview of Cowork tasks, skills and action controls. Optional tool guidance, not a Dynamics 365 Sales skills guide.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

resources.title: What to Use When
resources.description: Routes a request to the best-fit Copilot agent and reserves Cowork for longer multi-output work. Useful early in a role path when tool choice is still forming.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for a quick single answer when Copilot or a specialized agent is sufficient, and for work that should keep running on a schedule after you stop asking, which is Scout.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select Cowork beside Chat. Describe the outcome you want rather than a single question, then review the work at each checkpoint it presents.

primaryAgents.name: Researcher
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Deep research agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot that produces structured, source-cited reports.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Combines work content and web research across multiple steps.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Customer, market, competitor, industry, and strategic research requiring citations. Researcher is also reachable inside Sales Agent, which uses it to answer research questions; call Researcher directly when you want the full sourced report rather than an answer inside a sales conversation.
keyBenefits: Produces source-cited research reports rather than unattributed summaries, combining work content and web research across multiple steps so claims can be traced.

resources.title: Get started with Researcher in Microsoft Copilot
resources.description: Official guidance for complex, multistep research across the web and permitted work data, including clarifying questions, structured source-cited reports, and prompting guidance.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for quick summaries or lightweight drafting.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select the Researcher agent, then state the research question and sources.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.

activities.name: Separate demonstrated capability from roadmap aspiration
activities.description: A traceable baseline prevents ambition or incomplete reporting from silently becoming technical strategy.
activities.prompt: Using only [the approved partner capability/planning packet identifying the partner], build a technical landscape from the dated capability inventory, planning excerpt and up to three project summaries below. First reconcile duplicate capability names; then distinguish demonstrated capability, stated ambition and unknown. Produce a table with capability, cross-solution relevance, source/date, constraint and validation question, followed by the single uncertainty most likely to alter our roadmap. Preserve conflicting claims rather than choosing a convenient version. Treat supplied exports as snapshots, not live PMX or Partner Center access. Stop if the partner scope or evidence provenance is missing. Draft only; no writeback, outreach or readiness approval.
activities.expectedOutput: One-page landscape table plus one prioritized evidence uncertainty, with conflicting and missing claims explicitly labeled.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS checks that capability classifications match the supplied evidence and selects the one uncertainty worth validating. Stop if partner identity, provenance or permission is unclear; do not infer readiness from missing data.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; approved capability inventory with dates; PBP technical excerpt or equivalent notes; zero to three project summaries; source labels and sharing limits. Supply extracts manually; no connector assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Select one partner and paste approved, dated excerpts with source labels.
2. Ask Cowork to reconcile names and classify claims before synthesizing the map.
3. Trace the most consequential row to its supplied evidence and correct any inference presented as fact.
4. Retain the map with one PTS-owned validation question and a named human evidence owner.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: A traceable baseline prevents ambition or incomplete reporting from silently becoming technical strategy.

activities.name: Test one cross-solution opportunity hypothesis with citations
activities.description: Cited counterevidence helps the PTS avoid converting an attractive technology trend into an unsupported partner priority.
activities.prompt: Research [hypothesis and partner alias, or source reference identifying both] using only the approved source links or extracts I provide, alongside the attached capability baseline. Assess technical relevance across the named solution areas and distinguish current facts from forward-looking possibilities. Return a short evidence brief with supporting signals, counterevidence, dependencies and a now/next/later implication using my supplied horizon definitions. Cite each factual claim with source and date; if a source cannot be reached or citations are unavailable, label that explicitly rather than substituting unapproved research. Recommend one validation question, not an investment commitment. The PTS will decide whether the hypothesis belongs in the landscape. Stop before recommending direction if its key dependency is unsupported. No messages, publication or system updates.
activities.expectedOutput: Cited hypothesis brief containing supporting and contrary evidence, dependency gaps, horizon implications and a retain/qualify/park recommendation for PTS review.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS verifies source relevance and decides whether the hypothesis merits planning attention. Stop at an evidence-gap brief when the critical dependency or citation cannot be verified; no claim of validated feasibility.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; one cross-solution hypothesis; a dated capability baseline; user-defined planning horizons; an explicit approved source list or extracts, with source dates where known.
activitySteps: 1. State one opportunity hypothesis and define now, next and later for this partner.
2. Supply approved research links or extracts and the capability baseline to Researcher.
3. Check one supporting claim and one counterclaim against their citations.
4. Decide as PTS whether to retain, qualify or park the hypothesis and record the reason.

Fallback: If Researcher is unavailable, inspect supplied approved extracts or approved official URLs manually. Preserve citations/dates and mark inaccessible claims unresolved; do not broaden the source boundary.
activities.whyThisMatters: Cited counterevidence helps the PTS avoid converting an attractive technology trend into an unsupported partner priority.

activities.name: Choose the technical gap worth resolving first
activities.description: Selecting one evidence question protects strategic attention from a long, undifferentiated backlog of technical unknowns.
activities.prompt: From [the approved technical landscape identifying the partner], compare no more than three unresolved gaps using the decision criteria and constraints I supply. Work in two passes: identify which roadmap decision each gap blocks, then compare the value of obtaining evidence against effort and reversibility. Do not invent weights, delivery capacity or partner willingness; show any missing input explicitly. Return a gap-choice memo with the recommended first question, the minimum evidence needed to answer it, the human evidence owner and what we can safely defer. Stop if the comparison depends on an unsupported capacity or strategic-priority assumption. Draft only; no task assignment, messages or system writeback.
activities.expectedOutput: Gap-choice memo with a comparison table, one minimum evidence question, proposed human owner and a reason for deferring the other gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS confirms that resolving the selected gap could change a real roadmap decision. Stop if criteria conflict or an owner/capacity assumption is unsupported; retain a question rather than fabricate a ranking.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; one approved landscape; at most three gaps; PTS-supplied decision criteria; known effort constraints; evidence-owner names or explicitly unknown owners.
activitySteps: 1. Paste up to three gaps and the roadmap decisions they appear to block.
2. Add approved prioritization criteria, known constraints and available human evidence owners.
3. Review Cowork's comparison for invented weights or assumed capacity.
4. Select one gap as PTS and capture its minimum evidence request without sending it.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Selecting one evidence question protects strategic attention from a long, undifferentiated backlog of technical unknowns.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Start with one partner whose technical direction is harder to explain than its activity list. Ask what is actually demonstrated today and what is merely planned. This week establishes the evidence baseline for a cross-solution roadmap, not a customer-sales stage or an architecture review. AI can reconcile approved material and expose gaps; the PTS decides which gap matters. A partner's business ambition is useful context, but it is not proof of technical readiness. In the live practice, choose one bounded artifact, not the whole landscape-to-roadmap process.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Distinguish current technical capability, roadmap intent and unsupported assertion. Date the evidence and retain the partner's own description alongside Microsoft-side visibility.

2. Map across solution areas and planning horizons without assigning detailed architecture or delivery tasks. PTS sets direction; PSA executes scoped CSA-specific work; the partner owns delivery and operation.
3. Use PMX, PBP and Partner Center material only when the participant supplies an approved export or extract. Access, completeness and permission are not implied by naming a system.
discussionQuestions: Where does our current partner view confuse certification, stated capability and demonstrated delivery?
Which uncertainty could change the direction of the technical plan?
What must come from the partner rather than from Microsoft-side reporting?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Separate demonstrated capability from roadmap aspiration'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Give one minute to define the partner and question, five minutes to run one Featured practice, and two minutes to inspect the most consequential evidence gap. Treat the other practices as alternatives or later follow-ons. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Choose the technical gap worth resolving first', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Ask each participant to identify one claim they downgraded, retained or need to validate. Close on the evidence question rather than the apparent completeness of the AI output. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one partner identifier, a dated approved technical-plan excerpt or equivalent notes, a capability inventory and at most three project or offering summaries. Remove unnecessary customer identifiers. Mark source, date and disclosure permission; missing material is a valid starting point. Choose whether the immediate input supports a capability map, an opportunity hypothesis or a gap decision.
facilitatorQuestions: Which row is evidence and which is inference?
Does the proposed opportunity connect more than one technical capability, or simply restate a product name?
What can the PTS decide now without implying PSA capacity or partner commitment?
listenFor: An evidence gap being presented as a weakness, access to PMX being assumed, or a partner claim becoming a readiness score without corroboration. Ask participants to preserve an unknown rather than make the map look complete. Redirect implementation detail to a future scoped PSA handoff.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If approved data or agent access is unavailable, draw four columns: capability, evidence/date, uncertainty and next validation question. Populate one row from a clearly marked sanitized example. Do not imply the example describes the real partner and do not browse unapproved sources to fill the gap.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which assumption looked credible until you asked for its source, and how could it have distorted the roadmap?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a roadmap-relevant claim and its source/date, considering whether it changes the PTS planning judgment. Any later evidence request must use authorized human channels, not automated outreach. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized roadmap claim checked and whether it improved the planning judgment. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)
roles.description: Advances Enterprise solution-area opportunities through prospecting, discovery, proof, objection handling, and customer decisions. Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy and negotiation by assessing structural exposure, commercial risk, and renewal options. Verifies licensing, policy, and approval boundaries against authoritative sources, prepares decision narratives, and coordinates approvals and execution without assuming policy or exception approval authority.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads Enterprise commercial strategy, negotiation, and renewals within policy and approval limits.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Coordinates Enterprise customer success through outcome-based plans, milestones, and accepted owners. Combines health, usage, support, delivery, and stakeholder signals to align executives, orchestrate teams and partners, support adoption and growth planning, and manage delivery risks without owning technical architecture approval.
roles.descriptionSummary: Coordinates Enterprise success plans, adoption, milestones, teams, and delivery risk management.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. Shapes viable architecture with delivery owners, runs the smallest useful proof, transfers technical decisions into delivery, reuses assets, and addresses partner technical capability gaps.
roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: PDM
roles.description: Leads partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executive stakeholders and governance around growth priorities. roles.descriptionSummary: Leads EPS partner strategy and joint business planning, aligning executives and growth efforts.

roles.name: PMM
roles.description: Shapes partner marketing plans and campaigns around market needs, partner maturity, and joint business priorities. activities.name: Draft a traceable multi-horizon plan slice
activities.description: A small traceable plan is easier to co-create than a broad roadmap whose priorities and commitments are unclear.
activities.prompt: Use only [the partner ambition, technical baseline and horizon definitions] to draft a technical-plan slice with no more than three outcomes. First link each outcome to a stated partner priority; then sequence it by prerequisites rather than invented dates. Return a table of horizon, outcome, evidence gate, cross-solution dependency, proposed owner and unresolved decision. Distinguish PTS strategy from PSA execution and partner delivery. Label unsupported assumptions and unconfirmed commitments visibly, including any missing feasibility or capacity input. Stop before recommending a baseline when a critical dependency has no evidence or owner. Do not write back, message reviewers or approve commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Multi-horizon plan table with no more than three outcomes, source-linked rationale, evidence gates, proposed owners and unresolved decisions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS owns the proposed outcome set and horizon ordering. Stop if a critical prerequisite or owner cannot be established; leave the plan as a review draft with that blocker visible.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; approved ambition/PBP excerpt; technical baseline; horizon definitions; up to three candidate outcomes; known constraints and stakeholder roles. No live system access required.
activitySteps: 1. Supply one partner ambition, baseline and explicit now/next/later definitions.
2. Limit the plan slice to three candidate outcomes and run the synthesis.
3. Trace every outcome to a supplied priority and inspect its evidence gate.
4. Mark the PTS-selected draft and the one decision that requires co-creation review.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: A small traceable plan is easier to co-create than a broad roadmap whose priorities and commitments are unclear.

activities.name: Expose the dependency that could break the plan
activities.description: Surfacing the weakest dependency prevents a coherent-looking roadmap from failing at its first real handoff.
activities.prompt: Inspect [the partner technical-plan slice and dependency notes], covering at most three outcomes. In pass one, extract prerequisite relationships and their evidence; in pass two, look for circular sequencing, shared bottlenecks and assumptions about PSA or partner capacity. Produce a dependency register and identify the single dependency most likely to invalidate the proposed ordering. For that dependency, draft two planning responses and show the evidence needed to choose between them. Do not design the architecture, estimate unsupported effort or allocate anyone's resources. Mark missing and conflicting evidence explicitly. The PTS will validate the sequence and choose the response. Stop if the dependency chain rests on an unverified feasibility claim. Draft only; no assignments, notifications or system updates.
activities.expectedOutput: Dependency register plus one critical-dependency decision card with two planning responses and evidence needed for selection.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS verifies that the dependency genuinely changes roadmap ordering. Stop when feasibility or capacity is asserted without evidence; request scoped human input rather than invent an execution plan.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; at most three planned outcomes; known prerequisite notes; any approved PSA feasibility comments and partner capacity statements, each dated. Unknowns may remain unknown.
activitySteps: 1. Paste one approved plan slice and its dated dependency notes.
2. Ask Cowork to extract relationships before testing for bottlenecks.
3. Verify the highest-impact dependency against the source and inspect both proposed responses.
4. Record the PTS-selected planning question and the human feasibility input needed.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: Surfacing the weakest dependency prevents a coherent-looking roadmap from failing at its first real handoff.

activities.name: Prepare a co-creation review that resolves one choice
activities.description: A review designed around a choice produces better planning evidence than a meeting that merely walks through slides.
activities.prompt: Using only [the partner draft plan and dated stakeholder comments], prepare a decision-focused co-creation agenda around the unresolved choice. Reconcile the comments into agreement, disagreement and missing input, preserving who said what and when. Create a one-page review brief with the decision, two feasible planning options supported by the packet, tradeoffs, a question for the partner, and focused PDM and PSA review questions. Treat suggested owners, dates and commitments as unconfirmed unless explicitly evidenced. Include a blank decision record for the PTS to complete after review. Stop if the options require unsupported feasibility or partner intent. I will select and convene the review myself; do not schedule, message, approve, write back or claim agreement.
activities.expectedOutput: One-page co-creation decision brief with two supported options, role-specific review questions and an unfilled human decision record.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS verifies that the questions concern technical-plan choices and that agreement is not inferred from silence. Stop if the draft depends on unconfirmed partner intent; retain that as the review question.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; one draft technical-plan slice; one unresolved choice; approved dated comments from available partner, PDM and PSA reviewers; known meeting or disclosure constraints.
activitySteps: 1. Select one unresolved planning choice and provide approved stakeholder comments.
2. Run a reconciliation before asking for a review agenda.
3. Remove any option that assumes unconfirmed partner intent or technical feasibility.
4. Retain a PTS-reviewed agenda and blank decision record for a human-led conversation.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.

activities.name: Add a regional activation delta to a global plan
activities.description: A bounded regional variant extends a shared solution without fragmenting strategy or confusing activation with a new global build.
activities.prompt: Compare [the global partner-solution plan and named region's requirements]. Draft a regional activation delta, not a replacement solution roadmap. Separate reusable global decisions from regional prerequisites, local evidence needs and exceptions requiring the global technical owner. For each proposed delta, identify its source, the outcome it enables and whether the decision belongs to PTS strategy, PSA scoped execution or partner delivery. Do not assume local coverage, compliance, funding or access. Flag missing evidence and any request that would rebuild the global solution. The PTS will decide which deltas belong in the plan after owner review. Stop on an unresolved global/local conflict. No commitments, eligibility determinations, messages or writeback.

activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates local need against global intent and confirms the decision owner. Stop if global/local direction conflicts or the proposal assumes unverified local coverage; do not recreate the global build.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/solution and one region; approved global technical plan; regional activation requirements; known global/local owners and permission constraints. No implied region-wide source access.
activitySteps: 1. Supply one approved global plan and one region's dated activation requirements.
2. Ask Cowork to classify inherited decisions before drafting local deltas.
3. Inspect proposed changes for unnecessary global rebuild or unconfirmed regional coverage.
4. Keep the PTS-reviewed delta list and route unresolved exceptions through normal human governance.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Bring the landscape forward, but do not require last week's exercise as a prerequisite: an existing approved technical baseline is equally valid. Today connects one partner ambition to a small number of technical outcomes and the order in which they could become credible. The PTS owns cross-solution direction and planning choices. PDM contributes business alignment; PSA reviews feasibility and eventual scoped execution; the partner must validate its own priorities and responsibilities. AI prepares the conversation. It cannot make the conversation happen or turn proposed ownership into agreement.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Give each planning horizon a meaning for this partner; do not manufacture fiscal dates, funding or resource commitments. Link each technical outcome to the approved business ambition that justifies it.
2. Separate outcomes, evidence gates and dependencies. A roadmap milestone is not complete merely because a slide or activity exists.

3. Co-creation requires explicit human review. Mark proposed owners and unconfirmed partner commitments, and keep the resulting draft out of systems of record until the appropriate human process is complete.
discussionQuestions: Which technical outcome actually advances the partner's stated ambition?
Where does our plan depend on PSA feasibility input or partner capacity that has not been confirmed?
What should the next review decide rather than merely acknowledge?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft a traceable multi-horizon plan slice'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use one minute to name the planning decision, five minutes for one Featured plan, dependency or review-agenda practice, and two minutes to inspect the proposed human decision. Do not try to finish the partner plan live. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Add a regional activation delta to a global plan', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by distinguishing what the PTS has drafted from what the partner and reviewers have confirmed. The next useful step is one resolved planning question, not more roadmap detail. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring an approved partner ambition or PBP excerpt, the current technical baseline, existing horizon definitions, and at most three candidate outcomes. Add known constraints and the current review stakeholders. A manually supplied PMX/PBP export is a dated input, not permission to retrieve or update the system. Have one unresolved planning decision ready.
facilitatorQuestions: Can you trace the proposed outcome to a partner priority?
What evidence would distinguish an achieved outcome from completed activity?
Which proposed owner has not yet agreed, and how is that visible?
listenFor: Technical activities being labeled outcomes, an AI-proposed date becoming a commitment, or a partner role being silently assigned to Microsoft. Help participants express the disputed dependency rather than hide it behind a confident roadmap graphic.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: With no usable packet, outline one row: partner ambition, technical outcome, evidence gate, dependency, proposed owner and decision needed. Mark all unsupplied fields unknown. Use the row as a co-creation question, not a completed plan. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which proposed milestone changed when you required an outcome and an evidence gate rather than an activity description?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a technical-plan decision and the question a partner, PDM or PSA reviewer would need to resolve. Keep confirmed ownership distinct from proposals; do not automatically distribute a draft. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized milestone or ownership assumption changed in plan review and whether its evidence gate clarified the next decision. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.description: A conditional comparison makes the opportunity cost and uncertainty behind prioritization visible to the technical-plan owner.
activities.prompt: Compare [up to three approved technical candidates identifying the partner] against my stated criteria, constraints and any explicit weights. First assemble a fact-and-gap table; then provide a conditional priority order with rationale and the cost of deferring each candidate. Use no invented scores, weights, effort estimates or partner commitments. Distinguish strategic fit, technical readiness evidence and the credibility of a build-to-consume path. Show how the order changes under the single uncertainty I identify. If evidence cannot distinguish the candidates, recommend a hold and the minimum question needed to proceed. The PTS makes the priority decision. Stop before recommending allocation where capacity is unconfirmed. Draft only; no funding, eligibility approval, messages or system writeback.
activities.expectedOutput: Conditional portfolio comparison and PTS decision template covering priority/hold, defer consequences, gaps and a reconsideration trigger.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS owns the ordering and validates the criteria and capacity evidence. Stop at hold if a decisive input is missing; do not let a generated score authorize allocation.
activities.requiredContext: One partner; two or three candidate briefs; approved technical-plan priorities; PTS criteria and optional weights; known constraints; one uncertainty to test. All system material is user-supplied.
activitySteps: 1. Supply two or three candidate summaries for one partner and explicit criteria.
2. Add known constraints, optional human-chosen weights and one uncertain assumption.
3. Inspect the evidence table and conditional ordering for unsupported numeric precision.
4. Record the PTS priority or hold decision, one defer consequence and a revisit trigger.

activities.name: Challenge a candidate's build-to-consume bridge

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This week is about technical investment choices, not an automated score deciding a partner's future. Start with no more than three candidates from one partner and the actual constraints that matter. The PTS owns cross-solution prioritization and multi-horizon tradeoffs; PSA feasibility evidence and partner delivery capacity are inputs, not resources the PTS or AI can silently allocate. Build-to-Consume asks how technical work could lead toward usable, activated offerings and credible consumption evidence. It does not authorize an eligibility judgment or force this partner planning work into an MCEM stage.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Use human-supplied criteria and weights, or show an unweighted comparison. A precise-looking score is misleading when criteria, capacity or evidence are missing.
2. Compare build value with the path to activation and consumption; label hypotheses, partner-dependent steps and evidence gaps instead of forecasting unsupported outcomes.
3. Record the defer choice and revisit trigger as carefully as the top priority. Preserve PSA capacity confirmation and partner delivery decisions as separate human checkpoints.
discussionQuestions: Which candidate would we defer if available capacity fell tomorrow?
Where are we rewarding build activity without evidence of a usable offering or consumption path?
What new evidence would legitimately reverse our ordering?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Make an evidence-based priority or hold decision'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Allow one minute to bound the portfolio, five minutes to run one comparison, capacity or build-to-consume practice, and two minutes to challenge the strongest assumption. Only one practice is chosen live. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Compare reusable-asset investment with a bespoke build', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Ask participants to state the priority or hold decision, the candidate not pursued now and the evidence that would reopen the choice. Do not close on a score alone. If useful, you could revisit this evidence check in recurring work and choose whether to share a safe observation with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring at most three candidate summaries for one partner, the approved technical-plan priorities, explicit decision criteria, and a dated capacity or feasibility input if available. Include known activation dependencies and approved usage evidence where relevant. Supply PMX/PBP extracts manually and mark their date; do not imply native retrieval or a complete consumption view.
facilitatorQuestions: What drives the ordering: evidence, a weight you supplied or an assumption the agent invented?
Which partner or PSA dependency is still unconfirmed?
Is there a defensible hold decision rather than a forced winner?
listenFor: Unsupported numeric scores, capacity inferred from an org chart, and consumption claims inferred from a successful build. Coach toward conditional choices when the evidence cannot support a firm priority.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Create a three-row comparison manually using strategic fit, known constraint, evidence gap and defer consequence. Do not rank if the supplied criteria cannot separate the candidates. A documented hold with a minimum evidence request is a useful result. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What changed when you made the opportunity cost of the preferred candidate visible?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could examine the assumption most likely to change the portfolio order and consider a PTS priority, defer or hold judgment with a possible reconsideration trigger. Do not allocate PSA or partner resources automatically. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized portfolio assumption checked and whether it changed priority, hold or reconsideration; do not disclose the portfolio. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.prompt: Test [offering hypothesis and partner alias, or source reference identifying both] using only my approved source list or extracts and supplied capability baseline. Separate generally available capability from announced or uncertain future capability where the approved sources establish that distinction. Cite factual claims precisely; mark unavailable sources or citations unavailable and leave gaps open. Do not infer partner demand or commercial potential from a trend. The PTS will decide whether the signal warrants a roadmap discussion. Stop if the central claim cannot be substantiated. No new source browsing, commitments, outreach or publication.

activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS checks that citations support the actual hypothesis and that no trend has been recast as partner demand. Stop with a research-gap statement when the central claim or citation is unavailable.

3. Verify the central claim and counterevidence against their citations and dates.
4. Record the PTS decision to retain, narrow or park the hypothesis.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Start with one offering idea that could materially change the partner's technical roadmap. The question is not whether AI can describe an exciting solution; it is whether the supplied evidence supports choosing this direction over a plausible alternative. Researcher can test a specific signal against an approved source list. Cowork can connect the evidence, capability baseline and partner comments into a decision brief. PTS selects technical direction; PSA determines detailed architecture and scoped execution later; partner leaders validate their own intent and commitments. Keep exercise to one evidence test or one decision artifact.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Separate market or technology signals from verified partner demand. A cited source may support a trend without proving that this partner should invest in it.
2. State technical differentiation as a hypothesis and expose the dependency that could invalidate it. Do not turn a draft direction into promised features, timelines or revenue.
3. Partner commitment is human evidence. Prepare the questions needed to confirm priorities, sponsorship or operating ownership; never interpret a positive comment or absent objection as agreement.
discussionQuestions: What makes this direction technically distinctive for this partner rather than generically interesting?
What evidence would lead us to choose a different offering direction?
Which commitment are we assuming instead of asking the partner to confirm?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Test the signal behind an offering hypothesis'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Spend one minute naming the offering choice, five minutes running one Featured evidence, direction or commitment-question practice, and two minutes checking the strongest claim against its source. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Choose between two technical offering directions', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close on one direction to test or one reason to defer, not a list of exciting possibilities. Restate that the partner has not committed merely because the draft uses confident language. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one approved offering concept, a partner capability baseline, the technical-plan priority it supports and either an approved source list or approved stakeholder comments. Include a real alternative where possible. Mark source dates and distinguish external signals from partner statements. No public research beyond the user-approved list is required.
facilitatorQuestions: Does the citation support this claim or only a nearby idea?
Which feature or operating assumption remains a hypothesis?
Is the next step a PTS direction decision or a partner commitment question?
listenFor: Generic innovation language, current capability confused with a future roadmap, and market signals substituted partner intent. Ask for a counterargument and insist that unsupported claims remain visible.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Without accessible research, label citations unavailable and create a hypothesis card with the claim, supplied evidence, counterargument and minimum validation question. Do not invent market proof or use unapproved browsing to make the brief appear finished. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which sentence would have overstated our confidence if it had reached the partner unchanged?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a technical-direction assumption against an approved source and consider retain, revise or defer, keeping any needed partner confirmation explicit. Do not publish the offering brief through this exploration. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized direction hypothesis qualified and whether it prevented an overstated partner commitment. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports the customer's technical decision through discovery, architecture options, demonstrations and appropriate technical proofs. Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports technical decisions with architecture choices, proof evidence and clear delivery handoffs.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Delivers technical architecture, implementation, adoption and operational-health outcomes within the assigned specialty and engagement. Validates workload blockers, completes agreed technical work and supports measurable customer value, coordinating success-plan inputs and follow-on opportunities without assuming ownership of every forecast, consumption shortfall or customer review.
roles.descriptionSummary: Delivers technical architecture, adoption, health and workload outcomes within assigned scope.

roles.name: Digital Solution Area Specialist
roles.description: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline starting with installed-base telemetry and contract events, supplemented by customer, partner, and marketing evidence. Shapes customer strategy and decision criteria, coordinates multiworkload routing and proof, and connects conversion, delivery, activation, renewal, and expansion.
roles.descriptionSummary: Develops SME&C solution-area pipeline from installed-base evidence through conversion and expansion.

roles.name: Digital Solution Engineer
roles.description: Consolidates existing SME&C discovery from account, specialist, partner, and customer inputs, validating decision criteria and gaps. roles.descriptionSummary: Validates SME&C discovery, shapes architecture, runs proofs, and transfers decisions into delivery.

roles.name: PTS
roles.description: Shapes cross-solution partner technical direction through multi-horizon roadmaps and Build-to-Consume priorities. Guides offering innovation, establishes technical guardrails, and coordinates handoffs for scoped architecture and execution, inspecting plan progress and applying reusable learning without assuming ownership of partner business strategy or engineering delivery.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes EPS cross-solution partner technical strategy, roadmaps, and guardrails for scoped handoffs.

roles.name: PSA
roles.description: Translates scoped technical intake into offering architecture, designs, and reusable assets. Develops Customer Zero proofs and validates technical conclusions and offering readiness, coordinating accepted handoffs into commercialization and activation while keeping broader strategy, partner engineering delivery, and commercial approvals with accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Turns scoped EPS technical intake into offering architecture, reusable assets, and validated proofs.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Shapes USPSI account technical strategy using approved stakeholder, workload, KPI, and risk evidence. Prioritizes AI and cloud workloads, develops executive technical narratives, and aligns technical teams around readiness, impact, and customer decisions within organizational requirements, without default implementation ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Shapes USPSI technical strategy and workload priorities using approved evidence.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions through technical discovery, agreed criteria, architecture options, and grounded responses using approved evidence. Designs demonstrations, workshops, and proofs of concept with success and exit criteria, addressing technical risks within organizational requirements rather than assuming post-sale architecture ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Supports USPSI opportunity decisions with technical discovery and proofs using approved evidence.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Provides USPSI technical advice on production architecture, validation, technical health, and cost optimization using approved evidence and organizational handling requirements. Diagnoses consumption gaps, recommends targeted interventions, and demonstrates technical progress and customer value without owning every consumption shortfall.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advises on USPSI production architecture, health, and optimization using approved evidence.

activities.description: Clear return-to-PTS conditions reduce both unnecessary escalation and silent strategic drift during scoped execution.
activities.prompt: Review [the approved partner-project scope contract and decision constraints]. Create an escalation matrix for no more than three decision types: a change to cross-solution intent, a constraint that changes the technical-plan sequence, and a proposed expansion beyond the agreed deliverable. Use only supplied thresholds; when none exists, draft a question rather than inventing a numeric rule. Keep normal CSA-specific execution decisions with PSA. Flag missing evidence or conflicting authority. PTS will validate the escalation boundaries with the relevant owners. Stop if decision rights conflict. No automated alerts, task changes, approvals, messages or writeback.

activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates what changes strategic intent; PSA retains normal scoped execution choices. Stop where decision rights or thresholds are unresolved and seek human agreement before using the matrix operationally.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/project; approved scope contract; existing thresholds or explicit absence; technical-plan constraints; known decision owners and escalation process notes.
activitySteps: 1. Supply one approved scope contract and existing decision constraints.
2. Select at most three escalation decision types relevant to this project.
3. Review observable triggers and distinguish PSA execution discretion from PTS strategy decisions.
4. Retain a PTS-validated draft matrix and unresolved threshold/authority questions.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Bring one project whose direction is clear enough to discuss with PSA. The PTS task is not to solve the architecture in the huddle; it is to define why the work exists, what outcome and evidence are needed, where execution authority sits and when the scoped involvement ends. PSA must review feasibility and accept its own execution scope. The partner must confirm its delivery and post-activation responsibilities. AI can draft a scope contract or reveal an ownership gap, but it cannot allocate an architect, accept a handoff or approve release. Use the live practice to resolve one ambiguity.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Separate technical intent from implementation method. PTS supplies strategic outcomes and guardrails; PSA determines scoped CSA-specific architecture and execution.
2. Name deliverables, evidence gates, escalation triggers and exit criteria. A list of activities without an exit can turn scoped assistance into assumed ongoing operation.
3. Mark all proposed ownership and acceptance explicitly. Handoff readiness is a draft review judgment, not proof that PSA has capacity or the partner has accepted delivery obligations.
discussionQuestions: What must PSA understand about the technical intent without being told how to implement it?
Which decision must return to PTS because it changes scope or cross-solution direction?
What would show that the scoped work has ended and partner ownership is in place?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft a PTS-to-PSA scope contract'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use one minute to choose the handoff ambiguity, five minutes for one Featured scope, escalation or ownership practice, and two minutes to challenge the exit. Keep architecture design outside this segment. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Scope regional activation without rebuilding the global solution', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by reading the acceptance question and exit criterion aloud. Discuss the distinction between PTS strategy ownership, PSA execution ownership and partner delivery/operation ownership. Frontier Accelerator supports experimentation and shared learning, not a polished artifact. Where, if anywhere, could you adapt this judgment in your work?
preparationChecklist: Bring one approved technical-plan decision, project brief, known constraints and any dated PSA intake or partner ownership notes. Include the intended deliverable and evidence gate if they exist. Supply approved extracts only; no assumed PMX connector, automated intake or task assignment. Decide whether the biggest gap is scope, escalation or ownership.
facilitatorQuestions: Is this a PTS guardrail or an architectural instruction PSA should own?
Can the exit criterion be checked from evidence rather than sentiment?
Which owner or acceptance is still proposed rather than confirmed?
listenFor: PSA being treated as indefinite delivery capacity, partner operations assigned to Microsoft, and acceptance inferred because a name appears in a draft. Ask participants to make the stop or escalation boundary as concrete as the deliverable.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Write one handoff row manually: technical intent, expected evidence, in/out scope, proposed owner, escalation trigger and exit. Leave acceptance unconfirmed. If strategic intent itself is unclear, return to the technical-plan decision rather than fabricate intake detail. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which phrase in the original handoff could have made scoped technical help look like an open-ended delivery commitment?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a handoff boundary and the strategic guardrail a PSA or partner owner would need to review. Keep acceptance and scope changes unconfirmed unless evidenced; do not send or assign automatically. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized scope phrase or exit criterion clarified and whether it reduced ambiguity between PTS, PSA and partner ownership. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

primaryAgents.name: Scout
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Always-on agent that runs on your desktop. You set it up once and leave it running: it works to a schedule without being asked, remembers what it saw last time, and can reach work that sits outside Microsoft 365.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Recurring checks, follow-up nudges and work that reaches outside Microsoft 365. Watch a book of accounts for movement between reviews, catch commitments going quiet, notice a signal approaching its expiry, and carry what it found last week into this week rather than starting from nothing.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the work should keep running after you stop asking. Set it up and leave it running for anything recurring, anything that needs watching between reviews, and anything that reaches outside Microsoft 365. The test is whether you want an answer now or want to be told when something changes.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for a quick single answer that Copilot would handle in the app you are already in, and do not use it for a multi-step task you want done once and handed back, which is Cowork. activities.name: Audit milestone evidence without inventing a health score
activities.description: An evidence ledger exposes genuine progression without manufacturing precision or confusing activity with an achieved outcome.
activities.prompt: Inspect at most three milestones for the project identified in [the approved plan row, original evidence gates and dated progress packet]. First extract what each gate requires; then assess whether the supplied evidence supports, partially supports, contradicts or leaves it unknown. Keep activity completion separate from outcome proof and distinguish partner-provided evidence from Microsoft-side status. Return a progression ledger with source/date, evidence judgment, contradiction or gap, and the next human question. Do not invent traffic-light thresholds, completion percentages or missing results. Stop before declaring a gate met if required evidence is absent or contradictory. No status writeback, alerts, task assignments or approvals.
activities.expectedOutput: Milestone progression ledger with supported/partial/contradicted/unknown judgments, source references and one prioritized review question.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates the evidence judgment and its strategic implication, not execution completion on behalf of PSA. Stop before declaring a gate met when required evidence is missing or contradictory.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/project; up to three milestones; original approved evidence gates; dated progress notes/exports; available partner evidence; previous decision record where available.
activitySteps: 1. Supply one project and no more than three milestones with original evidence gates.
2. Add approved dated progress evidence and label source origin.
3. Trace the most consequential judgment back to the gate and source.
4. Retain the PTS-reviewed ledger and one unresolved human evidence question.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: An evidence ledger exposes genuine progression without manufacturing precision or confusing activity with an achieved outcome.

activities.name: Choose a strategic intervention rather than a task list
activities.description: A small intervention comparison focuses governance on the decision that changes trajectory instead of producing an unowned action backlog.
activities.prompt: For the blocked milestone identified in the supplied progression ledger, use my approved progression ledger, scope contract and constraint notes. Compare up to three responses: preserve the current direction while seeking evidence, change sequencing, or revise the technical scope. Include only responses justified by the packet. For each, show the strategic consequence, execution-owner boundary, evidence required and reversible versus hard-to-reverse effects. Do not invent resources or assign PSA/partner actions. Return one conditional intervention recommendation and the fact that would overturn it, with missing evidence explicit. PTS owns the strategic intervention and will validate it with relevant owners. Stop if the choice depends on unconfirmed feasibility or authority. Draft only; no notifications, commitments, approvals or system changes.
activities.expectedOutput: Intervention decision card comparing up to three responses, strategic consequences, owner boundaries and an overturning evidence trigger.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS chooses direction or sequencing changes while execution remains with PSA/project owners. Stop when feasibility or decision authority is unconfirmed; do not convert the recommendation into assigned work.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/project and one blocked milestone; approved progression ledger; scope contract; technical-plan constraints; known decision rights; available feasibility evidence.
activitySteps: 1. Select one blocked milestone and provide the approved evidence/constraint packet.
2. Ask Cowork to compare no more than three supported intervention responses.
3. Inspect decision rights and the assumption most likely to overturn the recommendation.
4. Record a PTS intervention or hold with a human validation owner and review trigger.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
activities.whyThisMatters: A small intervention comparison focuses governance on the decision that changes trajectory instead of producing an unowned action backlog.

activities.name: Rebaseline one horizon without erasing the original plan
activities.description: A transparent rebaseline preserves learning and accountability while allowing the multi-horizon technical plan to respond to real evidence.
activities.prompt: Compare [the project baseline and proposed revision] using only the dated change evidence and horizon definitions I supply. Produce a before-and-after plan row showing original outcome/gate, changed assumption, source of change, proposed horizon or scope, downstream dependency effects and decision still required. Separate a justified rebaseline from moving a date to conceal an unresolved blocker. Do not infer stakeholder acceptance, create dates or change the system of record. Preserve the original baseline and flag missing or conflicting evidence. The PTS will decide whether the revision belongs in the technical plan after owner review. Stop if the new horizon relies on unconfirmed PSA or partner capacity. Draft only; no writeback, commitments, messages or approvals.
activities.expectedOutput: Before-and-after rebaseline record retaining original assumptions, change evidence, downstream impact and the PTS decision pending or made.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates the rationale and confirms that changing a horizon is not hiding an unresolved gate. Stop on unsupported capacity or missing change evidence; retain the baseline and document the hold.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/project; one approved baseline outcome; proposed change; dated evidence; existing horizon definitions; known dependencies and capacity confirmations or explicit gaps.
activitySteps: 1. Supply one baseline row, a proposed revision and dated change evidence.
2. Add existing horizon definitions and relevant downstream dependencies.
3. Review the before-and-after rationale for hidden blockers or invented acceptance.
4. Keep a PTS rebaseline decision draft that preserves the original row and remaining review requirements.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.
