activities.name: Detect global-to-regional drift from two approved snapshots
activities.description: A bounded snapshot variant detects regional divergence without assuming continuous access or turning strategic governance into automated operational monitoring.
activities.prompt: Compare [the two dated snapshots identifying the partner solution and region] against the approved global technical guardrails. Work read-only on this packet; do not assume PMX integration, browse for updates or set up monitoring. Separate real changes from renamed fields or missing rows. Produce a drift log covering inherited global decisions, regional activation prerequisites and newly implied rebuild or support obligations. Cite the snapshot row supporting each change and mark uncertain comparisons unknown. Recommend one exception for PTS/global-owner review, not an operational action. PTS will validate whether the drift is material. Stop if snapshots are not comparable or a claimed change lacks evidence. No scheduling, alerts, messages, status updates or commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Read-only regional drift log with evidence references, uncertain comparisons and one PTS/global-owner exception candidate.
activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates materiality against global intent. Stop when snapshots are not comparable or supporting evidence is absent; do not interpret missing rows as completed or cancelled work.
activities.requiredContext: One partner/solution and one region; two dated approved status exports; global technical guardrails; field-mapping notes if needed. User supplies all material; no live connector or scheduled monitor.
activitySteps: 1. Supply two comparable approved snapshots for one solution and one region.
2. Add the global guardrails and known field-name changes.
3. Inspect the drift log for false differences caused by missing rows or renamed fields.
4. Retain one PTS-validated exception or a no-material-change conclusion with evidence.

Fallback: If the named assistant is unavailable, complete the same bounded evidence table or draft manually from the approved supplied packet. No additional assistant, connector, private-system access or automatic execution is required.

Include scope, sources, owner, cadence, recipients, expiry and approval gaps. For a first review, establish the baseline/access state; later, report only changed, missing or inaccessible evidence with dates and possible plan impact. Missing history means comparison unavailable, not ‘no change’. Don’t infer completion, change plans, send commitments or assign work.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated baseline-only or change-only supplied-evidence review draft with source/history/access gaps and an unactivated proposal for the named reviewer; zero scheduled jobs or notifications.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The named owner reviews every report; PTS alone decides whether the technical plan changes.
activities.requiredContext: An approved dependency, human-approved cadence, approved evidence locations, dated baseline, and named review owner. Provide authorized dated snapshots and user-maintained baseline/prior report if available. Source permissions, scope, cadence, recipients, review/expiry and automation approval are explicit proposed fields; missing inputs remain gaps and no tool access/state retention is assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm one bounded dependency/action and supply authorized dated snapshots; clearly labeled synthetic evidence is rehearsal-only.
2. Check the user-maintained baseline/prior report, comparable definitions and named reviewer; leave missing history, permission or criteria explicit.
3. Compare supplied evidence manually or with one already authorized tool; no schedule, live retrieval or persistent agent memory.
4. Produce a dated baseline-only/comparison draft and unactivated proposal with source, owner, cadence, recipients, expiry and approval fields.
5. Apply the unchanged HumanCheckpoint before interpretation/action; future automation, notifications and system changes require separate explicit authorization.

Fallback: Scout is optional and preview/prerelease. Compare supplied dated snapshots manually and retain the baseline/report yourself; no connector, persistent agent memory, scheduled job or notification permission is assumed.
activities.whyThisMatters: Persistent monitoring catches meaningful dependency movement without replacing the plan owner's judgment.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Rebaseline one horizon without erasing the original plan

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Select one project in the partner technical plan and compare its current evidence with the outcome and exit criteria already agreed. Do not ask AI to review everything or generate an overall partner health score. PTS governs cross-solution direction and the implications for the roadmap; PSA and project owners act on scoped execution issues, and the partner remains responsible for delivery and operation. Today's useful result may be confirmation that the milestone is supported, a targeted evidence request or a deliberate rebaseline. It is not a new promise about dates or resources.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Compare evidence against the original outcome gate, not the confidence of the latest status note. Keep source dates, contradictions and missing partner-side evidence visible.

2. Choose interventions by decision ownership. PTS changes direction or sequencing; PSA/project owners address execution within scope. Do not convert a governance review into automated task assignment.
3. Rebaseline only when a human decision changes the plan. Preserve the original assumption, the new evidence and the rationale so future reviews can see why the plan moved.
discussionQuestions: Which milestone appears complete because activity happened rather than because its evidence gate was met?
What is the smallest PTS intervention that could change the plan's trajectory?
When is a rebaseline honest governance, and when would it hide an unresolved dependency?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Audit milestone evidence without inventing a health score'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Use one minute to select the milestone decision, five minutes for one Featured ledger, intervention or rebaseline practice, and two minutes to audit the critical evidence reference. Extended snapshot comparison is optional follow-on work. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Choose a strategic intervention rather than a task list', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Ask participants to state the evidence judgment, the PTS decision and who owns any subsequent execution action. Close with a specific review trigger instead of an open-ended request to monitor progress. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
preparationChecklist: Bring one project's approved plan row or scope contract, the previous review snapshot, current approved progress notes and the defined outcome/exit evidence. Include human-supplied PMX or other status exports only if approved and dated. Keep the review bounded to at most three milestones and one project.
facilitatorQuestions: What changed since the previous review, and which source proves it?
Is this an execution issue or a PTS direction/sequence decision?
What would you need before accepting the proposed revised milestone?
listenFor: Completed meetings or documents being used as proof of an outcome, missing evidence treated as failure, and revised dates accepted without human ownership. Coach participants to preserve uncertainty and identify the precise decision rather than announce a red status.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Manually compare one milestone's original evidence gate with the latest approved evidence. Mark supported, partial, contradicted or unknown and write one review question. If no prior snapshot exists, establish a dated baseline rather than fabricate a change history. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the evidence inspection change that a conventional status update would have missed?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore a progression judgment or proposed intervention and the evidence/date that would support reconsideration. PTS judgment does not transfer execution ownership; make no automatic status updates or assignments. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized progression claim checked and whether evidence changed intervention rather than just status. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.prompt: Assemble a draft technical reuse package for the offering identified in [the approved architecture summary, validation evidence and asset-permission notes]. First separate reusable decisions and components from context-specific implementation; then create an inventory with original context, evidence reference, reuse condition, known limitation, rights status and lifecycle owner. Do not generalize one activation or early win into universal feasibility, and do not include customer identifiers or restricted content. Mark missing evidence and permissions explicitly. PTS will validate technical reuse scope and seek owner review. Stop before recommending reuse if rights, a critical limitation or support ownership is unresolved. activities.humanCheckpoint: PTS validates the reusable technical boundary; authorized owners must separately confirm rights and support responsibilities. Stop on unresolved permission, critical limitation or lifecycle ownership; no publication or reuse approval.

2. Ask Cowork to classify reusable versus context-specific elements before packaging.
3. Inspect the most valuable asset's evidence, limitation, rights and lifecycle owner.
4. Retain a PTS-reviewed reuse inventory with unapproved elements clearly held.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Take one offering with useful technical learning, whether it succeeded fully, partially or exposed a limit. This week is not a graduation or a claim that the partner is ready to scale everywhere. It asks what can responsibly be reused, what evidence supports that reuse and what should change in the technical roadmap. PTS validates cross-solution learning and reuse direction. PSA contributes architecture and execution evidence. The partner leads delivery and post-activation operation. AI can assemble a package or compare lessons, but permission, accuracy, reuse decisions and any publication remain human responsibilities.
keyTalkingPoints: 1. Separate reusable architecture decisions, bounded accelerators and context-specific implementation details. Keep rights, provenance, known limitations and support ownership attached to the artifact.
2. A successful activation or early win is not universal validation. Show the conditions under which it was observed and the evidence still missing for wider use.

3. Close the learning loop deliberately: retain, revise or retire one technical assumption and connect that judgment to the next roadmap review. Do not automatically publish proof points, update systems or transfer partner operation to Microsoft.
discussionQuestions: Which part of this offering would we reuse, and what context must travel with it?
What did the project teach us that should change a roadmap assumption?
Who owns delivery and operation after the scoped technical work ends?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Package one offering's reusable technical core'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Give one minute to choose the scale decision, five minutes for one Featured reuse, learning or ownership practice, and two minutes to check the evidence/permission boundary. The Extended variant is optional, not an additional live requirement. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Test a reusable asset in one new context before scaling', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close with one reusable insight and its limit, one PTS roadmap implication and the human owner of the next validation. Do not frame the package as published, approved or operationally handed over. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one offering's approved architecture/decision summary, validation or activation evidence, permission and asset-ownership notes, and one relevant technical-plan assumption. Include a human-supplied partner operating-owner statement where available. Remove customer identifiers and reuse-restricted content before the huddle. A partial outcome with clear limits is a valid case.
facilitatorQuestions: Which claimed reusable element has evidence and permission behind it?
What would fail if this artifact were applied in a different context?
Is the proposed next step PTS roadmap governance or partner delivery/operation?
listenFor: One early win being generalized to every partner context, reusable assets lacking rights or support owners, and an exit statement that assumes the partner has accepted operation. Encourage a bounded hold when the evidence or permission does not support scale.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Create a manual reuse card: artifact, original context, evidence, reusable boundary, known limit, rights/owner and next validation. If permission is absent, describe only the type of learning and hold the underlying material from reuse or publication. If no permitted inputs are available at all, sketch a clearly labeled synthetic version of the selected artifact to practice the review questions only. Leave real status, program criteria, authority and acceptance unknown; the example is not evidence for a live decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What limitation would you now insist travels with an early win or reusable asset?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore a reuse boundary, roadmap-learning change or partner operating-owner gap and consider retain, revise or hold. Permission and evidence are still required before broader use; do not publish or send the package automatically. If input or access is missing, you could explore a permitted sanitized example or leave the verification question open; do not infer approval, agreement or status. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized reuse limit or roadmap implication refined and whether it improved learning; publication or operational transfer is not required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

PLC-EPS-PTS-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on the team’s progress over the past eight weeks, identify the AI habits to keep building, and agree how to continue learning through team huddles.
PLC-EPS-PTS-W09.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
PLC-EPS-PTS-W09.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Reserve the final five-minute Close & Survey block for participants to complete their own Impact Survey through the approved link. Priorities and the continuing structure should already be agreed in Recap & What's Next.
2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Look back on experience from the first eight weeks without assuming everyone completed every huddle. This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion: keep sharing, explore workflows that matter, and build on what works.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the shared Transition HTML, not the ordinary AI-in-Action practice format. Share recent experience and journey-wide reflection; the facilitator or manager briefly explains why practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue. Then agree the ongoing huddle rhythm and a Week 10 topic, and close with feedback. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
discussionQuestions: Since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well or did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?

Looking back across the journey: Moments that mattered—what changed in how you think about or use AI, and what are you doing differently? Habits worth continuing—which habits and peer learning should we keep building? Make it our own—what has worked about our huddles, what would we change, and what should ongoing huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep a team-owned rhythm, and which topic will we use for Week 10?
suggestedTransitions: Open with the purpose (2 minutes). Use Share Your Experience (15 minutes) for both the since-last-huddle check-in and the journey-wide reflection. The facilitator or manager then presents Sustain (3 minutes): practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Move to What’s Next (8 minutes) to agree the ongoing rhythm and a Week 10 topic using All Topics or Huddle in a Box as appropriate. Close & Feedback (2 minutes) welcomes questions and points to the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the habits worth continuing, the team's ongoing huddle rhythm, and the agreed Week 10 topic. Use Close & Feedback for questions and the Team Member Impact Survey invitation. Participants who already completed the survey do not need to repeat it; this is the beginning of Sustain, not the end of the motion.
facilitatorQuestions: Share Your Experience—since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well, and what did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?
Looking back across the journey:
Moments that mattered: What experience changed how you think about or use AI? What are you doing differently today that you were not doing at the beginning?
Habits worth continuing: Which AI habits are becoming part of everyday work? What have you learned from one another that you want to keep building?
Make it our own: What has worked about our huddles, and what would we change? What should our ongoing team huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep learning together, and which topic will we choose for Week 10?
Close & Feedback: What questions, comments, or ideas would you like to share before we close?
listenFor: Listen for concrete changes, honest uncertainty, habits worth continuing, peer learning, and support needs. Include people with mixed experience or access gaps without assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Seek a shared Week 10 topic, not a tool quota or a ranking of participants.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If app, topic-library, customization, or survey links are unavailable, continue the team discussion and agree a Week 10 topic without a live build or download. Raise the access gap through the approved support route. Do not invent personal impact evidence or generate survey answers.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What has changed in how we think about and use AI, which habits should continue, and where would more practice or support help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Agree how the team will keep learning through huddles and choose a Week 10 topic. Existing All Topics content or Huddle in a Box are options described in the supplied HTML, not required live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; each person supplies their own feedback.
bringBackEvidence: Keep bringing useful experiences, questions, and friction into the existing team rhythm. No new individual report, artifact, or survey-completion proof is required. Distinguish an observed benefit from an untested idea and keep human judgment explicit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Help the team move from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Reflect on the first eight weeks, identify useful habits and remaining support needs, agree how huddles will continue, and choose a topic for Week 10. This is a shared team review, not account planning or technical strategy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the shared Transition HTML and its five-part agenda. With the manager, agree who opens the session, facilitates reflection, presents the brief Sustain explanation, and guides the Week 10 planning. Locate the All Topics, Huddle in a Box, and Impact Survey links before the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Follow the shared 30-minute agenda: Overview 2; Share Your Experience 15; Sustain 3; What’s Next 8; Close & Feedback 2. Sustain is a short facilitator/manager explanation of why ongoing practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue—not another open discussion or AI-practice block. Do not require a success story, a new artifact, or live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to draw out experiences and friction, reinforce why huddles continue, and help the team choose its Week 10 topic and continuing rhythm. Keep the same shared Team Review content across audiences; do not substitute a role-specific planning exercise.

PLC-EPS-PTS-W09.keyTakeaway: This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion. Keep sharing, explore workflows that matter to the team, and build on what works.

managerGuide.managerTeamRelevance: Help the team own its transition from guided Activation to Sustain: recognize learning, keep useful habits, agree how huddles continue, and choose a Week 10 topic. This shared review is not an account-priority or technical-strategy session.
managerGuide.managerPreparationGuidance: Review the Week 9 Team Review HTML and agree light handoffs with the facilitator before meeting. Be ready to support reflection, the continuing team rhythm, and choosing a Week 10 topic. Confirm the supplied Impact Survey link is available without asking for personal responses.
managerGuide.managerDuringHuddleGuidance: Make space for wins, dead ends, and friction without rating people or assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Agree who will present the brief Sustain explanation: practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Help the team agree its continuing rhythm and a Week 10 topic. Follow the shared five-part agenda rather than adding a live tool exercise.
managerGuide.managerFollowThroughQuestions:
What habits and support needs should we carry into our existing team rhythm?
Have we agreed how huddles will continue and which topic we will use in Week 10?
If the Impact Survey is still outstanding, do people know where to find it without repeating an already completed response?

PLC-USPSI-SE-W01.todayObjective: Understand why Frontier Accelerator matters, the roles that make huddles work, and what to expect as the team begins learning through real work.
PLC-USPSI-SE-W01.whyItMatters: Firsthand experience helps us bring real insights to customers. A consistent huddle rhythm builds confidence and helps teams learn from one another as AI becomes part of everyday work.
PLC-USPSI-SE-W01.desiredOutcome: Understand the huddle motion, the connected roles, where to find shared resources, and what to expect when workflow huddles begin in Week 2.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Welcome to the shared Frontier Accelerator Orientation. Understand why we go first as Customer Zero, how the huddle motion works, and how to participate. The Huddle Experience previews the repeatable weekly format from Week 2 onward.
keyTalkingPoints: Explain the Customer Zero purpose, the five connected roles, and the weekly rhythm of real work and peer learning. Distinguish today’s Orientation from the future weekly-format examples. Point to the HTML’s readiness checklist and shared resources; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2.
discussionQuestions: What questions do we have about the huddle motion and how to participate?
Where can we find the shared resources and access help?
What would help us feel ready for the first workflow huddle in Week 2?
suggestedTransitions: Move through the Orientation story, then use Huddle Experience to preview the familiar weekly structure. Explain that sharing prior experience and hands-on workflow practice start with the role-specific huddles, not as extra Orientation tasks. Close with readiness questions and the next huddle.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the team understands the motion, where to find the shared resources, and what to expect in Week 2. Point to existing Top 5 Agents readiness guidance in the learner HTML without adding a separate assignment. Make clear that the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional and the weekly pulse starts in Week 2.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the huddle motion for, and how will we learn from one another?
What will feel different when the role-specific huddles begin in Week 2?
What questions do we have about participation, the shared resources, or getting help?
listenFor: Listen for clarity about the weekly rhythm, the five connected roles, safe experimentation, and learning from wins and friction. Separate questions about future practice from Orientation participation; no expert knowledge, completed tool trial, or polished artifact is needed today.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a link or tool is unavailable, explain the motion from the supplied HTML and name the access blocker for support. Do not bypass permissions or invent a completed demonstration. Discussion and questions remain useful; never supply an AI-generated survey response.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What is clearer about how huddles work, and what question would help you feel ready to participate?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Confirm the shared next step into the first role-specific huddle. Use the learner HTML's existing readiness guidance as needed; the recurring-work discovery prompt remains optional. Do not require a tool trial or a new deliverable from every participant.
bringBackEvidence: Invite questions or learning to share at the next huddle. No new artifact, access screenshot, completed prompt, or proof of participation is required by this host guidance. Keep sensitive details in approved systems.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Introduce the shared huddle motion: why we go first as Customer Zero, how peer learning builds confidence, and what to expect from Orientation, role-specific Weeks 2–8, and team-owned Sustain. This is Orientation for everyone, not a role-specific work exercise.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the supplied Orientation HTML, including its Orientation and Huddle Experience tabs. Confirm the HTML and baseline-survey link are available; identify where to find the Top 5 Agents overview and access help. Agree the opening and handoffs with the manager before meeting.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Distinguish today’s Orientation from the weekly-format preview that begins in Week 2. There is no prior huddle experience to share today. Do not turn the preview into a required live tool exercise. Use the HTML for readiness guidance; the recurring-work discovery go-do is optional, not a required deliverable. The weekly usefulness pulse begins in Week 2; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree who introduces the why, who guides the Orientation and weekly-experience preview, and how questions or access blockers will be supported. Use the same shared content for every audience; local examples can add flavor without creating a maintained role-specific Orientation.

activities.name: Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief
activities.description: Synthesize approved customer and technical context into a brief that names the customer decision, constraints, evidence gaps, and criteria. Live huddle: choose ONE Featured practice, not the full menu; use an approved existing artifact for any prerequisite and leave additional builds for later.
activities.prompt: Use [customer and technical sources plus confirmed attendee list] to draft a discovery brief: business outcome, owner, architecture, constraints, open questions and five questions that advance the decision. Identify who must authorize funding/staffing and who is attending; flag unknowns. Separate customer-agreed decision criteria from proposed criteria, citing evidence and who must confirm each. Don’t turn hypotheses into agreement. Use supplied material only; don’t search, connect or take actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical discovery brief with questions, evidence gaps, the business outcome and its owner, decision-maker coverage, and explicit decision criteria. Each criterion identifies customer-agreed versus proposed status, supporting source where available, and the person who must confirm it or an unresolved ownership gap.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides which questions are appropriate to ask this customer. A technically sound discovery question can be premature or presumptuous given where the relationship is, and discovery is where that costs most. The SE also decides how directly to ask who can approve, since the question is fair to ask and can still land badly depending on who is in the room.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Selected approved customer and technical sources; the confirmed attendee list for the meeting, and any sourced information you hold about how the decision-makers are measured. Include any recorded customer-agreed decision criteria and their source; otherwise identify criteria as hypotheses to confirm.
activities.whyThisMatters: Discovery becomes useful when it produces decision criteria the customer and team can inspect.

activities.name: Rehearse the technical discovery conversation
activities.description: Practice questions, listening, objections and the intended next decision.
activities.prompt: Using only the supplied approved discovery brief, act as a hypothetical customer stakeholder. Let me open the conversation; then respond one exchange at a time and wait for my next question, for three exchanges. Test whether my questions uncover the customer outcome, a decision-changing constraint and who confirms the criteria. Do not invent customer facts; use an explicitly hypothetical answer when the brief leaves a gap. Then coach listening, premature solution claims and follow-up quality, and propose two revised discovery questions for SE review. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Three-exchange discovery rehearsal, coaching on listening and premature claims, two revised questions and factual/criteria gaps for validation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns what is said in the room. Rehearsal makes phrasing fluent, and fluency makes an unverified claim sound exactly as certain as a verified one.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. Approved discovery brief.
activities.whyThisMatters: Practicing discovery questions reduces the chance that the real meeting ends with ambiguity instead of criteria.

activities.name: Map evidence gaps against decision criteria
activities.description: Test each decision criterion in the discovery brief against the evidence you actually hold, so the gaps are visible before the customer finds them.
activities.prompt: Using the discovery brief, map each proposed decision criterion to supporting evidence, missing evidence, assumptions, and required reviewer input. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides which missing evidence actually blocks the decision. Discovery can always find another gap, and pursuing all of them delays the decision the criteria were built to enable.

activities.whyThisMatters: The gap map shows what must be proven before architecture, demo, or PoC work proceeds.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Discovery should end with decision criteria, not a second discovery meeting. Today focuses on making the customer decision explicit early.
keyTalkingPoints: Start from the customer decision and work backward to criteria and evidence.
Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and open questions.
Capture what must be validated before architecture, demo, or PoC work begins.
discussionQuestions: Which decision is the customer actually trying to make?
Who has to say yes for this to happen, and were they in the room last time?
What evidence gap would make the next technical step unsafe?
What criteria need to be agreed rather than inferred?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from discovery discussion to building the actual decision-criteria brief. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Map evidence gaps against decision criteria', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Technical discovery separates customer-agreed criteria from assumptions and identifies who can say yes. Write criteria before the conversation, then revise them as evidence changes. If this fits your work, you could adapt the useful step and choose whether to share a permission-safe lesson; no new habit or report is expected.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming or recent technical discovery conversation, approved context, known constraints, and any open technical questions.
facilitatorQuestions: Which discovery question would most change the technical decision?
What evidence is missing or only assumed?
Which criteria must be agreed with the customer?
Which question has a peer used to turn assumed criteria into a customer-confirmed decision?
listenFor: Vague decisions, inferred criteria, missing evidence, and questions that sound impressive but do not advance the decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one discovery-criteria brief: customer decision, confirmed versus assumed criterion, evidence needed, discovery question and confirmation owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What technical assumption did the practice test, and which proof or human decision is needed before advancing?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could explore discovery criteria and the approval question using existing context; a new customer conversation is not required. Any real discovery should keep proposed criteria distinct from customer-confirmed criteria. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized criterion confirmed or corrected and whether it focused discovery or clarified approval ownership; it need not have been wrong. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A demo or workshop should advance a customer decision, not tour a product. Today narrows the experience to proof that matters.
keyTalkingPoints: Anchor the experience in the customer scenario and decision.
Prepare evidence, objections, roles, environment needs, and fallback plan.
Do not rely on demo energy to cover unclear criteria.
discussionQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop make easier?
Which scenario proves the most important customer concern?
Where could environment, permission, or data issues derail the experience?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Build the decision-centered demo or workshop plan'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from scenario selection to the demo or workshop plan. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate demo evidence and known limitations', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Demos and workshops should provide the smallest relevant proof for the customer decision. Cut feature tours that do not test the criterion and keep prerequisites, limits and fallback visible. If a relevant case arises, you could adapt this approach and decide whether to compare what helped or failed with peers.
preparationChecklist: Bring one demo, workshop, or technical customer session and the decision it needs to advance. Supply any available run logs or test results with their date and environment; if none are available, plan the verification and keep execution status unknown.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop advance?
Which scenario proves that decision?
What could fail because of data, tenant, permission, or environment constraints?
What fallback has a peer used when a demo environment failed without claiming the proof succeeded?
listenFor: Feature tours, unclear audience, unsupported claims, missing fallback plans, and proof not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or approved context is unavailable, use a sanitized supplied example or a clearly labeled synthetic case. On paper, create one demo or workshop storyboard: audience decision, proof scenario, environment prerequisite, known limitation and fallback explanation. Mark evidence, assumptions and unknowns. This is a storyboard, not an executed demo, successful test or permission to use an environment. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient. Any later AI run must use project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot and approved supplied inputs.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What decision does the scenario test, and what feature or unsupported claim did you cut because it did not help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could revise a demo or workshop scenario to test the customer criterion, checking prerequisites, limits and fallback. Building or running the whole session is not required. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized scenario retained or cut and whether review made the decision clearer; a customer session need not have occurred. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

Which success criterion is measurable?
Which dependency or owner is missing?
How has another SE shrunk a PoC while keeping meaningful success and exit criteria?
listenFor: Vague success criteria, PoCs that duplicate demo work, unowned dependencies, and no exit path.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one PoC scope card: customer doubt, minimum proof, measurable success/negative result, exit condition, dependency and approval gap. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. This is a storyboard or proof contract, not an executed demo, successful test or permission to use an environment. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What would proof change, and what would justify no proof, a smaller test or an early stop?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If useful, you could explore whether proof would change a decision, including a no-proof option. If real proof is pursued, success criteria, a stop condition and an accountable execution owner must be agreed before it starts. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share the human proceed, revise or no-proof decision and a sanitized criterion that informed it; note avoided effort or a clearer proof boundary. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical responses move faster when supported answers, assumptions, confidence, exceptions, and required reviewers are visible.
keyTalkingPoints: Answer with sources and confidence, not just fluency.
Preserve unsupported areas instead of smoothing them over.
Use the response package to route review, not to bypass it.
discussionQuestions: Which technical answer needs evidence before it can be used?
Where do we usually hide uncertainty?
Who must review the response before it goes to the customer?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Draft the sourced technical answer matrix'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from answer drafting to response governance and exception routing. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Route unsupported technical answers for review', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Grounded technical responses distinguish sourced answers, uncertainty and claims needing specialist or formal review. A defensible answer matters more than filling every box. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring one technical ask, security or architecture question, or objection that requires a governed response. If a formal RFP or questionnaire is in play, bring the technical question inside it rather than the document; the formal response goes through the proposal process.
facilitatorQuestions: Which answer is most consequential?
What source supports it?
Where should the response show confidence, caveat, exception, or SME-needed flag?
What review habit has a peer used to catch an answer that sounded certain but lacked support?
listenFor: Confident but unsourced answers, hidden uncertainty, overbroad commitments, and missing reviewers.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one answer-matrix row: technical question, supplied authoritative source or unavailable, bounded answer or hold, caveat and SME reviewer. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. If current authoritative guidance or a required owner is unavailable, retain a decision hold or exact owner question; do not substitute remembered policy or a plausible ruling. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which answer is supported by its source, and which uncertainty belongs with a specialist or formal reviewer?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a technical response for an upcoming conversation: verify a consequential answer, flag source or uncertainty, and route unsupported claims to technical or formal proposal review. Review claims and decide personally what to say or send; do not imply customer agreement. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized answer qualified or routed and whether it prevented an unsupported technical claim. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical risk should be named while it is still a decision, not after it becomes a customer escalation.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect exit criteria, blockers, proof gaps, objections, dependencies, and handoffs.
Every risk needs evidence, owner, mitigation, checkpoint, and next decision.
Use AI to surface signals, but use your judgment to prioritize them.
discussionQuestions: What technical risk is blocking progression right now?
Which proof gap is being treated as if it were already closed?
Who owns the next technical action?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Inspect technical deal health and proof gaps'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Move from risk naming to action plan and handoff. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Validate the blocker evidence and mitigation path', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Early technical risk management turns evidence into a timely owner conversation, mitigation or accepted handoff. Inference is not a confirmed blocker or escalation rule. If useful, you could try a small test of better work and choose whether to share a benefit or correction rather than just a draft.
preparationChecklist: Bring one opportunity or technical workstream with a blocker, proof gap, objection, or dependency.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical risk is blocking progression?
What evidence would clear or confirm it?
Who owns the mitigation and next checkpoint?
How does another SE keep an untested proof gap visible in the technical handoff?
listenFor: Risks without owners, proof gaps treated as closed, delivery handoffs without requirements, and blockers framed too broadly.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one technical risk row: blocker, available evidence, untested proof gap, proposed mitigation owner, handoff requirement and next check. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which risk is supported by current evidence, what remains uncertain, and who is accountable for the intervention?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could identify one technical risk early enough to be a conversation rather than an escalation. Verify evidence and keep the next decision with the accountable human owner. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share an anonymized concern checked and whether acting early clarified mitigation or avoided a later surprise. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

activities.prompt: Using the supplied sanitized asset and repository context, create the reuse note, tags, owner, purpose, prerequisites, example use, limitations, and repository metadata needed for another SE to find and adapt the asset. Use [relevant dated material] only; no search, connectors or actions.
activities.expectedOutput: Reuse note and repository metadata.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE states the limitations alongside the purpose. An asset found without its constraints gets applied to a situation it was never validated for, and the next SE inherits the failure.
activities.requiredContext: Supply only minimum necessary evidence approved for this use/audience, sanitized as required, with source, account scope and as-of date. The sanitized asset; where it will be stored; the owner who will maintain it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Findability and context are what turn a useful file into a reusable asset.

agents.name: Microsoft 365 Copilot

agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Draft, summarize, analyze, prepare, and create within familiar Microsoft 365 experiences.
agents.whenToUseIt: Everyday work grounded in emails, meetings, chats, files and app content, in the app you are already working in. Ask and get: you want the answer or the draft now.

resources.title: Workforce Transformation Hub

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use as a substitute for a specialized agent when the work requires a specific system or workflow, for a multi-step task you would rather hand off and review, which is Cowork, or for work that should keep running on a schedule, which is Scout.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot from the app launcher or copilot.cloud.microsoft and start in Chat.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Reuse only works when an asset has enough context for someone else to trust and adapt it.
keyTalkingPoints: Package purpose, prerequisites, steps, parameters, validation checks, limitations, owner, and example use.
Remove sensitive content before reuse.
For a repeatable workflow that is not a validated asset, draft a written outline for human review.
discussionQuestions: What did you build recently that another SE will rebuild?
What context would make someone trust and adapt it?
What should not be reused without review?
suggestedTransitions: A suggested starting point is 'Package a reusable technical asset with context'. Other Featured practices can be used as alternatives rather than additional live steps. Inspect the selected asset's prerequisites, provenance and actual validation status. A written-workflow walkthrough is specification review, not an installed, executed or tested implementation. Name the human implementation/test owner before any promotion or publication. Optional Extended follow-up: 'Sanitize and validate the reusable asset', only if its prerequisites and role applicability are met; it is outside the live one-practice slot. USPSI execution is Microsoft 365 Copilot only within the approved project scope, using permitted supplied inputs, or manual practice. Do not assume live retrieval, background monitoring or writeback.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: USPSI: Technical reuse depends on provenance, permissions, prerequisites and validation limits. A workflow outline or written workflow outline is a draft, not an implemented or tested capability. Where, if anywhere, could this fit in recurring work, and what small, safe signal might help you explore its value?
preparationChecklist: Bring one demo, script, architecture, checklist, response, or pattern that could become reusable. Supply available validation results, date, and environment for asset packaging. For a repeatable workflow outline, bring a representative approved test case, expected outcome, and access constraints; the huddle drafts and reviews documentation rather than claiming an implementation exists.
facilitatorQuestions: Which asset is worth reusing?
What context would make it usable by another SE?
What must be removed, validated, or tested before sharing?
What did another SE need to know before reusing your asset safely?
listenFor: Assets without owner, missing prerequisites, sensitive content, unclear limitations, and reuse patterns that should become blueprints.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the selected tool, system or approved context is inaccessible, use a sanitized supplied example; if none is available, use a clearly labeled synthetic case. Work on paper to build one reusable-asset card: purpose, prerequisites, source/provenance, sensitive detail removed, validation status, limit and implementation/test owner. Separate evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A synthetic case rehearses the method only; it cannot establish live status, eligibility, agreement or approval. Record the source/access gap and who must validate it before real use. Keep reuse/publication on hold until rights, sanitization and actual validation are reviewed; no repository access is required for the draft. For USPSI, the manual route is sufficient; any later AI run remains project-scoped Microsoft 365 Copilot with approved supplied inputs only.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which technical lesson is reusable, what needs review before others apply it, and where should it live?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: If relevant, you could review a small reuse candidate from existing work or draft a workflow outline. Check provenance, permissions, prerequisites and technical limits with its owner; keep draft status until reuse is authorized. If inputs or access are missing, you could explore a sanitized manual example or leave the gap open; never invent facts. For USPSI, any Microsoft 365 Copilot use must be limited to authorized supplied information; manual exploration is also a choice. Do not assume connected-source or MSX access. You may adapt the idea or choose no next action; no follow-up evidence is required.
bringBackEvidence: You may share a sanitized reuse lesson and whether it reduced explanation or setup effort; no asset upload or distribution is required. A brief, anonymized verbal summary is enough; keep restricted details in approved systems. If blocked or untested, you could share a question or gap, or leave it open; no follow-up is required.

PLC-USPSI-SE-W09.todayObjective: Reflect on the team’s progress over the past eight weeks, identify the AI habits to keep building, and agree how to continue learning through team huddles.
PLC-USPSI-SE-W09.whyItMatters: Huddles make AI part of everyday work through shared learning, not a one-time push. Team-owned priorities keep the motion relevant as work changes.
PLC-USPSI-SE-W09.desiredOutcome: A shared understanding of what has changed, the habits worth continuing, how the team will keep learning together, and an agreed topic for Week 10.

activities.name: Reconnect to the Huddle Motion
activities.description: Reconnect to the shared purpose and move from guided activation into continuing, team-owned learning.
activities.expectedOutput: Shared understanding of how the team will carry learning into its next work priority.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Keep the transition non-evaluative. Participants choose what they share; do not use AI adoption or survey completion as an individual performance measure.
activities.requiredContext: An example or question about real work, if available. No separate role-specific preparation; use a sanitized or hypothetical example when the group cannot discuss the underlying details.
activitySteps: 1. Use the two-minute Overview to reconnect to why the motion matters: to take customers to the Frontier, we go first.
2. Frame the transition from guided Activation into team-owned Sustain, not the end of huddles; do not assume everyone completed every earlier week.
3. Preview the 30-minute agenda: Overview 2, Share Your Experience 8, Recap & What's Next 15, Close & Survey 5. These are coordinated components, not four alternative practices.
activities.whyThisMatters: A shared purpose helps the team connect prior learning to future work.

activities.name: Share Your Experience: look back on real work
activities.description: Compare current work with the start of the guided path; identify a useful change, a continuing friction point, or where support is still needed.
activities.expectedOutput: A practical learning insight and a support need that inform what the team should try next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Separate workflow benefit from tool usage. Share only permitted details and do not evaluate participants or collect individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: A permitted work example, attempted practice, or unanswered workflow question. Remove customer, partner, personnel, or commercial details the group is not authorized to receive.
activitySteps: 1. Use eight minutes to share what you tried with AI since the last huddle: a permitted task, prompt, workflow or moment.
2. Discuss what worked, what did not, and what you learned; no success story is required.
3. Name useful approaches, dead ends and process, data, tool, access or confidence blockers without ranking participants.
4. Carry observations into Recap & What's Next; the deeper eight-week recap and team prioritization share that following 15-minute block.
activities.whyThisMatters: Concrete examples show what to repeat and where the motion needs support.

activities.name: Recap & What's Next: choose team priorities
activities.description: Reflect on moments that mattered and friction from the first eight weeks, then choose two or three workflow priorities and agree how team-owned huddles will continue.
activities.expectedOutput: Two or three team priorities for manager and facilitator planning, an agreed continuing huddle structure, and a next topic or custom-draft starting point where available.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Use only tools and data permitted in the team project setting. AI assistance does not authorize access, policy changes, commercial commitments, or publishing. A named owner reviews a custom draft for accuracy, audience permissions, and privacy before distribution or publication.
activities.requiredContext: The work priorities raised in the reflection and the team project tool/data restrictions. App access is useful but not required to agree a priority; use permitted, sanitized, or hypothetical examples.
activitySteps: 1. Use the 15-minute Recap & What's Next block to name a real moment that changed work, a habit to keep and friction or session improvements. Do not assume all participants completed all weeks.
2. Explore where AI could change repeated work, not just speed up a task. Agree two or three useful or urgent team priorities that manager and facilitator can use in planning.
3. Agree the structure for continuing huddles and who coordinates the next planning step; do not turn all priorities into simultaneous individual commitments.

4. If useful and available, browse All Topics for a relevant existing huddle using the filters actually offered and tools permitted for the team. If no topic fits, consider Huddle in a Box: download the approved HTML, open it in a browser, build or edit with approved AI, and review before running it. This is a future-content route, not a requirement to finish a custom huddle live or to import it through the app's current HTML import option.

5. Confirm the priorities and structure before the final five-minute Close & Survey. If the app, filters, button or download is unavailable, record the priorities manually and locate approved content later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Starting from work value and team permissions makes the continuing motion useful rather than tool-led.

activities.name: Close and complete the Team Member Impact Survey
activities.description: Confirm the next work focus and invite participants to complete the Team Member Impact Survey themselves.
activities.expectedOutput: Participant-owned impact feedback opportunity with five minutes protected in-session; an access gap is recorded for follow-up if needed, without collecting individual responses.
activities.humanCheckpoint: Participants complete their own survey; do not collect individual responses or require proof of completion. Record only permitted team-level learning and next steps, never sensitive work examples or individual performance judgments.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed next priority and a participant-accessible survey link; survey access is not required to confirm the next work step.
activitySteps: 1. Reserve the final five-minute Close & Survey block for participants to complete their own Impact Survey through the approved link. Priorities and the continuing structure should already be agreed in Recap & What's Next.
2. Briefly reinforce that feedback helps understand change over time and shape what comes next; do not claim usage or survey completion proves impact.
3. Let participants answer privately. Do not collect individual responses or proof of completion, and never generate answers for them.

4. If the survey link or access fails, record the access gap and follow up through the approved process without extending the session or inventing a substitute survey. Continue team-owned Sustain; this is not the final huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: A clear next step and participant feedback sustain learning without turning the transition into a scorecard.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Week 9 is the shared transition from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Look back on experience from the first eight weeks without assuming everyone completed every huddle. This is the start of Sustain, not the end of the motion: keep sharing, explore workflows that matter, and build on what works.
keyTalkingPoints: Use the shared Transition HTML, not the ordinary AI-in-Action practice format. Share recent experience and journey-wide reflection; the facilitator or manager briefly explains why practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue. Then agree the ongoing huddle rhythm and a Week 10 topic, and close with feedback. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
discussionQuestions: Since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well or did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?

Looking back across the journey: Moments that mattered—what changed in how you think about or use AI, and what are you doing differently? Habits worth continuing—which habits and peer learning should we keep building? Make it our own—what has worked about our huddles, what would we change, and what should ongoing huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep a team-owned rhythm, and which topic will we use for Week 10?
suggestedTransitions: Open with the purpose (2 minutes). Use Share Your Experience (15 minutes) for both the since-last-huddle check-in and the journey-wide reflection. The facilitator or manager then presents Sustain (3 minutes): practice builds habits and confidence, peers learn together, and Customer Zero starts with us. Move to What’s Next (8 minutes) to agree the ongoing rhythm and a Week 10 topic using All Topics or Huddle in a Box as appropriate. Close & Feedback (2 minutes) welcomes questions and points to the Impact Survey only if not already completed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Confirm the habits worth continuing, the team's ongoing huddle rhythm, and the agreed Week 10 topic. Use Close & Feedback for questions and the Team Member Impact Survey invitation. Participants who already completed the survey do not need to repeat it; this is the beginning of Sustain, not the end of the motion.
facilitatorQuestions: Share Your Experience—since the last huddle: What did you try with AI? What worked well, and what did not? What did you learn, and where did you run into friction?
Looking back across the journey:
Moments that mattered: What experience changed how you think about or use AI? What are you doing differently today that you were not doing at the beginning?
Habits worth continuing: Which AI habits are becoming part of everyday work? What have you learned from one another that you want to keep building?
Make it our own: What has worked about our huddles, and what would we change? What should our ongoing team huddles look like?
What’s Next: How will we keep learning together, and which topic will we choose for Week 10?
Close & Feedback: What questions, comments, or ideas would you like to share before we close?
listenFor: Listen for concrete changes, honest uncertainty, habits worth continuing, peer learning, and support needs. Include people with mixed experience or access gaps without assuming everyone completed every earlier huddle. Seek a shared Week 10 topic, not a tool quota or a ranking of participants.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If app, topic-library, customization, or survey links are unavailable, continue the team discussion and agree a Week 10 topic without a live build or download. Raise the access gap through the approved support route. Do not invent personal impact evidence or generate survey answers.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What has changed in how we think about and use AI, which habits should continue, and where would more practice or support help?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Agree how the team will keep learning through huddles and choose a Week 10 topic. Existing All Topics content or Huddle in a Box are options described in the supplied HTML, not required live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; each person supplies their own feedback.
bringBackEvidence: Keep bringing useful experiences, questions, and friction into the existing team rhythm. No new individual report, artifact, or survey-completion proof is required. Distinguish an observed benefit from an untested idea and keep human judgment explicit.
facilitatorGuide.roleWorkflowContext: Help the team move from guided Activation to team-owned Sustain. Reflect on the first eight weeks, identify useful habits and remaining support needs, agree how huddles will continue, and choose a topic for Week 10. This is a shared team review, not account planning or technical strategy.
facilitatorGuide.facilitatorPreparation: Review the shared Transition HTML and its five-part agenda. With the manager, agree who opens the session, facilitates reflection, presents the brief Sustain explanation, and guides the Week 10 planning. Locate the All Topics, Huddle in a Box, and Impact Survey links before the huddle.
facilitatorGuide.facilitationWatchouts: Follow the shared 30-minute agenda: Overview 2; Share Your Experience 15; Sustain 3; What’s Next 8; Close & Feedback 2. Sustain is a short facilitator/manager explanation of why ongoing practice, peer learning, and Customer Zero continue—not another open discussion or AI-practice block. Do not require a success story, a new artifact, or live tool use. Invite the Impact Survey only if not already completed; participants provide their own feedback.
facilitatorGuide.managerFacilitatorAlignment: Agree how to draw out experiences and friction, reinforce why huddles continue, and help the team choose its Week 10 topic and continuing rhythm. Keep the same shared Team Review content across audiences; do not substitute a role-specific planning exercise.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Owns Enterprise account priorities and commercial execution across pipeline, renewals, expansion, and customer conversations. Creates and qualifies opportunities, maintains evidence-backed forecasts, and coordinates the account team; technical, policy, and approval decisions remain with their accountable owners.
roles.descriptionSummary: Owns Enterprise account priorities, pipeline, forecasts, renewals, and expansion.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Leads customer-backed technology strategy across relevant solution areas, translating readiness and business priorities into a technical roadmap and consumption plans. Aligns account, solution and customer-success teams around technical decisions and execution without assuming default implementation or commercial approval ownership.
roles.descriptionSummary: Leads customer technology strategy, readiness, technical roadmaps and consumption planning.

roles.name: Solution Area Specialist (SSP)

Builds value-based selling plans and competitive positioning, coordinating account owners, technical teams, partners, and investment preparation; funding decisions remain with authorized approvers.
roles.descriptionSummary: Advances Enterprise solution-area sales through discovery, proof, and customer decisions.

roles.name: Solution Engineer

Makes success criteria, actual findings, unresolved risks and handoff requirements clear, working with specialists and delivery teams without assuming all opportunity, forecast or production-delivery ownership.
